The web interface works through a REST API that b4 serves on the web server's port, under /api/. The API reference on this site lists every endpoint with its parameters and responses. With the address of a running b4 in its B4 Instance field, that page sends its requests to that instance; without one, it only shows the reference.

While a username and a password are set under Settings > System > Web Server, every request under /api/ needs a login token, except those to /api/auth/ and /api/version. Without a username and password, no token is needed. A page at another address or port then gets 403 for requests that change something and for connections under /api/ws/. A reverse proxy in front of b4 must pass the original Host header and X-Forwarded-Proto. Without them, the Logs and Traffic pages stay empty, and saving settings can fail. Step Request Log in POST /api/auth/login with {"username": "...", "password": "..."} returns {"token": "..."} Use the token An Authorization: Bearer <token> header on every request. WebSocket connections under /api/ws/ can pass it as the token query parameter instead Log out POST /api/auth/logout revokes the token A login token stays valid while it is used at least once every 24 hours, and is discarded when b4 restarts. After repeated failed logins from one address, b4 answers 429 for a while. The MCP endpoint has a token of its own, see MCP server.

Request What it does GET /api/metrics The dashboard snapshot GET /api/metrics/summary A short summary of the snapshot, with the connection totals since the last counter reset /api/ws/metrics WebSocket: a full snapshot, then one update per second, as the dashboard receives them POST /api/metrics/reset Reset counters on the dashboard POST /api/escalations/clear Clear on the dashboard's Active Escalations panel: every escalated host goes back to its set GET /api/ipbans The banned addresses the dashboard's Banned addresses panel lists POST /api/ipbans/clear Unban on that panel with {"key": "<address>:<port>"}, or Clear all without a key /api/ws/logs WebSocket: the live log the Logs page shows POST /api/logs/trace/start, POST /api/logs/trace/stop Start trace and Stop & save on the Logs page GET /api/logs/trace/status Whether a trace is recording GET /api/logs/trace/download The last trace file, as Download last trace saves it GET /api/config/download The configuration as it is, as Download as is under Settings > System > Backup saves it GET /api/config/download?safe=true The safe copy, as Download safe copy saves it GET /api/system/addresses The ports the Expose to internet switches opened, their firewall chains and errors, and the reason a switch that is on opened nothing GET /api/watchdog/status The watchdog's state for every watched set and domain, with the reason codes POST /api/discovery/start Starts a Discovery run. A run for a set that routes its traffic is refused with 400 and the code routed_set, and any run while b4 is still applying its DSCP rules with 409 and the code dscp_rules_pending POST /api/discovery/replace, POST /api/discovery/add, POST /api/sets/{id}/add-domain with tested Write a Discovery result into a set, create a set from it, or add its domains to a set. With the run's dscp_path, a set whose traffic takes another DSCP path is refused with 409 and the code dscp_path_changed, and a write while b4 is still applying its DSCP rules with dscp_rules_pending. replace and add take the page hosts to add in hosts. An entry that is not a host name on the internet is refused with 400 and the code bad_host, and more than 64 hosts with too_many_hosts POST /api/mcp The MCP server, see below

The watchdog reports why a set is in its state, or how its last heal ended, as one of these codes. The Watchdog page shows the same reasons in words. Code Meaning not_owned The set's addresses are handled by another set or by none, so a strategy written into this set does not affect them escalated An escalation sends the addresses to another set unusable A certificate error, a required client certificate, or a private or local destination. Never healed current_works Tested alone, the set's own strategy loads the addresses, yet the live check fails not_needed Tested alone, the addresses load without a bypass, yet the live check fails partial The search found a strategy for only some of the addresses, so nothing was written none The search found no working strategy incomplete The search ended without a confirmed result budget The search ran longer than 20 minutes and was canceled start_failed The Discovery run could not start verify_failed The strategy written did not pass the live check and was undone edited The set was changed during the check or the search, so nothing was written busy Another Discovery run holds the runtime, and the heal waits rules_changed b4 was applying or rewriting the firewall rules the search depends on, such as its DSCP rules, so nothing was written; the heal is tried again later

For an Expose to internet switch that is on but opened nothing, GET /api/system/addresses gives the reason as one of no_auth, web_no_auth, open_relay, shared_port, loopback, invalid_bind and not_listening. Securing the web interface describes the conditions of each switch.

POST /api/mcp serves the Model Context Protocol to AI applications, as JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP. Connecting an AI assistant covers the setup. Only POST is served: GET and DELETE return 405, which is normal for this transport. Situation Response Enable MCP server is off 404, mcp server is disabled An MCP token is set, and the request carries none or another one 401, invalid or missing MCP token No MCP token is set The web interface's login token is required, as for the rest of the API, while a username and password are set The request carries an Origin header that is not allowed 403 A request with an Origin header is accepted when that origin is b4's own address written as an IP address or localhost, or is listed in system.web_server.mcp.allowed_origins, where a single * accepts any origin. A host name is never accepted automatically: under DNS rebinding, a page on an attacker's name reaches b4 with matching Origin and Host headers. AI applications send no Origin header.

The server offers tools according to the two permission switches on the MCP server card and rebuilds the list when they change, without a restart. An application that was connected before the change keeps its old list until it reconnects. A tool that is not permitted is not offered at all, and the server tells the model which permission is off, so the model can say what to turn on. Permitted Tools offered Nothing (default) 14 Allow configuration changes 18 Allow active probes 16 Both 20 Tool What it does Needs b4_status Version, capture engine, firewall backend, how many sets exist and are enabled, the state of Telegram over WebSocket, uptime, the connections counted since the last counter reset, and which permissions are on - b4_metrics Connections in the last complete minute, in sets and not in a set, the totals since the last reset, dropped resets, blocked DNS lookups and connections, b4's CPU and memory use. Connections count as on the dashboard - b4_get_config The configuration, or one section of it - b4_list_sets Every set in priority order, with domain counts and primary strategy - b4_get_set One set in full - b4_check_domain Which sets target a domain, how the match was made, and whether the set is enabled - b4_recent_connections Connections b4 processed, with the set that matched each - b4_logs_tail The tail of errors.log, or of update.log with file=update - b4_diagnostics OS, kernel, interfaces, firewall backend and the rule groups b4 installed - b4_get_topic The description of a setting, see Topics - b4_list_writable_paths Which settings can be changed, with types, current values and accepted values - b4_geo_lookup Which GeoSite and GeoIP categories exist, what one holds, and which cover a domain or an address - b4_api_reference The REST API's operations, or one of them with its parameters, body and responses, see below - b4_watchdog The watchdog's verdicts, and its actions, see below Depends on the action b4_set_config_value Changes one setting and applies it at once, reporting the previous and the new value Allow configuration changes b4_revert_last_change Restores the configuration from before the last change made over MCP Allow configuration changes b4_edit_set_targets Adds or removes domains, addresses, geo categories, ASNs or source devices of one set Allow configuration changes b4_manage_set Creates, duplicates, moves, enables, deletes or resets a set Allow configuration changes b4_test_domain_now Fetches a domain through b4 and again with b4 bypassed, and says which of the two works Allow active probes b4_find_bypass_strategy Runs Discovery for a domain, a URL or a set, and applies the result Allow active probes to start a run, Allow configuration changes to apply it b4_check_domain answers whether a domain is configured in a set. b4_recent_connections answers whether traffic for it arrived and which set matched. The difference separates a targeting mistake from a routing one. A ready-made prompt, diagnose_domain, comes with the tools. It takes a domain and walks the model through the status, the error log, the coverage and the set's configuration. The model then asks the user to open the site again and reads the recent connections. They show whether the site's traffic reached b4 and which set took it. The model also names the installed version and looks for a newer release. With Allow active probes on, it offers a test fetch of the site. With the switch off, the prompt names it, and the model asks the user whether the site opens. The firewall rules are read only when the status shows a problem or no other step finds the cause. Applications that support prompts list it separately.

Reading the watchdog's verdicts emits no traffic and changes nothing, so the tool is offered at every level, and each action is permitted on its own. Without set, the actions work on the older per-domain list and the global watchdog switch: Action Effect Needs status The last verdict for every watched set and domain - add Adds a domain to the list Allow configuration changes and Allow active probes remove Removes a domain from the list Allow configuration changes enable Turns the global watchdog switch on, for the watched sets and the list Allow configuration changes and Allow active probes disable Turns the global watchdog switch off Allow configuration changes check Checks a domain of the list now Allow active probes With set, a set id or exact name, the actions work on that set's own watchdog and its Discovery addresses, passed as url: Action with set Effect Needs status The set's watchdog status, reason and per-address results - enable Switches the set's watchdog on and schedules a check; refused when the set cannot be watched Allow configuration changes and Allow active probes disable Switches the set's watchdog off Allow configuration changes add Adds url to the set's Discovery addresses Allow configuration changes and Allow active probes remove Removes url from them Allow configuration changes check Schedules a check of every address of a watched set and clears its cooldown Allow active probes; a give-up is cleared only when Allow configuration changes is on as well

domains takes up to five domains or full URLs, separated by commas, as the Discovery input does: a domain is fetched as https://<domain>/, a URL as given. A host that only serves files, such as an image or video CDN, can answer / with HTTP 400 and leave the run nothing to test. Such a host is probed by the URL of a file it serves. A run also tries the strategies the community hub publishes for the domains, as a run from the Discovery page does when the hub is on. action=start with set runs Discovery for that set: on the domains given, or on the set's Discovery addresses, at most five. The set's current strategy is tested first, and the search stops at the first strategy confirmed on every address. action=status reports the verdict, and action=apply with set writes the result into the set, the strategy only and only for the verdict covered. The same applies to action=apply without set when the run it refers to was a run for a set. A set that action=apply creates for free-form domains keeps the addresses they were found on as its Discovery addresses. A set with routing enabled is refused, and so is a result whose probes took another DSCP path than the set's traffic takes now, as on the Discovery page. A run also tests the other hosts each confirmed page loads, as the page hosts step on the Discovery page does. For a found domain, action=status names the hosts that fail without b4 and load with its strategy, and those that stay blocked with it. action=apply does not add them. b4_edit_set_targets with kind sni_domains does. While that step runs, action=apply is refused until the run ends, and action=cancel ends only the step: the run completes with every result kept.

With Allow configuration changes on, these become writable: every setting inside a set: targets, fragmentation, faking, TCP and UDP, DNS, escalation and routing; the MTProto and SOCKS5 settings, the Telegram over WebSocket switch system.mtproto.bridge.enabled among them; the logging settings, so the model can raise the log level, reproduce a problem and read the result. b4_list_writable_paths reports the exact paths with their types, current values and accepted values. A change goes through the same validation and live-apply path as a save in the web interface. An invalid result is rejected and nothing is saved, and an accepted one applies at once, firewall rules included. Writing a list, such as a set's domains, replaces the whole list, so a model reads the current value first and sends it back in full. b4_edit_set_targets adds and removes single entries instead, with kind naming the list: sni_domains, ip, geosite_categories, geoip_categories, asns or source_devices. An asns entry is written as AS15169 or 15169 and stored as the bare number; reserved numbers are refused. An ASN whose prefixes b4 has not fetched yet is added anyway and fetched at once, and the reply names it, because until the fetch succeeds the set matches none of its addresses. Whatever the switches say, the credentials of the web interface, SOCKS5, MTProto and a set's upstream proxy are refused, and so are these: Refused Reason Web server settings Moving or locking the interface removes the way to undo the change The MCP settings The model cannot widen its own permissions Capture engine and TUN Switching it under a live network can cut the machine off Firewall backend A wrong value leaves the machine with no rules at all Every Expose to internet switch, and any write that would open a port while one of them is on, such as turning the MTProto proxy on or changing its port An open port is reachable from the whole internet at once, and a revert does not undo what reached it Packet marks and routing tables b4's own traffic depends on them Set DSCP (system.tables.dscp) and a set's own DSCP (sets[].dscp) Rules on the next router act on the value, and a wrong one can send traffic down another route A set's id Escalation targets refer to it A set's Discovery addresses and watchdog switch Both make the router fetch sites on a timer; b4_watchdog with set changes them under its own permissions The log directory and the geodata file locations A wrong log directory silently stops file logging, and a wrong geodata path empties every category at once The dividing line is recoverability: a wrong value inside a set breaks some sites, visibly and reversibly, while a wrong web server port or capture engine can leave the machine unreachable. The writable areas are named as whole subtrees, and the exclusions are marked on the fields themselves, so a setting added to b4 later stays unwritable until it is opted in. Refusing a location does not refuse the contents: b4_logs_tail reads both log files wherever the directory points. b4_revert_last_change restores the configuration from before the most recent change made over MCP since b4 started, and applies it. Repeating it walks further back. It is refused, and the change stays on the list, when the configuration changed after that change, by a watchdog heal, the web interface or another tool. It is also refused when it would switch a set's watchdog or the global watchdog on, or bring back watched domains or the Discovery addresses of a watched set, while Allow active probes is off.

Several b4 settings have names that read as something other than what they do, and a zero usually means "use the fixed value" rather than "off". b4 carries a written description of such settings, and the server tells the model to read it before explaining or changing anything. The descriptions come from src/ai/topics.json, built into the binary; the web interface's AI explanations use the same text. The descriptions are published twice: the tool b4_get_topic, with topic for an exact key, path for the setting a b4_set_config_value path names (in sets[video].tcp.win.mode the set is ignored), or query for a search. With no arguments it lists every documented key; the resources b4://topics/<key>, with the same text. Most applications never show resources to the model; LM Studio and the OpenAI-compatible bridges list them for the user. The tool makes the text reachable for the model. A question about a setting without a description returns a note saying so, with the documented settings nearby. The note tells the model to say it is unsure rather than guess the setting's unit, default or meaning from its name.

The tool gives the model the reference that the API reference page shows, from a copy built into b4 that matches the installed version. It covers what the other tools leave out, and the model makes the API calls itself. The tool only describes the API. Arguments Answer None Every operation, by tag query The operations whose path, summary or description contain every word given operation, as PUT /api/sets/{id} The operation's parameters, request body and responses, with the types they use. A path with a real value, such as /api/sets/abc123, names the same operation schema One type from an earlier answer, with its fields A type too large for one answer is listed by name, for a later call with schema. An operation that another tool also performs names that tool. A REST write passes b4's own validation, but not the checks and refusals that the MCP tools add. Apart from schema, each answer also explains how to call the API. While a username and a password are set, that is the login, and the model is told to ask the user before using them. The MCP token is refused outside /api/mcp.

Every tool call writes one line to b4's log, shown on the Logs page: the tool, the caller's address and how long it took. A refused call is logged as a warning. A request turned away at the endpoint is logged too: the server off, a wrong or missing token, or a browser origin that is not allowed. The token itself is never written. Repeated refusals are collapsed into one line every 30 seconds, with a count. These lines go to the live log and the console, not to errors.log, which holds errors only. A change made or reverted over MCP also appears under Recent changes on the dashboard as AI agent changed a setting, with the path of the setting and without its value.

Tool output may be forwarded to a third-party model, so b4 removes these values from it or replaces them with [redacted]: the username and password of the web interface; the MCP token; the SOCKS5 username and password; the names and values of the MTProto secrets; the IPinfo token; the reference to the stored AI API key; the username and password of a set's upstream proxy; the path of the web server's TLS key. Host names and URLs are returned as configured. Download safe copy under Settings > System > Backup masks those as well. b4_diagnostics holds no credentials, but it reports the hostname, every interface address and the live firewall ruleset, which is enough to identify the network.

b4 accepts command-line flags, and they take precedence over the values in the configuration file. A flag overrides the setting for one run only. When b4 saves its configuration, a setting that came from a flag keeps the value the file already had.

Flag Description Default --config Path to the configuration file Discovered, /etc/b4/b4.json on most systems --verbose Log level: debug, trace, info, silent info -v, --version Print the version and exit - --clear-tables Remove b4's iptables/nftables rules and exit -

Flag Description Setting Default --queue-num The first netfilter queue number queue.start_num 537 --threads Number of worker threads queue.threads 4 --mark The queue mark, see Packet marks queue.mark 32768 --ipv4 Process IPv4 traffic queue.ipv4 true --ipv6 Process IPv6 traffic queue.ipv6 false --ipv6 is the Enable IPv6 Support switch under Settings > Core > Packet Engine. It decides whether b4 processes IPv6, not whether the router uses it. With it off, IPv6 connections pass the router without any set applying to them. In NFQUEUE mode, sets with Remove ECH keys from DNS answers on still remove ECH keys from IPv6 DNS answers. See The queue section.

Flag Description Setting Default --skip-tables Do not create iptables/nftables rules at startup system.tables.skip_setup false --tables-monitor-interval How often to check and restore the rules, in seconds. With NFQUEUE 0 turns the check off; in TUN mode the interval is at least 10, and 0 does not turn it off system.tables.monitor_interval 10

Flag Description Setting Default -i, --instaflush Flush log writes immediately system.logging.instaflush true --syslog Send log lines to syslog as well system.logging.syslog false --log-dir Directory for b4's log files. Empty turns file logging off system.logging.directory /var/log/b4
Flag Description Setting Default --web-port Port of the web interface. 0 turns it off system.web_server.port 7000

Variable Description Setting GOMEMLIMIT The memory limit of the Go runtime. While it is set, b4 does not apply Memory Limit system.memory_limit GOMEMLIMIT takes the Go runtime's format, not the field's: a byte count such as 268435456 or 256MiB, or off. With a value such as 256m, b4 does not start.

A custom configuration file and debug logging: b4 --config /opt/etc/b4/b4.json --verbose debug Removing b4's firewall rules: b4 --clear-tables Running without automatic firewall setup, with the rules managed by hand: b4 --skip-tables IPv6 processing for this run only, with the configuration file left as it is: b4 --ipv6
b4 keeps its configuration in one JSON file, /etc/b4/b4.json by default. The --config flag points it elsewhere.

Platform Path Linux /etc/b4/b4.json OpenWRT (with extroot or USB storage) /opt/etc/b4/b4.json OpenWRT (without USB storage) /etc/b4/b4.json ASUS Merlin /opt/etc/b4/b4.json Keenetic /opt/etc/b4/b4.json Docker /etc/b4/b4.json, inside the container Without --config, b4 looks for b4.json and config.json under /etc/b4 and /opt/etc/b4, and falls back to /etc/b4/b4.json. The log names the path it settled on at startup. The Download Configuration card under Settings > System > Backup saves the configuration in the form b4 writes to this file. Its safe copy masks credentials and private host names for sharing, and b4 refuses to load or save a configuration that still holds the safe copy's [redacted] placeholders.

The file is sparse. A setting that holds its built-in default is left out, so a fresh installation writes a very short file, and a section whose settings were never changed is absent. A missing key is not a missing setting, and adding it back with its default value changes nothing. Saves from the web interface, the API and MCP write the file the same way.
documents.s: Only what differs from the defaults is stored

documents.t: { "version": 52, "queue": { "start_num": 537, "threads": 4, "mark": 32768, "ipv4": true, "ipv6": false, "tcp_conn_bytes_limit": 19, "udp_conn_bytes_limit": 8, "interfaces": [], "mss_clamp": { "enabled": false, "size": 88 }, "devices": { "enabled": false, "vendor_lookup": false } }, "system": { "tables": { "skip_setup": false, "monitor_interval": 10, "engine": "", "masquerade": { "enabled": false, "interfaces": [] }, "dscp": { "enabled": false, "value": 0, "interfaces": [] } }, "logging": { "level": 1, "directory": "/var/log/b4", "instaflush": true, "syslog": false }, "web_server": { "port": 7000, "bind_address": "0.0.0.0", "expose": false, "tls_cert": "", "tls_key": "", "username": "", "password": "", "language": "en", "mcp": { "enabled": false, "allow_writes": false } }, "dns": { "tcp_disabled": false, "tcp_port": 5453, "query_timeout_sec": 5, "keep_ipv6_answers": false }, "socks5": { "enabled": false, "port": 1080, "bind_address": "0.0.0.0", "expose": false, "allowed_sources": ["192.168.1.0/24", "127.0.0.1/32"] }, "mtproto": { "enabled": false, "port": 3128, "bind_address": "0.0.0.0", "expose": false }, "checker": { "discovery_timeout": 5, "config_propagate_ms": 1500, "dns_server": "" }, "geo": { "sitedat_path": "", "ipdat_path": "", "sitedat_url": "", "ipdat_url": "" }, "timezone": "" }, "sets": [] } The sample shows some of the sections and some of their keys. A real file holds only the keys that differ from the default. system.mtproto.secrets is a list of named secrets, each with id, name, secret and enabled. A file written before configuration version 50 held a single mtproto.secret string, which the migration moves into the list as an entry named default. system.socks5.allowed_sources is absent while the list is empty, the default, and the proxy then accepts any source. Each entry is an IP address or a CIDR range. 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0 and malformed entries are refused when the file is loaded or saved.

Key Meaning Default start_num The first NFQUEUE number 537 threads Number of worker threads 4 mark The queue mark, see Packet marks 32768 ipv4 Process IPv4 traffic true ipv6 Process IPv6 traffic false tcp_conn_bytes_limit How many packets at the start of a TCP connection b4 inspects 19 udp_conn_bytes_limit The same for UDP 8 interfaces Capture Interfaces, a filter on the interface a packet passes. Empty means all of them [] tcp_conn_bytes_limit and udp_conn_bytes_limit apply to every set. A set's own tcp.conn_bytes_limit and udp.conn_bytes_limit have no effect, and the web interface has no field for them. queue.ipv6 decides whether b4 processes IPv6, not whether the router uses it. Off, the default, b4 processes IPv4 only and writes no IPv6 firewall rules for any set, so a client that reaches a site over IPv6 bypasses the sets. b4 then removes IPv6 addresses from DNS answers for the domains sets match, see DNS. The exception is NFQUEUE mode while an enabled set has dns.strip_ech on. In that mode b4 writes IPv6 rules for DNS answers and DNS over TCP, only to remove their ECH keys. A change takes full effect after a restart. --ipv6 sets the same thing for one run.

Each set is one object in the sets array, carrying its whole configuration. Its keys follow the tabs of the set editor: targets - domains, IPs, GeoSite and GeoIP categories, ASNs, source devices tcp - general TCP settings, desync, window, incoming, RST protection fragmentation - the fragmentation method and its parameters faking - SNI faking, SYN fakes, mutation udp - the QUIC filter, the port filter, the handling of calls and the UDP action mode dns - the set's resolver, DoH URL and pins routing - routing mode, output interface, upstream proxy or blocking dscp - the set's own DSCP value discovery - the set's Discovery addresses and its watchdog switch escalate - which set to escalate to when this one stops working The Import/Export tab of the set editor shows a set as JSON and takes a pasted one back. The exported JSON leaves out values equal to the defaults and the settings of switched-off features. It also leaves out the set's id, source devices, targets.ip_priority, watchdog switch and escalation settings, and, when the set has source devices, its dscp. A JSON imported into a set keeps that set's own targets.ip_priority.

Key Meaning Default dscp.enabled Enable per-set DSCP: write the set's own value into the packets to the set's addresses, see DSCP false dscp.value The value written into the DSCP field, 0-63. 0 clears the field 0 Each key is stored only while it differs from its default: the switch on with the value 0 is saved as "dscp": {"enabled": true}, a value kept with the switch off as "dscp": {"value": 12}. While dscp.enabled is true, a dscp.value outside 0-63 is refused, not clamped: the web interface refuses the save, and a file that holds one stops b4 at start. Neither key is writable over MCP or carried in a shared set.

Calls on a set's UDP tab is stored in two keys, see Sets for calls. Calls Stored as Pass call setup udp.filter_stun is true, the default Handle like other UDP udp.filter_stun is false Handle only calls udp.filter_l7 lists the calls of Which calls: ["discord", "stun"] for Discord app and browsers, ["discord"] for Discord app, ["stun"] for Browsers A non-empty udp.filter_l7 means Handle only calls whatever udp.filter_stun holds, and udp.filter_stun then has no effect. An empty list is not stored. A set with the list needs a udp.dport_filter, no targets.sni_domains, targets.ip, targets.geosite_categories, targets.geoip_categories or targets.asns, and an empty tcp.dport_filter. A set that breaks this is refused: the web interface refuses the save, and a file that holds one stops b4 at start. An escalate.to that names a set with the list is cleared, with a warning in the log. An unknown entry stays in the list, matches no traffic and is logged as a warning. (auto: STUN request) is "fake_payload_file": "@stun" under udp. udp.filter_l7 is writable over MCP, with discord and stun as its only entries, and is carried in a shared set.
documents.s: A set's calls: udp.filter_stun and udp.filter_l7

version at the top is the configuration format version. b4 reads it to decide what needs migrating, so it stays unchanged when anything else is edited. warning The values in the file are checked only when b4 starts, and a file that fails the check stops b4 with an invalid configuration error. b4 reads the file only at start, so a manual edit takes effect after a restart. Any save before then writes the running configuration over the file, and the manual edit is lost. Saves come from the web interface, MCP, a watchdog heal, a geodata download and an ASN prefix update.

When the format changes between releases, b4 migrates the file at startup: new fields arrive with their defaults, and renamed ones are carried over. Before it changes anything, it writes a backup next to the file, named after the version it migrates from, for example b4.json.v51.bak. A file that cannot be read at startup, for example one cut short by a power loss or left with a JSON syntax error, is copied next to itself as b4.json.corrupt. When an earlier copy with different content is there, the name is b4.json.corrupt.1 and onward. The log names the copy. b4 then starts on the defaults, and the next save replaces the original file, so the unreadable settings remain only in that copy. A file whose version is higher than the running binary understands is loaded as it is, with a warning. Settings that binary does not know are dropped at the next save.

TSPU (Technical Means of Countering Threats, ТСПУ) is the Russian deep packet inspection (DPI) system installed in internet providers' networks. It is the system that blocks access to sites and services.

A detailed technical description of the TSPU (ASBI) architecture, its components, how it works and how it filters is kept in a separate project: tspu-docs - a guide in 24 chapters, based on a lecture of about five hours on the architecture, configuration and operation of TSPU. The material is in Russian. Accuracy The documentation was generated with AI from the lecture transcript and checked by hand. It may be out of date: TSPU is updated continuously, and the current implementation can differ from the one described. Inaccuracies are possible. Main topics: The ASBI/TSPU architecture: balancers, filters, the DPI engine Blocking methods: DNS spoofing, SNI filtering, IP blocking Detection: how TSPU recognises bypass attempts Weak points: what b4's bypass strategies rely on Knowing how TSPU works helps when choosing and tuning bypass strategies. It is not needed for everyday use of b4: Discovery finds a working configuration automatically.

b4 downloads its releases, the installer and the GeoSite and GeoIP databases from GitHub. On some networks the host that serves the release files, release-assets.githubusercontent.com, is blocked, and an update stops with a connection timeout. There are three ways around it: mirrors, a personal Cloudflare Worker, and installing from a file.
documents.s: Downloading b4 when GitHub is blocked

documents.t: b4 tries GitHub first, then each mirror in Update mirrors, then the mirrors built into b4, then SourceForge. Every source serves the same archive, checked against the same published SHA256. On a network without blocks, the mirrors are never used.

Update mirrors under Settings > System > Service takes a comma-separated list of mirror addresses. They are tried before the built-in mirrors, and b4 passes them to the installer, so an update from the web interface uses them too. Only https addresses are accepted. An entry with a query string or a fragment is ignored. A mirror that works on one network can be blocked on another, because each provider blocks on its own. A list of several mirrors is tried in order. A mirror serves the binary that becomes b4 b4 checks every download against the SHA256 published next to it, but the checksum comes from the same host as the archive. A host that serves both can serve a matching pair. Only mirrors under one's own control, or trusted ones, belong in this field.

A Cloudflare Worker is a free mirror on a personal Cloudflare account, under a *.workers.dev name. It fetches from GitHub inside Cloudflare's network and passes the result on. Every account gets its own subdomain, so there is no single name to block. On some networks *.workers.dev names are throttled: small responses get through, while an archive crawls. b4 abandons a stalled download and moves on to the next source. The checks below show whether a Worker is usable from a given network. A Worker bound to a custom domain is not affected. This Worker is not the Cloudflare Worker relay for Telegram, which runs a different script.

Create a free Cloudflare account. Under Compute > Workers & Pages, create a Worker from the default template and deploy it. Replace the Worker's code with the script below and deploy again. In b4, add the Worker's address, such as https://name-1234.username.workers.dev, to Update mirrors under Settings > System > Service.

const REPO_OWNER = "DanielLavrushin"; const REPO_NAME = "b4"; const MIRROR_OWNERS = [ "DanielLavrushin", "Loyalsoldier", "runetfreedom", "XTLS", "Flowseal", ]; const MIRROR_HOSTS = [ "raw.githubusercontent.com", "github.com", "api.github.com", "objects.githubusercontent.com", "release-assets.githubusercontent.com", "codeload.github.com", "gist.githubusercontent.com", ]; const SF_BASE = "https://downloads.sourceforge.net/project/b4core"; const SEGMENT = /^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._+-]*$/; const RAW_PATH = /^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._/+-]*$/; const API_TTL = 300; function text(body, status) { return new Response(body, { status, headers: { "content-type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8" }, }); } function allowed(raw) { let url; try { url = new URL(raw); } catch { return false; } if (url.protocol !== "https:") return false; if (!MIRROR_HOSTS.includes(url.hostname)) return false; const parts = url.pathname.split("/").filter(Boolean); const owner = parts[0] === "repos" ? parts[1] : parts[0]; return MIRROR_OWNERS.includes(owner); } async function passthrough(request, target, ttl) { const headers = new Headers(); const range = request.headers.get("range"); if (range) headers.set("range", range); headers.set("accept-encoding", "identity"); headers.set("user-agent", "b4-mirror"); if (target.startsWith("https://api.github.com")) { headers.set("accept", "application/vnd.github+json"); } const init = { method: request.method === "HEAD" ? "HEAD" : "GET", headers, redirect: "follow", }; if (!range && ttl) init.cf = { cacheTtl: ttl, cacheEverything: true }; let upstream; try { upstream = await fetch(target, init); } catch (err) { return text(`upstream fetch failed: ${err}
`, 502); } const out = new Headers(); for (const name of [ "content-type", "content-length", "content-range", "accept-ranges", "etag", "last-modified", ]) { const value = upstream.headers.get(name); if (value) out.set(name, value); } out.set("access-control-allow-origin", "*"); return new Response(upstream.body, { status: upstream.status, headers: out }); } export default { async fetch(request) { const url = new URL(request.url); const path = url.pathname; if (request.method !== "GET" && request.method !== "HEAD") { return text("method not allowed
", 405); } if (path === "/b4/health") return text("ok
", 200); let m = path.match(/^/b4/dl/latest/(.+)$/); if (m) { if (!SEGMENT.test(m[1])) return text("bad file name
", 404); return passthrough( request, `https://github.com/${REPO_OWNER}/${REPO_NAME}/releases/latest/download/${m[1]}`, 0, ); } m = path.match(/^/b4/dl/([^/]+)/(.+)$/); if (m) { if (!SEGMENT.test(m[1]) || !SEGMENT.test(m[2])) { return text("bad tag or file name
", 404); } return passthrough( request, `https://github.com/${REPO_OWNER}/${REPO_NAME}/releases/download/${m[1]}/${m[2]}`, 0, ); } m = path.match(/^/b4/sf/([^/]+)/(.+)$/); if (m) { if (!SEGMENT.test(m[1]) || !SEGMENT.test(m[2])) { return text("bad tag or file name
", 404); } return passthrough(request, `${SF_BASE}/${m[1]}/${m[2]}`, 0); } m = path.match(/^/b4/raw/(.+)$/); if (m) { if (!RAW_PATH.test(m[1])) return text("bad path
", 404); return passthrough( request, `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/${REPO_OWNER}/${REPO_NAME}/${m[1]}`, API_TTL, ); } if (path === "/b4/api/releases") { return passthrough( request, `https://api.github.com/repos/${REPO_OWNER}/${REPO_NAME}/releases?per_page=25`, API_TTL, ); } if (path === "/b4/api/releases/latest") { return passthrough( request, `https://api.github.com/repos/${REPO_OWNER}/${REPO_NAME}/releases/latest`, API_TTL, ); } if (path.startsWith("/github/")) { const target = url.href.slice(url.origin.length + "/github/".length); if (!allowed(target)) return text("forbidden
", 403); return passthrough(request, target, 0); } return text("not found
", 404); }, }; The script fetches only from GitHub and SourceForge, and only for the repository owners it lists, so it cannot serve as an open proxy. Release archives pass through it without being cached.

curl -sI https://name-1234.username.workers.dev/b4/health curl -sL -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{size_download}\n' \ https://name-1234.username.workers.dev/b4/dl/latest/b4-linux-arm64.tar.gz The first command checks that the Worker answers. The second downloads a release archive through it and prints the status and the size. A download that stalls here means workers.dev is throttled on this network.

When no source can be reached, the archive can be brought in by hand, from a machine that has access. Requirements: A username and a password for the web interface, under Settings > System > Web Server. Without them the upload is refused, since it replaces the binary that runs as root. b4 running as a service, not in Docker. The installer script. b4 fetches install.sh, or uses the copy it saved at its last successful update. A router that has never been updated from the web interface needs install.sh reachable. Steps: Open the Version Management dialog from the version at the bottom of the side menu. Click Install from a file instead. On a machine with access, download b4-linux-<arch>.tar.gz for the router's architecture from the release page. The dialog links to it on GitHub, and SourceForge mirror opens the same release on SourceForge, with the same archives and .sha256 files. Click Choose archive and pick the file. Optionally, paste the SHA256 from the release page into Expected SHA256 (optional). Click Install. Before anything is replaced, b4 checks that the archive holds a b4 binary for this router's architecture, and refuses one built for another. The SHA256 read on the release page, on another machine, is an independent check of the upload. Hard-float and soft-float MIPS builds pass the architecture check alike, so on MIPS the archive name has to match the router, such as mipsle_softfloat. A wrong one is rolled back after the swap, as is any new binary that does not run.

The installer tries the sources in the same order and reads B4_MIRRORS from the environment. A mirror then works for a first install too, before b4 has any settings: B4_MIRRORS="https://name-1234.username.workers.dev" sh install.sh The value is a space-separated list. B4_SF_BASE replaces the SourceForge address the same way. When raw.githubusercontent.com is blocked as well, the Worker serves the installer itself: curl -fsSL https://name-1234.username.workers.dev/b4/raw/main/install.sh -o install.sh
All notable changes to b4 are recorded in this file.

The log names the set and the device when a TCP Timestamp fake goes out without its timestamp, as from a Windows PC by default or toward a server that refuses timestamps. #554 With Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup on, the log warns when the router's connection tracking would drop TCP Check fakes. #554 When Discovery finishes while b4 is in the background, the tab title marks it, and over HTTPS Notify me on the Discovery page adds a browser notification with how many sites got a strategy. #544
A set that an AI app creates through MCP b4_find_bypass_strategy is named after the site instead of an internal strategy name such as cached-5-tcpmd5. #559

With fake strategy TCP Check, or TCP Timestamp on a device without TCP timestamps such as a Windows PC, some sites on Cloudflare failed with an SSL error, because the server took the fake for the real start of the connection. #554 Fake strategy MD5 Sum broke the sites of its set, because the fake went out without the MD5 option. #555 A set with Fake SNI Packets on sent its fake again in front of later packets of a connection, and so did the Decoy Packet of Combo, so a server could close the connection right after it opened. #556 A fake meant to carry a wrong checksum could, in rare cases, carry a valid one and reach the server as data. #557 In the set editor, Fake TTL was greyed out while other features used it, Corruption Strategy stayed editable where it does nothing, and several faking help texts were wrong. #558

Discovery finds the other blocked hosts a site's page needs for its styles, scripts and images: the new Page hosts step tests them, and Apply as a set adds the ticked ones. A set can keep the connections to a provider's own servers, such as its Google Global Cache nodes, even when a lower set matches their domain. The IP priority switch for this is under Targets, Bypass IPs in the set editor and is off by default.

A set routed into an AmneziaWG interface leaves its packets alone while the interface is up, as a set routed into WireGuard does. The ASN tab of the set editor is gone: ASN targets are under Targets, Bypass IPs. Discovery shows a run's results again when its page is reopened within 30 minutes, and marks a strategy found during a run as the fastest so far. Deleting a payload that a set uses on the Payloads tab asks first and names the sets that depend on it. The diagnose_domain prompt for AI apps first checks whether the site's traffic reaches b4.

AI apps on the newest MCP protocol, such as Antigravity CLI, lost the connection before b4's tools appeared, and behind nginx they could wait a minute for them. An AI app could report one Discovery strategy and apply another, and b4's notes on settings did not turn up when searched in plain words. Many errors in the web interface showed only a bare status, such as 409 Conflict. In TUN mode, a device could keep waiting after b4 had cut its connection or answered its DNS query, because the router had moved the connection to another port. IP Block Detection and Escalation could cut off working sites: when a device reused a port, when a server asked the browser to repeat its first request, or right after Escalation moved a site to its backup set. IP Block Detection and Escalation missed some stuck connections: with RST or FIN fakes, or when the site name was in the second packet of the first request. A set using Combo with an Overlap Length could break connections soon after they opened, because the overlap was added to later packets too. On a busy network, connections could hang after b4 started, while b4 showed as running. A Discovery strategy could pass every test and then fail as a set, because captured ClientHello and Random fakes were tested with the built-in fake, or a site's QUIC capture went out in place of its TLS one. Applying a saved Discovery result whose payload had since been deleted gave the set the built-in fake without a warning. Discovery added DNS redirects that some sites did not need, and its result card and History could show another strategy's confirmation. A missing TCP fake payload also took away a set's UDP fake payload, so UDP fakes went out as zeros. In the set editor, Tab did not leave an empty entry field, and Manual Bypass IPs accepted text that is not an address, such as an AS number. A duplicated set was saved at the top of the list, ahead of its source, and took the connections to the sites both list. On a narrow screen, the history headers on the Discovery and DPI Detector pages could be unreadable.

Without a login for the web interface, any website opened on a device in the network could watch b4's live log and the sites each device visits. A dashboard on another site, such as Home Assistant, needs a web interface login and its token, and a reverse proxy must pass the original Host header and X-Forwarded-Proto.
The Captured ClientHello as the fake payload list in Discovery's options starts with Select all payloads and stays open, so several payloads can be picked in one pass. (#475, thanks @asovetov)

Videos and sites still froze on servers the provider blocks for every site, because IP Block Detection missed blocks that drop the server's answer, and apps that try QUIC first kept waiting on banned addresses. IP Block Detection could ban a server that refuses unknown site names, because b4 tests a suspect address with unrelated names, and re-tests never lifted the ban. In TUN mode, QUIC and other UDP connections that a set rejects through Block QUIC (force TCP), the UDP Action Mode or the Block action kept apps waiting instead of failing at once.

Sets with IP Block Detection and Cache Blocked IPs ban an address the provider blocks for every site on it, so connections to it fail at once instead of hanging, and the dashboard's Banned addresses panel lists the bans, an approach inspired by Ladon. Bans are on by default, and Remember blocked addresses under Settings, Core, Packet Engine turns them off. AI apps connected over MCP can look up b4's REST API with the b4_api_reference tool, for tasks the other tools do not cover, and are told to ask the user for the web interface login when one is set.
The MTProto Proxy's first answer to a Telegram app copies the cipher, key exchange and answer size of the Fake SNI Domain, and the log warns when that site has no TLS 1.3.

In TUN mode, b4 could load the router's processor fully until no device could open sites, because it read the router's whole connection list for almost every new connection and, since 1.88.0, every DNS answer. On Keenetic, connections to port 443 through a proxy set or Telegram over WebSocket stalled once they opened, so Telegram, for example, stayed on Updating. (#469, thanks @asovetov) Sites that need a bypass could stop loading until b4 restarted when the firmware or another service removed the firewall rules that pass traffic to b4. (#468, thanks @asovetov) With Telegram over WebSocket on, Telegram connections the bridge cannot relay, such as a bot's API requests, skipped the proxy sets that covered them, and where Telegram is blocked they were reset after about 13 seconds. Photos and videos through the MTProto Proxy or Telegram over WebSocket sometimes started loading only after 1-3 seconds. On some networks, Telegram over WebSocket and the MTProto Proxy stopped loading photos, videos and files, because those networks began to drop Cloudflare connections that open with a large first message.

On Keenetic, devices handled by Device Filtering could not open any site, even one in no set, because b4 took their first packets before Keenetic's firewall had marked them. #466 With Device Filtering on, a firewall rule from the firmware or another service could make b4 rebuild all its firewall rules every 10 seconds, and settings saves waited for each rebuild. The log showed four failed routing commands whenever the Telegram over WebSocket set, or a proxy set with Route UDP through upstream on, was rebuilt or removed.

Some AI apps could not use b4's MCP server: LM Studio, also through LobeHub, refused every request, apps using OpenAI's API did too with Allow active probes on, and b4 refused Gemini CLI's tool calls. b4_check_domain called a domain covered when a set listed only one of its subdomains and did not check links or hosts with a port by their host, and a very long name kept the router's processor busy for minutes, in the web interface too. Other MCP tools gave AI apps wrong information: b4_recent_connections misnamed its columns, b4_logs_tail called every error-log line an error and could skip newer lines, and b4_get_topic got some modes wrong. Settings changed through MCP could differ from what the AI app was told: a set switched on matched nothing until a restart, a set with a port filter and no targets acted on every connection on its ports, and invalid values were saved, some able to stop b4. Copy JSON copied a set as dozens of formatted lines, too long for a chat message, in the set editor since 1.88.0 and in Discovery's Apply as a set dialog.

MCP permission checks had gaps: a queued write was saved after Allow configuration changes was turned off, and an AI app could open a SOCKS5 server without a password to the network or point b4's Telegram server-list downloads at any address, local ones included. The tool hints also called b4_find_bypass_strategy read-only, although it can rewrite sets.

A set can handle only calls, such as Discord voice calls, with Handle only calls in the Calls field on its UDP tab, narrowed by Which calls to the Discord app or browsers; such a set has no targets and takes each call on its UDP ports from any other set. The dashboard lists devices again in its Devices panel, with each device's name, address, connection count and most visited sites, and clicking a device opens its traffic on the Traffic page. Devices that left the network can be forgotten under Settings, Core, Devices with Forget device or Forget offline: b4 deletes their name, selection and MSS value and removes them from the sets' source devices. Settings and the set editor mark unsaved changes with a dot and list each change with its old and new value before they are lost, and in the set editor Discard Changes replaces Cancel and keeps the editor open. (#434, thanks @alle-ox) A slider's value can be typed in by clicking the number next to the slider. (#434, thanks @alle-ox) For a site that needs no bypass, Discovery lists the other strategies that also loaded it under N other strategies worked, and any of them can be applied as a set, for when a browser still cannot open the site. #423

Filter STUN Packets on a set's UDP tab became the Calls field: on became Pass call setup, which passes STUN requests and the Discord app's voice packets unchanged, and off became Handle like other UDP. A set acts on QUIC to an address it learned only when the connection names a site the set targets, not on other sites that share the address, such as a CDN; By SNI or matched destination under QUIC Matching keeps the old behaviour. #437 The Traffic page and the dashboard show a device by its name, or by its IP address when it has none, where the Traffic page showed most devices by MAC address; the MAC address shows on hover. A set's JSON pasted on the Import/Export tab is not imported at once: it appears formatted in the box, which shows where broken JSON fails, Import applies it and Format JSON tidies hand-typed text. (#434, thanks @alle-ox) A Device Filtering change takes effect when the settings are saved, where it used to wait for a restart of b4 and could meanwhile make b4 process the same connections twice.

The Traffic page showed STUN and Discord voice packets that a set with Filter STUN Packets on let through unchanged as if the set had handled them. Some set editor help texts were wrong: the TCP Port Filter claimed port 443 is always included, the UDP Port Filter that an empty field turns it off, and the UDP Evasion Technique misdescribed None and TTL. The Connection Packets Limit sliders on a set's TCP and UDP tabs had no effect, because every set took the global limits under Settings, Core, Packet Engine. The import tool dropped a zapret port range with equal or reversed ends, such as 3478-3478, so a set with only that range acted on every port, and it left shared domains unused when every profile had its own host list. b4_test_domain_now and the Test button of a Community Hub set reported sites that redirect to their www. address, such as youtube.com, as failing with and without b4. #445 MCP answers did not say which setting to change or that Allow active probes and Allow configuration changes are in b4's web interface, and an undo that needed Allow active probes stayed refused after it was turned on. #446 A block set limited to Source Interfaces also blocked sites by name for other interfaces and the router itself, and a block set with an escalation target stopped blocking a site once a device retried it a few times. Block QUIC (force TCP) had no effect on a proxy set with Route UDP through upstream on, so videos loaded slowly over a slow upstream, and with that switch off, other UDP such as WebRTC requests, which can reveal the real address, left directly. #456 A proxy set with Route UDP through upstream off let QUIC go around the upstream on ASUS routers with Asuswrt-Merlin, and on any router it refused QUIC also from the devices it excluded with All devices except selected. On ASUS routers with AiProtection on, and for the devices KeeneticOS lists for its hotspot, b4 missed the replies of many device connections, because the firmware's connection marks covered b4's Packet Mark. #441 With the UDP action Coalesce QUIC Initial, apps that open a QUIC connection in a single packet could not connect at all, even to sites the network does not block. #427 b4 could stop on a malformed QUIC packet sent to an address a set covers. A site that a set drops, rejects or blocks over QUIC still opened when another set had learned its address, such as a shared CDN address. #437 In TUN mode, memory use grew with every new connection. On a phone, the set editor's Cancel and Save buttons covered the set name, and long section headers, Russian ones first, ran past the edge of their card. #448, #449 In the Russian interface, slider units and a new set's name stayed in English, and in both languages the SYN Fake TTL slider showed its value in milliseconds, although it counts hops. #450 Device Filtering ignored devices added under Manual Devices, such as clients of the router's own VPN server: a selected one got no DPI bypass, an excluded one still did, and selecting only such devices bypassed every device. #442 In TUN mode, Device Filtering kept the selected devices out of RST Injection Protection and Remove ECH keys from DNS answers. An unnamed device vanished from the device lists when it went offline, yet stayed selected with its MSS value, and a set's list showed a device with a lowercase MAC address as not selected. Discovery and the watchdog's heals for a set with its own DSCP value tested without that value, so where a router in front of b4 picks the provider by DSCP, they searched through another provider, a heal could write the strategy found there into the set, and applying a result could move its sites to a set with another DSCP value or none. With iptables and legacy iptables tables both present, b4 did not see a removed DSCP chain as gone, so the firewall monitor retried its DSCP rules every few seconds.

A set can Remove ECH keys from DNS answers, under DNS & Routing, DNS Redirect, so browsers open sites such as Cloudflare ones where the network drops connections that use ECH, and Discovery proposes such a set when a site needs it. With cloudflare-ech.com listed, the set covers every Cloudflare site. The dashboard warns under Recent changes when a set's TCP port filter makes b4 skip connections, which can happen with Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup on or without the kernel's conntrack match. System Info shows whether the router can hold a dropped QUIC connection, in the row QUIC drop holds for the whole connection, and names what is missing, on OpenWrt the package kmod-nf-conntrack-netlink. A set routed through an interface can send its traffic to a gateway on that interface's network, such as a VPN gateway or another router, set in Gateway (optional) under DNS & Routing, Traffic Routing. (#401, thanks @alle-ox)

On Keenetic and on routers with an older kernel where b4 cannot hold DNS queries, they reach the resolver the device asked, and b4 replaces its reply for names a set blocks, pins or sends to its own resolver, so that resolver still sees those names, even for a set with an encrypted resolver. System Info shows the row DNS queries copied, not held (NFLOG) where this applies. In NFQUEUE mode, a connection that another service sends through a WireGuard, AmneziaWG, TUN or TAP tunnel, or with legacy iptables reroutes as MagiTrickle does, gets no strategy from its set and is marked tunnel->wg0 or reroute->ppp1 on the Logs page. Block sets still block it, and a tunnel that carries the router's default route keeps strategies.

On Keenetic, a device that asked for a name's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses at once, and the router itself, still often lost the second answer after 1.85.1, though System Info showed DNS queries queued before conntrack (raw) as available. #402 On routers with an older kernel, a device that asked at once for the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses of a name in a set with a DNS redirect occasionally got only one of the answers. On routers with iptables and an older kernel, such as Keenetic, SYN Fake Packets made connections open about a second slower, and the UDP mode Fake & Fragment lost most fakes, often with the real first QUIC packet. A device that sends several DNS lookups from one socket, such as a DNS server on the local network, had its later lookups skip b4 once b4 had answered or changed one of them, for example by removing IPv6 addresses. A set with Domain-only matching on applied its strategy only to the start of each connection, and the rest showed no set on the Traffic page. #428 A set that drops or rejects QUIC, or blocks a site, did not stop a browser such as Chrome from opening the site over QUIC, because Chrome sends the start of a QUIC connection in two packets. #428 With the UDP action Coalesce QUIC Initial, sites did not open over QUIC in Chrome, because the padding went in front of every handshake packet. #427 Discovery reported some sites, such as Cloudflare ones, as loading without b4 while Chrome could not open them, and could propose a remembered packet strategy for a site that only needed its DNS answer fixed. System Info listed tools such as jq, sha256sum and ipset without a version when they were on the USB drive b4 is installed on. A regexp: entry listed in two sets, such as a set and its copy made with Duplicate, worked only in the higher set, so with one of them limited by source devices, some devices got the wrong set or none. A device added by hand with an IPv6 address typed in another form, such as in capitals or with leading zeros, was not recognised, so a set that selects it under source devices skipped it and one that excludes it applied to it. Apps that use TCP Fast Open could not open sites through a set with a strategy. #431 Window Mode sent malformed fake packets on connections that use TCP timestamps, which Linux turns on by default. SYN MD5 Signature could send its fake SYN without a usable MD5 option, such as for an app that uses TCP Fast Open, so a server could take the fake for a real SYN. b4 could stop on a malformed TCP packet sent to an address a set covers. A set whose TCP port filter covered the ports devices pick for their own connections, such as 1-65535, made b4 skip some or all TCP connections of every set. #429 Since 1.71.1, on the router's own connections and on IPv6 connections without address translation, RST Injection Protection, Incoming Response Bypass and escalation on Forged resets stopped working once b4 had sent fakes or split segments. Since 1.26.1, with Device Filtering off, the router's own connections showed up twice on the Traffic page, and IP Block Detection could mark their addresses as blocked after fewer failed attempts than its thresholds. Since 1.22.0, connections from the internet to a local server behind a port forward failed once a set matched them, such as a set that matches port 443 alone. Since 1.39.1, on nftables, Global MSS Clamping and the MSS Clamping of a set without source devices had no effect on devices or on the router's own connections. On routers whose firmware overwrites b4's connection mark, such as some ASUS models, a forwarded port gave no answer to connections from an address in a set routed through an interface. Connections that another service on the router had marked, such as those of devices KeeneticOS lists for its hotspot or those MagiTrickle routes, got no strategy from b4's sets, because b4 took those marks for its own. (#422, thanks @asovetov; #276)

The Discovery page shows a run started through MCP or by the watchdog while the page is open, and its history marks such runs via MCP or via watchdog. Copy JSON in Discovery's Apply as a set dialog copies the proposed set without creating it, ready to import on another device through the set editor's Import/Export tab. System Info shows the version of each tool it lists, such as iptables, nft, ipset, curl and wget, and its Copy JSON and the MCP tool b4_diagnostics include it as version. A set can write its own DSCP value into the packets sent to its addresses, in place of the Set DSCP value, so a router in front of b4 can route each set's traffic separately; the switch is under DNS & Routing, Traffic Routing. The browser tab title names the open page, such as Traffic - B4, and the open set in the set editor, so several b4 tabs can be told apart. The Devices panel on the Traffic page sorts by name by default, or by latest activity or packet count with its sort button, where devices used to swap places whenever one of them sent a packet.

A device on the dashboard's Blocked panel shows its IP address under its name, with the MAC address on hover. The dashboard arranges its panels in full-width rows, each panel as tall as the tallest in its row, instead of packing them into free spots, and in Customize panels can be resized and moved between rows.

Discovery tried every strategy for minutes on a link that gives an error even without b4, such as the bare address of an image host, then reported the site as if it were blocked. Discovery started through MCP cut a link at a comma inside it and lowercased its path, so a link such as a YouTube image link failed on every attempt, and it never tried the Community Hub strategies. On Keenetic, b4 was sometimes not running after a router reboot, with no errors.log, and could stop when it restarted itself to retry its packet engine. #404
With iptables, other services' firewall rules for DNS queries, such as an Xray TPROXY rule or mwan3 and KVAS marks, also apply to the queries b4 has already seen.

On routers with an older kernel, a device that asked for a name's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses at once often got no second answer, so apps such as a TV's video player never connected, and the router's own lookups could stall for seconds.

Discovery takes a Trusted DNS server, under Settings, Discovery or for one run, as 9.9.9.9, 127.0.0.1:53053, tcp://, tcp+udp:// or an https:// URL, checks DNS against its answers and gives it to a proposed set as its DNS where the set can use one. Discovery tests a site through pinned addresses, given for a run under Pinned addresses or taken from the set the run is for, keeps them in a proposed set, and reports a name that has no address in DNS as such instead of as misspelled. Download Configuration under Settings, System, Backup saves the running configuration as is, or as a safe copy to share when asking for help, with passwords, tokens, user names, host names and credentials in URLs replaced by [redacted]. b4 refuses to load or save a configuration that still holds these placeholders. System Info shows in its Routing Sets row how many routing sets are installed and, while installing them fails, the error and the next retry, and the log warns when no firewall tool can install routing at all.

The settings are regrouped: the Core tab has sub-tabs for Packet Engine, Devices, Firewall, DNS and SOCKS5, and a new System tab holds Service, Web Server and Backup, which used to be a tab of its own. The dashboard shows connections per minute in and outside sets, each set's matches in the last hour and the problems that need attention, Runtime moved to System Info, and Reset Stats became Reset counters, with a separate Clear on Active Escalations. MCP b4_status and b4_metrics and the metrics API count each connection once, with per-minute connection counts, cpu_percent and rss_bytes in place of connections_seen, current_cps, current_pps and memory_percent. /api/metrics and /api/ws/metrics carry the new dashboard snapshot, and POST /api/escalations/clear clears escalations.

Discovery's Fallback UDP DNS servers list and the unused Reference domain setting are gone. The dashboard's Device Activity and Domains Not In Any Set panels are gone, in favour of links into the Traffic page.

Dashboard figures misled: Active flows only grew, Throughput counted only the first packets of each connection, Workers always read all active, Uptime started over at Reset Stats, and Domains Not In Any Set stopped taking new domains. Reset Stats on the dashboard also sent every escalated site back to the set that had failed for it. Discovery for a domain that does not exist, such as a misspelled one, ran through every strategy for minutes, each test failing with DNS resolution failed (no such host). Discovery could report a site as needing no bypass when its resolver gave a wrong address and no DNS server it tried answered honestly, and could propose a DNS redirect that gave a wrong address too. Applying a Discovery result could switch off the set's Fail closed when the resolver is unreachable. After a Discovery run, DNS queries over TCP for sets with a DNS redirect went to the original resolver from the next firewall rebuild until a restart, and during a run the Active Escalations list kept emptying. A set whose DNS redirect pointed at a resolver on another local device made its lookups wait out the timeout, or end in SERVFAIL with Fail closed when the resolver is unreachable on, whenever that resolver asked its upstream over plain DNS. Switching Time Zone back to Auto (system default) kept the previous zone in log timestamps until b4 restarted. A NAT Masquerade interface that was down or renamed disappeared from its card, which then looked as if masquerading covered every interface while it was limited to the missing one. Set cards gave target counts such as 1 domains, and in Russian the longer labels in the panel a set card opens ran into their values or wrapped onto a second line. An update from the web interface failed with Could not fetch the installer: mkdir /tmp/b4update-...: no such file or directory when nothing could be created in /tmp, as in a MikroTik container after a restart, and with /tmp mounted noexec it seemed to start while nothing happened. On a kernel that rejects b4's nftables routing table, such as Synology DSM with b4 in Docker, b4 logged a routing error at every start and save and retried every 10 minutes, even when no set used routing. The Docker image lacked ipset, so on a host without working nftables routing sets failed and the NFQUEUE engine left out packet duplication and per-set MSS clamping by address, and the TUN engine gave each packet duplication address a capture rule of its own.
A request to /api/system/update with a version such as --remove or --arch=mips removed b4 or installed a binary for another architecture, because b4 passed the version to the installer unchecked.

Expose to internet switches, off by default, open the ports of the web interface, the MTProto and SOCKS5 proxies and the Telegram Desktop WEB proxy in the firewall, and the MTProto share dialog can put the internet address in its link. System Info, the log and the Telegram over WebSocket card name the network bridges, such as br-lan, whose devices cannot use proxy sets or Telegram over WebSocket while net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables is 1, as the dockerd package sets on OpenWrt. The Bridge netfilter row in System Info names the setting to turn off. Set DSCP, off by default, writes a DSCP value into the packets the host sends out, so a router in front of b4 can recognise b4's traffic; the switch is under Settings, Core, Firewall Features.

The settings page asked for a restart of b4 after changes that need none: to the SOCKS5 proxy, to the web interface's username, password or language, or to the MCP settings. Discovery, including the watchdog's runs, lost some probe packets and ran several times slower on a site an enabled set already covered, on iptables and on nftables with some mark settings, such as a changed Packet Mark. A changed Packet Mark took effect only in part: routing sets kept the old value until the next firewall check or a restart, on iptables the old CONNMARK rule stayed even after b4 stopped, and a save from the web interface left Discovery's marks at the old value plus 1 and plus 2. On iptables, b4 deleted masquerade rules it had not added at every start, stop and firewall refresh: a plain -j MASQUERADE in nat POSTROUTING and -o <interface> -j MASQUERADE for each interface listed under NAT Masquerade. One malformed address, such as 10.0.0.0/99 or a name, in a set with packet duplication kept the NFQUEUE packet engine from starting. In TUN mode, a set with packet duplication over many addresses, such as a GeoIP category or an ASN, delayed the web interface by a minute or more after start and, with a routing set, paused the bypass about as long again, while stopping b4 in that time timed out and left capture rules behind. In TUN mode on a kernel without the raw table or the CT target, such as Synology DSM, connections the device forwarded for others, such as Docker containers on a bridge network or LAN clients, failed past the local network. In TUN mode on a kernel without xt_connbytes, a set applied its DPI bypass to every packet of a connection instead of only its first ones, which slowed traffic through it many times over and wrote a log line per packet. The first connection to an address a routing set learned from a DNS answer could leave outside the set, directly instead of through a proxy set's upstream or the set's interface. Connections a proxy set sent to its upstream showed no site name on the Traffic page and in the log while Send domain name to upstream was off, or when the set listed only addresses and b4 had seen no DNS answer for the address.

When the packet engine fails to start, b4 keeps running so the web interface stays reachable, and the dashboard shows the reason with a button that switches to the other engine; b4 also retries three times within about two minutes. b4 can be restarted from the web interface without a service manager, for example in Docker, in a MikroTik container or after a manual start, and keeps its process ID, so the container keeps running.

b4 could exit at startup without showing the reason on the console, some startup errors read %!w(...), and when the packet queue failed to open, proxy sets kept sending traffic to a listener that was gone. On routers where b4 runs from an init script, such as ASUS Merlin and Keenetic, every restart or update from the web interface carried the old b4's packet-sending sockets into the new one, so open sockets piled up. With Device Filtering limited to selected devices, connections through b4's SOCKS5 server and others the router opened itself went out directly instead of through proxy sets and Telegram over WebSocket. On iptables, a routing set that Device Filtering limited to selected devices left without any, for example because its only selected devices were manually added IPv4 ones while IPv6 is on, kept its previous devices and made b4 rebuild routing at every firewall check. In TUN mode, a proxy set's site opened through b4's SOCKS5 server timed out unless its exact name was listed in the set, and a .onion address never worked through the SOCKS5 server in any mode. Where iptables is the nf_tables variant, as on Debian, Ubuntu and some OpenWrt builds, the router's own connections to a proxy set's addresses went out directly while b4 captured traffic for DPI bypass. A routing set with a resolver of its own under DNS Redirect could fill with the addresses the router's resolver gave for its domains, fake ones on a network with spoofed DNS, and turning that resolver on did not look the domains up again. On nftables, routing sets dropped each address learned from DNS when its time to live, an hour by default, ran out after it was first seen, however often DNS returned it, which cut live proxy connections and let traffic past block sets. On iptables, an address listed in a routing set by hand dropped out of it an hour after DNS also returned it. With net.ipv4.conf.all.src_valid_mark set to 1, as XrayUI does for a WireGuard outbound and wg-quick does, Telegram over WebSocket and proxy sets passed nothing from LAN and VPN devices, while the MTProto Proxy kept working.

A set can target whole networks by their ASN, such as AS15169, on the new ASN tab of the set editor or from the Traffic page and the DPI Detector, and b4 refreshes their address ranges daily. Telegram over WebSocket can be turned on with one switch under Settings, Telegram, without a set or GeoIP and GeoSite files, and its card shows whether the bridge works and what is missing. Two options under Settings, Telegram, both off by default, help where Telegram's WebSocket servers are blocked or workers.dev is slowed down: Fronting name for Telegram's WS edge (advanced) and Let sets process Worker connections. Find a strategy in a set card's menu runs Discovery on the addresses kept on the set editor's new Discovery tab, and with Keep this set working with the watchdog on, the Watchdog applies a new strategy when they keep failing. System Info shows how many of TUN's capture rules are in place and how often b4 restored its rules, and in TUN mode the firewall monitor interval appears under Settings, Core, Firewall Features.

The MTProto Proxy settings tab is renamed Telegram, and the Traffic page labels Telegram over WebSocket connections Telegram bridge instead of -ws. Replacing a set's strategy from Discovery works on any set and changes only what Discovery tested, keeping the set's UDP settings and routing; adding the site to the set, and out of every other set, is a checkbox, on by default. TUN picks its routing tables from the free ones below 100 instead of 9999 and 9998, which busybox ip refused, so TUN did not start there. queue.tun.route_table still sets a table by hand, and busybox ip older than 1.33 cannot run TUN.

A set whose GeoIP or GeoSite file or category was missing acted on every connection to the ports in its port filter, and its MSS clamp on every HTTPS connection from its source devices. A cut-off download of geosite.dat or geoip.dat stopped b4 from starting until the file was fetched again by hand, and the installer could default to a source whose file did not fit on the router. Settings could be lost when a save was cut short, for example by a power loss, or when an address was added from the Traffic page during another save. Overlapping packet duplication addresses such as 8.8.0.0/16 and 8.8.8.0/24 stopped the bypass on nftables, and packet duplication and the MSS clamp picked up new addresses late. Saving settings took seconds with large routing sets on nftables. IPInfo and RIPE NCC lookups on the Traffic page could hang, and a failed add there showed a JSON parse error instead of the reason. Telegram through the MTProto proxy and the WebSocket bridge dropped connections and loaded media slowly where Telegram's own servers are blocked or unreliable, and on Android some channels' photos and videos did not load through the bridge. Telegram through the WebSocket bridge kept failing where workers.dev is slowed down, a working Cloudflare Worker was cut off mid-session, and Telegram's Cloudflare routes failed while a set covering Cloudflare was on. b4 contacted core.telegram.org (or proxy.b4core.app when that failed) and raw.githubusercontent.com on every start, even with every Telegram feature off. A heal by the Watchdog could damage the set it healed, and with Cache Blocked IPs on, the sites the old strategy had failed on stayed refused for up to five minutes after any strategy change. Discovery could pass a strategy that ended on the ISP's block page, probe the router's own network, and wait out the whole timeout on a connection that froze mid-page. The Watchdog and the DPI Detector reported blocking that was not there, and the DPI Detector said port 53 queries reached their resolvers when one redirect answered them all. Proxy sets and Telegram over WebSocket could stop carrying traffic, for example after XrayUI restarted xray, and a proxy set whose targets included the server of an upstream in the network cut off every device behind it. Send domain name to upstream changed nothing for most connections, so an upstream such as Tor got only an address and, with SafeSocks on, refused the connection. A set with an output interface sent its fake and split packets out the main uplink after some saves on iptables, and could delete every routing rule on the router and replace its default route when routing tables 100 to 249 were all taken. In TUN mode, a router firewall restart, such as after a port-forward change on Xiaomi, cut b4 off from traffic until b4 was restarted, some setting changes also needed a restart, and on iptables 1.8 device filtering briefly dropped LAN devices from capture. In TUN mode with NAT Masquerade on and no interface selected, or with a router masquerade rule that names no outgoing interface, b4 captured traffic but no site opened.
The IPInfo token could end up in b4's log when an IPInfo request failed.
