Discovery and the DPI Detector recognise a gateway in front of b4 that answers connections in the site's place: Discovery leaves its addresses out, and the DPI Detector reports the site as GATEWAY. Discovery keeps up to twelve other strategies that worked for a site in its History, not only the winner, and any of them can be applied from there later.
Apply as a set starts on replacing the strategy of the set a site is already in, keeping its name, sites and routing, instead of only creating another set.

A site with Pinned addresses opened in a browser drifted after about a minute to an address b4 never handed out, and the tab ended in a timeout. A pinned address the router could not reach was handed out first every time, and a browser waited on it for over two minutes before trying the next one. A site outside every set that shares an address with a pinned name went out unprotected for two minutes after each lookup of that name. Discovery wasted a run on an http:// check address whose port 80 answers everyone with a short error, and swept fake TTLs a second time after the first sweep had found none.

A rule restore after a firewall rewrite announced by the Keenetic hook is logged at INFO level, and the remaining warning means the hook is missing on Keenetic, or elsewhere that something other than b4 removed the rules. Mirrors learned from the hub are tried after hub.b4core.app instead of before it, and Settings, Integrations, Community Hub lists the addresses in the order they are tried and marks the one that answered last.

Saving a setting that rebuilds the firewall could leave the rules absent or half-built for up to twenty seconds on a slow router, with Tables rules missing, restoring... in the log. The hub never synced where a set covering it, such as a regexp:.* catch-all, stalled b4's own connection to it, and a failed sync was reported as did not answer the health check for one address only, whatever the reason.
b4 re-checks its firewall rules on SIGUSR1, and on Keenetic the installer hooks this into the router's firewall rebuilds, which used to leave b4 without its rules for up to ten seconds.

A rule restore that ran while another program was rewriting the firewall reported xt_connbytes kernel module is not available and skipped IPv4, although the module was loaded. A custom list of five fallback UDP DNS servers under Settings, Discovery was lost after the next restart. On nftables, a duplication set or a set with MSS clamping that held more than a few thousand addresses stopped b4 with argument list too long.

Sets can be shared through the Community Hub, off by default under Settings, Integrations: published to hub.b4core.app after moderation, then browsed, applied and rated on the new Community page, and Discovery tries them before its own presets. The new Coalesce QUIC Initial UDP mode sends a padding-only QUIC packet ahead of the real handshake in the same datagram, so DPI that reads only the first packet stops on it. The new Empty line before HTTP method TCP option puts an empty line before a plain HTTP request, for sites filtered by their Host header; it covers port 80 only and needs a User-Agent header. The Telegram Desktop WEB proxy can have its own Relay port, for a forwarded WAN port 443 that otherwise showed the b4 login page, and its placeholder page can be replaced with an uploaded HTML file.

Stop and confirm ends a Discovery run early and still confirms the strategies found so far, and a second press during confirmation ends the run at once. Match Fake Size copies the real ClientHello into the fake with only the domain name replaced, instead of stretching the payload to its size, and Discovery tries this shape too. The Compare Sets dialog shows the same rows as the set cards, picks and swaps both sets inside it, names every setting that differs and has a Differences only switch. #356

Discovery could name a winning strategy for a site that stayed blocked, and kept searching with a fake it had already proved harmful. A passphrase-protected TLS key was accepted under Settings and the web interface silently stayed on plain HTTP, while a certificate file missing at start stopped the service altogether.
Without a login for the web interface, any website opened on a device in the network could read and change b4's configuration.
After a service restart on OpenWrt, b4 could be left running and deaf to everything but kill -9, or run twice after an update. #351

Discovery looks for a site's addresses that the block does not cover, among those served to some five hundred other regions, pins the site to them, and can fix a site by DNS alone with a set that changes no packets.

The DPI Detector page is rebuilt around the sites typed into it: each is fetched directly and through b4, so a row shows whether the ISP blocks it and whether b4 fixes it, and a button hands still-blocked sites to Discovery. The Discovery page is rebuilt around the sites typed into it, with one card and a plain verdict per site, the found strategy shown as on the Sets page, and the last run's log kept after a restart for download.

Discovery could apply a set that did not match what it had found, and a stopped run left the page stale until it was reloaded. A proxy set that matched every address cut the device it was bound to off the network, and taking the address back out did not bring it back. #322 A set routed through an interface sent only the first packet of each connection that way, and every packet after it by the ordinary uplink.

Changing anything on a routing set took it down for about a second, and connections opened in that window left by the ordinary uplink for as long as they lived. Every setting changed through the MCP server kept a whole copy of the configuration, so memory climbed by tens of megabytes until b4 was restarted. A proxy set that resolves its upstream by domain went back to sending bare addresses a few minutes after any settings change, until b4 was restarted. #338 On Keenetic, the proxy and mtproto-ws routing modes were reported as unavailable after every reboot, although the firmware ships the modules they need. #342

A routing table named in /etc/iproute2/rt_tables, as ASUS firmware names tables 100 and 200, was not recognised as a set's table, so b4 reported its own rule as missing on every pass and TUN left rules behind on shutdown. On iptables, a set in proxy or mtproto-ws mode diverted nothing on port 443, so Telegram sat at "Connecting" while the same set still worked on its other ports. On kernels up to 4.17, as on Keenetic, Padavan and older OpenWrt and Merlin builds, a set routed through an interface never got the rule that sends its traffic to its table, so everything it matched left by the ordinary uplink. A domain in a proxy-mode set failed through b4's built-in SOCKS5 server, while the same domain worked for a client passing through the router. A set in proxy mode with a hand-set fwmark took the router's whole network down.

A set routed through an interface has a Kill switch, so its traffic does not leave by the ordinary uplink with the router's real address when the interface goes away. The MCP server can act on b4, not only describe it: AI apps can search geosite and geoip, edit sets and their targets and, with Allow active probes on, test whether a domain loads and run Discovery. The Update mirrors field under Settings, Control takes https addresses that b4 and the installer try ahead of the built-in ones when GitHub cannot be reached, and the docs carry a Cloudflare Worker script to run one. The update window installs an update from a b4-linux-<arch>.tar.gz file fetched on another machine, with an optional SHA256 check, for a router that can reach no download source.

A set routed into a tunnel leaves its packets alone, without fakes, fragmentation, desync, SYN health checks, dead-IP escalation, IP Block Detection or TCP duplication; a set routed to a plain second uplink, or whose interface is down, keeps its strategy.

After the b4 binary was replaced without a restart, the web interface reported the older version with nothing to say why. A set routed to a tunnel or an upstream proxy could take the router down within seconds of the service starting, because its traffic looped back into the proxy. A routed set could carry nothing at all with no sign of it in the interface, for example when no interface or upstream port was chosen, the firmware rebuilt its firewall, or a Broadcom router overwrote b4's routing mark. A routed set could send the start of a connection by the ordinary uplink and the rest by its route, take a routing table another program was using, or take over addresses another proxy set targeted. b4's own firewall work could take down the whole network: its commands raced the firmware where iptables has no lock, an overloaded b4 let the kernel drop packets, and on such routers pages stalled after their first fifty kilobytes once b4 stopped. Picking network interfaces to monitor could switch the bypass off for the whole network without a sign, once a VPN client or a transparent proxy moved the traffic to another interface. On the TUN engine, b4 captured a transparent proxy's own upstream connection instead of the network's traffic, sent LAN requests for a device on another bridge to the internet, and never saw DNS answers, so routing sets learned no addresses. Telegram kept reporting the MTProto proxy as incorrectly configured and switching it off, and on a router without IPv6 the bridge gave up on some of Telegram's servers. A Discovery result became unreachable once its run ended, stopping a run early threw away what it had found, the history file grew by about half a megabyte per domain, and the Watchdog judged domains on a check that skipped the bypass. A downloaded backup could be empty on drives prepared from Windows, because b4 skipped files marked as programs. Importing a zapret or byedpi configuration converted only a fraction of what was pasted, and misdescribed what it did convert. The MTProto settings page asked for a WEB proxy relay hostname while the MTProto proxy that serves it was off. Installing or updating b4 failed where the network blocks GitHub's download hosts, and the update window could come up with no versions listed.
The settings folder, which holds the web interface login and the MCP token, was readable and writable by every account on the router, and restoring a backup could write files anywhere.

The MTProto proxy has a WEB carrier under Settings, MTProto Proxy that Telegram Desktop 7.1.1 reaches over ordinary HTTPS, for networks that block MTProxy and fake-TLS outright. The SOCKS5 proxy under Settings, SOCKS5 Proxy has Allowed Sources, a list of IP addresses and CIDR ranges allowed to connect, for clients such as Chrome that cannot send a username and password. A set's UDP tab has a Block QUIC (force TCP) switch, and a UDP action that leaves matched packets alone, for a set that matches QUIC only to learn a site's addresses. Force IPv4 for matched domains under Settings, Core, DNS drops the IPv6 records from DNS answers for names a set matches, so a dual-stack site cannot skip the set over IPv6. A set can have an Egress IP under Routing that replaces the source address of its traffic, for routers that pick their path by source address. The dashboard's Runtime card shows the operating system thread count, and b4 writes a goroutine dump to the log directory once it passes half the limit.

A set's DNS redirect falls back to the last good answer or the client's own resolver when its DoH server is unreachable, instead of answering SERVFAIL; Fail closed when the resolver is unreachable keeps the old behaviour. The two QUIC Matching values that both matched by server name are one value, By SNI, and stored sets are converted on the first start. The API settings tab is renamed Integrations and gives IPinfo, the AI assistant and MCP one card each, with its switch in the header, a masked credential field and, for MCP, a client configuration to copy.

Discovery offered strategies for domains that were never blocked, and declared a strategy working on a single page fetch that may not have succeeded, such as a 502 error page longer than a kilobyte. On a router with working IPv6, Discovery stopped after about twenty tests and reported that no bypass was needed. Discovery built sets with a DNS redirect and geo categories they did not need, so a result for a CDN domain could not be added without a geo database. On systemd, restarting the service from the web interface left Restart command failed: signal: terminated in the error log, and a stop could hang for ten seconds and kill b4 during its firewall cleanup. An update could leave the service unable to load, or a second b4 running outside the service manager. A malformed IPv6 packet with extension headers could crash b4 and stop the service for every device on the router. A DNS answer that b4 rewrote never cleared the failure count for that name, so a site that had recovered moved to its backup set on the next single failure. A device added by hand, which has no MAC address, was ignored everywhere devices are matched, and an MSS clamp on it clamped every other forwarded connection instead. A routing set limited to source devices diverted traffic it was never meant to touch, such as the router's own outgoing traffic, and one matched only by port lost every DPI countermeasure. A routing set with no domain or IP target was built in full and quietly matched nothing. b4 took the router down after a few minutes on a busy line, leaving runtime: program exceeds 10000-thread limit in the log.

The SOCKS5 proxy switched authentication off when only a username or only a password was set, its UDP relay could be pointed at another host on the network, and turning it off left open connections running.

An MCP server at /api/mcp lets an AI app read b4's status, configuration, sets, recent connections, log and diagnostics; it is off by default and uses its own token. A second switch, also off by default, lets the app change set, MTProto, SOCKS5 and log level settings, and the last change can be reverted. MCP server

Encrypted traffic on port 53, such as a VPN tunnel, was matched against sets as if it carried a domain name, and a site name read from QUIC traffic was accepted whatever bytes it held. Telegram could report the MTProto proxy as misconfigured and switch it off, because a session was accepted before b4 reached a data center and a blocked route was tried for longer than the client waits. Telegram sessions to data center 203 and others waited for a new connection, because spare connections were kept for only two data centers, and a route that went silent made every later session wait in full. A connection to a name with several addresses stalled on the first address that did not answer, while another address of the same name answered in under a second. The API reference on the documentation site rejected the b4 username and password in its Authorize window and accepted only a pasted login token. Turning the SOCKS5 proxy on or off, or moving it to another port, had no effect until b4 was restarted, although the save was reported as successful.

Customize on the dashboard reorders panels by dragging, widens or narrows them on a twelve-column grid and hides them, and the layout is kept in b4's configuration, the same in every browser. Escalation also moves a site to its backup set when its name lookup fails or returns no address, or when its address answers no connection attempt, and the backup set answers that lookup. A log trace begins with the enabled sets, with domain lists counted rather than listed and proxy credentials left out.

Unanswered TLS handshakes, forged resets and failed name lookups each have a threshold on the Escalation tab, in place of one control for forged resets and a threshold taken from IP Block Detection. Editing a set keeps the Escalation switch-overs that the edit does not affect, instead of dropping all of them. A firewall mark picked by hand for a set is refused and replaced with an assigned one when it holds every bit of b4's own packet mark, which made the set's traffic look like b4's own packets. A connection through a set's proxy is closed after an hour without data, or five minutes after one side has finished sending, and a proxy the set cannot reach shows up in the log and the diagnostics.

Fake and split packets that b4 sends itself ignored the set's routing: on two WAN links the site reset the connection, and a set routed through a tunnel sent them, site name included, over the plain uplink. A set routed through a proxy leaked open files for each connection that died without closing, so within about an hour b4 hit the router's limit and stopped working until restarted. A set with an MSS limit for IPv4 addresses also capped every IPv6 HTTPS connection from the devices it names. A site moved to its backup set still used the failing set for its name lookups, the opening packet of each connection and connections that never reached TLS, so the backup set's DNS and SYN settings never applied. Escalation gave the backup set's routing only the one address a connection used, which expired while the switch was in force, and one device's failure moved every device to the backup set. Turning a backup set off erased the link to it, a set routed through a proxy could not escalate any further, and the chain-length warning was logged again for every packet.
b4 resolves only a limited number of DNS queries at once and passes the rest to the device's usual resolver unchanged, as one slow DNS-over-HTTPS server could leave thousands of queries waiting.

In TUN mode, devices got no reply to DNS queries that a set handled, blocked names, pinned addresses and curated answers included, because b4 read the device's address only after the router had replaced it. Every DNS query was listed under the router's address on the Traffic page, and a set limited to certain devices had nothing to match a query on. In TUN mode, a set routed through a proxy or an interface could add another packet's addresses to the firewall.

Your own Cloudflare Worker is the last WebSocket route tried instead of the first, because Cloudflare can take a Worker back partway through a session, so it passed every check while video failed. b4 asks a Cloudflare Worker for a data center address without a port, because media from data center 203 failed on port 5222. The Worker script in the Telegram documentation needs a compatibility date of 2026-04-07 or later.

Telegram photos, videos and stickers stopped loading in 1.76.0 and 1.76.1, because media sessions were sent to a data center that could not serve them. b4 knew too few of Telegram's address blocks, so nearly half the connections matched no data center and had almost no routes to try, and two addresses went to the wrong data center. A route that took a request and returned nothing kept getting new connections, while sessions closed by the client counted against a route and pushed a working Cloudflare Worker below all others.

In the WebSocket bridge routing mode, Telegram could stay on loading with an empty chat list, because the bridge used only Cloudflare Workers and never Telegram's own route. The WebSocket bridge kept giving new Telegram connections a Cloudflare Worker that had stopped passing traffic, and sent traffic to a different data center address than the device asked for. Connections that b4 opens itself, such as a fail-open connection to a destination already in trouble, went out without any of b4's bypass applied. b4 put its routing rules back only when all of them were gone, and treated a partly missing rule set as healthy.

A set can pin addresses for its domains under Pinned addresses, written in hosts file order, for a CDN that keeps answering with a blocked address; a pin for a name the set does not match offers to add it.
b4 remembers every address seen in a DNS answer, not only those it connected to; before, a name with a single address, such as Meta's CDN, had nothing to fall back to once that address was blocked.

Every DNS lookup took five seconds once a set was routed through a proxy or an interface, because b4 stopped reading packets while it wrote each answer's addresses to the firewall. System diagnostics reported jq and other tools as missing when they were installed on a USB drive. A curated DNS answer could hand a device an address that b4 had since marked unreachable, so the connection was reset on its first packet. In the WebSocket bridge routing mode, Telegram messages arrived but photos, videos and stickers did not, because every media session was announced to Telegram as an ordinary one. The Traffic page listed a TCP connection under a set whose port filter excludes it, and showed nothing about which resolver answered a DNS request or whether it was pinned, curated or dropped. On some systems, b4's firewall rules were torn down and rebuilt every few seconds, because the chain for the router's own DNS over TCP failed to load, and each rebuild left a moment with nothing intercepted.

Import on the Sets page turns a byedpi or zapret command line into one set per profile and reports each option as carried over, approximated or without an equivalent. Match any domain and Match any IP address make a catch-all set with IPv6 included, typing *, any or all into a target field does the same, and *.example.com is saved as example.com. A warning appears when several enabled sets name the same domain, since only the one placed higher in the list handles it. A DNS section in Settings sets the port for DNS over TCP, how long to wait for an answer and an off switch, and warns about ports other services already use. A log trace records whether each DNS request reached the set's DNS server or slipped past it. An IP Health section in Settings controls how long an address stays marked unreachable, with one verdict shared by all sets. A switch removes unreachable addresses from DNS answers, so a device does not hang on the one blocked address of a CDN while another device loads the site. A ready spare connection to your Cloudflare Worker for each data center saves the 65-90 ms setup that every new Telegram connection paid.

IP Block Detection also catches an address that never answers a connection request, and the router tests the address itself before treating it as blocked. Several Cloudflare Worker addresses are tried in random order instead of as written, which sent all traffic and all rate limiting to the first.

A set applied from Discovery had no effect until b4 restarted, and two applied results could claim the same domains, so a domain got another result's strategy. When two sets listed the same IP range, the one stored last took it rather than the one higher in the list, and a set limited to source devices could lose it to a general set below. On routers with iptables, 0.0.0.0/0 in a set's IP targets never reached the firewall and took the set's MSS and duplication entries with it, and a set routed through a TCP-only proxy left no rules at all. DNS queries that a device sent over TCP skipped the set's DNS server and went to the router's usual resolver. One refusal from Telegram's WebSocket servers switched off a working Cloudflare Worker, and a paused data center address was refused at once, so Telegram reconnected in a loop and flooded the log. System diagnostics reported jq, sha256sum and nohup as missing while they were installed, and flagged flow offloading even when it was set up to leave b4 alone. An address marked as blocked stayed blocked for as long as a device kept retrying it and was never tested again, so a false alarm or a lifted block held on.

A Remove button deletes a downloaded geosite.dat or geoip.dat and clears its path and source URL, and downloading into another directory deletes the copy b4 wrote at the old one. An IPv4/IPv6 switch in the DC Relay socat helper produces TCP6: commands for a VPS that reaches Telegram's data centers over IPv6, and an IPv6 DC Relay address switches the listening side too.

A set routed through a TCP-only upstream proxy refuses QUIC on port 443 so that the browser falls back to TCP, instead of letting it go out directly past the proxy. Turn on Route UDP through upstream if the proxy supports UDP ASSOCIATE.

b4's logs could fill a router's memory or storage: init scripts from older installers kept the full log in a RAM file on OpenWrt, and the error and update logs and trace files kept growing. A restart could leave a second copy of b4 running alongside the first. Turning Route UDP through upstream off had no effect until a restart, and matched UDP kept going to a port with nothing behind it, so HTTP/3 sites waited out a timeout instead of falling back to TCP. An upstream proxy that cannot relay UDP was reported only at trace level, so a set with Route UDP through upstream on looked like a broken site rather than a setting to change. Connections meant for a routing set could leave directly: the first one after each redirected DNS answer, and with an upstream SOCKS5 proxy, one for each address of a subdomain the set matches by suffix. An update could run out of space on devices with little storage, and a failed update left a second copy of b4 behind.

New set options shape the fake ClientHello: fake_len_mode: "match" sizes it to the real one, apply_ttl gives it the set's TTL with any faking strategy, and md5_on_fake adds the TCP MD5 option to it. With the tls fragmentation strategy, middle_sni places the split inside the domain name instead of at a fixed offset. Discovery also tries fake-only strategies, a low-TTL fake without any fragmentation, which reach filters that see through every split. The STUN fake payload is built in as Preset: STUN under Fake Payload Type, in place of a capture file uploaded to every device. Importing a shared set names the payload files it uses that are missing on the device, with a link to Payloads.
A fake packet and the real one carry different IP identification numbers, since a shared number gave away that both came from the same source.

The Watchdog showed a newly added domain as healthy before any check, and indefinitely while the watchdog was off. A Watchdog healing run could declare a site healed after one lucky fetch, and overwrite a hand-tuned set's TCP, UDP, fragmentation and faking settings while logging only the strategy name. Discovery counted a fetch that returned no data as a working strategy. On an OpenWrt router without the packet-queue kernel module, b4 failed to start with a raw firewall error that did not point to the module, and the installer reported such a router as ready. #275 A kernel without connection packet counters stopped b4 from starting, and a failed start left part of b4's firewall rules behind. The diagnostics report left out the queue number, worker count and queue mode, and System Info listed the wrong kernel modules on nftables-only routers. Telegram on Android could stay at "Connecting" when a set routed it through the built-in Telegram bridge, because the bridge closed connections that were silent for five seconds. #277 The Already exists in other sets warning missed overlaps by domain suffix, such as example.com in another set for www.example.com. #273 The DC Relay socat helper generated commands for Telegram servers that drop the connection right after it opens. A request after an idle spell could hang for twenty seconds and YouTube on Android could take minutes to appear, because b4 missed a site name split across two packets and the connection got no strategy. #279, #280 The first connection to an address b4 had just resolved for a device could miss the set that owns the domain, and one device's traffic on a shared CDN address could decide the set for every other device. #279 A set built from a large geosite category took several times more memory than its domains, about 90 MB to read a few categories from a 51 MB file.

The MTProto Proxy settings have a TCP user timeout and an idle timeout, for carrier networks or router kernels where the defaults of about two and five minutes need adjusting or turning off. Two API endpoints, GET /api/mtproto/sessions and GET /api/mtproto/active-clients, list live MTProto client connections and group them by secret with each secret's client addresses.
An MTProto proxy session could stay stuck for many minutes after a phone lost signal or put Telegram in the background, or when its link to Telegram over the WebSocket bridge stalled.

The MTProto proxy holds several named secrets, each switched on or off and shared as its own link or QR code, and the Traffic page and a dashboard panel show which secret each connection uses. All devices except selected in a set's Source Devices applies the set to every device except the ticked ones. Domain-only matching in a set's targets picks the set only from the domain it sees and does not learn or route the addresses behind it, for shared CDN addresses such as YouTube's and Google's.
A set's Source Devices table shows each device's MSS limit from Device Filtering.

Memory use jumped after saving settings, even for changes unrelated to the blocked-site lists. On some routers, such as b4 in a container on MikroTik, a set routed through an interface, a proxy or the Telegram bridge gradually stopped working, because the router rejected newly found addresses. #267 With NAT Masquerade on, the log repeated Tables rules missing, restoring... every few seconds, and b4 re-applied all its rules although they were in place.
System Info has a Kernel Capabilities section that shows whether the router supports the features advanced modes rely on.

The Telegram bridge could be slow to connect or cut transfers short, because b4 interfered with its own connection to Telegram. A named device that was off the network, for example connected over VPN, showed as its hardware address on the dashboard and the Traffic page.

Lines on the Logs page are coloured by level, and each level can be shown or hidden with one click. Start trace on the Logs page records everything until Stop & save and downloads one file with system details to attach when asking for help; recording stops by itself after 15 minutes. NAT Masquerade can apply to any combination of network interfaces, not only to one or to all of them. A runtime panel on the dashboard charts b4's memory use over time.
The live signal panel on the dashboard shows throughput, total data, the targeted share and active connections in place of connections and packets per second.

In TUN mode, Device Filtering had no effect, and every device's traffic was processed whatever the selection. Memory use could creep up the longer b4 ran, because logging, AI chat streaming and Discovery did not always clean up after themselves. After an unclean stop in TUN mode, new sites could stop loading while open ones kept working, because a routing rule for the removed TUN interface stayed behind.
System diagnostics show whether b4 runs in NFQUEUE or TUN mode and list the firewall rules b4 maintains.
b4's own firewall marks moved to high bits, out of the range that Tailscale and some other router apps use, which could misroute traffic when they ran alongside b4.

On gateway or container setups with NAT Masquerade, the bypass stopped working for mobile apps such as YouTube on Android, because b4's fake and split packets did not get the gateway's public address. b4 refused to start when a set mixed a country or service list with addresses added by hand that the list already covered, such as Instagram addresses next to the Facebook list. In TUN mode, every device appeared under the router's public address, so connection logs, per-device statistics and per-device set rules could not tell devices apart.

A TUN engine, chosen in the settings, runs b4 on devices whose kernel lacks the NFQUEUE modules, sending target traffic through a virtual interface whose uplink follows the default route when left on Auto. Discovery still needs NFQUEUE and does not run in this mode. Columns in the Aggregated view of the Traffic page sort by a click on their header.
The dashboard is rebuilt in one consistent style and opens with a live signal panel that combines connection rate with the key counters.

On gateway and container setups with NAT Masquerade, such as b4 in a container on MikroTik, a set's DNS-over-HTTPS redirect could time out or return nothing, so pages did not load. On some setups, such as b4 in a container on MikroTik, a routing set filled in its addresses only on restart or when toggled, and stopped refreshing them once they expired. A set using the Telegram bridge kept failing after an internet outage until b4 was restarted by hand.
The web interface password was stored as plain text and shown on the settings page. The field stays empty: leave it blank to keep the password, or type a new one to change it.

The Sets page seemed frozen after enabling, reordering, duplicating or deleting a set, because the screen changed only after the save and a full reload a second or two later. The MTProto proxy in 1.69.0 stopped connecting to Telegram on networks that block Telegram's data center addresses, so Telegram did not load through it.

System diagnostics, in System Info and in the installer, show whether flow offloading is on: this router speed feature, common on OpenWrt, sends traffic past b4 so that nothing is bypassed. Max Connections in the MTProto Proxy settings caps how many clients the proxy serves at once, and the default limit is 2048 instead of 512.

A set routed through a proxy or the Telegram bridge could be handled by another router app such as XrayUI instead, so it worked only while that app was installed. Discovery split a web address containing a comma into broken pieces, lost its log on a page refresh or after a search ended, and offered only the best result per group once a search finished.
A set saved by Discovery sends its DNS lookups over DNS-over-HTTPS by default.

On networks where the provider tampers with DNS, Discovery could not look up its test sites and reported that nothing worked, even when a working setup existed. Pressing Cancel while Discovery was testing several sites at once could crash b4. Stopping b4 could leave its firewall rules in place, and stopping it or running --clear-iptables left changed network settings, stray routes from sets sharing an interface and piled-up proxy or bridge rules. When a set's outgoing interface, such as a VPN or a modem, got a new address, the set's traffic kept using the old one until b4 was restarted. Changing the SOCKS5 proxy or a set (adding domains or IPs, creating, editing, reordering, deleting or toggling several) could save a configuration that did not match what was running.
Every update from the web interface writes a step-by-step trace to update.log in the log folder, reset at each attempt. The web interface shows the changelog in the selected language.
The log setting under Settings, Service is a folder (default /var/log/b4) instead of the path to errors.log, and existing configs are converted. An empty field turns file logging off.
Each web interface update left a finished helper process behind, and where no system service runs b4, such as directly in a container, the update reported success but the old version kept running.

The Traffic page grew sluggish as more addresses had their AS label looked up. When a set's DNS-over-HTTPS server was briefly unreachable, lookups hung until they timed out, so pages failed slowly. Pressing Cancel did not stop Discovery, so starting another search ran two at once with mixed-up results.

A set's DNS tab can send lookups over DNS-over-HTTPS to a built-in or custom server, for services that need a specific resolver such as xbox-dns.ru and for providers that tamper with DNS. A set can be limited to IPv4 or IPv6 traffic, so a site can have its own set over each, and Discovery can search over one and limit its result to it. The choice appears when both IPv4 and IPv6 are on in Settings.
RST Injection Protection also drops the fake reset aimed at the server, not only the one aimed at the device.

A set that routed its traffic to an upstream proxy or the Telegram bridge failed to open connections while its DPI bypass options were on. RST Injection Protection did nothing on a set that also used some SYN-based TCP techniques, because those connections were not tracked. Dummy network interfaces, such as dummy0, were missing from the interface lists in Settings, so they could not be picked for monitoring or NAT masquerade. Telegram Desktop reconnected every 30-60 seconds over the Telegram bridge, because a keep-alive added in 1.66.0 sent a signal that Telegram's servers rejected. Watchdog could repair a monitored site by adding it to a blocking or routing set that listed one of its subdomains, so the site got blocked. A site an earlier version added to such a set has to be removed from it by hand.

When a Block set blocks something, the Dashboard shows a Blackhole panel with blocked attempts, top domains and devices, and the Traffic page marks those connections block. DC list fallback mirror under Settings, MTProto Proxy turns off or replaces the b4 author's backup copy of Telegram's data center list on lavrush.in, used only when Telegram's own address is blocked. A set can have its own device list, so its routing, Telegram bridge or block applies only to those devices.

A set's Routing ignored the devices chosen under Settings, Devices, so its interface, proxy, Telegram bridge or block applied to every device. The router itself showed up on the Traffic page as a separate device, sometimes named after a phone brand, holding the router's own connections. On a set with UDP on Drop or Reject, Discord voice and video calls could break, because b4 did not recognize their traffic. On some Asus Merlin firmware b4 quit right after starting with a misleading message about a missing xt_connbytes, because it used a firewall command option the router's tool did not understand. The Traffic page could show an empty list and empty activity bars when the viewing computer's clock was off by as little as 30 seconds. A device could still appear twice on the Traffic page, once under its name and once under its bare IP. Discovery found no working strategy for any site when the domains were entered in quotes, such as a pasted "discord.com","youtube.com". #241
The Block mode in a set's Routing tab blocks the matched domains, IPs or GeoSite categories, such as category-ads-all, for every device and the router itself (Blocking).
A set routed to an upstream SOCKS5 proxy also sends its UDP traffic from LAN devices, such as QUIC and DNS, through the proxy. The proxy must accept UDP.

In the Aggregated view of the Traffic page, a device could appear twice, under its name and its bare IP, and devices added by hand under Settings, Devices showed a raw IP instead of their name. Starting b4 with a command-line option such as --skip-tables saved it into the config, so it kept applying on later starts without it.

MTProto Proxy can use a Cloudflare Worker as a free personal relay, with no domain to buy, for accounts where media, reactions or stickers still fail to load. The DPI Detector also measures how fast DNS servers answer and tests Telegram's download speed and servers, with a Legend for its results. It is based on dpi-detector.

Telegram routing over WebSocket in bridge mode works on phones as well as desktop, loads media more reliably and always prefers WebSocket, whatever the proxy's transport setting. The DPI Detector tells apart more of the ways a provider blocks or tampers with a connection, and tests a refreshed list of sites and servers.

When a set sent its DNS lookups to a chosen server on its DNS tab, names failed to resolve and the internet seemed to hang. Telegram data centers without a WebSocket edge stalled when the shared fallback domains were rate-limited. Copy buttons did nothing when the web interface was opened over plain HTTP, such as http://192.168.1.1, because browsers allow the clipboard only over HTTPS. Memory and CPU use slowly climbed while Watchdog repaired a site again and again, until b4 was killed. #227 The Traffic page's Aggregated view lumped devices without a known MAC address, such as those behind another router, into one Unknown device, and usually showed nothing for a filter such as !github + !google, which it read as plain text.

A switch in the top bar of the Sets page turns every set on or off at once. Test direct TCP under Settings, MTProto Proxy checks Telegram directly, bypassing the DC Relay, to tell a relay problem from one between b4 and Telegram. Auto-update under Settings, Geo Databases can download both files on every start and on a daily, weekly or monthly schedule. Missing files are downloaded at startup whenever a source URL is set. A set's TCP tab has MSS Clamping for the set's connections, such as a small MSS for a smart TV streaming YouTube. The set must target by IP, GeoIP or source device.

Watchdog keeps checking every site while it repairs one, and repairs sites that break close together in one go. Test connection for the MTProto proxy also completes the MTProto handshake and shows whether connecting failed, the handshake failed, or Telegram or the relay dropped the link right after.

In rare cases the installer saved the geo database path as b4/geosite.dat instead of a full path, and the web interface then refused to download new files. MTProto Proxy dialled internal Telegram addresses that dropped direct TCP connections, ignored a configured DC Relay in Auto mode, and could not load media from data center 203 through the relay. A geosite or geoip file downloaded or uploaded in the web interface took effect only after a set was next edited. Some sites, such as YouTube, failed to load through b4's built-in SOCKS5 server while they worked directly. On iptables routers such as Merlin, Keenetic and OpenWrt without nftables, the global MSS overrode the per-device MSS when both were on.

Memory Limit under Settings, Logging caps how much memory b4 may use, with values such as 128MiB, 1g or off. Empty keeps the automatic limit of half the system RAM. MTProto Proxy can reach Telegram over WebSocket as well as direct TCP, or through Cloudflare with a custom domain when Telegram's WebSocket endpoint is blocked too.
On upgrade, the MTProto proxy switches to the new Auto transport, which tries WebSocket first, then TCP. The JSON in a set's Import/Export leaves out the settings of features that are turned off.

Some Telegram clients could not connect to the MTProto proxy, because it accepted only one of Telegram's three transport variants. On some OpenWrt setups, the traffic of a set routed to an upstream SOCKS5 proxy skipped the proxy and went straight out, because two kernel modules were missing. #221
b4 could refuse to start with a false "another b4 instance is already running" error after a crash, after a restart from the web interface, or inside containers such as on MikroTik.

A set's UDP fakes can carry a payload picked in Fake Packet Payload: a captured or uploaded .bin, a random QUIC Initial made for each fake, or a bundled QUIC preset. Uploads under Payloads are marked TLS or QUIC. A ? button next to DC Relay under Settings, MTProto Proxy shows the current Telegram data center list and ready-to-copy commands for the VPS. b4 refuses to start when another b4 process is already running on the same host, and names that process's PID. Combo and Disorder splitting have an Overlap Length: that many pattern bytes go in front of a real fragment, with its sequence number shifted back by the same amount. Small AI buttons next to some fields explain what the field does. This is experimental: few fields are covered and the answers can be wrong.
When saving the configuration or a set fails, the web interface shows the reason, such as a port already in use.

Routing a set through an upstream SOCKS5 proxy failed on BusyBox routers, because the 1.49.0 fix for routing table numbers had missed it. Blocking all QUIC let through the newer QUIC variant that Chrome on Android uses, so YouTube on phones kept using QUIC. On MikroTik containers, routing failed for interface names with dashes, and interface routing went nowhere when several container interfaces shared one bridge with a single gateway. Safari on macOS greyed out the downloaded .tar.gz backup in the restore file picker. In UDP fake mode b4 split every matched UDP packet, which could break voice calls, screen sharing and games.

A set's Escalation tab picks a set to fall back to: when the set keeps failing for a host, b4 moves that host to the other set on its next connection, for an hour by default. Share connection link under Settings, MTProto Proxy shows a tg:// link with a QR code to scan with a phone, and buttons to copy it, open it in Telegram or share it.

Enable Packet Duplication could stop b4 from starting on routers without ipset, such as some Keenetic and Merlin setups. Duplicating whole connections needs ipset (opkg install ipset on Keenetic or Entware). On some setups, Update in the web interface did nothing, and the version stayed the same after a restart. Adding an IPv6 address from the Traffic page cut it to its first group, such as 2a01, put the port into the suggested CIDRs and broke its IPInfo and ASN lookups.

The error log keeps its history across restarts instead of being wiped at every start, so a crash leaves a trace. The Connections page is renamed Traffic, and old /connections links redirect to it. The Traffic page keeps updating at any log level, such as Warn or Error, and shows the last few hundred events as soon as it opens.
A set routed through an upstream SOCKS5 server, local or remote, sent its traffic directly instead of through the proxy.

Combo fragmentation's overlap can be tuned in the web interface again, with a preset (TLS handshake, HTTP GET, zeros) or a custom byte pattern. A set's Routing tab can forward matched traffic to a local or remote SOCKS5 proxy, such as Xray or sing-box, with the Upstream SOCKS5 proxy mode.
The web interface is redesigned, with cleaner type and spacing, calmer colours, larger numbers and better keyboard access.

Routing broke until b4 was restarted when the proxy's network interface, such as that of tun2socks or sing-box, was recreated or was not ready when b4 started. In the Aggregated view of the Connections page, the set name showed twice when a set matched by both domain and IP, and the SOCKS5 proxy label could overlap the domain.

Devices behind another router that are missing from the ARP table can be added by IP under Settings, Device Filtering, for per-device filtering and MSS clamping. #185 TCP fake settings can generate a fake TLS handshake from any domain typed in, such as example.com. Refresh Telegram DC list under Settings, MTProto Proxy fetches Telegram's current data center list, which b4 also fetches on every start. #190 The Connections page opens in a new Aggregated view that groups packets by device, protocol and domain or IP, with an activity chart per group and a device list to filter by. The old table is under Raw feed. The set editor has a save button that stays in the bottom-right corner while scrolling. Reset Config to Defaults under Settings, Core Controls is back, and keeps the sets, the web server settings and the geo file paths.
When one strategy works for every tested domain, Discovery shows them as one group that is applied in one click. RST Injection Protection uses more checks to tell real resets from injected ones.
The separate mac_aliases.json file is gone: device names are stored in the main config, and existing names are moved there on upgrade.

Traffic routing failed on Keenetic routers, because routing table numbers could go above 255, which BusyBox does not support. With Syn Fake on, the fake SYN packet always carried the built-in payload instead of the one picked in the set. When the router forwarded DNS through a local proxy such as https-dns-proxy, domains from GeoSite categories were not added to routing sets. The Error log level set in the web interface went back to Info after a restart. Some Telegram pictures and files did not load through the MTProto proxy, because b4 did not know Telegram's media data centers such as DC 203. #190 When another service, such as a VPN, QoS or policy routing, put its own marks on packets, b4 missed its own mark, so queued packets could loop and masquerade on VPN interfaces broke with routing on.
A Reject option for QUIC and UDP answers matched packets with an ICMP Port Unreachable instead of dropping them, so clients fall back to TCP almost at once.
A device that changed its IP address appeared twice in the device list, under its old and its new IP.

Before an update b4 saves a copy of its config file, such as b4.json.bak.v1.47.2, and the update dialog suggests downloading a full backup from Settings, Backup. Watchdog checks listed domains or URLs and, after repeated failures, runs a quick Discovery and applies the first working setup. It is configured under Settings, Discovery and has its own page. IP Block Detection notices when a destination IP is blocked outright and resets the connection, so the device tries another server sooner instead of waiting for a timeout. RST Injection Protection in a set's TCP settings drops fake TCP resets injected by DPI, spotted by their TTL, by arriving before any server reply, or by repeating on one connection.
Sequence Offset appears only for the Past Sequence and Random Sequence strategies, and Timestamp Decrease only for the Timestamp strategy.

Adding an IP by hand that a GeoIP category in the same set already held caused a firewall error. Traffic routing stopped working after about an hour, because GeoIP and static IPs were added to the firewall with an expiry.
Discovery tests several domains at once instead of one by one, which makes it noticeably faster.
System Info in Settings shows full system diagnostics, such as the kernel, network interfaces, firewall status with an NFQUEUE test and b4's paths, and copies them as JSON for sharing.

Discovery tests on its own isolated path, so the network's normal traffic is not affected while it runs. The Discovery page is redesigned: domains that share a strategy form one group applied in one click, logs open in a window, and raw MB/s figures are replaced by ranked presets and improvement percentages. The built-in Swagger UI is gone, which shrinks the binary from about 27 MB to 13 MB: the API docs are at docs.b4core.app/swagger, and /swagger/ redirects there. All sets can be deleted, since b4 no longer keeps a default set, and an empty Sets page offers Create Set. The config file stores only the settings that differ from their defaults, so it is much shorter.
The Reset to defaults button is gone from Settings.

Restarting WireGuard or another VPN while b4 was running broke routing until b4 was restarted. Cancelling Discovery did not reliably stop it at once or remove all of its firewall rules. Discovery history showed every entry as run a moment ago, because timestamps were not saved correctly.

With many sets and hundreds of thousands of IPs, b4 failed to start after a restart, because all the IPs went into a single firewall command. Routing ignored IP ranges, such as 10.0.0.0/24, in a set's target IPs and routed only single IPs. Updating from the web interface appeared to succeed, but the version stayed the same. The update dialog showed a prerelease version, such as 1.46.6rc, as a downgrade.

Domain-based routing failed on routers that run their own DNS, such as dnsmasq on OpenWrt, and the firewall monitor did not restore b4's DNS rule for routing when it went missing. A set whose routing was turned off and on again did not route until new DNS traffic came in.

A built-in Telegram MTProto Proxy disguises Telegram traffic as HTTPS and can go through an external DC Relay when Telegram's data centers are blocked by IP. It is set up in Settings with a fake SNI domain and a generated secret to paste into Telegram. The SOCKS5 proxy splits the first data packet of matched connections, which helps with protocols other than TLS.
Connections matched by a learned IP keep fragmentation and desync on even when their traffic is not TLS.
An interactive Swagger UI at /swagger/ lists every REST API endpoint and can test them.

A set's Routing tab sends the traffic of its matched domains through a chosen network interface, using the IPs b4 resolves for them. The SNI, OOB and TLS record split positions, First Segment Delay, Jitter Max and Fakes Per Segment accept ranges, and several splitting strategies can be selected, so each connection gets a random pick. Domains and IPs can be edited as bulk text, and long lists collapse behind a +N more button. ASN details for a destination IP can be looked up straight from the connections table, and they are stored on the router, so every browser and device sees the same.

Fake packets look more like the real connection: RST, FIN and ACK fakes keep the original TCP options, their TTL never exceeds the real packet's, and they combine a bad checksum with that TTL. The log shows the domain and TLS version for every packet of a connection, not only the first.

Uploaded and downloaded payloads got wrong file names, and disabled sets caused needless payload loading errors. Turning on syslog in a Docker container made b4 crash in a loop, because the syslog socket does not exist there. The time zone set in Settings had no effect on some routers, such as Keenetic, that lack time zone data. The log level set in Settings went back to Info after a service restart. A wrong certificate or key path in Settings made b4 crash on the next restart.

A specific Time zone for the logs can be picked under Settings, Logging. Firewall Engine in Settings picks nftables, iptables or iptables-legacy by hand when automatic detection does not work for a device.
Log timestamps use the system's local time instead of UTC.

Download on a captured payload did nothing, and an uploaded payload was saved with its extension twice, such as tls_payload_bin.bin. Update in the web interface seemed to run, but b4 restarted with the same version. With a set's TLS version filter on Any, connections broke right after they opened, because encrypted data packets were handled as new TLS handshakes. b4 failed to start on some Xiaomi routers, such as the BE7000 and AX3200, with a "Could not process rule" error, because it picked nftables where nftables does not fully work. #132, #133
The web interface can be switched between English and Russian in Settings.

With a web interface login set, an update got stuck on "Waiting for service to restart" forever. On busy routers, packet queue overflows flooded the log with repeated errors and wasted CPU. Some QUIC connections showed a blank TLS version in the log and the connections table.
On some routers with older kernels, such as the ASUS RT-AC68U, b4 started but captured no traffic. Copy JSON in Import/Export did not work in Safari on Mac.

Settings, Backup downloads a .tar.gz with the config, the Discovery and detector history, device names and captured payloads, and restores it from an upload followed by a restart of b4. The web interface can be protected with a username and password under Settings, Web Server, Authentication or during installation. TLS Version Filter under Targets limits a set to TLS 1.2 or 1.3 traffic, a Discovery run for one version sets it on its result, and the connections log shows each connection's TLS version.
After an import in Import/Export, a green banner confirms it and reminds the user to save, instead of the page silently switching to another tab.

DPI Detector results are saved under Previous Results, where past runs can be expanded or deleted, and the page remembers which tests were selected. Discovery keeps its results on the router under Previous Results, where a past strategy can be applied without re-testing, a domain re-tested or entries deleted, and a page refresh during a run reconnects to it. Adding a domain or IP to a set warns when another set already has it, including inside GeoSite categories.

A failed Discovery preset takes about 5 seconds instead of 35. Discovery spots a domain blocked by IP early, marks it Blocked and skips the extended search for it. Errors read in plain words, such as "connection timed out" instead of "context deadline exceeded", and firewall errors name the rule that failed and why.

Traffic could get the wrong set when sets had overlapping IP ranges, and later packets of a connection matched by domain could fall back to a set chosen by IP alone. Discovery reported DNS as poisoned on routers using encrypted DNS such as DoH or DNSCrypt, and could count a Russian provider's block page as a working bypass. Discovery could hang after detecting DNS poisoning, because its DNS workarounds waited for an answer with no timeout.

Several sets can be selected and deleted at once with Select in the toolbar, and Select All picks every set. With Fake Per Segment in the Combo or Disorder settings, b4 sends the chosen number of fake overlap packets before every real segment, not only the first, and Discovery tests this mode too. Faking has two new fake payload types: All Zeros and Inverted Original, a flipped copy of the real data. GeoIP and GeoSite .dat files can be uploaded from the computer with Upload under Settings, Geo Databases. A set can capture TCP ports other than 443, such as 80,5222,8000-9000, with the TCP Port Filter on its TCP tab; port 443 is always included, and no restart is needed.

There is no special main set any more: all sets are equal, and an existing main set becomes a regular set. TCP and UDP connection bytes limits moved from the sets to Settings, Core, Queue Settings. The device list is sorted by name, with selected devices at the top. An exported set lists only the settings that differ from the defaults, plus a b4_version tag, and pasted set JSON applies at once, with buttons to copy and paste it.

Pasting a set from the clipboard did not work on Android. b4 had several memory leaks that made its memory use grow. veth interfaces, which MikroTik containers use, were missing from the network interface list.

MSS Clamping makes packets smaller so blocked content such as YouTube on smart TVs loads, for all devices under Settings, Network or per device under Settings, Device Filtering. The new DPI Detector page checks whether the provider tampers with traffic, with tests for DNS spoofing, blocked websites and dropped connections. NAT Masquerade under Settings, Feature Flags sets up NAT for b4 in a container such as Docker, LXC or MikroTik CHR, also as --masquerade and --masquerade-interface. Discovery remembers the strategies that worked before and tries them first for a new domain. One Discovery run can test several domains or full URLs and finds a configuration for each. A button opens the Discovery logs in a large window.

Discovery tests real-world combinations of techniques instead of single tricks, finds the Fake TTL for Combo from preset values and tries every faking strategy, timestamp included. Saving in the set editor keeps the current tab and scroll position instead of returning to the sets list. The --config flag is optional: b4 looks for its config in /etc/b4/ and /opt/etc/b4/ and creates one on first run if there is none. The SOCKS5 proxy received updates. (#64, thanks @remmody) Devices are found from the system ARP table instead of DHCP lease files, so they show up on any router; their names still come from DHCP when available.
The Decoy SNI Domains setting of Combo is gone: the decoy packet uses the fake payload set in Faking.

Discovery used built-in payloads such as duckduckgo in place of the selected custom ones, and a configuration added from it lost its captured payload file and showed the wrong payload type. A configuration that passed in Discovery could fail once added, because the saved configuration differed from the tested one. The TTL search in Discovery did not change the fake packets' TTL, so every attempt was the same.

TLS Version in Discovery chooses the TLS version for probing: Auto, TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3. A built-in SOCKS5 server under Settings, Network Configuration lets apps such as browsers, curl or torrent clients send traffic through b4, with an optional login. (#48, thanks @remmody)

The device manufacturer database, about 6 MB, is not downloaded at startup any more: turn on Vendor Lookup under Settings, Device Filtering to see device brands. In Docker, b4 shows docker pull instructions in place of the update button.

The Settings page crashed to a white screen in containers such as Docker and MikroTik, because the interface list did not expect container interfaces such as veth. (#44, thanks @kakosmakos) The DNS check could report "DNS poisoned" when DNS was fine: it timed out before trying the system resolver, and CDN domains such as YouTube got different but valid addresses from different resolvers. #46
The web interface can use HTTPS, set under Settings, Network, Web Server, and the installer offers it with the router's own certificate on OpenWrt and Asus Merlin. (#40, thanks @Shiperoid)
A Reset Statistics button on the dashboard clears all counters without a restart and replaces the restart button, which stays under Settings, Core Controls.
Downloading a geo database failed with error 500 on routers with little free storage.

The play and stop control of the Connections table is a floating button in its bottom-right corner instead of a control in the top bar. The set editor has 5 tabs instead of 7: TCP holds General, Splitting and Faking, and Faking groups its settings in collapsible sections that show their status.

Edits to a new set could be undone at random, and its tabs reset, while it was being created. Custom TCP window values added or removed in the Oscillate or Random window modes were not saved. Packet Duplication connections showed wrong data in the connections table.

Packet Duplication sends several copies of each packet, against providers that throttle addresses such as Telegram's by dropping packets. It replaces the set's other DPI bypass and uses more bandwidth.
The GeoSite and GeoIP databases download separately and from different sources, so either can be used alone, and b4geoip is a built-in source.
Connections to matched domains sometimes showed as not matched, because learned addresses were lost when settings were saved or geo databases updated.

Segment 2 Delay takes a min-max range, and each packet waits a random delay within it; equal values keep a fixed delay. The redesigned Dashboard shows device activity per domain, domains in no set with Add to set, bypass statistics and active sets, and counts all traffic, not only bypassed connections. The TCP Timestamp faking strategy sends fakes with an outdated timestamp, so the server ignores them while DPI still reads them, inspired by youtubeUnblock.
The set editor opens as a full page instead of a popup.
UDP and QUIC traffic stopped matching its set after a while, because b4 dropped the link between a server and its domain even while traffic was flowing.
Discovery can require 1 to 5 successful connections before it accepts a configuration, with the validation tries setting (default 1).
Connection logs show the domain of QUIC traffic that no set handles.

A set with a domain such as youtube.com handled only the first UDP connection to it, not all UDP traffic to that domain's addresses. A UDP port filter such as 443 for one service could match all UDP traffic on that port, including other services.
Custom payload files did not work in Discovery for older configurations with relative paths such as captures/payload.bin.
Support for the TCP MD5 option, which Discovery also tests as a strategy.
b4 uses the iptables multiport module for rules with several ports when it is available, and the installer detects it. Importing a set made before 1.29 converts it to the current format.
Importing a set saved before 1.29 gave a white screen.
Discovery can test strategies with captured TLS payloads instead of the built-in ones.
Discovery could crash when its status was checked during a run, for example on Create Set or a page refresh (reported by Andrew B.).
Incoming Response Bypass works around throttling that stalls downloads after about 15 KB; the TCP incoming fake mode suits most cases.
The Discovery progress bar could go over 100%.

Bind Address sets the address the web interface listens on, such as 127.0.0.1 for local access only or 0.0.0.0 for all interfaces, IPv6 included. Skip DNS in Discovery skips the DNS checks for faster results when DNS is not blocked. Support for MIPS devices with soft float. Post-ClientHello RST in the TCP Desync settings sends a fake connection reset after the ClientHello, to confuse DPI that tracks connection state.

Discovery finds the best TTL for the network instead of using a fixed value. On shutdown, b4 waits up to 5 seconds for packets in progress to finish. Fragmented IP packets pass b4 untouched, since it cannot inspect them in full. Combo can send a decoy, a fake ClientHello with an allowed domain such as ya.ru or vk.com, before the real split request; it is on the set's fragmentation tab.
The DPI fingerprinting phase of Discovery is gone, as it was slow and unreliable, so testing starts at once. The overlap fragmentation strategy is gone; Combo covers it.

DPI bypass did not work for LAN devices on routers with nftables, such as OpenWrt. The TCP Desync modes rst, fin, ack, combo and full sent malformed packets over IPv4 and IPv6, so they failed or were ignored. The Packet Mark setting was missing from the network settings. Connections could hang when packets got stuck in b4's processing queue. Packet sending could go on after b4 stopped, which could crash it or make it unstable during a restart. On routers with several network interfaces, b4 could make wrong filtering decisions because of a race in its interface name cache.
Adding several services with many UDP ports, such as Discord or WhatsApp, could make the iptables rules fail, so b4 did not start or restart.

DNS poisoning detection could report poisoning when the system resolver and encrypted DNS returned the same addresses in a different order. UDP and QUIC traffic of services matched by address, such as YouTube, could be handled wrongly when another set had a port filter, which could break video. Downgrading from the web interface reported success but kept the current version.

A Discovery Logs panel shows the progress of a run as it happens, through DPI fingerprinting, DNS checks and strategy tests. For more than 20 major services such as Instagram, YouTube, Telegram, Discord and Netflix, Discovery tests their full IP ranges instead of a single DNS answer. When it finds geo-blocked addresses for a CDN service, b4 sends split DNS queries to external resolvers to find working servers. Discovery detects when the provider returns fake addresses for blocked sites, by checking with encrypted DNS from Google, Quad9 or Cloudflare, and then tests against the real server.

QUIC traffic, used by YouTube, Google and many other sites, was ignored when any set had custom UDP ports. UDP traffic to an address could go to a set that matched only its port instead of the set that defined both the address and the port.
Several domains can be pasted into Targets at once, separated by spaces, commas or pipes.
UDP port ranges such as 50000-50032 could stop b4 from starting on older devices, with iptables or nftables.
UDP port ranges written with a dash are converted to the colon form that iptables expects.
Discovery missed DPI that cuts a download mid-transfer, for example after 16 KB, and could report a false success. Payload capture always reported a timeout, even when the target site was visited.

Payload files can be uploaded on the Capture tab of Settings, and My own Payload file in Faking uses a captured or uploaded payload. Adding a configuration from Discovery also adds the matching geosite category, such as youtube for youtube.com. A set can filter UDP by port, and b4 listens only on those ports. Changes to UDP ports, connection limits and other core settings update the firewall rules without restarting the service. Discovery accepts full URLs such as https://youtube.com/watch?v=xyz, not only domain names. A sequence overlap pattern (seqovl) in Fragmentation mixes custom bytes into TCP segments to confuse DPI while the real data reaches the server intact; it works with Disorder and Combo.
By default b4 handles UDP only on port 443 (QUIC), not on all UDP ports. Device names in the Connections tab appear only when Device Filtering is on in Settings.

b4 crashed on startup when geosite.dat or geoip.dat had been deleted by hand. Re-downloading geodat files did not reload the domain and IP targets until the service restarted. Turning IPv6 off in the config did not stop IPv6 packet processing.
Kernel module errors flooded the system log on OpenWrt routers.
Forwarded traffic got no bypass with nftables on OpenWrt, because b4 caught the packets after NAT.
When the fake SNI does not fit, the overlap strategy falls back to plain TCP fragments.
The overlap strategy could crash b4 on 32-bit ARM devices.

The Connections table names the device behind each connection, from DHCP or a custom name under Settings, Devices, and Device Filtering limits DPI bypass to chosen devices or excludes them. Filters in the Connections table combine with +, exclude with ! and match one field with domain:, asn: or device:, as in domain:youtube+!asn:cloudflare.
The --skip-local-traffic option is gone: it caused connection problems and did not solve the problem it was added for.

--skip-local-traffic, on by default under Core, leaves the router's own traffic alone so a transparent proxy such as Xray, Clash or Sing-Box on it keeps working; a change needs a restart. b4 can be limited to chosen network interfaces, such as eth0 or tun0, under Core without a restart; none selected means all.
Errors other than crashes were written to errors.log.
The overlap fragmentation strategy crashed b4 when the SNI went past the end of the packet. Crash errors were not written to errors.log.
An error log for crash diagnostics, /var/log/b4/errors.log by default, with a configurable path. The Connections table can filter by ASN name, everywhere or with the asn: field filter.
A set's TCP and UDP connection byte limits cannot exceed the main set's, in the web interface and in the service.
The web interface could leak memory.

Discovery showed "0 of 0 checks" and "NaN%" while checking DNS, and a run that finished too fast ended with "Failed to fetch discovery status". DNS poisoning detection falsely triggered for CDN domains, because it compared addresses literally instead of testing whether they connect.

DNS Redirect in a set sends its DNS queries to a clean resolver, to get around DNS poisoning by the provider. Discovery checks DNS and manages DNS settings, with support for custom DNS servers. Enter starts Discovery. (#5)
Discovery has better fragmentation configurations and new presets for Combo and Disorder.
A SYN Fake TTL slider in the TCP settings.

With the randseq or pastseq faking strategies, SYN fakes went out with full TTL, reached the server and broke connections. Config validation compared a set's connection bytes limit with the main set's default instead of its saved value. The web interface crashed when a set was created with Overlap fragmentation.
New fragmentation strategies for modern DPI: Combo (recommended), Disorder, Overlap, Extension Split, First-Byte Desync and Hybrid.
b4 leaves packets to private addresses alone.
Saving a set was slow.
Discovery measures a reference domain first and requires the target to download at least 4 KB at 30% or more of its speed; the reference domain is under Settings, Discovery, yandex.ru by default.

Discovery finds the TTL and split position with a binary search, cutting its second phase from about 50 tests to 15. The save button of the set editor shows a spinner and is disabled while saving, so a set cannot be saved twice. Sets are reordered by drag and drop instead of up and down arrows.
Discovery trusted the first successful response and missed DPI that throttles, stalls or blocks resources mid-transfer.

Experimental DPI fingerprinting in Discovery tries to identify the DPI type and blocking method and tests the likely strategies first, falling back to the full scan when unsure. Faking offers a choice of fake payload: Random, Custom or a built-in one, FakeSNI1 (google, the default) or FakeSNI2 (duckduckgo). Discovery tries both built-in fake payloads, since DPI may react to only one, and uses the one that works for the rest of the run.

QUIC fragmentation splits at the site name inside the encrypted QUIC packet, against DPI that decrypts the first QUIC packet to read it. The OOB strategy supports the tcp_check and md5sum faking strategies, for when TTL-based faking is unreliable.
In fragmentation settings, "Middle SNI" is renamed Smart SNI Split, a packet diagram shows the split, and the manual position is in a collapsible advanced section.

IP-level fragmentation broke in several ways: IPv4 UDP fragments had a wrong offset, IPv6 fragments split at the wrong place, and Smart SNI Split was ignored. QUIC fragmentation sent fragments in reverse order when the reverse option was off, and in normal order when it was on. The OOB strategy broke connections: its extra byte reached the server, and the second segment had a wrong sequence number.
Discovery tests more than 150 configurations. The SNI split position in fragmentation is a number field instead of a slider.
New sets with geosite or geoip categories did not match traffic until the service restarted.

Sets can be filtered by name, domain, geosite category or geoip category. Two sets can be compared side by side, with the differences grouped by TCP, UDP, fragmentation, faking and targets. Discovery names a new set after its preset, such as tcp-frag-rev-fake, and offers to add the domain to a similar existing set instead. Discovery shows working configurations as tests finish, so they can be applied before the scan ends, and skips the later phases when no DPI is detected.

New sets are added at the top of the list. Sets moved from the Settings menu to the main navigation. Creating, editing, deleting, duplicating, reordering and turning sets on or off save at once, without Save Changes.
Refreshing the Settings page lost the selected tab.
The fake SNI payload is back to the earlier one, for better compatibility.
The default Desync mode of a set is off.
The Domains table stopped updating with new packets, and its columns were cramped.
ClientHello Mutation works for IPv6.
Discovery presets lacked default values for the SNI Mutation, TCP window and Desync settings.
The ClientHello Mutation mode could not be changed in the Faking settings.

TCP Window Manipulation (--tcp-win-mode) sends fakes with altered TCP window sizes to confuse DPI that tracks connections, in the modes oscillate, zero, random and escalate. TCP Desync Attack (--tcp-desync-mode) injects fake RST, FIN or ACK packets with low TTL and broken checksums to throw off DPI connection tracking: rst, fin, ack, combo or full. SNI Mutation changes the structure of the ClientHello to get past DPI fingerprinting, in the modes duplicate, grease, padding, reorder, full and advanced.

The Out-of-Band (OOB) strategy (--frag=oob), with configurable position, reverse order and character, which Discovery also tests. TLS Record Splitting (--frag=tls) splits the ClientHello into several TLS records, against DPI that expects one. SACK dropping (--tcp-drop-sack) strips Selective Acknowledgment options from TCP headers to force full retransmissions and confuse DPI that tracks connections.

The fake SNI payload, the default included, uses a TLS 1.3 ClientHello for staticcdn.duckduckgo.com. For domains longer than 30 bytes, the SNI split falls 12 bytes before the end of the name, so suffixes such as googlevideo.com are split across packets. Sets with large geosite or geoip categories use 70-90% less CPU. Downloaded geodat files are available in the sets manager at once, without a restart. The Fragmentation tab of a set is reworked. --frag-sni-reverse is renamed --frag-reverse.
Changing the log level needed a reload of the web interface. b4 failed to start with the error TCP ConnBytesLimit greater than main set, because config validation compared the main set with itself.

YouTube and other video could buffer or hang and sites loaded slowly, because with default settings each QUIC packet held up the kernel queue for at least 6 ms. IPv6 QUIC packets used the TCP delay settings instead of the UDP ones. A set created from the Domains page lost its custom name and got a generic one such as "Set 1".
A set can be turned off without deleting it. A clear button next to a set's IP and CIDR list. GeoSite and GeoIP files can be downloaded from Settings, with preset sources.
Test domains are managed on the redesigned Test page instead of in Settings. Discovery has new test strategies.
The Domains page slowed down badly when ASN filters were added.

Fake SYN packets with a configurable payload length go out before the real connection opens, to confuse DPI; set them with --tcp-syn-fake and --tcp-syn-fake-len or in the TCP settings. With an IPInfo token under Settings, API, clicking a destination address on the Domains page shows its location, ASN, organization and network. RIPE Stat integration shows the prefixes an ASN announces and details about the network, to help target address ranges. Sets can be exported as JSON files and imported on another device.
Discovery results show a configuration card for each domain instead of a single recommended configuration.
Adding a domain or an IP or CIDR address from the Domains page asks which set it goes to. A Discovery result can be added to the sets with one click.
Discovery testing is rebuilt to be more reliable and faster.
b4 leaked memory over time. Updating b4 through the web interface could fail.

Clicking a destination address on the Domains page adds the exact IP or its CIDR range to a set, without a reload or restart. A switch on the Domains page shows all packets or only those with a known domain, which helps when checking UDP traffic. Sets show how many domains and addresses their geodat categories contain. A new tab on the Test page shows a Discovery configuration card for each domain instead of a single recommended configuration.

In the reworked UDP tab of a set, port filtering takes one field such as 80,443,2000-3000 instead of from and to, and --udp-dport-filter replaces --udp-dport-min and --udp-dport-max. The packet count badge on the Domains menu counts only packets handled by b4's targets.

UDP entries were not logged when UDP packets were set to be ignored. The web interface crashed when the filter on the Domains page was used. Manually added domains needed a service restart when no geodat files were configured. The tests reported failure when a site answered with an HTTP status other than 200, even though DPI was bypassed.
Configuration sets give different targets their own TCP, UDP, fragmentation and faking settings, matched by domain, IP or CIDR range, or UDP port range. Support for geoip.dat.

A DPI bypass test on the Test page checks the configured domains and measures download speed, with its settings under /settings/checker. A button in the Core tab of Settings resets b4's settings to their defaults.
The restart button moved to the Core tab of Settings, under Core Controls.
