Restarting the service from the web interface did not work with some service managers (Entware, OpenWrt, systemctl). The pause shortcut P on the domains and logs pages fired while typing in the search field.
Blocked sites could fail to load at random in Safari, Firefox and Chrome.
b4 restores its iptables or nftables rules when they disappear, without a manual restart; --tables-monitor-interval sets how often it checks (10 seconds by default, 0 turns it off).
b4 keeps connection state for longer and with a larger buffer, and checks the characters of detected domain names more strictly.
The geosite path field was missing from the settings.

Hotkeys on the Domains and Logs pages: Ctrl+X or Delete clears the entries, and P or Pause pauses the stream. Regex entries in geosite files are read. TCP and UDP connection bytes limits in the network settings.
The settings showed a wrong total number of domains.
Support for nftables.
--skip-iptables and --clear-iptables are renamed --skip-tables and --clear-tables. TCP connections are split into fragments after the domain name (SNI) is found.
A Restart Service button in Settings restarts b4 from the web interface. The Domains table sorts by a column when its header is clicked. b4 can update to a new version from the web interface.
The iptables rule in the OUTPUT chain.
The unused --conntrack and -gso flags.
The Dashboard did not work.
--clear-iptables removes b4's iptables rules. IPv6 support, with --ipv4 (on by default) and --ipv6 (off by default) to choose the protocol versions.
Domains from geodata files are handled better.

The Community page lists sets that other b4 users published, with reports on whether they work, and turns one into a local set in one step. The page is in the menu while the Community Hub is on, see Switching it on. Finding a community set Applying a community set Reports and complaints Publishing a set and Sharing a set

The Community Hub at https://hub.b4core.app keeps the catalogue: the newest approved version of every published set, with the reports on it. A moderator approves every version before it is listed. The catalogue is signed with the hub's key, which is built into b4, and a list signed with another key is refused. The router keeps a copy of the catalogue. It syncs the copy every hour, again 5 minutes after a sync that no hub answered, and at once on Sync now. The search runs on this copy, so a domain typed into it is not sent to the hub. The copy expires when no hub has answered for two weeks. The page then shows a warning above the last catalogue received. Applied sets are ordinary sets in the configuration and keep working. Reports count per strategy, not per set. Two sets with the same strategy share one score, and a new version that changes only the targets keeps the score of the previous one.

Action What the hub receives Sync A request for the catalogue. The hub sees the router's public address and b4 version, and answers with the network it sees the router on: ASN, country and ISP. Works or Broken The set and version, the kind of report, the domain the list was filtered by, if any, the router's ASN and country, its capture engine and b4 version. Complaint The set and version, and the reason typed in. Publication The shared set. The names and targets of other sets, and the devices behind the router, are never sent. Every record is signed with the router's author key. The hub knows a router by this key, not by an account.

The line at the top of the page shows the catalogue date, the number of sets, the last sync, the network the hub sees the router on and the number of reports waiting to be sent. Sync now fetches the catalogue and sends the waiting reports. Message Meaning The Community Hub is off. Enable Community Hub is off, and the list is hidden. No trusted hub key is available, so the catalogue cannot be verified. Hub public key holds a key that cannot be read, and the list is hidden. Pointing a router at it describes where the key comes from. The catalogue expired on ... No hub has answered for two weeks. The last catalogue received stays listed. Last sync error: ... The last sync failed, for the reason the message names. The next successful sync clears it.

The Domain field narrows the list to the sets that cover a domain. A pasted URL is reduced to its host name. A set covers a domain through a domain entry, a regexp: entry or a geosite category, and the card names the entry it matched through. Categories are looked up in the geosite database of this router. A category named after the domain, such as youtube for www.youtube.com, matches without a database. The closest match comes first: an exact domain, then a parent domain, a regexp: entry, a category. Among equal matches, the order is the nearest network with reports, the higher score, the more reports, then the newer update. With the field empty, the whole catalogue is listed, best rated first.

The header shows the title, the author label, the version, the technique family, the b4 version the set needs and the targets. The strategy summary below says what the set does to packets, in the same form as a Discovery result. Reports on the right shows the score, see Reading the score. Badge Meaning Applied A local set was created from this one, and its strategy is unchanged. A click opens the local set. Applied, edited The strategy of the local set was changed after it was applied. needs payload The fake packets use a captured ClientHello. Applying fetches the file from the hub. block A block set. pins The set pins domains to fixed addresses, listed under Details. blanket The set targets geosite categories only. catch-all At least one domain entry is a regexp: pattern. Button What it does Apply Creates a local set from this one, see Applying a community set. On an applied set it reads Applied, and Open set opens the local set. Update to version N, Reapply Replace the local set with the published version, see Updating and reapplying. Details Shows everything the catalogue holds about the set: all targets, the strategy, the payload files, the dates, the fingerprint and the set JSON. Report Sends a complaint to the moderators, see Complaints. Works, Broken Shown on an applied set. They report whether the set works on this network, see Reports and complaints. Disabled while the local strategy is edited. Test Shown on an applied set. Fetches a domain through b4 and around it, see Testing an applied set. A link to a set that is not in the local catalogue, such as one still waiting for a moderator, opens Set details with a note saying so.

The connection to the hub is set under Settings > Integrations > Community Hub. Field What it does Default Enable Community Hub Adds Community to the menu, starts the sync and shows the Share with other b4 users section in the set editor. A shared set pasted into Import is accepted with the switch off as well. Off Hub mirrors Other addresses of the same hub, one per line, tried in order until one answers. Mirrors the hub approved are learned from it and added automatically, see A mirror of another hub. Empty, which means https://hub.b4core.app Hub public key Only for a hub of one's own, together with its address in Hub mirrors. The key of hub.b4core.app is built in. Empty Hub status shows the catalogue and when it expires (Fresh until), the last sync and its error, the key the catalogue was verified with (Signed by), the network the hub sees the router on, and Unsent reports, kept for 30 days. Hub lists the addresses in the order they are tried: the ones entered by hand, the built-in one, then learned mirrors. Author identity next to it shows the router's author key. b4's own requests to the hub pass through its packet processing like any other traffic. A set that matches everything, such as one with a regexp:.* entry, applies its strategy to them as well and is listed under Matched by set. A set for the hub addresses with no strategy, placed before it, keeps the hub out of that strategy. When such a strategy stalls the sync, b4 syncs over a connection its own rules leave alone and shows Own traffic. The sync keeps working, but a set or rule on this router breaks b4's own connections.

A set applied from the Community page is an ordinary set with a Community set chip on its card. The chip opens the set on the Community page. Once the strategy differs from the published one, the chip reads Community set, edited, see Applied and edited.
documents.s: Applied sets on the Sets page

documents.t: Apply creates a local set from a published one. The hub is not changed: the set is created on this router and starts working at once, without a restart.
The Community Hub is on, and the set is listed on the Community page, see Finding a community set. A hub answers, when the set has the needs payload badge: applying fetches the payload file from it.

Click Apply on the set's card, or in Details. Read the message that follows. It names everything applying changed, such as domains moved out of other sets. Click Open set to review the new set in the editor, or Undo to delete it. Open the sites the set covers. When one does not open, run the test.

The set goes through the checks of a shared set pasted into Import. Unknown settings are dropped, values this b4 does not accept are replaced by defaults, and unsafe pins and DNS redirects are dropped. Payload files are installed and appear under Settings > Payloads. Geosite and geoip categories missing from this router's databases are named. Without a database, the categories are removed. A set left with no targets is refused, unless it handles only calls. The set is created enabled, at the top of the Sets page, named after the published title. Domains the set lists are removed from every other enabled set that listed them. warning Undo deletes the new set and nothing else. Domains removed from other sets stay removed.

The local set stays linked to the published one, and the link is what allows reports and updates. The card on the Community page shows Applied, and the set's card on the Sets page shows a Community set chip. Editing the strategy changes the badge to Applied, edited and the chip to Community set, edited. The strategy here means the TCP, UDP, fragmentation, fake packet, MSS clamp and DNS redirect settings. Works and Broken are disabled on an edited set. Targets, port filters, pins, the name, routing and device filters are not part of the strategy. A community set can be narrowed to a few domains or sent through a proxy and stays linked and unedited. Calls and Which calls on the UDP tab are part of the strategy, see Sets for calls: changing either changes the badge to Applied, edited.

When the author publishes a new version, the card of an applied set shows Update to version N. An edited set on the newest version shows Reapply. Both replace the local set with the published version, after a confirmation. The set keeps its place in the list, its enabled state, its Discovery addresses, the watchdog switch and its own DSCP value. Every other setting comes from the published version, and local edits are lost. The IP priority switch is turned off. warning Routing to a proxy or an interface, device filters and escalation are not part of a publication. Update to version N and Reapply return them to their defaults, so the set has to be routed again afterwards. A router keeps running the version it applied until Update to version N is clicked. The score on the card belongs to the newest version.

Test on the card of an applied set fetches one domain twice: through b4 with the set active, and with b4 bypassed. The domain defaults to the one the list was filtered by, otherwise to the first domain of the set. Any domain the set covers can be entered. The test sends nothing to the hub. Through b4 Bypassing b4 Verdict OK OK Nothing blocks the domain right now, so the set is not needed for it. OK FAIL The set does its job. FAIL OK The set breaks the domain. FAIL FAIL The address may be blocked outright, or the site is down.

Discovery has the option Try community sets first, shown while the Community Hub is on and enabled by default. A run with it first syncs the catalogue when the router's copy is older than ten minutes. It then takes up to three sets per site, best rated first, and tests them after the strategies remembered from earlier runs and before the built-in presets. Community strategies appear in the run as community-<title>-v<version>. One that wins is applied like any other Discovery result. The set it creates stays linked to the hub set: it shows as Applied on the Community page and accepts reports.

When applying fails, the message names the reason. When the set applies but a site does not open, the test shows whether the set or the site is at fault. A set that breaks the domain gets a Broken report, see Reports and complaints, and Discovery searches for a strategy on this connection.

Other b4 users may already have published a set that opens a blocked site. The search on the Community page finds the sets that cover a domain, and the score shows how they do on networks near this one.
The Community Hub is on, see Switching it on. The catalogue has synced at least once. The status line at the top of the Community page shows its date.

Open Community. Type the domain, or paste a URL, into Domain. Compare the sets in the list. The closest match with reports from the nearest network comes first. Click Details on a set to see all its targets and the full strategy. Click Apply on the set chosen, see Applying a community set. The fields of the page are described under Community.

Reports on a card shows the share of reports that say the set works, such as 75% works. The card uses the nearest network with enough reports: on your ISP: routers on the same ASN as this one; in your country: routers in the same country; worldwide: all routers. A set without enough reports in any of them shows no reports yet. Until the router knows its own network, only worldwide reports are shown. The hub tells the router its network at the first sync, and before that the last DPI Detector run supplies it. Under the percentage, the card shows the weight of the reports, written as a number of reports, the number of devices that sent them and the date of the last one. Older reports count for less, so that number shrinks as they age, and the score follows recent reports. A set that stopped working falls within a couple of weeks of the first Broken reports, whatever it collected before. Few reports give a cautious figure: two Works reports and nothing else show 75%. The score describes other networks. DPI differs between regions of one ISP and changes without notice. A high score makes a set worth trying, and Test on an applied set checks it on this connection, see Testing an applied set.

What happens Cause and next step No published set covers ... Nobody has published a set for this domain yet. Discovery searches for a strategy on this connection. Community is missing from the menu The Community Hub is off, see Switching it on. A warning takes the place of the list See the messages under Status line. A link opens Set details with a note that the set is not in the catalogue The set is still waiting for a moderator, or the catalogue has not synced since it was approved. Sync now fetches the newest catalogue.

A Works or Broken report tells the hub whether an applied set does its job on this network, and it feeds the set's score. A complaint tells the moderators about a problem with the set as published, and does not change the score.
For a report: the set is applied, and its strategy is unchanged since. For a complaint: nothing. A set can be reported without being applied.

Apply the set and use the sites it covers for a while. When a site does not open, click Test on the card, see Testing an applied set. A site that fails both through b4 and around it is down or blocked outright, which says nothing about the set. Click Works or Broken on the card. The pressed button stays marked, and its tooltip shows the date of the report. Clicking the other button replaces the report.

The hub keeps one current report per router, strategy and network each week. A report counts for the network the hub sees the router on, so it shapes the score that routers on the same ISP and in the same country see first, see Reading the score. On an edited set the buttons are disabled, because a report would not describe the published strategy. Reapply restores the published strategy and enables them again, see Updating and reapplying. A report made while no hub answers is saved and goes out with the next sync. The status line on the Community page shows how many reports are waiting. They are kept for 30 days.

Report on a card or in Details opens a complaint, with a reason of up to 500 characters. Complaints are for: a strategy that does not do what the title says; targets the set has no reason to cover, such as a regexp: pattern under a narrow title; a pin that points at an address that does not belong to the site; a duplicate, or spam. A set that does not work on this network gets a Broken report, not a complaint. Three complaints about one version, from routers on different networks, take it out of the catalogue without waiting for a moderator. A complaint made while no hub answers waits for the next sync, like a report.

The hub accepts a limited number of shared sets, reports and complaints from one router a day. Some limits count per network, so a router new to the hub can be refused because other new routers on the same network came first that day. The hub operator sets the limits. A record over a limit is refused with a message that names the limit and when it resets. Reports and complaints are saved and go out with a later sync. A shared set is not saved, and has to be published again once the limit resets.

Message Meaning Apply the set first; reports are accepted only for sets in use. The set is not applied on this router. Report saved; it goes out with the next sync. No hub answered, or a limit was reached. The report waits in the queue. Could not send the report: ... The report was not sent. The message names the reason, such as a key the moderators banned.

b4hub is the service behind hub.b4core.app. It keeps the catalogue, accepts what routers send, signs what it publishes and serves the moderation console. It is a separate binary from b4, released on its own, and never runs on a router. A hub of its own A mirror Command b4hub serve b4hub mirror Catalogue Built from the sets its moderators approve, signed with its own key Copied from an upstream hub, with the upstream signature Records from routers Stored and counted, with a database and the console Checked and passed on upstream What routers need Its address and key id, entered by hand Nothing, once the upstream hub approves the mirror A hub of its own is a second catalogue, with its own sets and scores. A mirror serves the same catalogue at another address, for networks where the hub does not answer. Hub mirrors on the router has nothing to do with update mirrors.
documents.s: Hosting a hub or a mirror

documents.t: One static binary with the console embedded. Every command takes --data, the directory that holds everything the service owns. Command What it does b4hub keygen Creates the signing key and prints its key id. Refuses to overwrite an existing one b4hub serve Runs a hub: the catalogue builder, the endpoints routers use and the console b4hub mirror Runs a mirror of another hub b4hub build Builds and signs the catalogue once, then exits b4hub moderate Moderates from the command line, see Without the console b4hub version Prints the hub version and the b4 source it was built from Flag Variable Default --data B4HUB_DATA data --listen B4HUB_LISTEN 127.0.0.1:7100 --public-url B4HUB_PUBLIC_URL empty --geosite-url, --geoip-url B4HUB_GEOSITE_URL, B4HUB_GEOIP_URL the v2ray-rules-dat and b4geoip releases --upstream B4HUB_UPSTREAM empty, required by mirror --upstream-key B4HUB_UPSTREAM_KEY empty: the key built into b4 --trusted-proxies B4HUB_TRUSTED_PROXIES empty none B4HUB_ADMIN_PASSWORD empty: the console is closed none B4HUB_TELEGRAM_TOKEN, B4HUB_TELEGRAM_CHAT, B4HUB_WEBHOOK_URL, B4HUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET empty, see Notifications --new-epoch, --revoke, --new-database, --announce, --refresh and --queue-limit exist on the command line only. The data directory holds hub.key (the signing key), hub.db (the SQLite store), secret, blobs/ (payload files), public/ (the signed files routers download) and geo/. warning b4hub speaks plain HTTP and expects a reverse proxy for TLS, so it listens on loopback by default. The b4hub repository publishes a deployment bundle with an nginx vhost, a systemd unit and a Compose file. Routers use /b4/health and the paths under /b4/hub/. The console is at /admin.

b4hub keygen --data /var/lib/b4hub B4HUB_ADMIN_PASSWORD=... b4hub serve --data /var/lib/b4hub \ --listen 127.0.0.1:7100 --public-url https://hub.example.org keygen prints the key id, the only thing that identifies the hub to a router. The key cannot be rotated. --public-url is the address routers reach, which the hub announces in its manifest. The console password comes from the environment only. Without it, the console refuses every sign-in, and b4hub moderate is the only way to moderate. A new hub starts with an empty catalogue: nothing is published until a moderator approves it.

On the router, under Settings > Integrations > Community Hub: Enter the hub's base URL in Hub mirrors. Enter the key id in Hub public key. Save the settings, then click Sync now. Both fields are needed. With the key alone, the router keeps syncing from hub.b4core.app and refuses its catalogue for the wrong signature. The address must be https://. Plain http:// is accepted only for localhost and for loopback, private and link-local addresses, and an address b4 does not accept is dropped without a message. A wrong key fails every sync with "manifest is not signed by a trusted key".

A build runs within about 10 seconds of a moderation action, and at least once a day. The signed manifest is valid for 14 days. Routers that hear from no hub for that long mark their copy expired and keep running the sets they applied. Routers accept only a manifest newer than theirs: a higher epoch, or the same epoch and a higher sequence number. The hub refuses a build that would not be newer than the catalogue in public/ or the one an approved mirror serves, and the build history gives the reason. A database that has never published refuses to publish over an existing catalogue, or to sign an empty one with a key built into b4. That is what serve with the production key on the wrong data directory looks like. --new-database on serve or build confirms that a new database is intended.

A record counts for the ASN and country of the address it comes from. The hub looks them up over DNS, so it needs working outbound DNS. Behind a reverse proxy, the hub sees the proxy's address, unless the proxy is on loopback or listed in --trusted-proxies as an address or a CIDR. With an untrusted proxy, every record counts for the proxy, and all routers share the per-network limits. A mirror with its own key, on b4hub 1.3.0 or newer, signs the records it forwards. When the mirror is approved and its clock is within 10 minutes of the hub's, such a record is stored without a network. A vote then counts only worldwide, at reduced weight, and a complaint never counts toward the automatic hide. The mirror's address gets 10 times the per-network request limit and 20 times the new-key limit. Any other record from a mirror counts for the mirror's own address.
documents.s: The network a contribution is attributed to

documents.t: b4hub mirror --data /var/lib/b4hub-mirror \ --upstream https://hub.b4core.app \ --listen 127.0.0.1:7101 The mirror checks the upstream manifest every five minutes, or at the interval set with --refresh. It copies a newer catalogue and the payload files it lacks, verifies the signature, sizes and hashes, and serves them unchanged. A failed check keeps the previous copy. With the upstream down, the mirror keeps serving the last catalogue it copied. A mirror of a self-hosted hub needs --upstream-key with that hub's key id. Without it, the mirror trusts only the built-in key of hub.b4core.app. The page at / of a mirror shows what it holds and when it last checked the upstream. A mirror cannot alter what it serves. Routers verify the hub's signature and every hash and reject a changed byte. A manifest or a catalogue that fails the check sends them to their next address.

Routers learn mirrors from the signed manifest of the hub, up to 32 of them. They try them after the addresses entered by hand and the built-in one. A mirror gets into the manifest by announcing itself: b4hub keygen --data /var/lib/b4hub-mirror b4hub mirror --data /var/lib/b4hub-mirror \ --upstream https://hub.b4core.app \ --public-url https://mirror.example.org --announce --announce needs the mirror's own key and --public-url, the address being announced. That address follows the rules of a router's hub address. The announcement is sent at start and daily, and arrives at the hub as pending. The mirror is advertised only after a moderator approves it on the Mirrors page. Announcing again never changes a decision. An announcement signed by a key other than the one the decision was made for is refused with mirror_key_mismatch. The hub checks every approved mirror every 10 minutes: /b4/health must answer ok, and the manifest must verify against the hub's key. A mirror stays listed while a check passed in the last 24 hours.

A mirror passes shared sets, reports and complaints on to the hub and returns the hub's answer. It refuses a record with a bad signature itself. One client network, a /24 for IPv4 or a /48 for IPv6, may send up to 600 records an hour. While the upstream does not answer, reports and complaints wait in the mirror's queue, and a shared set is refused with 502 hub_unreachable. The queue holds up to --queue-limit records, 5,000 by default, with at most 200 a day from one client network and 40 a day from one key. A record over a limit stays in the router's own queue. Behind a proxy that --trusted-proxies does not name, all routers share the limits of one client, and the mirror logs a warning. A mirror does not serve /b4/hub/v1/network, so a router that syncs only through mirrors takes its network from the DPI Detector.
They are separate processes and deployments: nothing merges two catalogues, and a router trusts one hub key at a time. On one machine they need two data directories and two listen addresses.
documents.s: A hub and a mirror on one host

documents.t: The data directory moves as a unit: hub.key, hub.db, secret, blobs/ and public/ belong together. danger secret keys the HMAC that stands for every contributor's key in the database, and it is created silently when it is missing. A database restored without its original secret recognises nobody: bans, trust marks, the authorship of sets and the de-duplication of reports all come apart. Restoring an older database rolls the epoch and sequence number back. Routers refuse a catalogue older than theirs, and the hub refuses to build one while public/ or an approved mirror holds a newer one. Start a new epoch on the console's Catalogue page, or b4hub build --new-epoch --data <dir>, publishes the restored database. A lost hub.key cannot be replaced from the hub's side. Every router pointed at the hub then needs a new key id entered by hand.

Every version of every set waits for a moderator before it reaches the catalogue, and the console is where that decision is made. It is part of b4hub, served at /admin on the hub's address, in English and Russian. A mirror has no console, see Hosting a hub or a mirror. The console names two things differently from the router: a vote here is a Works or Broken report on the router, and a report here is a complaint.

The password is B4HUB_ADMIN_PASSWORD from the service environment. There are no accounts or roles: whoever has the password is a moderator. A session lasts seven days, and changing the password ends every open session. An address gets ten sign-in attempts in 15 minutes. The session cookie is marked secure when the request carries X-Forwarded-Proto: https, which the reverse proxy is expected to set. Without the password, every sign-in is refused, and b4hub moderate is the only way to moderate, see Without the console.

A decision changes the store at once. The catalogue routers download is rebuilt in the background within about 10 seconds, so a burst of decisions ends in one build. A failed build does not undo a decision: routers keep the previous catalogue until a build succeeds. Health on the Overview page lists what needs attention, each item with a link: a failed build, a manifest about to expire, a version pending for over 72 hours, a failing mirror or open reports. The menu counts pending versions, listed sets that need attention, pending mirrors and open reports.

One card per pending version, oldest first, laid out like a set card on the router. The strip across the top lights the parts the set configures: Target, Split, Fake, Route or Block, and DNS. A click on a part opens its settings. The tooltip of the line under the title gives the network the upload came from. The author is a 16-character HMAC of the contributor's key under the hub's secret. The key itself is never stored. The version's tooltip says what approving would do, such as New version of a set listed as vN. A version Older than the listed vN is outlined in orange: approving it changes nothing in the catalogue. Marks under the targets point at what needs a closer look: Mark Meaning blocks traffic, pins addresses, categories only, pattern match, needs payload What the set does, explained in each tooltip. blocks traffic is red; categories only and pattern match are orange similar sets: N The hub holds sets with the same targets, strategy, domains, title or author. Orange for a likely duplicate author banned, set withdrawn The version stays out of the catalogue even when approved edited, open reports: N A moderator changed the version, or reports wait on it A click on the card opens the set's panel at this version, with everything it holds. Compare with listed vN in the card's menu shows the difference from the listed version.

Action Reason Effect Approve none The version becomes active and is listed at the next build Reject required The version is refused, and the reason is recorded Hide optional The version leaves the catalogue at the next build Edit none Opens the editor, see Editing a pending version Ban uploader optional See Banning a key Every dialog states the effect on the catalogue before anything changes. Hiding a listed version lists the newest older active version instead, unless Also withdraw the whole set is ticked. Open reports on the version are closed with the decision, unless Keep the open reports open is ticked. Reject as duplicate fills the reason with the set that is duplicated. A rejection is a verdict on a submission. Its reason stays in the console: the author's router only sees that the set is not in the catalogue. Hiding takes a version out of circulation, and a hidden version still counts as a duplicate of later shares with the same strategy. A checkbox on each card, or Select all, applies one decision to up to 200 versions at once. Each reason dialog offers the reasons saved for that action, and Save as a preset keeps a typed one.

A submission with a good strategy and flawed targets can be corrected instead of rejected. The editor holds the title, the description, a Moderator note visible in the console only, and one field per kind of target. Show the full set JSON edits everything else the set carries. The router's Publish to hub sends no description, and one can be written here. Check runs the result through the checks of a fresh share. A change to the targets, title or description keeps the fingerprint, so the recorded votes still count. A change to the strategy changes the fingerprint and drops the votes for this version, and the published set no longer matches the author's copy. A result that duplicates a set the hub holds is refused. Warnings appear under the fields they concern, such as private domains, a /0 range or a dropped pin. b4 has no wildcards, and a plain entry covers every subdomain. Under Domains, the editor flags four mistakes, and Apply suggestions fixes them in one step: Check Example Suggestion Entry that never matches *.example.com example.com www. entry with no apex www.example.com alone example.com, which covers both Repeated entry Example.com. after example.com Drop it Entry already covered cdn.example.com beside example.com Drop it Save keeps the version pending, and Save and approve approves it at once. Both need a check of the current content that found a change and no duplicate. The received set is kept, so the card and the panel show what changed.
Edit title on a version outside the queue changes its title and description and nothing else. Routers see no new version, the votes keep counting, and new users get the new title from the next build.
documents.s: Editing the text of a listed version

documents.t: Five tabs hold what was decided: Listed, the version of each set in the catalogue; Superseded, older approved versions; Withheld, sets withdrawn or by a banned author; Hidden and Rejected, with their reasons. Versions hidden by reports wait on Hidden for a review. The cards add the score routers got in the last build: green from 70%, orange from 40%, red below. next: follows it when the next build changes the score. On Listed, Needs attention keeps the sets with a mark that routers never see: Mark When low score At least 3 weighted votes and a score under 30% stale No vote for 60 days, and almost no weight left under 50% Enough independent votes to show a score, and it is under 50% open reports The listed version has open reports A card opens the set's panel with every version, its votes and its History. A hidden version can be restored there, and a rejected one approved after all. Withdraw set in the panel takes the whole set out of the catalogue at the next build, and Reinstate brings back exactly what was listed. A new version of a withdrawn set still enters the queue. Delete permanently removes the set with its versions, votes, reports and unused payload files, once the set id is typed in. It is meant for an entry that should never have existed. Routers that applied the set keep their copy.

One row per contributor, by HMAC, with its activity and last network. The search also takes the key id a router shows under Author identity. Operator notes attach a name shown in place of the HMAC, a note and a tag. The tag staff is a label only. The tag test stops the key's votes and reports from counting, and leaves its activity out of the statistics. Trust stops counting the key against the per-key daily limits; its sets still wait for a moderator, and the per-network limits still apply. Untrust reverses it.

A ban is a reversible quarantine. From the moment it is set: every new record signed by the key is refused; at the next build, its sets leave the catalogue for the Withheld tab; its votes stop counting, and its reports stop counting toward the automatic hide; its pending versions can be approved only with a second confirmation, and stay out of the catalogue. Nothing is deleted, and Unban restores it all at the next build. The ban dialog counts what is affected, and names the mirrors the key announced. A ban leaves them announced; rejecting them on the Mirrors page takes them off.

Every hub that announced itself as a mirror of this one, pending first, with the key that announced it. Status Meaning pending Waiting for a decision rejected Never announced. The tooltip gives the reason announced Approved and in the manifest joining, leaving Joins or leaves the manifest at the next build kept Failing, and kept in the manifest while no mirror passes its check not announced Approved, and joins the manifest after its next passing check Approve runs a health check at once, and the mirror is listed once one passes. Reject needs a reason, and the mirror is never announced. Remove forgets the mirror, which can then announce itself again. Check now and Check all run the health check on demand, and the tooltip of a failed check names the step that failed. Serves compares the mirror's catalogue with this hub's: current, behind by some builds, stale, or ahead of this hub.
Votes lists every vote with the weight it carries, filtered by kind, ASN or Country. A vote that does not count says why, for example that its key is banned or tagged test.

Votes count per strategy, in three cells: the ASN and the country the hub saw the vote come from, and worldwide. Vote Weight Works +1 Broken -1 The publication itself, as a works vote by the author +1 A vote without a known network, such as one relayed by an approved mirror a quarter of the above A vote from a key first seen less than a week ago a quarter of the above The two reductions multiply. Every vote loses half its weight every two weeks. The score is (works + 1) / (all + 2). A router uses a cell once at least two devices voted in it with a total weight of at least one. The hub also defines capped weights for automated votes from the DPI detector, the watchdog and Discovery, which b4 does not send yet.

Reports is the inbox of complaints. A report is open until a moderator marks it dismissed or handled, and Reopen returns it. Hiding, rejecting, restoring and withdrawing close the open reports of what they touch. A listed version is hidden automatically once three open reports against it come from independent keys and networks. Only reports with a known network count, from keys neither banned nor tagged test. Restoring a version dismisses its open reports, so the count starts again.

The page shows the published files, the mirrors and revoked keys the manifest lists, and Build history: every build, why it ran, its result and what it changed. Operation What it does Build now Builds from the store even when nothing changed Start a new epoch Resets the sequence number. Every router treats the new epoch as newer and downloads the catalogue again Revoke a hub signing key Adds a key id to the list every manifest carries. Routers stop trusting anything signed with it A build that would not be newer than the published catalogue, or than one an approved mirror serves, is refused. That follows a restore from an older backup, and a new epoch publishes it, see Keeping the data. Otherwise, a new epoch only makes every router download again. danger Routers keep a revocation forever. The hub refuses to revoke its own signing key, and revoking the key built into b4 needs a separate confirmation, because it cuts off every router that trusts that key. Revoking names the signing key of a hub or a mirror and reaches every router. Banning names a contributor and affects only this hub.

Statistics shows activity per UTC day, the spread of published scores and where votes come from. Audit log records every action with its time, actor, target, reason and changed fields. The actor is console, password login, command line or automatic.

Six limits apply from the next request: Limit Per Default Shares per key day 5 Votes per key day 20 Reports per key day 20 Mirror announcements per key day 48 New keys per network day 5 Requests per network hour 2000 A day is the UTC day and an hour the clock hour. The counters live in memory and start over when the service restarts. A network is the sender's /24, or /48 for IPv6. A refused record or a duplicate share does not spend the quota. What a router shows at a limit is described under Limits. Saved reasons edits the preset reasons of each decision dialog.

The hub sends a digest of new events to a Telegram chat, a webhook, or both. Telegram needs a bot token and a chat id: a number, or @name of a public channel, with the bot a member of the chat. A supergroup, a forum and a channel have a chat id of -(1000000000000 + n), where n is the number in a t.me/c/ link, so such an id starts with -100. A webhook needs a URL, https:// or plain http:// to a loopback or private address, and an optional signing secret. B4HUB_TELEGRAM_TOKEN, B4HUB_TELEGRAM_CHAT, B4HUB_WEBHOOK_URL and B4HUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET in the service environment override the console, which then shows the field read-only. Values entered in the console are stored encrypted with a key derived from secret. The events are new sets in the queue, reports, versions hidden by reports, failed builds and new mirrors. New sets and reports are selected until the settings are first saved. The first event after a quiet period goes out at once, and later ones at most once per digest interval: 60 seconds by default, from 30 to 3600. A failed delivery is retried with a growing delay, up to 30 minutes. Send a test checks a saved channel. The webhook receives a POST with a JSON body: { "hub": "https://hub.example", "sent_at": "2026-09-27T12:41:15Z", "counts": { "share": 2, "report": 1 }, "events": [ { "kind": "share", "at": "2026-09-27T12:40:58Z", "set_id": "01J9...", "version": 1, "title": "Example", "author": "70837b639d58b777", "asn": "12389", "country": "RU", "url": "https://hub.example/admin/sets/01J9.../v/1" } ], "more": 0, "console": "https://hub.example/admin/queue" } Every request carries X-B4hub-Timestamp, the Unix time of the send. With a secret set, it also carries X-B4hub-Signature: sha256=<hex>: the HMAC-SHA256, under the secret, of the timestamp, a dot and the raw body. Redirects are not followed, and any status outside 2xx is a failure.

b4hub moderate does from the command line what the console does, with the same checks and audit entries. It opens the database directly while the service runs. Every change leaves a build request that b4hub serve picks up within about 10 seconds. Commands What they do list, approve, reject, hide, restore The queue and the version decisions. A set is named as <id> or <id>/<version>. Several can be given at once, and approve is all or nothing withdraw, reinstate, delete Whole sets. delete needs --confirm <id> ban, unban, trust, untrust Keys, named by their HMAC reports, dismiss-report, resolve-report, reopen-report The report inbox mirrors, approve-mirror, reject-mirror, remove-mirror, check-mirror Mirrors status, builds, epoch, revoke Publishing, the build history, a new epoch, and revoking a hub signing key with --confirm <key_id> audit The audit log Editing a version, key notes and tags, saved reasons, notifications and the limits are in the console only.

A set that works can be published to the Community Hub. Other b4 users find it on their Community page once a moderator approves it. b4 publishes the set as a shared set: the strategy and the targets, without anything tied to this router.

The Community Hub is on, see Switching it on. The set is saved. Unsaved changes are not published. The set was tested on the targets it lists. A domain it was never tried on collects Broken reports. A set that handles only calls has no targets and is tested with a call through it.

Open the set and go to the Import/Export tab. In Share with other b4 users, click Prepare shared set. Read Check before sharing and Left out of the shared set, and correct the set where needed. Click Publish to hub.

Prepare shared set shows what is sent. Check before sharing lists what deserves a second look, such as domains that look private to this network or pins everyone importing the set will use. Left out of the shared set lists every dropped setting with the reason. Routing to a proxy or an interface, device filters, escalation and the DNS server address are always dropped, see What leaves the router. The JSON below, with Copy and Download, hands the set over directly. The hub refuses a set without targets, except one that handles only calls. Such a set is published with its Which calls choice and its UDP ports. The published title is the set's name. The router sends no description, and a moderator can add one on the hub.

The section shows the id the hub gave the set and its status, pending moderation. The set appears in the catalogue, for other users and for this router, once a moderator approves it and the router syncs. There is no notification of the decision. Until then, Open in Community opens Set details with a note that the set is not in the catalogue. The published set is now linked to the hub set, like an applied one: its card on the Sets page shows Community set. A version that a moderator hides later leaves the catalogue, and routers that applied it keep it.

After the strategy of a published set changes, the button reads Publish as new version. Publishing then adds the next version to the same hub set, and routers that applied the previous one see Update to version N. When the original set was published by someone else, the hub creates a new set instead. A publication whose strategy and targets match a version the hub already holds is not stored. The hub names that set, and the upload counts as a Works report for it. For a set that handles only calls, the Which calls choice and the UDP ports count as its targets, both for new versions and for duplicates.

Every record the router sends to the hub is signed with its author key. The hub knows the router by this key: new versions of a set can be published only under the key that published it, and the moderators can trust or ban the key. The catalogue shows an author label derived from the key, never the key itself. The key is created on first use and kept in .hub/ in the configuration directory. A backup made under Settings > System > Backup does not include it. A router restored from a backup starts with a new key, and the hub gives a key it first saw less than a week ago less weight in the scores. Settings > Integrations > Community Hub > Author identity shows the key and two actions: Show recovery code shows the code the key is rebuilt from. Anyone with the code can publish and report as this author, so the code is kept private. Restore from code replaces this router's key with the one the code describes. The sets published under it can then get new versions from this router.

Message Meaning Linked to community set ... nothing to publish. The set is linked to a hub set, and its strategy has not changed since. The hub refused the set: ... The message names the reason, such as a set without targets that does not handle only calls, or the daily limit, see Limits.
The terms below appear throughout the web interface. Each section links to the page that covers it in full.
A set ties a list of targets to what b4 does with their traffic. b4 changes nothing until a set targets sites. Sets are created on the Sets page or from a Discovery result, see Sets.

Targets decide which traffic a set applies to: domains, IP addresses and ranges, GeoSite and GeoIP categories, ASNs and source devices. They are edited on the set's Targets tab, see Targets. How sets match traffic explains which set handles a connection that several sets match.

A strategy is the set of packet changes a bypass set makes, such as splitting a request into pieces or sending fake packets ahead of it. It is configured on the set's TCP and UDP tabs, see TCP. Discovery tests strategies and suggests the one that loaded the sites.

The dashboard shows each set's kind. Enable Routing and Routing mode on the set's DNS & Routing tab decide it. Kind Setting What the set does Bypass Enable Routing off Applies its strategy to its traffic. See Unblocking a site Route Network interface Sends its traffic out through another interface, such as a VPN. See Routing sites through a VPN or another interface Proxy Upstream SOCKS5 proxy or Telegram over WebSocket (built-in) Hands its traffic to a SOCKS5 proxy, or to b4's Telegram bridge. See Sending sites through a SOCKS5 proxy Block Block (blackhole) Stops its traffic, for every device and for the router itself. See Blocking ads and sites A proxy set applies no strategy, and neither does a route set whose interface is a tunnel such as a VPN: the tunnel or the proxy carries the traffic to the site. A set routed to a plain interface, such as a second uplink, keeps its strategy, see Network interface.

Discovery tests b4's strategies against sites that do not open. It turns the strategy that loaded them into a new set, or writes it into an existing one. It is the usual way to make a first set, see First steps and Discovery.

The watchdog fetches a set's pages on a schedule. When they keep failing, it runs Discovery for the set and writes the new strategy into it. It is turned on under Settings > Discovery, and for each set with Keep this set working with the watchdog on the set's Discovery tab. See Watchdog.

Escalation moves a site to a backup set when its own set keeps failing to reach it, and tries the original set again after a while. The backup can use another strategy, a VPN or a proxy. The watchdog repairs a whole set on a schedule, while escalation reacts to the failing connections of one site. It is set up on the set's Escalation tab, see Escalation.

Community sets are sets that other b4 users published to the Community Hub. The Community page lists them, applies one in one step, and collects reports on whether it works. An applied set is a normal set marked Community set. The page appears once Enable Community Hub is on under Settings > Integrations, see Community.

The packet engine is how traffic reaches b4: NFQUEUE, the default, has firewall rules hand packets to b4. TUN interface routes the traffic through a virtual interface instead. It is the alternative on kernels without the NFQUEUE modules. Either way, b4 reads only the first packets of each connection. The engine is chosen under Settings > Core > Packet Engine and changes after a restart, see Packet engine. When the engine does not start, the dashboard shows the error and offers the other engine.

The Traffic page shows the connections b4 inspects as they happen: the protocol, the domain, the destination, the device and the set that matched. It shows whether a site's connections reach a set, and adds domains, addresses and networks to sets. DNS for sets uses it to check DNS. b4 sees only the first packets of each connection, up to the per-connection limits under Settings > Core > Packet Engine. One connection therefore gives several entries, and the packet counts say nothing about speed or volume. DNS queries that match a set appear too, with what b4 did with each, while Log Level is Info or more detailed. A connection that a proxy set sends to its upstream appears once. The page opens in Aggregated mode. Raw feed in the top right corner shows single packets instead.

Packets are grouped by device, protocol and domain, and a packet without a domain by its destination address. The groups build up while the page is open. Leaving the page, switching to Raw feed or clearing starts them over. Column Shows Protocol TCP or UDP Domain The domain from the handshake or (no domain), the TLS version (1.2, 1.3) and the labels. A domain outside every set has a + button, see Adding domains to sets Destination The latest destination address, +N when there were several, and its ASN Set The set matched by domain, and the set matched by IP when it is another one Source The device, see Devices Activity Packets per second over the last minute Packets The number of packets in the group Seen Time since the latest packet A click on a row opens the Detail panel: activity, packet count, the time from the first packet to the last, the source, every destination address of the group and the matched sets. For a domain outside every set it also has Add domain to a set. Providers may block TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 differently, and a set can be limited to one TLS version on its Targets tab.

Control Effect Filter field Keeps the matching rows, see Filter 30s, 1m, 5m, 15m, All Shows the groups with packets within that period. 1m is the default Unmatched only Keeps only the groups no set matched Domains only / All packets See Domains only and all packets Trash can Clear Packets, see Pausing and clearing The dashboard opens this page with Unmatched only on from Domains not in any set on Activity, and with a device selected from Blocked, both with the period at All.

The Devices panel on the left lists the sources seen within the period, with the time since the latest packet, the activity and the packet count. A click on a device limits the list to its groups, and All devices removes the selection. Hide devices collapses the panel. Sort devices orders it By name, the default, By latest activity or By packet count. A device is identified by its MAC address. When the MAC is unknown, as for a device behind another router, the source shows by its IP address. Aliases from the device filtering table are always shown. With device filtering or vendor lookup turned on there, the names of discovered devices are used too, and the router's own addresses show as Router.

Raw feed shows the latest 1000 packets one by one, the newest at the bottom. Column Shows Time The time of the packet Protocol TCP or UDP and the labels Set The set matched by IP, or by domain when no set matched by IP Domain The TLS version and the domain. A domain outside every set has a + button Source The device name, or the source IP address and port Destination The destination address and port, the ASN, and a + button for an address outside every set

Labels mark special cases: next to the domain in Aggregated mode, and next to the protocol in the raw feed and in the Detail panel. Label Meaning dup The packet was duplicated, see Packet duplication ip The destination was found blocked by IP. An outlined label means the address was already in the cache of blocked addresses ban The destination is a banned address, and b4 reset the connection or, for QUIC, refused it block A block set blocked the packet voice A call packet passed through untouched: by a set with Calls on Pass call setup, or by a set that handles only calls, as a later packet of a call the set took. The packet such a set takes itself carries no voice label and shows that set in the Set column proxy The connection came through b4's SOCKS5 proxy Telegram icon A connection of b4's MTProto proxy, with the secret's name Telegram icon with Telegram bridge A connection relayed by Telegram over WebSocket doh, forward, pin, sinkhole and others What b4 did with a DNS query, see DNS for sets

The switch in the control bar applies to both modes. Mode Shows Domains only Packets with a recognised domain. The default All packets Every inspected packet, also the TCP handshake before the ClientHello, connections without SNI and traffic to addresses that have no name

The filter field works in both modes. + joins conditions, and all of them must hold. ! before a condition excludes what it matches. field:value checks one field. Several conditions on the same field hold when any of them matches. An empty value, such as set:, matches an empty field. A word without a field is looked up in every field. Matching ignores case and looks for a substring. The fields of both modes are protocol, domain, destination, tls, flags, asn and device (also alias). set works only in Aggregated mode, source only in the raw feed. Filter Shows protocol:udp UDP packets domain:youtube Packets with "youtube" in the domain protocol:tcp+!domain:google.com TCP packets, except google.com domains asn:AS13335 Destinations in AS13335 (Cloudflare) whose ASN has been looked up flags:dns DNS queries and what b4 did with them set: Groups that no set matched

The + button next to a domain opens Add Domain to Manual List. Pick the domain or one of its parent domains, listed from the most specific to the broadest. For rr1---sn-ab5l6ne7.googlevideo.com these are the name itself and googlevideo.com. Under Target Set, choose one of the enabled sets, or Create New Set and enter a Set Name. Click Add Domain. A domain in a set covers its subdomains too. A service that serves content from many subdomains, such as YouTube or a CDN, is covered by its parent domain, such as googlevideo.com.

The + button next to a destination address, and in the raw feed a click on the address itself, opens Add to a set. b4 looks up which network announces the address, through RIPEstat. The dialog then shows the address, the announced prefix that covers it and the network, such as AS15169 Google LLC. When several networks announce the prefix, one of them is picked in the dialog. A private address has no network. A failed lookup can be repeated with Retry, and the address can be added either way.
documents.s: Adding addresses and networks to sets

documents.t: Choice What goes into the set Single IP The address alone, as /32, or /128 for IPv6. The default Announced prefix that covers this address The prefix, such as 142.250.0.0/15, when it is known and wider than the address A wider range The address with a mask such as /24 or /16, for IPv6 /64 or /48, saved as its network: 142.250.120.139/24 becomes 142.250.120.0/24 The whole network The ASN itself, see ASN. b4 fetches its prefixes and keeps them up to date daily For the whole network, the dialog shows the ASN's prefix count and roughly how many IPv4 addresses it holds, and warns about a large network as the set editor does. The choice is unavailable when the set already has that ASN. An ASN whose prefixes are not known yet is added anyway, and b4 fetches them in the background. The set is chosen under Target Set, as in the domain dialog, and the confirm button names what is added, such as Add AS15169. With an IPInfo token on the Settings > Integrations tab, Enrich with IPInfo shows the address's hostname, organization and location from ipinfo.io, and the hostname can be added to a set's domains. The DPI Detector opens the same dialog from its hosting and CDN results, with the network of the affected provider already chosen.

The network icon next to a destination address looks up its network without opening the dialog. b4 finds the ASN that announces the address and fetches its prefixes into its ASN cache. Addresses of that network then carry a label such as AS15169 Google LLC, and the asn: filter finds them. Every browser sees the same labels, and the ASNs that sets target label their addresses too. The cross on a label deletes that ASN from the cache. An ASN that a set still targets is not deleted: b4 names the sets that use it, and the label stays.

The round button in the bottom right corner pauses and resumes the stream. While it is paused, new packets are not collected. Clear Packets, the trash can in the control bar, removes the collected packets, groups and devices. The number next to Traffic in the side menu counts the packets that matched a set. A click on Traffic in the menu, or clearing the packets, resets it, and it does not grow while the stream is paused.

The dashboard is the first page of the web interface. It shows whether b4 is running, whether the sets match traffic, and what needs attention. The figures update every second. Some panels appear only when they have something to show, such as Blocked while a block set is enabled.

The strip at the top shows the state of the service. Cell Shows Status Running in normal operation. Engine failed means b4 is up but does not process traffic, see below. Engine How b4 captures traffic, NFQUEUE or TUN, and the number of worker threads. Firewall The firewall b4 works with, iptables or nftables. restored N times means something on the router removed b4's rules and b4 put them back. Some router firmware does this routinely, and it is not an error. Set up externally means Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup is on, so b4 installs no rules of its own. Uptime, b4 RAM, CPU How long b4 has been running and what it uses. Hovering a cell shows the peaks. When the live updates stop, a line under the strip says so and the panels dim. The page reconnects by itself, and Retry reconnects at once. After Session expired - sign in again, Sign in opens the login page.

When the packet engine fails to start, the web interface keeps working, but traffic passes through the router untouched: no set applies. A card under the strip shows the error. b4 retries by itself up to three times, and the card shows when the next retry is. Switch to TUN or Switch to NFQUEUE tries the other capture mode, for example TUN when the kernel lacks the modules NFQUEUE needs. Restart b4 starts again once the cause is fixed, such as a missing kernel module. Engine settings opens Settings > Core > Packet Engine.
documents.s: If the packet engine did not start

documents.t: The list appears only when something needs action, errors first. The link on each line opens the place where the problem is fixed. Message Meaning and action Set X: proxy ... unreachable The proxy of a proxy set does not answer: the proxy server is down, or its address on the set's DNS & Routing tab is wrong. Telegram bridge: ... Telegram over WebSocket cannot work. The message names the cause, and Troubleshooting explains each one. Watchdog checks fail for X Some pages of the set stopped opening. The watchdog keeps checking and searches for a new strategy if the failures continue. The watchdog is looking for a working strategy for X A search for the set is waiting or running. No action is needed. The watchdog cannot check X None of the set's pages can be checked, for example because another set handles them. The second line gives the reason. The watchdog gave up on X; its sites may not open Three attempts in a row to find a new strategy failed, and the watchdog stopped searching for this set. Searches resume after Check now on the Watchdog page, or once a check finds every page loading, for example after a manual Discovery run for the set. The watchdog is off, but N sets ask for it Either the watchdog is turned on under Settings > Discovery, or Keep this set working with the watchdog is turned off in those sets. No packets reached b4 in the last N min While devices are in use, this means their traffic is not reaching b4, and no set applies. The link opens the packet engine settings. No packets reached b4 lists the causes and fixes. SOCKS5 server did not start, MTProto server did not start, Web server error That part of b4 did not start. The second line shows the error, for example a port that another program already uses. Web server TLS is not usable, serving plain HTTP instead The certificate or key under Settings > System > Web Server cannot be used, so the web interface runs over plain HTTP. The second line shows the error. Some set targets could not be loaded Some set targets were not loaded. The second line shows the error, and the link opens Sets. b4 was updated on disk; restart to run it Restart runs the new version. b4 skipped the bypass for N packets, b4's packet queue overflowed b4 could not keep up with the traffic for a moment, and some connections got no bypass. The router's connection table is N% full The router is close to its limit of open connections, and new connections may fail. The limit belongs to the router, not to b4. b4 holds N OS threads b4 uses far more threads than normal and may stop. A restart clears the state. For a bug report, goroutines.txt in the log directory holds the details when file logging is on. IPv6 traffic skips all sets The router has IPv6, but b4 handles only IPv4, so connections over IPv6 skip the sets. Enable IPv6 Support under Settings > Core > Packet Engine brings IPv6 into the sets. In TUN mode the message reads TUN mode does not handle IPv6; IPv6 traffic skips b4, because that mode never handles it. The cross on a start failure or on the IPv6 message hides it.

The chart shows how many connections b4 checked each minute: in your sets when a set matched the connection, not in a set otherwise. 1 h and 24 h switch the time window, and Table shows the same numbers as rows. Live traffic opens the Traffic page. Domains not in any set opens the Traffic page with only the connections no set matched: the sites that are not in a set yet. The history is kept in memory and starts over when b4 restarts.

Each TCP connection or UDP flow counts once, when it starts. b4 sees only the first packets of a connection, so the dashboard does not show how long a connection lasted or how much data it carried. Only connections to the ports b4 watches count: 443 and the ports the sets add. Connections count whether they come from devices on the network or from the router itself, and connections through proxy sets count too. DNS queries, Discovery's test connections and devices that device filtering leaves out do not.

One row for each enabled set. A row shows the set's kind (Bypass, Route, Proxy or Block), how many connections it matched in the last hour, and when it last matched. Proxy sets also show their open connections, and upstream down while their proxy fails. Block sets show how many DNS lookups they blocked. A set's name opens it. When a set shows no matches although its sites are in use, the Traffic page shows which set, if any, their connections get. A set that the watchdog keeps working shows its status: Healthy, Failing, Healing, Gave up, Can't check, Not checked yet or Watchdog off. The status opens the set's Discovery tab.

What happened since b4 started, newest first: starts, applied settings, firewall rules restored, strategies the watchdog switched, settings an AI assistant changed over MCP, warnings and errors. Most entries link to the related page. The list is kept in memory and starts over when b4 restarts. The warning TCP port filters cover the source ports of client connections means that b4 passes some connections unprocessed. A set's TCP port filter covers the ports devices pick for their own connections, and on this router b4 tells a device's packets from the server's by their ports. The second line names the ports. A filter below 32768 avoids it, and When b4 tells the direction by port lists the cases.

Top domains lists the names devices connect to most. Top addresses lists connections without a name, such as Telegram apps, voice calls, games and VPN servers. Badges show the sets that matched. + marks a name or an address that no set matched, and adds the domain, or the address, its network or its ASN, to a set. Both lists count from the last reset.
Shown while a host is moved to a backup set because its own set kept failing, see Escalation. Each row shows the host, the set it moved to and when it goes back. Clear sends every host back at once.
Shown while a block set is enabled. Domains lists what was blocked, Devices the devices that tried to reach it. A device opens its traffic.

Shown while IP block detection has banned addresses. Each row shows the address, the domain and set it was caught on, how many times it was caught and the time left. Unban lifts one ban at once, and Clear all lifts every ban.

Shown while the MTProto proxy or Telegram over WebSocket is on. For the proxy, it shows the connected networks, open connections and traffic of each secret. For the bridge, it shows the relayed sessions and failures, and not working when the bridge cannot work. The gear button opens Settings > Telegram.

Customize in the menu at the right end of the status strip switches the panels into edit mode: Drag a panel by its handle to move it, or drop it on another panel to place the two side by side. Drag the border between two panels to change their widths. Click the eye button to hide a panel. Hidden panels are listed in the edit bar, where a click brings one back. Click Done. Reset layout returns to the default. The layout is saved in b4, so every browser shows the same one.

Reset counters in the menu at the right end of the status strip starts the counters from zero. It clears Top domains, Top addresses, the Blocked counts, the count of resets dropped by RST protection and the escalation count. It keeps the Activity history, Recent changes, the uptime, the Telegram figures, the banned addresses and the hosts escalated right now. Clear on Active Escalations sends those back.

The DPI Detector shows what the ISP does to traffic leaving the router. It finds which sites are blocked and how, whether DNS answers are forged, whether long connections to hosting networks are cut, and whether Telegram is reachable. Every site is fetched twice, directly and through b4, so the result shows both the block and whether a set fixes it. Unblocking a site shows where the detector helps. The checks and the target lists come from the dpi-detector project.

Sites to check takes domains or URLs, separated by spaces or new lines. A URL with a path is checked at that path. Without sites, the built-in list is checked. Fill from: fills the field with the built-in list, or with the domains listed by hand under Targets in the enabled sets. What to check offers four scopes: Scope What it answers Default Sites Whether each site loads, how it is blocked, and whether b4 fixes it. On DNS Whether resolvers answer blocked names honestly, whether port 53 is hijacked, and which DoH and DoT servers work. On Hosting and CDN Whether long connections to Hetzner, Cloudflare, Akamai and other networks are cut after the first kilobytes. Off Telegram Whether the datacenters are reachable, and the download and upload speed. Off Advanced holds the rest: Option What it does Default IP family IPv4, IPv6 or both. Shown while the capture engine handles both. With both, a site with an IPv6 address gets a second row. both Parallel checks How many checks run at once. A lower number is easier on a small router. 5 Fetch mode direct and through b4, or direct only. direct and through b4 Also try TLS 1.2 When a site is blocked over TLS 1.3, checks whether TLS 1.2 gets through. On Look for a working SNI on blocked hosting For each network that cuts long connections, tries known whitelisted names as the SNI. Off Run check starts the check, and Stop and keep results ends it early.

The verdict comes first, with the counts of sites blocked by the ISP, fixed by b4 and still blocked. Fix N with Discovery opens Discovery with the still-blocked sites filled in. Copy report copies a plain-text report for an issue or a forum post.

The table has a row per site, with the result Direct, the result Through b4 and the Outcome: Outcome Meaning Works Loads both ways. Fixed by b4 Blocked directly, loads through b4. The row names the set. Still blocked Blocked both ways. The row says whether no set targets the site, the set is disabled, or the set does not help. Broken by b4 Loads directly but not through b4. The matching set does harm. Site-side error The site itself answered with an error, both ways. No address from the resolver The resolver of b4's host gives no address for the site, while DoH does and the site loads at it. The direct result says how a site is blocked: Status Meaning Reset A TCP reset on the TLS handshake. Dropped The TLS handshake is never answered. Unreachable The connection is never established. Throttled The transfer stops after the first kilobytes. Fake DNS The resolver answers with a stub address. The DoH address is shown next to it. No address The resolver gives no address for the name. ISP page A redirect to, or a page from, the ISP. Fake certificate The certificate is substituted. TLS alert, Garbage reply A forged TLS alert, or injected garbage in place of TLS. Refused, Timeout The connection is refused, or nothing answers in time. Gateway The first hop in front of this host answers the connection itself, as a transparent proxy does. Nothing b4 does on this host reaches past it. Sites with Gateway or No address from the resolver have counters of their own and are left out of Fix with Discovery, since no strategy helps them. Names are resolved with the resolver of the host b4 runs on, from its /etc/resolv.conf. Devices on the network may use another resolver, so what the table shows about DNS applies to b4's host. The line above the table names the resolvers used.

The table has a row per resolver, with the resolvers of b4's host first. Latency cells show the fastest answer over UDP, DoH and DoT. Honest compares the resolver's answers for blocked names with the answers of encrypted resolvers: Value Meaning Honest The answers match. Substituted A stub or reserved address where encrypted resolvers give a real one. No answer Ordinary names resolve, while blocked names time out or return an error. Filters NXDOMAIN or an empty answer for blocked names, without a forged address. Port 53 answered by is the network that answered a query sent to the resolver. A network that is neither the provider's own nor a known public resolver marks the row as hijacked. copy DoH URL copies a working DoH server, for a set's DNS redirect.

The table has a row per network, with the number of targets cut and the point of the cut (Drops at). Working SNI, when the search was on, lists names that got through, for a set's fake SNI. Add <ASN> to a set opens the add dialog of the Traffic page with that network chosen.
The panel shows how many datacenters are reachable, and the download and upload speed.

The lists of sites, hosting targets and resolvers are built into b4 and dated. Fetch the project's current lists downloads the current lists from the dpi-detector repository and keeps them next to the configuration. Dead sites and addresses are then replaced without a b4 update. Use the built-in lists goes back to the built-in copy.
Up to fifty runs are kept with their verdict. A run can be opened again, copied as a report or deleted.

Discovery searches for a bypass strategy for the sites named in its field, or for the pages of one set. The result becomes a new set or goes into an existing one. Configured sets keep working during a run. Unblocking a site walks through a first run, and Keeping sets working shows how the watchdog runs Discovery on its own. How Discovery searches explains a run in detail.

Site or URL takes domains or full URLs, separated by commas or new lines. A domain is fetched as https://<domain>/, a URL as given. Local and private addresses are refused. Find a strategy for a set runs Discovery for one set instead and fills the field with the set's Discovery addresses, or with suggestions. A run for a set tests at most five addresses. A set that routes its traffic to a proxy or an interface cannot be picked. When another set handles an address in the field, a warning names that set. Find a strategy in a set card's menu, or on the set editor's Discovery tab, opens this page with the set picked.

The defaults are the usual choice. Option What it does Default Check DNS for tampering Compares each site's address with a trusted resolver's answer, adds a DNS fix for a forged one and looks for alternative addresses. Turning it off shortens the run when DNS is known to be clean. On Trusted DNS server The resolver the DNS check trusts, for this run only. Empty uses the one in Settings. Empty Pinned addresses Hosts-file lines, the address and then its names. Those names are tested through these addresses, and the set keeps them as pinned addresses. Empty Stop at the first strategy that works for every address Shown while a set is picked. Turned off, the search tests every strategy, which takes longer and can find a faster one. On Try community sets first Shown while the Community Hub is on. Tests up to three published sets per site before the built-in strategies. On Try strategies that worked before Winners of earlier runs go first. Forget them clears that list. On Confirm each strategy Fetches in a row a strategy has to pass during the search, 1 to 5. 1 TLS version for the probes Limits the probes, and the created set, to TLS 1.2 or 1.3. Auto IP version for the probes The same for IPv4 and IPv6. Shown while the capture engine handles both. Auto Captured ClientHello as the fake payload Fake packets carry a ClientHello captured under Settings > Payloads. None

Start begins a run through six steps: DNS, Without bypass, Strategies, Tuning, Combining and Confirming. A run that finds a strategy goes on to a seventh step, Page hosts, see Page hosts. A row per site shows what has been found so far, with the quickest strategy yet as Fastest so far. The card at the end can offer another strategy, see Results. Show log opens the log. A run takes from one to ten minutes, depending on the network. Stop and confirm ends the search and confirms what was found, without tuning it. Stop ends a run that has found nothing. Stop now, during the confirmation, ends the run at once and keeps the results unconfirmed. Skip host check ends only the Page hosts step. A run stops when b4 rewrites its DSCP rules during it, for example after a set's new DSCP value is saved. Its results cannot be applied, and the history marks the row stopped: firewall rules changed during the search, run it again. One run is in progress at a time, the searches of the watchdog included. A watchdog search shows on this page but cannot be stopped here.

A run for a set ends with one verdict for the whole set, above Results per address. The set's own strategy is tested first, as Current strategy of the set, and a strategy is confirmed on all addresses together. For a set with its own DSCP value, the probes carry that value, as the set's traffic does, and take the set's route through the router in front of b4. The progress and the results show DSCP <value>, as the set's traffic. The probes of any other run carry the value of Set DSCP under Settings > Core > Firewall while it is on, or none, also to the addresses of such a set. Verdict Meaning and what the card offers one strategy covers every address Apply to <set> writes the strategy into the set, see Writing into an existing set. current strategy works The set's strategy loads every address. For sites that still fail in a browser, the card names the addresses another set handles. It also notes that the browser may use QUIC (HTTP/3), which Discovery does not test, or another IP version than the run, such as IPv6. IP version for the probes sets the version a run tests. covers some addresses Apply to <set> anyway writes the best strategy. Remove them from this set's Discovery addresses drops the uncovered addresses. no bypass needed Every address loads without b4, so these pages cannot show whether the set works. nothing worked The cards below show what happened to each address. stopped before a result Nothing to apply. The set's Discovery tab shows the last run for it.

Every site gets one card, under Results per address in a run for a set. Badge Meaning and next step confirmed 3 of 3, not confirmed A strategy, a DNS fix, an alternative address or removing an ECH key made the site load. The card describes the set it creates and, for a confirmed strategy, lists the page hosts it can add. no bypass needed The site loads without b4. address blocked Connections to every known address fail, so no strategy can help. The site needs a VPN or a proxy. intercepted by the gateway The first hop in front of this host answers the connection itself. b4 has to run on that gateway, or this host has to be excluded from its redirect. When b4 is the router itself, only a proxy helps. does not resolve The name has no address, as with a misspelled domain. link answers 400 The link answers HTTP 400 even without b4. A link to a page or a file the site serves is needed. nothing found No strategy worked. A new run with TLS 1.2 or a captured ClientHello sometimes helps.
