Sites that one strategy loaded share one card and one set. The card offers the strategy that loaded the most sites. Speed does not decide, see Which strategy a card offers. N other strategies worked lists up to twelve other strategies that loaded every site of the card, fastest first, each with Use instead. When the last run to end was started from this page, reloading the page or opening it again within 30 minutes of the end shows its results again. New search clears them in the browser where it is clicked. The history keeps them, also after b4 restarts.

The Page hosts step reads the page of each site with a confirmed strategy and tests the other hosts the page takes its stylesheets, scripts, images and other files from. A host that fails without b4 and loads with the strategy is listed on the card with a checkbox. The ticked hosts are added to the set by exact name when the result is applied. Host marked Ticked by default stylesheet, script, image, media, CSS or preload, with or without tracker that holds the page until it loads Yes in page code, frame, icon, preconnect, base address or redirect No part of <service>: a set of its own fits better, whatever its type. A tracker that belongs to a service, such as googletagmanager.com or connect.facebook.net, gets this note too. No handled by set <set>, whatever its type. Another enabled set already handles the host. No Only the page itself is read. Hosts that its stylesheets and scripts load in turn, or that a script builds while the page runs, are not found. How Discovery searches explains how the hosts are found and tested. The hosts are tested with the card's strategy only, and Use instead opens the dialog without them. In a run for a set, the hosts are on the cards under Results per address, and Apply to <set> on the verdict writes only the strategy. Watchdog searches skip this step.

Apply as a set, Apply in the history and Use instead open one dialog. It previews the set and offers: Create a new set, then Create set: see Creating a set. Write the strategy into an existing set, then Replace strategy: see below. This is the default when the run was for a set or a set lists the site exactly. Add to <set>, which already uses the same strategy, then Add to set: adds the sites to that set. When the set's strategy changed after the dialog opened, nothing is added. Copy JSON copies the set without creating it, in the Import/Export format. Page hosts in the dialog repeats the card's page hosts with their ticks. When a host marked handled by set <set> is ticked, applying moves it out of that set if the set lists it by its exact name, as with a site. Each of the three choices adds the ticked hosts, even when Add <sites> to this set is off, and Copy JSON includes them. A result is applied only to a set whose traffic takes the network path the run tested: the DSCP value of the run's probes, written on the same interfaces. A change to the set's DSCP value, to Set DSCP or to its interface list after the run can change that path. The error then names the difference, and a new run for the set tests the new path. For a few seconds after such a change is saved, while b4 applies its DSCP rules, applying and starting a run are refused.

Which set to change lists the run's set and the enabled sets without routing that already match the site. Another set picks any other set without routing. Only the bypass strategy is written: TCP, fragmentation, fake packets and, when the result uses them, a DNS redirect, pinned addresses and removing ECH keys. The port filter, RST protection, UDP, routing and escalation stay as they are. Use these addresses as the set's discovery URLs also replaces the set's Discovery addresses. When the set does not match the sites, Add <sites> to this set adds them and moves them out of other enabled sets. The dialog warns when another set actually handles a site, since the new strategy has no effect there.

The suggested Set name is the site without its prefix and top-level domain. Match can shorten a single site to a parent domain, so the set also covers its subdomains. A site listed in another enabled set moves into the new one. The new set goes to the top of the list, enabled. It gets a DNS redirect or pinned addresses only for a site that needed them. The tested addresses become its Discovery addresses, so the set can be searched again or watched.

Some blocks hand out an address that refuses every connection, while clients in other regions get addresses that work. With Check DNS for tampering on, Discovery looks for such addresses when every known address of a site fails. The set pins the site's name to up to three addresses that complete a TLS handshake, so devices get those in DNS answers. The pins are fixed at the time of the run. When the block moves, a new run with the DNS check on finds new ones. Watchdog searches skip the DNS check and do not refresh pins.

A site that publishes an ECH key is probed the way a browser with the key connects, so the ClientHello names the key's public name, such as cloudflare-ech.com. The set targets that name as well. When the network drops ClientHellos with ECH and the site loads without it, the card is marked ECH blocked. The result is ECH keys removed: a set that turns on Remove ECH keys from DNS answers and changes no packets. A browser with its own secure DNS still sends ECH, so it needs one of the other strategies listed under the result.

The history keeps the latest result of each site, newest first. Apply creates the set the run built, without a new run. +N page hosts under the strategy counts the page hosts the run offered, and Apply offers them again with the default ticks. Run again repeats the run for the site, or for the set the row came from. Remove from history and Clear history remove one row or all of them. A row expands to the other strategies its run's card listed, up to twelve, fastest first, each with Use instead. Tried marks a strategy that has been applied as a set, also after the set is deleted. via watchdog and via MCP mark runs that the watchdog or an AI assistant over MCP started. Last run log opens the log of the last run, also after a restart, and can download it as a text file.

A set can answer DNS for the domains it targets: send them to another resolver, answer them with fixed addresses, or remove parts of the answers. Names that no set targets go to the resolver the device chose, unchanged. The options are on the set's DNS & Routing tab, under DNS Redirect, see DNS & Routing.

b4 sees DNS that goes to port 53, from the devices on the network and from the router itself. Encrypted DNS that a device sends by itself (DoH, DoT or DoQ) passes b4 unseen, and the sets do not apply to it. The usual sources are secure DNS in a browser such as Chrome or Firefox, Android Private DNS, and a DoH resolver set up on the device. The sets apply to such a device once encrypted DNS is turned off on it. An encrypted forwarder on the router is not a problem, since devices still ask the router on port 53. The interception itself is described in How b4 handles DNS.

A query name matches a set the way a server name does: a domain covers its subdomains, and a domain listed in one set wins over a regexp: entry in another. A block set answers first, then the set's pins, then the set's resolver while Enable DNS Redirect is on. Otherwise the query goes to the device's resolver unchanged. b4 can then remove ECH keys and IPv6 addresses from the answer, see the full sequence.
documents.s: How a set handles a query

documents.t: A set's resolver helps when the provider's DNS answers the set's domains with wrong addresses. Open Sets and open the set. On the DNS & Routing tab, under DNS Redirect, turn on Enable DNS Redirect. Under Resolver type, choose Plain DNS (UDP) and a DNS Server IP, or DNS-over-HTTPS and a DNS-over-HTTPS URL, typed in or picked from the recommended list. Click Save Changes. Resolver type When it fits Plain DNS (UDP) Plain DNS to other servers arrives intact. Fragment DNS Queries splits each query into IP fragments, for DPI that reads the names in DNS queries. DNS-over-HTTPS The provider tampers with plain DNS to other servers too, or the resolver serves only DoH. The queries leave encrypted. Queries from the set's own resolver go on unchanged, so a resolver on the local network can serve a set. A resolver on the router itself has one more condition, see When it does not work. A service that checks the address a connection comes from needs another exit rather than another resolver, see Routing sites through a VPN.
documents.s: Sending a set's domains to another resolver

documents.t: When b4 looks up a set's names itself, for routing, a DSCP value or a proxy upstream, it uses the set's resolver while Enable DNS Redirect is on, and the router's resolver otherwise, see How b4 handles DNS.

When the set's resolver does not answer, b4 answers from the last good reply it holds for the name, or else asks the resolver the device was addressing. Query timeout under Settings > Core > DNS sets how long b4 waits. Fail closed when the resolver is unreachable turns the fallback off. The device then gets an error (SERVFAIL), and the set's names resolve through its resolver or not at all. warning With fail closed on, an unreachable resolver stops every name of the set from resolving, even while the bypass strategy works. On a censored connection, the DoH server itself can get blocked.

A pin answers a name with fixed addresses, with no hosts file to edit on every device. It helps when DNS keeps handing out an address that does not answer. Domain and addresses under Pinned addresses takes hosts file lines, one per address: the address first, then the names it answers for. 157.240.0.174 www.instagram.com 157.240.205.63 scontent.cdninstagram.com scontent-a.cdninstagram.com A pin covers each name and its subdomains. The longest matching entry wins. A pin applies only to a name the set targets. For other names the editor offers Add to this set's domains. Pins work with Enable DNS Redirect off too, and win over the set's resolver. The pins are the whole address answer: a name pinned to IPv4 addresses only gets no IPv6 addresses. In a set without routing, b4 leaves out pinned addresses that do not answer on TCP port 443, checked at start, on save and at the Retest interval (seconds) of IP Block Detection. When none answers, the pins are used anyway.

While Enable IPv6 Support is off, b4 processes IPv4 only, and a site with IPv6 addresses would be reached over IPv6, past every set. b4 therefore removes the IPv6 addresses (AAAA records) from the answers for names a set matches, and the device connects over IPv4. Other names keep their full answers. The switch is Force IPv4 for matched domains on the IPv4 / IPv6 card under Settings > Core > Packet Engine. It is on by default and unused while Enable IPv6 Support is on. A set limited to IPv6 by its IP Version Filter keeps its IPv6 answers. An address the device already has from its cache, a hosts file or its own encrypted DNS still leads over IPv6. Enable IPv6 Support closes that path.

Sites behind some CDNs publish an Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) key in DNS. A browser that gets the key, such as Chrome, sends a ClientHello that names the CDN's shared name instead of the site: cloudflare-ech.com for every Cloudflare site. Where DPI drops such ClientHellos, all these sites stop loading at once. Remove ECH keys from DNS answers, under Encrypted ClientHello (ECH), takes the key out, and the browser sends an ordinary ClientHello naming the site. It works with Enable DNS Redirect off too. The key is removed when: the name asked matches the set, such as steamdb.info listed in the set; the key's public name is a domain the set matches. A set listing cloudflare-ech.com removes the key from every Cloudflare site's answers. While Enable IPv6 Support is off, b4 in NFQUEUE mode also removes the key from answers that arrive over IPv6. A set that uses Source Devices leaves such answers alone, since b4 cannot tell which device they go to. A device added by hand by its IPv6 address is the exception. Discovery proposes such a set, with no packet changes, for a site that loads without ECH but not with it. A key already in a browser's cache is used until it expires.

A set that targets every name sends the DNS of the whole network and of the router to one DoH resolver. Domains listed in other sets keep their own sets' resolvers. Open Sets and click Create Set. On the Import/Export tab, paste the configuration below into Set Configuration JSON and click Import. To use another resolver, change DNS-over-HTTPS URL on the DNS & Routing tab. Click Create Set. { "b4_version": "dev", "name": "all DOH", "tcp": { "dport_filter": "53" }, "udp": { "dport_filter": "53" }, "fragmentation": { "strategy": "none" }, "faking": { "sni": false }, "targets": { "sni_domains": ["regexp:.*"] }, "enabled": true, "dns": { "enabled": true, "doh_url": "https://wikimedia-dns.org/dns-query" } } The set changes no packets, and its port filters of 53 keep it off TLS and QUIC connections. Router host names and .lan names stop resolving, since the public resolver does not know them; pins keep the ones that matter working. When the resolver is unreachable, every name falls back, so a resolver reachable from the connection matters more than its features.
documents.s: Sending every DNS query to DoH

documents.t: Settings > Core > DNS holds the interception of DNS over TCP and the timeouts for all sets. Without Intercept DNS over TCP, a device that retries a query over TCP reaches its own resolver, past the set.

Open Traffic. Enter flags:dns in the filter to keep only DNS queries. Open a site of the set on a device. Each query shows the set that matched it and a label: Label Meaning doh <server>, forward <address> Resolved through the set's DoH or plain DNS server pin, pin empty Answered from the pins, empty when they hold no address of the type asked ipv4 only, no ech IPv6 addresses or the ECH key removed from the answer heal, heal + ipv4 only Unreachable addresses removed or replaced by Heal DNS answers, or banned addresses removed or replaced sinkhole, block A block set answered "does not exist" or dropped the query fallback-cache, fallback-upstream The set's resolver did not answer: the last good reply was used, or the device's resolver answered servfail The set's resolver did not answer and nothing else could, or the set fails closed passthrough, bad target, from target, ipv6 off Passed on unchanged: the set has no resolver, DNS Server IP is not a valid address, the query came from the set's own resolver, or it came over IPv6 while IPv6 support is off escalate <set> Lookups for the name kept failing, and the backup set of Escalation answered The log records the same decisions, as dns-doh->, dns-pin and so on. Both show DNS decisions while Log Level is Info, the default, or more detailed.

What happens Cause and fix A device's lookups never show on the Traffic page The device uses encrypted DNS. Turning off secure DNS in its browser, or Android Private DNS, sends its lookups to the router. The site still goes to the old address The device keeps an answer it already has until the answer expires. servfail, fallback-cache or fallback-upstream The set's resolver is unreachable from this connection. Another resolver, or DoH in place of plain DNS, is the next try. The set's names resolve slowly or not at all, with the set's resolver on the router A resolver on the router, and the router's resolver when a resolver on the network uses it upstream, has to reach its own upstream over DoH or DoT, which b4 does not intercept. A browser still uses ECH, with a resolver on the network that checks DNSSEC, such as BIND or Unbound The resolver gets the original answer on a path b4 does not see: DoT or DoH to its upstream, an interface left out of Capture Interfaces, or TCP while Intercept DNS over TCP is off. With Intercept DNS over TCP on, plain DNS through a captured interface closes these paths, see ECH keys.

On KeeneticOS and some other routers with an older kernel, b4 works on copies of DNS requests and replaces the resolver's reply with the set's answer. The row DNS queries copied, not held (NFLOG) in System Info shows when. The resolver the device asked then still receives every request, and a resolver outside the router has to reply before the device gets the set's answer. Requests that a nat rule moves to another port, or that NAT sends from another source port, get no set handling, see Copied requests.
A set acts only on the traffic its targets name. Sites are added on the set's Targets tab, or with the + buttons on the Traffic page and the dashboard, which add one domain or address at a time.
A set to add the sites to. The + buttons can create one as well. For GeoSite and GeoIP categories, the databases loaded under Settings > Geodat Settings.

Target Use it for Sub-tab Domain A site reached by name, which is most sites. A domain covers its subdomains, so a service that serves content from many subdomains is covered by its parent domain, such as googlevideo.com for YouTube. Bypass Domains GeoSite category A ready-made list of a service's domains, such as youtube or discord. Bypass Domains IP address or range Connections made straight to an address, without a name, such as those of Telegram apps, voice calls or games. Bypass IPs GeoIP category The address ranges of a country or a network, from the GeoIP database. Bypass IPs ASN Every address range a network announces, kept up to date by b4. A cloud, hosting or CDN network also carries many unrelated sites. Bypass IPs

Open Sets and click the set's card. On the Targets tab, open Bypass Domains, type a domain into Add Bypass Domain and press Enter. Several domains can be pasted at once, separated by commas or new lines. For a GeoSite category, pick it under Add Bypass Category. For addresses, open Bypass IPs and use Add Bypass IP/CIDR or Add Bypass GeoIP Category. For a network, open Bypass IPs and, under Networks (ASN), enter its number, such as AS15169, or an IP address of the service. For an address, b4 offers the networks that announce it. Click Save Changes. Targets describes every field of the tab.

The Traffic page lists the connections b4 sees, and the dashboard's Top domains and addresses panels list the names and addresses that devices use most. A + next to a name or an address opens a dialog that adds it to a set. On the dashboard, + marks the names and addresses that no set matched. For a domain: Click + next to the domain. Pick the pattern: the domain itself or one of its parent domains. A parent domain covers every subdomain. Under Target Set, pick a set, or Create New Set and enter its name. Click Add Domain. For an address: Click + next to the address. The dialog looks up the network that announces it. Under What to add, pick the address alone, the announced prefix that covers it, a broader mask, or the whole network, its ASN. Under Target Set, pick a set or create one. Click the button that names what is added, such as Add 142.250.120.139 or Add AS15169. Adding domains to sets and Adding addresses and networks to sets describe both dialogs. The DPI Detector opens the address dialog from its Hosting and CDN results.
documents.s: Adding from the Traffic page or the dashboard

documents.t: The set's card on the Sets page shows the new targets. An ASN whose prefixes are not fetched yet shows as N ASN unresolved. On the Traffic page and the dashboard, the next connections to the site carry the set's badge. The dashboard's Sets panel counts the connections the set matched.

The connections carry another set's badge. Another set targets the same site and takes its connections, for example a set limited to the device. A set higher in the list with IP priority on also keeps the connections to the server addresses it lists. When a domain is already in another set, the Targets tab names that set. How sets match traffic describes how b4 chooses. The connections carry no set at all. The set may be turned off, or the site may load from other domains. The Traffic page shows the names it really uses, and Domains not in any set on the dashboard opens it with only the connections no set matched. A category or an ASN adds nothing. The GeoSite or GeoIP database is not loaded, or the ASN's prefixes could not be fetched yet. b4 retries an ASN in the background. The site is matched but still does not open. The set's strategy does not work for it, see Unblocking a site.

The b4 skills are instructions that an AI assistant follows while it uses the tools of b4's MCP server. A skill uses the open Agent Skills format. The skills are published in the b4-agent-skills repository.

Skill What it does b4-connect Connects the AI app to b4's MCP server and fixes the connection when b4's tools are missing: the app's entry, the token, certificate errors, a reconnect after a switch. Works without b4's tools. b4-troubleshoot Finds out why a site, an app or b4 itself does not work: a site that does not open, Discovery that finds nothing, a problem that began after an update, a clash with firmware features or another proxy. b4-unblock-site Confirms the block with b4's own test of the site, runs Discovery after the user agrees and applies an approved result as a set. Then tests the site again and says how to undo the change. Stops when the router already loads the site. b4-proxy-routing Sets up or fixes sets that send sites or devices through a VPN interface or a SOCKS5 upstream, and works out which set takes a connection. b4-find-app-hosts Finds which hosts and protocols an app on one device uses, such as a TV's YouTube app, Discord voice or a game. Says whether b4 sees that traffic, which set takes it and what to add to a set. Reports only that device. b4-report-issue Writes a short bug report for b4's GitHub issues, without the router's host name, addresses and other private data. Checks first whether a newer release fixes the problem. Without b4's tools, it works from text pasted into the chat. Every skill has the assistant: read b4's state and b4's own description of a setting before it answers; test a site, run Discovery or change a setting only on request, and only while the matching switch is on; say that a site opens only after b4's own test of that site succeeded; leave other devices' traffic and the router's private data out of answers and reports.

b4's MCP server is on and connected to the AI app, as described in Connecting an AI assistant. Reading b4's state needs nothing more. Testing a site and running Discovery need Allow active probes. Changes to settings and sets need Allow configuration changes. Both switches are on the MCP server card under Settings > Integrations, see Allowing changes and probes. An AI app from the table below that loads skills and runs on a computer that reaches the router.

App Works with the skills Note Claude Code yes Installs with the skills CLI or as a plugin. Claude Desktop yes The Code tab works like Claude Code. In Chat, the plugin installs under Customize > Plugins, and b4's MCP server goes into the app's configuration file through a local bridge such as mcp-remote. Connectors added in its settings connect from Anthropic's cloud and cannot reach the router. ChatGPT desktop app yes Installs as a plugin. b4's MCP server goes into the MCP configuration that the app shares with the Codex CLI. Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, VS Code with GitHub Copilot yes Installs with the skills CLI. Antigravity CLI yes The b4 plugin loads with its skills. claude.ai, ChatGPT on the web no They connect to MCP servers from the vendor's cloud and cannot reach a router on a home network. LM Studio and Jan desktop apps no They use b4's MCP tools without the skills. Ollama no It does not connect to MCP servers on its own. b4's AI Assistant card no It explains settings in the web interface and does not use the skills.

The skills CLI needs Node.js. Open a terminal in the folder that the AI app works in. Run: npx skills add DanielLavrushin/b4-agent-skills Choose the skills and the AI apps when the command asks. With -g, the skills are installed for the user account instead of one folder. Options answer the questions in advance, for example every skill for Claude Code: npx skills add DanielLavrushin/b4-agent-skills --skill '*' -a claude-code -y The other app names are codex, gemini-cli, cursor and github-copilot.

In Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add DanielLavrushin/b4-agent-skills /plugin install b4@b4-agent-skills From a terminal: claude plugin marketplace add DanielLavrushin/b4-agent-skills claude plugin install b4@b4-agent-skills

The marketplace is added with the Codex CLI. Run in a terminal: codex plugin marketplace add DanielLavrushin/b4-agent-skills Restart the ChatGPT desktop app. Open Plugins, choose the b4-agent-skills source and install b4.

A request in plain words is enough, and the app loads the matching skill by itself. Examples: "discord.com stopped opening after the b4 update" "make meduza.io open through b4" "route youtube.com through the wg0 interface" "which servers does Discord on my PC use, and does b4 handle them?" "help me write a bug report for b4" "the AI app does not show b4's tools" In Claude Code, a skill can also be called by name, for example /b4-troubleshoot. With the plugin, the name is /b4:b4-troubleshoot.

A question such as "is b4 running?" gets an answer with b4's version once the MCP connection works. In Claude Code, calling a skill by name, such as /b4-troubleshoot, shows whether the skills are installed.

The app does not load the skills. The app does not support skills, see the table, or the skills CLI installed them into a folder the app does not open. With -g, they are installed for every folder. The app shows no b4 tools. A request to connect to b4 loads b4-connect, which works without b4's tools. When it does not work on the MCP page lists the usual causes. The assistant says it cannot test a site or change a setting. The matching switch is off, or the app connected before the switch was turned on. Reconnecting the app to the MCP server fetches the current list of tools. The problem is still there. The assistant lists what to attach to a report, and b4-report-issue writes it. Reporting a problem covers where to send it.

By default b4 handles the traffic of every device on the network. Device filtering under Settings > Core > Devices decides which devices get DPI bypass at all. The Source Devices of a set limit that one set to some devices.
The devices are on the router's network, where b4 finds them in the ARP table. A device behind another router has a fixed or reserved IP address, since it can be added only by that address.

Open Settings > Core > Devices. Turn on Enable Device Filtering. Under Available Devices, select the devices. A device missing from the list is added under Manual Devices by its IP address. To exclude the selected devices instead of limiting DPI bypass to them, turn on Exclude Selected Devices (Blacklist). Click Save Changes, then Restart Service. The selection applies after a restart. What the filter covers: DPI bypass matches devices by MAC address. A device added by hand does not count for it, and a selection made only of such devices leaves DPI bypass on for every device. Routing sets and Telegram over WebSocket use the same selection for traffic from the network. There a device added by hand is matched by its IP address. The router itself is not a device. Its own connections, those of the SOCKS5 proxy included, get DPI bypass in both modes. While devices are selected, sets do not write their own DSCP value. The fields are described under Devices.
documents.s: Choosing the devices that get DPI bypass

documents.t: Open the set, then Targets > Source Devices. Select the devices. To apply the set to every device except the selected ones, turn on All devices except selected. Save the set. A set limited to source devices takes priority over a set without that limit. Source devices narrow whom a set applies to, but they do not select traffic. A routing set still needs a domain, IP or ASN target, and Match any IP address under Bypass IPs routes everything from those devices. See Source devices.
documents.s: Applying one set to some devices

documents.t: Open Traffic. In the Devices panel, select a device. Its connections show the set that matched each of them. Devices that device filtering leaves out get no DPI bypass, and the dashboard does not count their connections.

Nothing changed after saving. The device filter applies after a restart of b4. A device added by hand gets no DPI bypass. DPI bypass matches MAC addresses only. Such a device can still be the source device of a set. A device added by hand is not matched. Its IP address changed, or a router in between replaces the source address of its traffic. The first needs a fixed or reserved address; the second cannot be matched at all. A phone stops being matched. Many phones use a randomized MAC address, shown as Private, and a new address is a new device for b4. Turning off the private address for this network on the phone keeps its MAC address fixed. A device that is gone stays in the list as offline. b4 keeps a device's name, selection and MSS value until the device is forgotten under Available Devices. A replacement device, or a phone with a new random MAC address, is a new device and needs its own selection.

The setup adds a set that sends fakes before the UDP packets that open a Discord voice call. It is needed when a call sends its voice packets but gets no answer, or drops after a few seconds, while the rest of Discord works. A call that hangs at RTC Connecting fails on TCP instead, see When it does not work. The address of a voice server is not known in advance. The set therefore has no targets and handles only calls on the voice ports, see Sets for calls. Once it takes the packet that opens a call, the rest of that call belongs to the set and passes untouched, whatever other sets match its address.

b4 is installed and running. A set that already opens Discord itself, the app and text chat. Adding sites to a set adds Discord's domains to a set, and The Discord set's TCP ports lists the ports that set needs.

Open Sets and click Create Set. Enter a name for the set, such as Discord voice. Leave the Targets tab empty. On the UDP tab, in Calls, select Handle only calls. Which calls stays at Discord app and browsers, and a warning asks for a port filter. Click Use Discord ports in the warning, or enter 19294-19344,50000-50100 in Port Filter. Leave Action Mode at Fake & Fragment. Fake Packet Payload now shows (auto: STUN request). On the TCP tab, leave Port Filter under General empty. Click Create Set. Ports Voice servers 19294-19344 Discord's voice servers on Cloudflare 50000-50100 The other voice servers, for example in Finland With Discord app and browsers, the set takes calls and voice channels in the Discord app, and calls in a browser, Discord in a browser included. Fake Packet Count and Fake Packet Size keep their defaults.

The JSON below creates the same set without the steps above. Settings it leaves out keep their defaults. { "name": "Discord voice", "udp": { "dport_filter": "19294-19344,50000-50100", "filter_l7": ["discord", "stun"], "fake_payload_file": "@stun" } } Open Sets and click Create Set. Go to the Import/Export tab, paste the JSON into Set Configuration JSON and click Import. Click Create Set. The Community Hub can carry a set of this kind as well. A zapret line for Discord voice with no host list or ipset of its own, such as --filter-udp=19294-19344,50000-50100 --filter-l7=discord,stun --dpi-desync=fake, converts into the same set on import.

The Discord app, text chat and the signalling connection of a call run over TCP. They belong to the set with Discord's domains: the GeoSite category discord, or domains such as discord.com, discord.gg and discord.media. b4 captures TCP port 443 and the ports that any set lists. Discord's other TCP ports therefore have to be in that set's list. Open the set with Discord's domains. On the TCP tab, enter 443,2053,2083,2087,2096,8443 in Port Filter under General. Click Save Changes. The list limits the set to these ports, and 443 keeps it on HTTPS. The voice server picks one of these ports for the signalling connection of a call, and the set's strategy has to work on each of them. A strategy that opens discord.com on port 443 can still fail on the port of a voice server, and Checking the voice server tests that port. The watchdog checks a new strategy only on the set's Discovery addresses, and an address given as a domain is checked on port 443. A strategy it writes can then open Discord and break calls, so keeping the watchdog off for this set is the usual choice.

Join a voice channel in Discord. Open the Traffic page. Turn on All packets. Voice packets carry no domain and show only with it on. Switch to Raw feed in the top right corner. The packet that opens the voice connection and the STUN requests show the voice set's name in the Set column, with a destination port from the two ranges. The packets that follow on the same connection show the voice set as well, with a voice label: the set passed them through untouched.

Before the first voice packet, Discord opens a TCP connection to the voice server. Its domain ends in discord.media, and its port is one of the ports in The Discord set's TCP ports. Join a voice channel in Discord. On the Traffic page, switch to Raw feed and enter domain:discord.media in the filter field. Note the domain of the latest row, such as c-xxx.discord.media, and the port in its destination. On a computer behind the router, run the command below with that domain and port. curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}/%{size_download}\n' https://c-xxx.discord.media:2087/ Output Meaning 403 and a few thousand bytes, such as 403/4548 The server's answer passes. 000/0 or 403/0 The connection to this port is cut.

While a call hangs, the Traffic page with All packets on shows which side fails. The Traffic page shows Cause No TCP row with a discord.media domain b4 does not capture the voice server's port: it is missing from the Port Filter of the set with Discord's domains. A TCP row with a discord.media domain, and no UDP packet to the voice ports The TCP connection to the voice server fails, and Discord sends no voice packet. Checking the voice server confirms it, and the set with Discord's domains needs a strategy that works on that port, see Unblocking a site. UDP packets to the voice ports with the voice set's name The voice server does not answer them, see the causes below. On some networks no strategy opens the voice server's port when it is not 443. The check then reads 000/0 whatever the strategy, and calls through that server need a proxy or a VPN for discord.media. b4 refuses to save the voice set. A warning on the UDP tab names the cause: the set has targets, its Port Filter is empty, or the TCP tab lists ports. The set saves with no targets, both port ranges in the UDP Port Filter and an empty TCP Port Filter. No packet to the voice ports shows the voice set. The voice set took neither the packet that opens the call nor the STUN requests. Their port is missing from its Port Filter, Which calls leaves that kind of call out, or the set is turned off on the Sets page. The IP Version Filter on the set's Targets tab can also exclude one IP version. No packets to the voice ports appear. All packets is off, or the port is missing from the voice set's Port Filter: b4 sees UDP only on port 443 and on the ports that sets list. With Enable IPv6 Support off under Settings > Core, b4 sees no IPv6 packets at all. Calls through one Discord server fail, and calls through other servers work. A voice channel uses the region Discord picks automatically. When a provider blocks the addresses of that region's voice servers, no strategy helps. Someone who can manage the voice channel sets another region for it in the channel's settings in Discord. The voice server check passes over IPv4 and fails over IPv6. With the TTL strategy, or with Apply Fake TTL on, the set with Discord's domains sends its fakes with one Fake TTL for IPv4 and IPv6. A voice server can be fewer hops away over IPv6, and a fake that reaches the server breaks the connection. A lower Fake TTL on the Faking sub-tab, checked over both IP versions, is the fix. Discord does not open at all. The set with Discord's domains does not cover the TCP side. Its Port Filter needs the ports from The Discord set's TCP ports, and its strategy has to open Discord, see Unblocking a site.

A set can write a DSCP value of its own into the packets sent to the set's addresses. DSCP is a field of the IP header, so the value leaves the host with the packet. The router in front of b4 tells the set's traffic apart by it and sends it, after b4 has processed it, through a route of its own, such as a VPN or a second uplink. b4 itself does not route by the value.

A router in front of b4 that can match DSCP and route by a connection mark, such as Linux with nftables or RouterOS. b4 installs its firewall rules: Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup under Settings > Core > Firewall is off. With iptables, the ipset command and the xt_set and xt_DSCP kernel modules are present; on OpenWrt xt_DSCP comes with kmod-ipt-ipopt and iptables-mod-ipopt. A set with routing off or in Network interface mode, with no source devices and no source interfaces. When the value is not written lists every case. Device Filtering under Settings > Core > Devices off, or on with no device selected. While it has a device selected, in either mode, no set writes its value; Set DSCP still applies.

Open Sets, open the set, then DNS & Routing > Traffic Routing. In the DSCP block at the bottom, turn on Enable per-set DSCP. b4 fills in DSCP value with the first of 7, 31, 6 and 25 that no other set and no Set DSCP uses. Click Save Changes. Optionally, turn on Set DSCP under Settings > Core > Firewall. It writes its own value into every other packet, so no device whose traffic passes through b4 can pick the set's route by writing the set's value itself. Each route needs a value of its own. The field is described under DSCP.

Every device on the path sees the value until something resets it, and some act on it. Linux Wi-Fi drivers, and access points that follow the same mapping, pick the WMM queue from it: Values Wi-Fi queue 7, 31, 6, 25 Best effort, as for traffic without a value 8 and several other values below 24 Background 32-63, and from Linux 6.8 on 24, 26, 28 and 30 Video and voice 7, 31, 6 and 25 keep normal priority in cake and pfifo_fast as well. The hint under DSCP value lists where the other values land, and Choosing the value gives the values for pfSense.

The router in front of b4 has to: Decide on the first packet of a connection and keep the decision, with a connection mark. Routing each packet by its own field moves a connection to another route when the value appears in the middle of it, and behind NAT that breaks the connection. With flow offloading on b4's host, such as an nftables flowtable, FLOWOFFLOAD or hardware NAT, only the first packets of a connection carry the value. Compare the whole field. nftables ip dscp and RouterOS dscp= compare all six bits. The tos selector of ip rule compares only some of them for IPv4: to it, 7, 15, 31 and 63 look the same. Reset the field on the internet uplink and on the tunnel, so the provider and the far end of the tunnel do not see it. A reset in the forwarding path misses the packets that FastTrack, an nftables flowtable or hardware NAT carries past it. Accept the value only from b4, by its address or MAC address. Devices whose traffic passes through b4 are kept out only by Set DSCP on b4. Let in the replies of the second route. Strict reverse-path filtering, Linux rp_filter 1 or RouterOS rp-filter=strict, drops them. While b4 is stopped, restarting or running without its packet engine, new connections carry no value and take the main route. A router that uses the Set DSCP value to keep b4's traffic out of a route leading to b4 sends that traffic back to b4 meanwhile; a match on the interface or the MAC address does not depend on b4 running.
documents.s: Reading the value on the next router

documents.t: One nftables table reads the value. In the example the router reaches b4 through br-lan, the main uplink is wan, the second route is the uplink wanb, and the set's value is 31. The table goes into a file such as /etc/dscp_route.nft, loaded with nft -f /etc/dscp_route.nft; loading it again replaces the table. table inet dscp_route delete table inet dscp_route table inet dscp_route { chain prerouting { type filter hook prerouting priority mangle; policy accept; iifname "br-lan" ip saddr 192.168.50.2 ct state new ct status & confirmed == 0 ip dscp 31 ct mark set ct mark | 0x01000000 iifname "br-lan" ip6 saddr { fd50::2, fd10::/64 } ct state new ct status & confirmed == 0 ip6 dscp 31 ct mark set ct mark | 0x01000000 iifname "br-lan" ct mark & 0x01000000 == 0x01000000 meta mark set meta mark | 0x01000000 } chain postrouting { type filter hook postrouting priority mangle; policy accept; oifname { "wan", "wanb" } ip dscp != 0 ip dscp set 0 oifname { "wan", "wanb" } ip6 dscp != 0 ip6 dscp set 0 } chain srcnat { type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; oifname { "wan", "wanb" } masquerade } } The marked connections take routing table 100, whose default route leads out of wanb: ip rule add fwmark 0x1000000/0x1000000 iif br-lan lookup 100 priority 1000 ip route add default via 100.64.2.1 dev wanb table 100 ip -6 rule add fwmark 0x1000000/0x1000000 iif br-lan lookup 100 priority 1000 ip -6 route add default via 2001:db8:b::1 dev wanb table 100 The ip applet of busybox 1.37 takes the same lines. Neither the table nor these commands survive a reboot by themselves; they belong in the router's startup scripts. In the example Stands for br-lan The kernel device name of the interface toward b4, not OpenWrt's interface name 192.168.50.2 b4's IPv4 address, best fixed with a static lease. Forwarded IPv4 traffic carries it only while Enable NAT Masquerade is on in b4 (NAT Masquerade); without it, the subnet behind b4 joins it: ip saddr { 192.168.50.2, <subnet> } fd50::2, fd10::/64 b4's own IPv6 address and the IPv6 prefix of the devices behind b4. The line is left out when no IPv6 passes through b4 31 The set's value. Each further value needs its own pair of marking lines 0x01000000 A bit of the connection mark and the packet mark that nothing else on the router uses. A further route takes another bit and another table 100, 1000 The table of the second uplink, and a free rule priority below the main table's 32766 and ahead of other policy rules 100.64.2.1, 2001:db8:b::1 The gateways of the second uplink Chain srcnat Masquerading on both uplinks, which the router's own firewall may already do ct status & confirmed == 0 matches only the packet that creates the connection; ct state new alone also matches a repeated SYN and moves the connection in the middle. nft 1.0.2 and later print it as ct status ! confirmed, which nft 0.9.8 does not accept. The marking lines change only their own bit, so programs that change only their own bits of the connection mark coexist with the table; a program that overwrites the whole connection mark breaks it. The reset keeps the two ECN bits and also clears the values LAN devices write for themselves. With b4 on the same Ethernet segment, its MAC address can replace its addresses, for both families and with NAT Masquerade on or off: iifname "br-lan" ether saddr 02:00:00:00:00:b4 ct state new ... in both marking lines. With software flow offloading, a flowtable takes over a connection and its packets skip the reset in postrouting. Two more rules and a table that resets the field on the way out of the uplinks fix that: ip rule add oif wanb lookup 100 priority 1001 ip -6 rule add oif wanb lookup 100 priority 1001 table netdev dscp_wash delete table netdev dscp_wash table netdev dscp_wash { chain egress { type filter hook egress devices = { "wan", "wanb" } priority 0; policy accept; ip dscp != 0 ip dscp set 0 ip6 dscp != 0 ip6 dscp set 0 } } The egress hook needs Linux 5.16 or later; nft 1.0.2 and later load the table, nft 0.9.8 does not. Instead of the table, cake with wash on both uplinks resets the field: tc qdisc add dev wan root cake wash, and the same for wanb. Without the oif rules every offloaded UDP flow through wanb loses a datagram, and without iif br-lan in the fwmark rules offloaded IPv6 replies go back out through wanb and the connections fail. The example was tested outside OpenWrt's firewall4 and without hardware flow offloading. With net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_checksum at the kernel default 1, fakes with a broken TCP checksum, such as those of the TCP Check strategy, are not tied to their connection: on the second route they leave through the main uplink with b4's address. OpenWrt sets the value to 0, and the fakes follow their connection.
RouterOS reads the value with mangle rules. Routing a set's traffic by its DSCP value gives them with the names of the container setup.

Discovery for the set and the heals of the watchdog test strategies with the set's value, so on the set's route. A run for sites without a set tests the main route, also for the set's addresses. When a change to the set's value, to Set DSCP or to its interface list moves the set's traffic to another path after a run, the run's strategy is not applied, and the set needs a new run.
documents.s: Finding a strategy for the set

documents.t: The DSCP block of the set shows no reason under the switch. System Info on Settings > System > Service shows a Per-set DSCP group under Firewall, with applied for the set and the number of addresses written for it. With ipinfo.io added to the set's domains, https://ipinfo.io/ip on a device shows the address of the second route.

The first connection to a site takes the main route. b4 had not learned the address yet. IP, CIDR, GeoIP and ASN targets carry the value from the first packet. See The first connection. The value does not arrive through a tunnel. With a WireGuard output interface on b4, the router in front sees only the tunnel's packets, and WireGuard writes 0 into their DSCP field. IPv4 connections over the second uplink fail. Strict reverse-path filtering drops the replies. The kernel takes the larger of net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and the interface's own value, here net.ipv4.conf.wanb.rp_filter; 2 or 0 lets the replies in. The provider sees the value. A flowtable or hardware NAT carries packets past the reset; see the flow offloading part of Linux with nftables.

Three settings take an interface name: the capture filter of the packet engine and two fields of a routing set. They sit in different places of the web interface and do different things. Setting Where What it filters None selected Capture Interfaces Settings > Core > Packet Engine Which packets the engine inspects Every interface Source Interfaces DNS & Routing > Traffic Routing of a set Which arriving traffic the set's rules are offered Any interface Output Interface DNS & Routing > Traffic Routing of a set Where a matched packet is sent The set routes nothing The first two are filters and narrow what b4 does. Only the third sends traffic anywhere. The interface lists of NAT Masquerade and DSCP, and the Uplink interface of the TUN engine, take interface names as well.

The field is described under Capture Interfaces. For forwarded traffic the engine compares the interface a packet leaves by, because its capture rules run after the kernel has chosen the route. Only the reply direction and DNS are matched on the interface they arrive on. The leaving interface comes from the routing table. A VPN client, a policy route or a transparent proxy that moves the default route changes it without touching this list, and a selection made before that stops matching. While the selection matches nothing, b4 inspects nothing and no set applies.

Each name becomes an iifname qualifier (-i on iptables) on the set's marking, TPROXY and block rules, so it selects which arriving traffic those rules are offered. The match is on arrival: A WAN interface here never matches traffic from the local network. A LAN client's traffic arrives on the bridge, br0 on most consumer routers, not on the uplink. Traffic the router originates arrives on no interface, so a set with a source interface does not route, proxy or block the router's own connections. See Router's own traffic. Source devices listed under Targets > Source Devices have the same effect, unless the list is an exclude list. No selection is the usual choice; a name here belongs to a set meant to cover one segment.
The set's addresses are marked, and an ip rule sends the mark to a routing table whose default route points at this interface. See Network interface and How routing sets work.

Symptom Setting to check Nothing on the Traffic page, or only traffic from the router itself Capture Interfaces Sets apply to the router but never to a client Capture Interfaces, then Source Interfaces A set's marking rule shows zero packets in the firewall counters Source Interfaces Traffic is marked but leaves by the wrong path Output Interface, and any other service with ip rule entries The Traffic page answers the first two. When the router is the only source (Router in the device list, or its own address in the raw feed), the engine sees only the traffic the router originates. When another service also does policy routing, a set can mark traffic correctly and still not use its own table. Using b4 with Xray or XrayUI covers that case.

A strategy that works today can stop working later. The watchdog checks a set's pages on a schedule. When they keep failing, it heals the set: it searches for a new strategy with Discovery and writes it into the set. Escalation adds a second safety net: it moves a site that keeps failing to a backup set for a while, then tries the original set again.

A set that applies a bypass strategy. A set that routes its traffic to a proxy or an interface cannot be watched. The set targets domains or GeoSite categories, and is not limited to specific devices by an include list. Up to five pages that represent the set and do not open without b4, such as the main page of each service it covers.

Open Settings > Discovery, turn on Enable Watchdog and click Save Changes. Open Sets and open the set. On the Discovery tab, enter a page under Address and press Enter. Repeat for the other pages. Suggest offers candidates, and Add puts one in the list. Turn on Keep this set working with the watchdog. Click Save Changes. A backup set for escalation is optional: On the set's Escalation tab, pick the backup set under Switch to. A set that sends sites through a VPN or a proxy can be the backup. Click Save Changes. The fields of these tabs are described in Discovery tab and Escalation.

The Watchdog page lists the set under Watched sets. When the first check passes, its status reads Healthy. The set's card on the Sets page carries a Watchdog badge, and the dashboard's Sets panel shows the same status. When the watchdog writes a new strategy, the row shows it under Last heal, and the dashboard lists it under Recent changes. While escalation sends a site to the backup set, the dashboard's Active Escalations panel lists it.

Status or message Cause and fix The watchdog is off, but N sets ask for it, on the dashboard Enable Watchdog is off under Settings > Discovery. Turning it on starts the checks. The switch cannot be turned on A condition fails, and the caption under the switch names it, see Watchdog. Cannot verify No page can be checked: another set handles them, an escalation sends them elsewhere, or they are unusable. The set needs pages that it handles itself. Cooldown or Gave up, with the reason that the current strategy loads the addresses Tested alone, the set's strategy loads the pages, yet the live check fails. Something outside the strategy is in the way: another set, DNS or IPv6. The Traffic page shows which set the connections get. Gave up Three heals in a row failed, and the reason shows the last cause. A manual run with Find a strategy on the set's Discovery tab shows what works, and Check now on the Watchdog page resumes the heals. When no strategy helps any more, the sites need a VPN or a proxy. A set routed that way, as the escalation backup, catches the sites that keep failing.

A mark is a 32-bit number the kernel keeps with a packet. Firewall rules set it and match it, ip rule picks a routing table by it, and a socket can put one on every packet it sends. Conntrack keeps a second 32-bit mark for each connection. b4 uses marks to tell the packets it sent itself from the ones it still has to handle, to send a set's traffic to its route or to its own listener, and to keep its own connections out of its routing rules and, for some of them, out of its packet processing. Services that route by policy or proxy transparently use the same 32 bits: Xray and XKeen, sing-box and mihomo, XrayUI, podkop, Tailscale, WireGuard, mwan3. When two of them use the same bit, one can take the other's packets for its own, and a service that writes the whole mark erases the bits the others put there. The sections below list the bits b4 writes and reads, the routing rules that go with them, and the values some other router services use.

Form Meaning 0x5aef/0x27fff The bits covered by 0x27fff equal 0x5aef; the other bits are not compared 0x8000/0x8000 Bit 0x8000 is set, whatever the rest of the mark holds fwmark 0x5aef/0x27fff lookup 119 in ip rule Packets whose mark matches 0x5aef/0x27fff are routed by table 119 fwmark 0x111 lookup 111 in ip rule No mask: the whole 32-bit mark has to equal 0x111 A rule that writes a mark with a mask changes only the bits under the mask and keeps the rest. In iptables that is MARK --set-xmark 0x5aef/0x27fff or CONNMARK --save-mark --nfmask 0x27fff --ctmask 0x27fff. nftables prints the same write as meta mark set meta mark & 0xfffddaef | 0x00005aef: the AND keeps every bit outside 0x27fff (nft folds the value's own bits into that constant), and the OR writes 0x5aef. A rule without a mask, such as nftables meta mark set 0x00021546 or iptables MARK --set-mark 0x111, replaces all 32 bits and erases whatever another service wrote there. nft list prints every value padded to eight digits, 0x00008000 for 0x8000. Kind Where it lives Shown by Packet mark (fwmark) One packet, from the rule or socket that set it until the packet leaves the router meta mark in nftables, -m mark and MARK in iptables Connection mark The conntrack entry, shared by every packet of the connection in both directions ct mark, -m connmark and CONNMARK, mark= in /proc/net/nf_conntrack Socket mark (SO_MARK) A socket; every packet it sends starts with this packet mark fwmark: in the output of ss -e, run as root on kernel 4.9 or later (4.10 for raw sockets)

Both require these bits clear, and a packet that carries one of them is taken neither for such a connection nor for b4's own packet. The rules that write the whole mark, those of proxy sets on nftables and of Discovery, clear them on the packets they take. Bit 16 is left free for XrayUI's 0x10000.

b4 rules A packet is left alone when Packet processing, nftables (inet b4_mangle) b4_chain, the rules for outgoing ports, returns it when its mark reads as b4's own (see The queue mark), its bits under 0x27fff equal 0x24bab, or it matches 0x240000/0x8efd8000, and during a Discovery run when its mark is exactly the flow or injected mark. postrouting jumps to b4_chain, or, when device filtering selects devices, forward for their packets and output for the router's own. output accepts a packet with every bit of the queue mark, above that jump. Below its returns, b4_chain drops UDP whose addresses and ports are in the set b4_udp_drop4 or b4_udp_drop6, the QUIC connections a set drops, rejects or blocks; see Packet capture. prerouting, with the rules for DNS answers and other replies, tests no packet mark. It skips a reply that reaches a socket on the router when its connection mark has every bit of the queue mark, and, while no enabled set uses an incoming mode, the TCP packets without SYN or RST of connections whose connection mark has bit 0x2000000 and none of the queue mark's bits. raw_prerouting and raw_output, which queue DNS queries at priority -300, ahead of conntrack, return a packet whose mark reads as b4's own, and during a Discovery run one whose mark is exactly the flow or injected mark; raw_output also returns one that leaves through lo. While they queue DNS queries, b4_chain returns UDP to port 53. The MSS clamp rules come first in prerouting, output and forward, apart from the rules a Discovery run adds above them Packet processing, iptables (B4, B4_PREROUTING) B4, the rules for outgoing ports, first returns a packet whose mark reads as b4's own, as b4_chain does on nftables. The jumps to B4 come from mangle POSTROUTING, or, when device filtering selects devices, from mangle FORWARD for their packets and from mangle OUTPUT for the router's own. Mangle OUTPUT accepts a packet the router sends with every bit of the queue mark, above that jump. B4 also returns a packet whose bits under 0x27fff equal 0x24bab or the mark of a proxy set, or whose mark matches 0x240000/0x8efd8000, and during a Discovery run one whose mark is exactly the flow or injected mark. B4_PREROUTING and the rules for DNS answers test no packet mark; with the connmark module, B4_PREROUTING skips the same packets as prerouting on nftables. DNS queries are queued from B4_RAW in the raw table, which raw PREROUTING and OUTPUT jump to for UDP to port 53 and which returns a packet whose mark reads as b4's own, and during a Discovery run one whose mark is exactly the flow or injected mark; while it queues them, B4 returns UDP to port 53. On KeeneticOS, where b4 never uses B4_RAW, and on a kernel before 4.18 (4.14 before 4.14.173) whose raw table cannot queue packets, DNS queries are copied instead: mangle INPUT and FORWARD jump at their top to B4_DNSCOPY for UDP to port 53, and mangle OUTPUT for such UDP that does not leave through lo. B4_DNSCOPY returns a packet whose mark reads as b4's own and copies every other one to NFLOG group queue.start_num, 537 by default, with the prefix b4dns, and b4 ignores a copy from mangle OUTPUT whose mark has every bit of the queue mark; while it copies them, B4 returns UDP to port 53 as well, and, as with B4_RAW, the rules for DNS answers skip UDP to port 53. When b4 can neither queue DNS queries from the raw table nor copy them, the rules for DNS queries sit in B4_PREROUTING and mangle OUTPUT instead and test no packet mark The queue itself, both backends b4 releases a packet unchanged when its mark matches 0x240000/0x8efd8000, has 0x24bab under 0x27fff, or has every bit of the queue mark with the rest made only of bits of 0x27fff and 0x2000000, and is not exactly one of Discovery's two marks. On kernels 3.14 and later it also releases a packet that a socket on the router sent with every bit of the queue mark, unless the mark is exactly one of Discovery's two marks. A packet that leaves through a tunnel gets no strategy either, and neither does one that another service's mark sends by another route than the packets b4 injects would take. With legacy iptables that check covers every mark, as long as no other service on the router keeps nftables tables and Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup is off. Otherwise it covers only marks with every bit of the queue mark; see Packets that leave by another route Routing sets other than block sets, packets entering the router (b4r_*_pre), including the router's own packets a proxy set loops through lo Its mark has every bit of the queue mark or bit 0x40000, or its bits under 0x27fff are not zero and, in a proxy set's chain, differ from that set's own mark Routing sets, the router's own packets (b4r_*_out) Its mark has bit 0x40000 or any bit under 0x27fff. A packet with every bit of the queue mark is left alone as well, after a set routed through an interface has given it the set's mark when its destination is in the set; a set that leaves the router's own traffic alone and lists its devices only by IP address does this only for packets from those addresses. The IPv4 ICMP redirects that a set with a gateway drops, as sets routed through an interface describes, are dropped whatever their mark QUIC refusal of a proxy set with Route UDP through upstream off or Block QUIC (force TCP) on, for forwarded packets (b4r_*_q) and the router's own (b4r_*_qo) Its mark has every bit of the queue mark, or bit 0x40000; in b4r_*_q also when it comes from a device outside the set's source devices Block sets Never: they test no mark, only the destination and, when the set has them, its source interfaces and source devices TUN capture (B4_TUN) Its mark has every bit of the queue mark or bit 0x20000000, matches 0x240000/0x8efd8000, or has 0x24bab as its bits under 0x27fff; on iptables also when its destination is in a routing set other than a block set. A packet to a network in which the router has an IPv4 address of its own is left alone as well, unless it is UDP DNS or a TCP reset the chain captures; while b4 captures only the router's own connections, such a packet is always left alone, except a UDP DNS query to the uplink gateway TUN on the whole default route Only packets with bit 0x10000000, and with bit 0x20000000 when ip accepts suppress_prefixlength, leave by b4's rules; every other packet that follows the default route enters b4tun0 NAT Masquerade (b4_masq, B4_MASQ) Its mark has bit 0x20000000. On iptables that RETURN sits at the top of nat POSTROUTING, so such a packet skips every later rule there, other services' included Set DSCP and the sets' own DSCP values (B4_DSCP, inet b4_dscp) Its mark has bit 0x20000000, it leaves through lo, or it travels in the reply direction of its connection. On iptables the jump to B4_DSCP sits at the top of mangle POSTROUTING; on nftables inet b4_dscp runs in postrouting at priority 150. The sets' values are written in the same chain or table, after the Set DSCP value, by rules that choose the value by the destination address alone DNS over TCP redirect Its mark has every bit of the queue mark Discovery, during a run At the top of the chain, a packet whose mark is exactly the injected mark is accepted, and a packet whose mark or connection mark is exactly the flow mark goes to Discovery's queue; either way it skips the rest of the chain. On iptables that is the built-in mangle PREROUTING and OUTPUT, so it skips every later rule there. Its DSCP chain, B4_DISCOVERY_DSCP or b4_discovery_dscp, leaves alone every packet whose mark is not exactly one of the two Where the kernel has the conntrack direction match, the TCP queue rules, those for a set's packet duplication addresses included, also test the direction: ct direction original in b4_chain and -m conntrack --ctdir ORIGINAL in B4, ct direction reply in prerouting and -m conntrack --ctdir REPLY in B4_PREROUTING. See Packet capture.

b4 rules What they write Sets routed through an interface The packet mark's bits under 0x27fff; the connection mark's bits under 0x27fff and bit 0x40000000. Masked, the other bits stay Proxy sets, iptables The packet mark's bits under 0x1027fff. Masked Proxy sets, nftables The whole packet mark Packet processing The queue-mark bits into the connection mark of every connection on which the router itself sends a packet with every bit of the queue mark, such as b4's own lookups. Bit 0x2000000 instead when the packet also has that bit, as the fakes and split segments b4 sends into a device's connection do. Nothing for a packet whose mark has bit 0x20000000 that the queue mark lacks, such as a DNS answer b4 sends to a device. NFQUEUE mode only; on nftables not for packets sent to lo, on iptables only with the connmark module. Masked TUN capture Bit 0x40000000 of the packet mark. Masked Discovery, during a run The whole packet mark of a packet whose connection mark is exactly the flow mark, and the whole connection mark of a connection that carries a packet whose mark is exactly the flow mark; both get the flow mark Set DSCP and the sets' own DSCP values write the DSCP field of the IP header, not a mark. A set's own value adds no packet mark, connection mark or routing rule: its rules sit in the chain or table Set DSCP uses, B4_DSCP or inet b4_dscp, which b4 installs while Set DSCP is on or a set writes its own value, and they choose the value by the destination address alone.
documents.s: What b4 writes on packets it did not create

documents.t: The queue mark is the Packet Mark setting under Settings, Core, Packet Engine, queue.mark in the configuration file and --mark on the command line. The default is 0x8000 (32768); the web interface takes the value in decimal, and 0 stands for the default. b4 sends every fake, split segment and packet it puts back on the wire from raw sockets carrying this mark, with bit 0x2000000 added in NFQUEUE mode and bit 0x10000000 in TUN mode. The packets toward a device in TUN mode carry 0x20000000 alone, and those of a Discovery run carry Discovery's injected mark, with 0x20000000 added on the packets it sends back toward its probes. The DNS queries b4 sends for clients and for its sets carry the queue mark too; its lookups through the router's own resolver carry no mark. Every rule below tests all bits of the queue mark at once, so the bits b4 adds on the same packet do not hide it. The rule that writes the connection mark for the router's own packets also wants bits 0x2000000 and 0x20000000 clear, so neither a packet b4 sends toward a device nor one it sends into a device's connection marks that connection as one of b4's own. A second rule writes bit 0x2000000 for the latter, see connections b4 sends packets into. With a queue mark that has bit 0x2000000 or 0x20000000 itself, the rules do not tell such packets apart. Rule nftables iptables Router's own packets output: meta mark & 0x22008000 == 0x8000 ct mark set ct mark | 0x8000, then meta mark & 0x8000 == 0x8000 accept mangle OUTPUT: -m mark --mark 0x8000/0x22008000 -j CONNMARK --save-mark --nfmask 0x8000 --ctmask 0x8000 (with the connmark module), then -m mark --mark 0x8000/0x8000 -j ACCEPT Queue chain b4_chain: meta mark & 0x8cfd8000 == 0x8000 return B4: -m mark --mark 0x8000/0x8cfd8000 -j RETURN Packets entering the router prerouting: ct mark & 0x8000 == 0x8000 ct direction reply socket wildcard 0 return B4_PREROUTING: -m connmark --mark 0x8000/0x8000 -m conntrack --ctdir REPLY -m socket -j RETURN (with the connmark module) DNS queries, ahead of conntrack raw_prerouting, raw_output: meta mark & 0x8cfd8000 == 0x8000 return B4_RAW: -m mark --mark 0x8000/0x8cfd8000 -j RETURN DNS query copies - B4_DNSCOPY: -m mark --mark 0x8000/0x8cfd8000 -j RETURN Routing sets other than block sets meta mark & 0x8000 == 0x8000 return -m mark --mark 0x8000/0x8000 -j RETURN Sets routed through an interface, router's own packets meta mark & 0x8000 == 0x8000 ip daddr @<set> meta mark set ... -m mark --mark 0x8000/0x8000 -m set --match-set <set> dst -j MARK --set-xmark <mark>/0x27fff DNS over TCP redirect, while it is on meta mark & 0x8000 == 0x8000 return B4_DNSTCP: -m mark --mark 0x8000/0x8000 -j RETURN TUN capture - B4_TUN: -m mark --mark 0x8000/0x8000 -j RETURN, written with iptables on both backends In the queue chains b4_chain and B4 and in the rules that queue or copy DNS queries, a mark reads as b4's own when it has every bit of the queue mark and no other bit outside 0x73027fff. Those are the bits b4 itself may add to its own packets. With the default queue mark this is the match 0x8000/0x8cfd8000. The 0xffffaaa that KeeneticOS writes has every bit of the default queue mark and bits outside 0x73027fff. These rules do not take it for b4's own. The rule for packets entering the router takes a packet only in the reply direction of its connection, and only when the packet reaches a socket on the router, as the replies to b4's own lookups and probes do. The replies of a device connection reach no such socket, whatever value another program writes into its connection mark, and they go to the queue rules. ASUS firmware with AiProtection on often writes values with every bit of the default queue mark, and KeeneticOS does for the devices of its hotspot. -m socket on iptables and socket wildcard 0 on nftables pass over sockets bound to every address. Where nftables has no socket wildcard, b4 uses socket transparent 0, which also matches such sockets. Without the socket match, xt_socket or nft_socket, the rule takes every reply whose connection mark has every bit of the queue mark, and b4 logs a warning. Without the conntrack direction match it tests no direction. The rule for sets routed through an interface sends the fakes and split segments of a connection such a set routes out of the same interface as the connection itself. It matches the destination, and the source address only in a set limited to source devices that are all given by IP address, so it does the same for the injected packets of connections to the set's destinations that the set does not route, such as those from a device outside its source interfaces. The source address is matched per address family: in a family for which such a set lists no device address, the rule matches the destination alone, so with Enable IPv6 Support on, a set whose devices are all given by IPv4 address gives its mark to every queue-marked IPv6 packet to its destinations. Saving a changed Packet Mark moves the packet processing rules, the rules of routing sets and the DNS over TCP redirect to the new value at once and removes those of the old value. While a Discovery run is active, the packet processing rules and the redirect wait for it to end; after a run that ends more than five minutes after the save they move at the next check of the firewall monitor on iptables, and at the next start of b4 on nftables or with the monitor off (system.tables.monitor_interval at 0). Until they move, b4 queues its own DNS queries, which already carry the new value, like those of a device, so the DNS redirect of a set can stop applying. The raw sockets, b4's release of its own packets from the queue and, in TUN mode, the B4_TUN chain take the new value at the next start of b4, which the web interface asks for. Discovery's two marks follow the new value unless system.checker sets them to something other than the Packet Mark plus 1 and plus 2. A configuration saved from the web interface of a version before 1.84.0 can hold them at values that no longer follow it, such as the old value plus 1 and plus 2, after a save that changed the Packet Mark or one made while --mark was in effect. Deleting discovery_flow_mark and discovery_injected_mark from system.checker while b4 is stopped lets them follow again. b4 refuses a value that: is made only of bits of 0x240000, the marks of its own connections; is made only of bits of 0x27fff and 0x1000000, the bits of set marks; overlaps 0x70000000 in TUN mode; has bit 0x20000000 in NFQUEUE mode while NAT Masquerade or Set DSCP is on, or while an enabled set has Enable per-set DSCP on; has bit 0x2000000 in NFQUEUE mode, the bit b4 adds there to the packets it sends into a connection. A configuration that already runs NFQUEUE mode with such a value still loads and saves, and b4 logs a warning; has 0x24bab, the Telegram over WebSocket mark, as its bits under 0x27fff; equals the flow or injected mark of Discovery; is above 0xffffffff, or, while either Discovery mark is left out of the configuration, is above 0xfffffffd or gives that mark (the value plus 1 for the flow mark, plus 2 for the injected mark) a value that matches 0x240000/0x8efd8000 or equals the other Discovery mark. A packet another service marks with every bit of the queue mark reads to the other rules as one b4 sent itself. Proxy sets, Telegram over WebSocket and the QUIC refusal leave it alone. A set routed through an interface gives it the set's mark when the router sends it to an address in the set and its mark has no bit under 0x27fff and not 0x40000, unless the set is limited to source devices that are all given by IP address, and a block set rejects it by destination as usual. TUN capture skips it whatever the rest of its mark holds; the queue chains of both backends, b4_chain and B4, skip it only when its mark reads as b4's own, and on kernels 3.14 and later b4 releases it from the queue unchanged when a socket on the router sent it. In NFQUEUE mode, when the router sends it, b4 also copies the queue-mark bits into its connection mark (on nftables not for packets sent to lo, on iptables only with the connmark module), so the replies that reach the socket that sent it are skipped as well. A mark that also has bit 0x2000000 puts that bit into the connection mark instead, as b4's fakes do, and one with bit 0x20000000 that the queue mark lacks puts nothing there. A packet that reaches the queue anyway, on both backends through the rules for packets entering the router, which test no packet mark, is released unchanged only when the rest of its mark is made only of bits of 0x27fff and 0x2000000, or when the mark matches 0x240000/0x8efd8000 or has 0x24bab under 0x27fff. wg-quick's 51820 (0xca6c), which it puts on the WireGuard socket when a peer routes /0, has bit 15 set, and the rest of it, 0x4a6c, lies within 0x27fff.

In NFQUEUE mode the fakes, split segments, re-sent SYNs and other packets b4 sends into a connection carry the queue mark with bit 0x2000000 added, 0x2008000 by default. b4's own lookups and probes carry the queue mark alone. The connection mark keeps the two apart: the queue-mark bits mark a connection of b4's own, bit 0x2000000 a connection b4 has sent packets into. With the default queue mark, the rules for the bit are: Rule nftables iptables Connection mark output: meta mark & 0x22008000 == 0x2008000 ct mark set ct mark | 0x2000000 mangle OUTPUT: -m mark --mark 0x2008000/0x22008000 -j CONNMARK --save-mark --nfmask 0x2000000 --ctmask 0x2000000 The server's packets prerouting: ct mark & 0x2008000 == 0x2000000 tcp flags & (syn|rst) == 0 return B4_PREROUTING: -p tcp -m connmark --mark 0x2000000/0x2008000 --tcp-flags SYN,RST NONE -j RETURN On iptables both need the connmark module. Both rules that write the connection mark, for b4's own connections and for this bit, sit above the accept for the queue mark in output and in mangle OUTPUT. The rule for the server's packets sits right below the return for b4's own connections, above every queue rule there. It matches a connection whose connection mark has bit 0x2000000 and none of the queue mark's bits. The connection's SYN-ACK and resets still reach b4, for RST Injection Protection and the escalation on forged resets, and the server's other packets stay out of the queue. nftables 1.1.6 lists its flag test as tcp flags ! syn,rst. While an enabled set uses an incoming mode, the rule is left out. The server's packets of every connection b4 sends packets into then reach the queue rules, whichever set the connection belongs to. Firmware that writes the whole connection mark can remove the bit. ASUS firmware rewrites the connection mark of device connections, for example while AiProtection or QoS is on, and the bit is gone when that rewrite comes after b4 set it. The server's packets then reach the queue rules as on any other connection. While AiProtection is on, the value the firmware writes often has every bit of the queue mark. The replies of such a connection reach no socket on the router, and the return for b4's own connections does not take them. Without the socket match it does, and none of the connection's replies reach b4, the SYN-ACK and resets included. A queue mark that has bit 0x2000000 itself makes the two kinds of connection look the same. A connection b4 sends packets into then counts as one of b4's own, and its replies skip b4, the SYN-ACK and resets included. b4 refuses to save such a mark when the save would put it on NFQUEUE mode for the first time; a configuration that already runs NFQUEUE mode with one keeps working, and b4 logs a warning.

A set routed through an output interface gets a mark and a routing table from the interface name, the egress IP, the gateway and the kill switch. Sets that agree on all four share both. Item Value Mark From a hash of the four, in 0x100-0x7eff and never equal to the queue mark's bits under 0x27fff; if every hashed candidate is taken, counted up from 0x66 instead Table 100-249, skipping tables named in rt_tables, looked up by another service's rule, or holding routes b4 did not add Rule ip rule add fwmark <mark>/0x27fff lookup <table> priority <10000 + table>, for IPv4, and for IPv6 when Enable IPv6 Support is on Table contents A default route through the interface, via the set's gateway in the gateway's address family when b4 can use it, plus blackhole default metric 4096 with the kill switch Pinned values routing.fwmark and routing.table in the configuration file or through the API, used only when both are set, the mark lies within 0x27fff, is not 0x24bab, does not contain every bit of the queue mark and does not equal its bits under 0x27fff The set marks the first packet of each connection to its destinations and saves the mark in the connection mark, with bit 0x40000000 as b4's claim. Later packets of that connection sent in the direction of its first packet get the mark back from the connection mark; replies get no mark. The set's chain for packets entering the router, b4r_<set>_pre, in this order: Returns packets that carry the queue mark, bit 0x40000, or any bit under 0x27fff. Returns packets that arrive on the output interface itself, narrowed for a set with a gateway as described below. Restores the mark from the connection mark on later packets of claimed connections that travel in the direction of the first packet. Marks new connections to the set's destinations and saves the mark with the claim. With an IPv4 gateway that b4 uses, on an output interface of the Ethernet type (Ethernet, bridge, VLAN, Wi-Fi, TAP), step 2 is narrower. The set first returns packets to local, broadcast, multicast and IPv6 link-local addresses, whatever interface they arrive on. It then returns the IPv4 packets that arrive on the output interface from the usable IPv4 gateway of any set routed through that interface, its own included, and every IPv6 packet that arrives on it. Other IPv4 packets from the output interface go on to steps 3 and 4. A refused gateway, an IPv6 gateway and an interface of another type leave step 2 as it is. A set that excludes source devices returns their packets before step 2, only the packets of its devices enter the chain of a set limited to source devices, and a set limited to source interfaces applies steps 3 and 4 only to packets arriving on them. Device filtering under Settings, Core, Devices narrows the chain the same way. b4r_<set>_out does the same for the router's own connections when the set carries them, and gives the set's mark to b4's own queue-marked packets addressed to the set; a set limited to source devices that are all given by IP address does this only for packets from those addresses. With the narrower step 2, the first rule of b4r_<set>_out drops the IPv4 ICMP redirects that leave through the output interface, whatever their mark and whether or not the set carries the router's own traffic. With net.ipv4.fwmark_reflect set to 1, the kernel gives a redirect the mark of the packet that caused it.
