Masquerade matches the set's mark and the output interface; with an egress IP present on the interface, SNAT to that address takes its place and also requires the destination to be in the set. On a router whose firmware overwrites the connection mark b4 writes, the restore never matches. b4 on iptables notices this while the firewall monitor runs: when several connections have been claimed, the restore has never matched, and no answered connection in /proc/net/nf_conntrack still carries bit 0x40000000, on two checks in a row, b4 writes 0 to .conntrack-mark next to the configuration file. From then on, and at every later start on either backend until the file is deleted, the set marks every packet to its destinations that travels in the direction of its connection's first packet and has no bit under 0x27fff, not only the first. While a set uses an output interface whose effective rp_filter is 1, b4 writes 2 to net.ipv4.conf.<interface>.rp_filter, and writes the old value back when the last set on that interface goes. On a test box the two sets on wg0 got: 10119: from all fwmark 0x5aef/0x27fff lookup 119 10123: from all fwmark 0x69cf/0x27fff lookup 123

Sets in the Upstream SOCKS5 proxy and Telegram over WebSocket routing modes, and the Telegram over WebSocket switch, divert connections to transparent listeners of b4 with TPROXY. Each has a mark, and the mark gives the listener port. Item Value Mark 0x20000-0x27dff, from a hash of the set's ID, or the value after it when the hash equals the queue mark's bits under 0x27fff; routing.fwmark replaces it when it lies within 0x27fff, is not 0x24bab and does not equal the queue mark's bits under 0x27fff Telegram over WebSocket switch 0x24bab, port 13443 Listener port 13000 + mark % 50000 Rule, priority 3 fwmark <mark>/0x27fff lookup 252, for IPv4, and for IPv6 when Enable IPv6 Support is on; table 252 holds local default dev lo and is shared by every proxy set. When 252 belongs to another service, b4 takes 251, 250, then 300-399 Rule, priority 2 fwmark <mark>/0x1027fff iif lo lookup main, IPv4 Router's own packets <mark> + 0x1000000, TCP in the original direction; none for a set limited to source devices or source interfaces b4r_<set>_pre returns packets that carry the queue mark, bit 0x40000, or bits under 0x27fff other than the set's own mark, and packets to local, broadcast, multicast and IPv6 link-local addresses. Of the packets to the set's destinations, it then marks TCP packets of connections already held by a transparent socket and accepts them, and hands the other TCP packets, and UDP ones when Route UDP through upstream is on, to TPROXY with the set's mark; a set limited to source interfaces hands over only packets arriving on them. When the set refuses QUIC, with Route UDP through upstream off or Block QUIC (force TCP) on, the chain accepts its UDP to port 443 instead, so no later set's chain takes it and the QUIC refusal rejects it; on iptables that accept also skips every later rule in mangle PREROUTING. Source devices limit this chain as they do for sets routed through an interface. iptables writes the mark under the mask 0x1027fff; nftables writes the whole mark. The router's own connections reach a proxy set by a loop, unless the set is limited to source devices or source interfaces. b4r_<set>_out marks their TCP packets in the original direction with the set's mark plus bit 0x1000000, the priority 3 rule sends them to lo, and they come back through prerouting, where TPROXY takes them. Once new connections to the set's destinations exceed 200 per second (burst 400), b4r_<set>_out leaves the first packet of each further connection unmarked, but marks its later TCP packets in the original direction as usual. With src_valid_mark at 1, in net.ipv4.conf.all or on the interface a connection arrives on, the kernel checks the source of every diverted connection in the table its mark selects, and table 252 answers every address with the router itself. The priority 2 rule sends that check to main. Bit 0x1000000 keeps the router's own packets out of it, so they still loop through lo. XrayUI sets net.ipv4.conf.all.src_valid_mark to 1 when Xray has a WireGuard outbound, wg-quick and awg-quick when a peer takes the IPv4 default route, and Tailscale in its default netfilter mode. b4 also adds an accept for each proxy mark to the input chains. On iptables it is -m mark --mark <mark>/<mark> -j ACCEPT at the top of filter INPUT and of mangle INPUT, through ip6tables as well and through the -legacy variants when they are installed. Mangle INPUT runs before filter INPUT, and the accept there keeps a diverted connection from a drop lower in that chain, such as the KeeneticOS chain that drops TCP to port 443 on the router. When a jump to B4_DNSCOPY heads mangle INPUT, the accept goes right below it, and a DNS query that a proxy set diverts is still copied. On nftables it is meta mark & <mark> == <mark> accept at the top of inet fw4 input, or of inet filter input when fw4 is absent, and nowhere when neither chain exists. Installing a proxy set writes 0 to net.ipv4.conf.lo.rp_filter and 2 to net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter; b4 does not write the old values back. On a test box the Telegram over WebSocket switch and one proxy set got the following; the other proxy set and a set in the Telegram over WebSocket mode each added the same pair of rules with its own mark: 2: from all fwmark 0x24bab/0x1027fff iif lo lookup main 2: from all fwmark 0x21546/0x1027fff iif lo lookup main 3: from all fwmark 0x24bab/0x27fff lookup 252 3: from all fwmark 0x21546/0x27fff lookup 252
documents.s: Proxy sets and Telegram over WebSocket

documents.t: b4 opens these connections with 0x40000: to the upstream of a proxy set and the direct connections a proxy set opens in its place, to Telegram, for the address and domain lists the Telegram features download, the MTProto proxy's forward to its fake SNI domain, and requests to the Community Hub, ipinfo and RIPEstat. The chains of interface, proxy and Telegram over WebSocket sets return on it, so none of these sets routes such connections and they never loop into b4's own listeners; they follow the rest of the router's routing rules, normally the main table. Block sets still block them, and in TUN mode they can still pass through b4tun0. Packet processing does not skip 0x40000: a set whose targets match the destination applies its strategy to b4's own connections as it does to a device's. A set in a proxy or Telegram over WebSocket mode, or one routed into a TUN, TAP or WireGuard tunnel that is up, lets them through unmodified instead, and since its routing chains skip them, they leave by the main route with no strategy at all. 0x240000 adds bit 0x200000, and packet processing skips a packet whose mark matches 0x240000/0x8efd8000: 0x240000 exactly, apart from bits under 0x71027fff. A mark of another service that only shares bit 0x200000 with it does not take a packet out of packet processing. The MTProto proxy and Telegram over WebSocket put 0x240000 on their connections through Cloudflare-proxied domains or a custom WebSocket domain, and to a Cloudflare Worker unless Let sets process Worker connections is on; see DPI processing. Lookups and probes carrying the queue mark skip packet processing, and proxy sets leave them alone. The DPI Detector's direct mode uses the queue mark to measure the network without b4's processing. A set routed through an interface gives such packets its mark when their destination is in the set, as it does to the packets b4 injects, so they leave by that set's interface; a set limited to source devices that are all given by IP address does this only for the packets b4 injects for those devices. Lookups through the router's own resolver carry no mark, and a service that exempts b4 by its marks still sees them as ordinary router traffic. In TUN mode, when the default route itself points at b4tun0, the router's own packets with the queue mark, 0x40000 or 0x240000 enter b4tun0 like any other whenever they follow the default route. b4 reads them there without their mark, so neither the queue mark nor 0x240000 takes them out of packet processing; in TUN mode they do so only with port capture, where B4_TUN returns such packets.

In TUN mode (queue.mode: "tun") packets reach b4 through a TUN device, b4tun0 unless queue.tun.device_name says otherwise, instead of a queue. These rules are written with iptables also on the nftables backend, and cover IPv4 only. Item Rule Capture Chain B4_TUN, jumped from mangle OUTPUT and PREROUTING (from PREROUTING through B4_TUN_GATE when device filtering selects devices), or only from OUTPUT while b4 captures only the router's own connections (see Packet engine): sets 0x40000000/0x40000000 on UDP DNS queries and answers, on the first packets of connections to the capture ports (on every packet of them where xt_connbytes is missing; TCP only in the direction of the connection's first packet where xt_conntrack is available), on every TCP packet to the capture ports of a set's packet duplication addresses (only in the direction of the connection's first packet where xt_conntrack is available), and on TCP resets from the capture ports, only in the reply direction where xt_conntrack is available, while a set has RST Injection Protection on or an escalation target Rule fwmark 0x40000000/0x40000000 lookup <table> at priority 10, or one less than the lowest rule another service has at 5-9, but not below 4 Table default dev b4tun0; chosen from 96 down to 61, skipping 77 and tables in use, or next to queue.tun.route_table Packets b4 writes back Socket mark queue mark + 0x10000000, not tracked by conntrack (raw OUTPUT ... -j CT --notrack) unless system.tables.skip_setup is on or the kernel has no raw table or no CT target. When system.tables.skip_setup is off and b4 cannot install this rule, the one for packets toward a device or the SNAT into b4tun0, it captures only the router's own connections Packets toward a device Socket mark 0x20000000, not tracked by conntrack under the same conditions When xt_connbytes is not available, b4 counts the packets of each connection itself and processes only the first ones, as the match would. While b4 captures only the router's own connections it keeps port capture, and B4_TUN marks every packet of the connections to the capture ports; otherwise b4 points the default route itself at b4tun0 instead. No setting selects either mode. With the default route at b4tun0, b4's own packets leave through rules 88 and 89 (0x20000000) and 99 and 100 (0x10000000): the first of each pair looks in main without its default route, the second in the uplink table, which holds the uplink's default route and is chosen from 97 down to 62 in the same way, or is queue.tun.route_table itself. Rules 88, 89 and 99 need an ip that accepts suppress_prefixlength; without it only rule 100 is added.

While a Discovery run is active, including runs the watchdog or the MCP server start, a chain at the top of b4's prerouting and output chains in inet b4_mangle (b4_discovery, nftables) or of mangle PREROUTING and OUTPUT (B4_DISCOVERY, iptables and ip6tables) steers its probe connections to a queue of their own, numbered after the main queues (541 with the defaults). Discovery uses this queue in TUN mode as well. The probes carry the flow mark, the queue mark plus 1 by default; the packets Discovery sends carry the injected mark, the queue mark plus 2. Both are compared as whole 32-bit values, and the flow mark is copied between the packet and the connection whole. They are set by system.checker.discovery_flow_mark and system.checker.discovery_injected_mark in the configuration file. The default values have bits under 0x27fff, so no routing set routes Discovery's traffic. For the length of a run, b4's queue chain, b4_chain on nftables and B4 on iptables and ip6tables, returns a packet whose mark is exactly the flow or injected mark as well, so packet processing leaves Discovery's packets alone on their way out of the router. The DNS query chains, raw_prerouting and raw_output on nftables and B4_RAW on iptables and ip6tables, do the same, so b4's sets never answer Discovery's name lookups. B4_DNSCOPY gets no such rule: with the default values, 0x8001 and 0x8002, its return for the queue mark covers Discovery's packets, and b4 ignores a copy whose mark is exactly the flow or injected mark. While a set writes its own DSCP value, a run also writes a DSCP value into its packets: the chain B4_DISCOVERY_DSCP in mangle (iptables and ip6tables), jumped to from POSTROUTING right after the jump to B4_DSCP, or b4_discovery_dscp in inet b4_mangle (nftables), hooked at postrouting priority 151, after inet b4_dscp. It sets the DSCP field of every packet whose mark is exactly the flow or the injected mark, on the interfaces the list of Set DSCP allows: in a run for a set with its own value, to that value in the IP versions the set's traffic carries it in, and otherwise to the Set DSCP value, or 0 while it is off. It runs after the sets' rules, so its value replaces the one they chose by destination. See DSCP rules. During a run, a connection of another service whose mark is exactly the flow mark goes to Discovery's queue too, and a packet whose mark is exactly the flow or injected mark skips the rest of these chains; on iptables that includes every rule below them in mangle PREROUTING and OUTPUT, other services' rules as well.

Priority Rule Table Present for 2 fwmark <mark>/0x1027fff iif lo main Proxy sets and Telegram over WebSocket, IPv4 3 fwmark <mark>/0x27fff 252; 251, 250, 300-399 Proxy sets and Telegram over WebSocket 4-10 fwmark 0x40000000/0x40000000 96 down to 61, or next to queue.tun.route_table TUN mode with port capture, IPv4 88, 89 fwmark 0x20000000/0x20000000 main without its default route, then the uplink table: 97 down to 62, or queue.tun.route_table TUN mode on the whole default route, IPv4 99, 100 fwmark 0x10000000/0x10000000 The same TUN mode on the whole default route, IPv4 10000 + table fwmark <mark>/0x27fff 100-249, or the pinned routing.table Sets routed through an interface The kernel walks the rules from the lowest priority number up and stops at the first one that gives a route. A rule added without a priority gets the priority of the rule after local, minus one; on kernels before 4.3 an IPv6 rule gets 16383 instead. Added after b4's priority 2 rule, such a rule gets priority 1 and sits above every rule of b4; on a system with only the standard rules it gets 32765 and sits below them. XKeen, XrayUI and OpenClash outside their TUN modes, MagiTrickle, mihomo in iptables mode, the Xray guides, wg-quick and awg-quick all add their rules that way, so their rules sit above b4's when they are added while b4 is running, a restart of that service included. Added before b4 starts, they sit below b4's only when no rule other than the standard ones was there: next to Tailscale's 5210, for example, such a rule gets 5209, above b4's interface sets at 10100-10249. On kernels before 4.3 their IPv6 rules get 16383 and sit below b4's either way.

A mark with any bit under 0x27fff on a packet before b4's routing chains keeps interface and proxy sets off that packet; only a proxy set still takes a packet whose bits under 0x27fff equal its own mark. Block sets and the QUIC refusal of a proxy set do not look at those bits. An upstream proxy running on the router is kept out of a set that matches its server this way, for example with Xray's sockopt.mark at 255. Packet processing still applies to its connections unless the mark is one of those in the next point, or its bits under 0x27fff equal 0x24bab or, on iptables, the mark of a proxy set. A mark with every bit of the queue mark reads as b4's own packet to the routing sets, TUN capture and the DNS over TCP redirect; the queue chains and the rules for DNS queries also need the rest of it within 0x73027fff, see The queue mark. Such a packet that reaches the queue is released unchanged when the rest of its mark is made only of bits of 0x27fff and 0x2000000 or, on kernels 3.14 and later, when a socket on the router sent it. A mark that matches 0x240000/0x8efd8000 reads as one packet processing leaves alone; a mark that has bit 0x200000 without matching it does not. On nftables, b4's routing chains run at priority mangle - 1 (-151), ahead of chains at the mangle priority (-150): b4 marks first, and a service that later writes the whole mark replaces b4's, so the packet follows whichever rule matches the new value. A packet of the router itself is rerouted only when that rewrite happens in a chain of type route, as iptables mangle OUTPUT is. On iptables, b4 inserts its routing jumps at the top of mangle OUTPUT. In mangle PREROUTING it puts them right above its own B4_PREROUTING jump, which it inserts at the top when it installs its rules, or above an earlier rule of another service that matches local sockets; with neither, as in TUN mode, it appends them, and it moves them back when they end up below either. A rule another service inserts at the top afterwards runs first, unless it matches local sockets. On iptables, the jump to the QUIC refusal of a proxy set for forwarded packets (b4r_*_q) sits at the top of filter FORWARD, so the router firewall's own rules, such as Asuswrt-Merlin's accept for traffic from br0, run after it. The jump in filter OUTPUT to its refusal for the router's own packets (b4r_*_qo) and the jumps of block sets are appended, and a rule above them that accepts a packet keeps it from them. On nftables these chains hang off b4's block_fwd and block_out, filter chains at priority -150, ahead of the filter priority (0). On iptables in NFQUEUE mode, a packet b4 releases from its queue skips every later rule of the built-in chain it was queued from, so another service's rules lower in that chain never see it. That covers the UDP packets from port 53 that B4_PREROUTING and b4's rules near the top of mangle OUTPUT queue unless the packet carries the queue mark or answers a lookup of b4's own, and the first packets of connections on b4's ports. UDP packets to port 53 are queued from the jumps b4 appends to raw PREROUTING and OUTPUT: other services' raw rules run before them, a raw rule another service appends after b4 is skipped for them, and once b4 releases them they pass conntrack and every mangle rule, so the DNS the Xray guides take with TPROXY reaches that rule. On KeeneticOS, and on a kernel before 4.18 whose raw table cannot queue packets, b4 copies them instead, from the jumps to B4_DNSCOPY it inserts at the top of mangle INPUT, FORWARD and OUTPUT: NFLOG does not end the chain, and every later rule there, b4's or another service's, sees the query. In mangle INPUT, b4's accept for a proxy mark sits right below the jump and ends the chain for a query that a proxy set diverts. Another program bound to the NFLOG group b4 uses keeps b4 from copying. When b4 can neither queue them from the raw table nor copy them, it queues them from B4_PREROUTING and mangle OUTPUT, and they skip the later rules there as well. b4's fakes and split segments carry the queue mark and bit 0x2000000, and b4 accepts them near the top of mangle OUTPUT, so a service whose rules come later in that chain, such as mwan3 or KVAS, never marks them either: for a connection such a service routes by its mark, they follow the router's main routing instead. In TUN mode the fakes and split segments carry the queue mark and bit 0x10000000, mangle OUTPUT has no such accept, and those rules see them. When b4 picks a table itself, it skips one it has not claimed yet if the table is named in rt_tables, looked up by another rule, or holds routes b4 did not add. A table pinned with routing.table is used as given only together with routing.fwmark, and a queue.tun.route_table that is taken is refused. Some services use fixed table numbers in b4's ranges without such a check: XKeen 111, podkop 105, the Xray guides 100 and 106, XrayUI 250 in TUN mode. Started after b4 has taken one of them, XKeen flushes the table and adds its own routes, and XrayUI replaces b4's route in it; podkop and the Xray guides fail to add their route (File exists) while b4's default route is in the table. XKeen, podkop and XrayUI flush the table when they stop, and XrayUI also deletes every rule that looks up 250, b4's priority 3 rule included when b4 uses that table. Values used by other services, read from their source code: Service Marks Rules and tables Xray-core 26.3.27 streamSettings.sockopt.mark: the whole socket mark of an outbound, only when set; no firewall rules of its own. The transparent proxy guides write 1, whole value, with TPROXY and on the router's own TCP and UDP in OUTPUT, and exempt Xray's own traffic only by an exact mark of 2 or 255 Guides: fwmark 1 lookup 100, and fwmark 1 lookup 106 for IPv6, no mask, no priority XKeen 2.0.1 Beta TPROXY and MARK 0x111, whole value, in TProxy mode and for UDP in Hybrid mode; Redirect mode and TCP in Hybrid mode use nat REDIRECT without a mark. CONNMARK saves and restores the whole mark. With router traffic on (proxy_router), takes the router's own TCP and UDP the same way, except a mark of exactly 255, a Keenetic policy mark, or bit 0x40000000 fwmark 0x111 lookup 111, no priority XrayUI 0.70.2 0x10000/0x10000 in DIVERT, TPROXY and the connection mark fwmark 0x10000/0x10000 lookup 77, no priority; TUN mode: 49 from <LAN> to <LAN> lookup main and 51 from <LAN> lookup 250, no mark sing-box 1.14.2 route.default_mark, routing_mark: socket marks. TUN auto_redirect: 0x2023 and 0x2024, whole values, on the packet and connection mark of UDP and ICMP and, when NFQUEUE 100 is available, of TCP connections it judges on the first packet; 0x2025 on a TCP first packet it resets; every outbound socket 0x2024 TUN auto_route: 9000-9010 to table 2022; with auto_redirect instead 9000 fwmark 0x2024, 9001 fwmark 0x2023 lookup 2022, 9002, and 32768 not fwmark 0x2024 lookup 2022 mihomo 1.19.32 routing-mark: socket mark, 2158 when iptables mode is on and it is unset. iptables mode: 0x2d0 (TPROXY under 0x2d0, MARK whole). TUN auto-redirect writes 0x2023 and 0x2024, and puts 0x2024 on every outbound socket, only with route-address-set or route-exclude-address-set TUN: 9000-9010 to table 2022, and 32768 to table 2022 when auto-redirect writes marks; iptables mode: fwmark 0x2d0 lookup 720, IPv4 only, no priority OpenClash 0.47.156 0x162, whole value: on UDP in the default TPROXY mode, where TCP goes through nat REDIRECT without a mark, and on TCP, UDP and ICMP echo in TUN mode fwmark 0x162 lookup 354, no priority; TUN mode: 1888 nikki 1.26.1 0x80/0xff for TPROXY, 0x81/0xff for TUN 1024 to table 80, 1025 to table 81 podkop 0.7.22 0x100000, whole value 105: fwmark 0x100000/0x100000 lookup podkop (table 105, named in rt_tables), IPv4 only zapret 72.13 and zapret2 1.0.5.2 Generated packets: the queued packet's mark plus 0x40000000. With FILTER_TTL_EXPIRED_ICMP=1, the default, 0x40000000 is added to the connection mark: in nftables POSTNAT mode, also the default, of every connection queued to nfqws, otherwise of connections nfqws sent generated packets on. In POSTNAT mode 0x20000000 is added to the packets queued after NAT. NFQUEUE 200 and 300 None MagiTrickle 0.8.2 0x4d616769 and up, one per group, whole value, packet and connection mark fwmark <mark> lookup <mark>, no priority KVAS 1.1.9 0xd1000, whole value, packet and connection mark 1778: fwmark 0xd1000/0xd1000 lookup 1001 Tailscale 1.102.5 Its own sockets 0x80000; packets forwarded from tailscale0 get 0x40000/0xff0000 and are masqueraded; bits 0xff0000 of the router's new connections saved in the connection mark and restored on later incoming packets, masked on iptables, whole value on nftables (the OpenWrt package's default) 5210, 5230, 5250 on 0x80000/0xff0000; 5270 to table 52; 1310-1370 instead on OpenWrt with mwan3 wg-quick 1.0.20260223, awg-quick 3.1.20260812 With a /0 peer and Table unset or auto: 51820 (0xca6c) on the WireGuard socket, or its FwMark, or the next number up when table 51820 holds routes; the whole connection mark copied to the packet mark of every UDP packet of that address family in prerouting not fwmark 51820 lookup 51820, lookup main suppress_prefixlength 0, no priority mwan3 2.12.2 Interface N as N << 8 under 0x3f00; connection mark saved and restored under the same mask 1001-1060 by incoming interface, 2001-2060 by mark, 3001-3060 unreachable by mark, 2061 and 2062 blackhole and unreachable pbr 1.2.2 0x10000, 0x20000 and on per interface under 0xff0000 30000, 29999 and down: fwmark <mark>/0xff0000 Where these meet b4: Xray, XKeen. 255 lies under 0x27fff, so routing sets leave Xray's outbound connections alone and packet processing still handles them. The QUIC refusal of a proxy set with Route UDP through upstream off or Block QUIC (force TCP) on, which tests only the queue mark and 0x40000, and block sets, which test no mark, reject Xray's packets to their addresses as well. XKeen's whole-value writes replace b4's bits on the connections it takes. With router traffic on, it also takes b4's own connections: none of its exemptions covers 0x40000. The nftables variant of the Xray guides starts with flush ruleset, which removes b4's nftables tables too, and the iptables tproxyrules.service of the IPv4 and IPv6 guide runs iptables -t mangle -F and ip6tables -t mangle -F when it stops, which removes b4's mangle rules. XrayUI. Its bit 16 is outside b4's. Its DIVERT rule and the order of the two services in mangle PREROUTING are described in Using b4 with Xray or XrayUI. sing-box, mihomo. Their default marks lie under 0x27fff; only sing-box's bridge outbound, when it falls back to iptables, uses bit 0x40000000, b4's TUN capture bit. auto_redirect, in mihomo only with route-address-set or route-exclude-address-set, writes whole marks after b4's routing chains: on UDP and ICMP, and in sing-box also on TCP connections it judges through NFQUEUE. With auto_route a rule at 9000-9010 sends forwarded traffic to table 2022, before b4's interface sets at 10000 and above. The router's own connections, b4's included, are taken as well: auto_redirect exempts only a mark of exactly 0x2024. nikki. Its mask, 0xff, lies inside the marks of b4's interface sets. A set whose mark has 0x81 in the low byte, or 0x80 when nikki uses a TPROXY mode, matches nikki's rule first, since its priorities are lower. nikki's own writes change only bits 0-7, but these lie under 0x27fff, so on destinations both cover nikki's route wins, whichever runs first. nikki's proxy.bypass_fwmark option takes mark and mask pairs; 0x40000/0x40000 and 0x8000/0x8000 there exempt b4's marked connections and packets from its proxying, but not from its router DNS hijack, which runs before that check, and not b4's connections that carry no mark. mwan3. Its mask, 0x3f00, lies inside the marks of b4's interface sets. A set whose mark has an active mwan3 interface number in bits 8-13 matches mwan3's rule at 2001-2060 first; with 61 or 62 there it matches mwan3's blackhole or unreachable rule, 2061 or 2062, whenever mwan3 runs. A set mark with no bit in 0x3f00 gets an interface number added by mwan3's policy, and then mwan3's rule matches it instead of b4's. With legacy iptables in NFQUEUE mode, a connection that mwan3 sends through another interface than the main table's route gets no strategy; see Packets that leave by another route. zapret, zapret2. Bits 30 and 29 are b4's TUN capture bit and its bit for packets toward a device, and bit 30 of the connection mark is b4's claim. Neither service skips the packets the other generates by their mark. On nftables in zapret's default POSTNAT mode, though, zapret takes its generated packets out of conntrack, and b4 does not queue them: its queue rules count a connection's packets or test its direction. Only on a kernel without the conntrack direction match does b4 still queue them toward a set's packet duplication addresses. On nftables both queue the packets they select, b4 first (priority -150 against zapret's 99 or 101). With Set DSCP or a set's own DSCP value on, b4 writes no value into a packet with bit 0x20000000, so in POSTNAT mode the packets zapret queues after NAT, and the packets it generates from them, leave without b4's DSCP value. On iptables the NFQUEUE rule that sits higher in mangle POSTROUTING takes the packets both select there, and the other never sees them. With device filtering, b4 queues the router's own packets earlier, in mangle OUTPUT, and forwarded packets in mangle FORWARD, so zapret can still process those after b4. zapret drops ICMP time-exceeded messages of connections whose connection mark has bit 0x40000000, which includes every connection a b4 interface set claims. In TUN mode with port capture, b4's rule fwmark 0x40000000/0x40000000 also matches zapret's generated packets and sends them into b4tun0. MagiTrickle. Its marks, 0x4d616769 and the ones after it, have bit 0x200000 but do not match 0x240000/0x8efd8000, so in NFQUEUE mode packet processing sees its connections. A connection it sends into a WireGuard, AmneziaWG, TUN or TAP interface gets no strategy. On legacy iptables, neither does one it sends by another route than b4's injected packets for that address would take; see Packets that leave by another route. On nftables such a connection gets the strategy, and the packets b4 injects for it carry the queue mark instead of MagiTrickle's and do not follow its route. MagiTrickle's marks also have bit 0x40000000: in TUN mode with port capture, b4's rule fwmark 0x40000000/0x40000000, IPv4 only, matches every packet MagiTrickle marks, and when it sits above MagiTrickle's fwmark <mark> rule in ip rule, those packets go into b4tun0, b4 processes them, and they leave by the router's own routing instead of MagiTrickle's table. KeeneticOS. _NDM_HOTSPOT_PREROUTING_MANGL in mangle PREROUTING writes a whole mark, such as 0xffffaaa, on the packets of the devices it lists by MAC address. Such a value has every bit of the default queue mark, bit 0x40000, bits under 0x27fff and bits outside 0x73027fff. The queue chains and the rules for DNS queries do not take it for b4's own, so the connections and DNS queries of these devices reach packet processing. KeeneticOS also saves the mark into the connection mark. The replies of these connections reach no socket on the router, and B4_PREROUTING passes them to packet processing as well. Without the socket match it skips them, DNS answers from resolvers outside the router included; see The queue mark. Interface sets do not route these devices: the whole mark takes the place of b4's route mark, and KeeneticOS's own rule fwmark 0xffffaaa lookup 4096 picks the route. The rule of an interface set still sends the packets b4 injects to the set's addresses through the set's interface. A connection of these devices therefore gets no strategy while an enabled interface set routes addresses through another interface than the connection leaves by. A set with Domain-only matching on and no IP address listed, or a set without destinations, routes nothing and does not count. A proxy set takes their connections when b4's routing chains come before _NDM_HOTSPOT_PREROUTING_MANGL in mangle PREROUTING, where b4 puts them. These connections then leave through b4's proxy, not by the device's KeeneticOS policy. When KeeneticOS sends a connection by that mark through another interface than b4's injected packets would take, the connection gets no strategy; see Packets that leave by another route. zapret, MagiTrickle and b4's connection-mark check. Both put bit 0x40000000 into connection marks. b4 takes any answered connection that carries that bit as proof that the router keeps its connection mark, so they can hide firmware that overwrites b4's claim. KVAS. 0xd1000 contains 0x40000: a packet that already carries it when b4's chains run reads to b4 as one of its own connections. With acceleration on, KVAS also marks the router's own connections to its unblock destinations, b4's included, and its rule 1778 routes them into table 1001. Tailscale. 0x40000 is Tailscale's mark for packets from tailscale0. Its masquerade rule, present by default, matches every packet carrying that value under 0xff0000, so b4's own connections marked 0x40000 are masqueraded to the address of the outgoing interface; those marked 0x240000 are not. Rule 5270 (1370 on OpenWrt with mwan3) comes before b4's interface sets, so a destination that table 52 routes leaves through Tailscale even when an interface set of b4 marked it. wg-quick, awg-quick. With the default queue mark, 0xca6c has every bit of it, so b4 treats WireGuard's own packets as its own. Their prerouting rule replaces the packet mark of every UDP packet with the connection mark. When both they and b4 use nftables, it runs after b4's routing chains: packets of an interface set still match its rule, since b4 saved the set's mark in the connection mark, but UDP that a proxy set diverts loses the set's mark, so the priority 3 rule no longer sends it to b4's listener. Brought up after b4, their two rules sit above every rule of b4, for IPv6 only on kernel 4.3 or later. pbr. 0x40000 is its fourth interface's mark, so with four or more interfaces pbr's rule routes b4's own connections that carry 0x40000 by that interface's table. A pbr policy that matches a packet a b4 interface set has marked adds its interface byte; when that byte has bit 17, b4's rule no longer matches and pbr's rule routes the packet. OpenClash, podkop. Their writes replace b4's mark: whole values, and in OpenClash's default mode nat REDIRECT for TCP, so on destinations both cover, their route wins. OpenClash takes the router's own connections while router self-proxy is on, the default; podkop always takes those to addresses in its lists. Neither exempts b4's own connections. The values in the table come from the releases named there and change between versions. ip rule and the firewall listing on the router show what is actually installed.

# b4's rules with their marks nft list table inet b4_mangle nft list table inet b4_route nft list table inet b4_dscp iptables -t mangle -S iptables -t nat -S iptables -t raw -S # the ipsets of the sets' own DSCP values on iptables, and the entry count of one ipset list -n | grep '^b4d_' ipset save b4d_u_v4 | grep -c '^add' # routing rules of every service, and b4's tables ip rule ip -6 rule ip route show table 252 # socket marks of b4's own connections ss -tanpe | grep b4 # connection marks in decimal, where the kernel exposes them grep -o 'mark=[0-9]*' /proc/net/nf_conntrack | sort | uniq -c The addresses of the sets' own DSCP values live in these objects: iptables, ipsets nftables, in inet b4_dscp Holds b4d_u_v4, b4d_u_v6 - Every address of the sets' IP, GeoIP and ASN targets; a packet to none of them and to no learned address leaves B4_DSCP before the sets' rules b4d_s<value>_v4, b4d_s<value>_v6 Maps s4_<n> and s6_<n>, and a chain v<value> for each value The same addresses, grouped by the value they get b4d_ul_v4, b4d_ul_v6 - Every address b4 learned for the sets' domains b4d_l_<set>_v4, b4d_l_<set>_v6 Sets l_<set>_4 and l_<set>_6 The addresses b4 learned for one set, each with its own timeout System Info in the web interface lists b4's firewall rules and the output of ip rule. While an enabled set has its own DSCP value switched on, its Per-set DSCP group gives each such set's value and why it is refused, or whether it is applied, with the number of its static entries and of the learned addresses b4 wrote for it from each source.

A set in Upstream SOCKS5 proxy mode hands the connections of its sites to a SOCKS5 proxy, such as Xray or sing-box on the router or on another host in the network. The devices need no proxy settings. The mode also helps where blocking is whitelist-based and direct connections to other addresses are dropped.
documents.s: Sending sites through a SOCKS5 proxy

documents.t: A SOCKS5 proxy the router can reach, and its address and port. Xray and sing-box carry UDP only when UDP is turned on in their inbound. TPROXY support in the kernel. On OpenWrt with nftables: opkg install kmod-nft-tproxy kmod-nft-socket On builds with apk, apk add takes the same packages. Other systems are listed under Requirements. System Info on Settings > System > Service shows under Kernel Capabilities whether Transparent proxy (TPROXY) is available. A set with the sites as domains or addresses. See Adding sites to a set.

Open Sets and open the set, or click Create Set and add the sites on the Targets tab. Open the DNS & Routing tab, then Traffic Routing. Turn on Enable Routing. Set Routing mode to Upstream SOCKS5 proxy. Enter Upstream SOCKS5 host and Upstream SOCKS5 port: for a proxy on the router itself, 127.0.0.1 and the port of its SOCKS5 inbound. Fill in Username (optional) and Password (optional) if the proxy requires them. Turn on Route UDP through upstream only if the proxy supports UDP. Click Save Changes, or Create Set for a new set. Send domain name to upstream is on by default: the proxy gets the site's name and resolves it itself. The fields are described under Upstream SOCKS5 proxy. The set's bypass strategy does not apply in this mode, since the proxy reaches the sites.

Add ipinfo.io to the set's domains for the test. On a device, run curl -s https://ipinfo.io/ip or open the address in a browser. It shows the proxy's exit address. Open Logs. The connection ends with [proxy]: TCP 192.168.1.37:20854 → 34.117.59.81:443 ipinfo.io sni-set=ipinfo.io [proxy] Without a [proxy] line the connection was not diverted, usually because its address was not in the set. A single address is the clearer test, since a full web page loads parts from other hosts.

Fall back to direct on upstream failure connects directly while the proxy cannot be reached. The sites keep opening, without the proxy, and the provider sees where the connections go. Off, the default, suits whitelist-based blocking, where a direct connection cannot work anyway, and setups where a failure has to be visible.

While the proxy does not answer, every connection to the set's addresses hangs and then fails, on every TCP port. A CDN address the set shares with other sites breaks those sites as well. b4 shows it: under Needs attention on the dashboard: Set X: proxy ... unreachable, with "this set's traffic is not getting through", or "traffic goes direct" while the fallback is on; as upstream down next to the set in the dashboard's Sets panel; in the log, at most once a minute, and once more when the proxy answers again. The cause is on the proxy's side: it is not running, it listens on another port, or the address on the set is wrong.

No [proxy] line. Usually the address the device connected to is not in the set. A device with encrypted DNS hides its lookups from b4; turning off secure DNS on it, or listing the site's domains in the set, fixes it. Devices on the network hang, the router's own connections work. Bridge netfilter is on, as OpenWrt's dockerd package sets it. The Bridge netfilter row in System Info shows it, and Bridge netfilter gives the fix. UDP or QUIC does not work. With Route UDP through upstream on and a proxy without UDP support, the set's UDP is dropped, and the log names the set. Tor's SOCKS port has no UDP support either. Off, b4 refuses the set's QUIC, and browsers use TCP through the proxy. Video is slow through the proxy. With Route UDP through upstream on, QUIC goes through the proxy too, and a proxy that carries UDP slowly, such as one behind a TCP-only VPN, slows video down. Block QUIC (force TCP) on the set's UDP tab makes browsers use TCP. The set's other UDP, such as WebRTC, still goes through the proxy. With the option off, QUIC is refused as well, but the set's other UDP leaves directly, and WebRTC can show the router's public address. Some connections bypass the proxy over IPv6. While Enable IPv6 Support is off, b4 handles only IPv4, and the dashboard shows IPv6 traffic skips all sets. The proxy runs on another device and the set covers its server. b4 recognises the proxy's own connections on the router by its process. On another device it recognises them only for a set that targets 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, or while a connection to the same destination is relayed through the proxy. Excluding that device under Targets > Source Devices keeps its traffic out of the set.
Discovery searches for a bypass strategy that makes a blocked site load and turns it into a set. When no strategy helps, the site can go through a VPN or a proxy instead.

b4 is running: Status on the dashboard reads Running. The devices' traffic reaches b4: the dashboard's Activity chart shows connections while they are in use. The address of the site, or of a page on it that does not open.

Open Discovery. Enter the site in Site or URL, for example youtube.com, and press Enter. Sites of one service, such as youtube.com and googlevideo.com, can go in together. Click Start. A run takes from one to ten minutes. On a card with a strategy, click Apply as a set. Choose Create a new set, check the name under Set name, and click Create set. The new set is enabled at once. The defaults under Options are the usual choice for a first run; the fields are described on the Discovery page.

Open the site on a device behind the router. Open the dashboard. The Sets panel lists the new set with the connections it matched in the last hour. Open Traffic. The site's connections show the new set in the Set column. When several strategies worked, Use instead under N other strategies worked, or in the Discovery history, tries another one. Its dialog offers to write the strategy into the set that already handles the site, so no second set is needed.

The card's badge says why no strategy was found: Badge Cause and fix address blocked Connections to every address of the site fail, and no bypass strategy can help. The site needs a VPN or a proxy. intercepted by the gateway The first hop in front of b4's host answers the connection itself. When that hop is another router, b4 has to run on it, or b4's host has to be excluded from its redirect. When b4 runs on the main router, only a proxy helps. does not resolve The name has no address, as with a misspelled domain. link answers 400 The link answers HTTP 400 even without b4. The link of a page or a file the site serves is needed. nothing found A new run with TLS version for the probes set to TLS 1.2, or with a captured ClientHello, sometimes helps. Otherwise a VPN or a proxy is left. The DPI Detector shows how the ISP blocks a site: by resetting connections, dropping them, forging DNS answers or cutting long transfers. It checks many sites at once, and Fix N with Discovery opens Discovery with the sites still blocked filled in. When the set exists but the site still does not open: Traffic shows another set in the Set column: that set handles the site, and the new strategy has no effect there. Applying the result with Write the strategy into an existing set and that set puts the strategy where it applies. The browser can reach the site over QUIC (HTTP/3), which Discovery does not test. Block QUIC (force TCP) on the set's UDP tab makes the browser use TCP. The browser can connect over another IP version than the run, for example over IPv6 while the run tested IPv4. A new run with IP version for the probes set to the browser's version tests the site the way the browser reaches it. The page opens without its styles or images: the other hosts they come from can be blocked too. The result card lists the page hosts that the strategy opens, and Apply in the Discovery history offers them again. The site opened before and stopped later: Keeping sets working shows how the watchdog searches for a new strategy on its own. The full list of checks, from the quickest to the slowest, is under A site does not open.
A set in Network interface mode sends the traffic of its sites through an interface of the router, such as a WireGuard or OpenVPN tunnel or a second uplink. Everything else keeps the normal route.
documents.s: Routing sites through a VPN or another interface

documents.t: An interface that is up on the router: a VPN client set up outside b4, such as WireGuard or OpenVPN, or a second uplink. The ip command and a firewall backend: nftables, or iptables with the ipset command. A set with the sites as domains, or with their IP addresses, CIDR ranges, GeoIP categories or ASNs. See Adding sites to a set.

Open Sets and open the set, or click Create Set and add the sites on the Targets tab. Open the DNS & Routing tab, then Traffic Routing. Turn on Enable Routing. Set Routing mode to Network interface. In Output Interface, select the VPN interface, such as wg0. Turn on Kill switch if the set's sites must never use the normal uplink. Click Save Changes, or Create Set for a new set. The fields are described under Network interface. To send everything a device sends through the VPN, select the device under Targets > Source Devices and turn on Match any IP address under Targets > Bypass IPs.

Add ipinfo.io to the set's domains for the test. On a device, open https://ipinfo.io/ip or run curl -s https://ipinfo.io/ip. The address shown is the VPN's exit address, not the router's. A single address like this is the clearer test: a full web page loads parts from other hosts, and it can look broken while routing works. With a tunnel as the output interface, the set's connections end with [routed->wg0] on the Logs page. System Info on Settings > System > Service shows the number of installed routing sets in the Routing Sets row under Firewall.

Without the Kill switch, the set's traffic leaves through the normal uplink with the router's real address while the VPN is down. With it, that traffic is dropped until the interface returns. Router's own traffic decides whether connections the router opens itself follow the set. Automatic is the usual choice. A setup with Xray, sing-box or another proxy reading a TUN device is covered in Using b4 with Xray or XrayUI.
documents.s: Kill switch and the router's own traffic

documents.t: The VPN can run on another device in the router's network, such as a Raspberry Pi or a second router. The set then sends its sites to that device, which forwards them into its VPN. Follow steps 1 to 4 of Setup. In Output Interface, select the interface that faces the device, such as the LAN bridge. In Gateway (optional), enter the device's address in that network, such as 192.168.1.10. Click Save Changes, or Create Set for a new set. Devices in that network follow the set over IPv4, and the device's own traffic keeps the normal route. IPv6 from that network never follows the set. With an IPv4 gateway and Enable IPv6 Support on, the set's IPv6 traffic leaves through the output interface by that interface's own route, as without a gateway. b4 ignores a gateway outside the network of the output interface, and the log says why. When the sites stop opening once the gateway is set, the address in Gateway (optional) is not a device that forwards the traffic, or the VPN on the device is down. The log shows no error then: packets leave, and no reply comes back. See Gateway.
documents.s: Sites through a VPN on another device

documents.t: The set routes nothing. Routing matches destination addresses, and the tab warns when the set has no domain, IP or ASN target. Source devices alone select no traffic. The output interface is marked unavailable. The VPN is down, or its interface has another name now. Routing resumes when the interface is back. A device uses encrypted DNS. b4 does not see that device's DNS answers, and the first connection to a new address can take the normal route. Turning off secure DNS in the browser, or Private DNS on Android, fixes it. See DNS. Another service routes the traffic first. VPN and proxy tools add their own ip rule entries, and a rule with a lower priority takes the packets before b4's. See Using b4 with Xray or XrayUI. The Routing Sets row shows an error. The firewall rejected the rules. When the rules cannot be installed lists the causes.

Xray with a TUN inbound and a b4 set in Network interface mode both put a route in front of the kernel's normal one. Run together, they meet in three places, and b4's web interface shows only one of them. The same applies to any service that terminates connections behind a TUN device: sing-box, a tun2socks client, or Xray run by hand instead of by XrayUI.
documents.s: Using b4 with Xray or XrayUI

documents.t: Xray's TUN inbound creates a network device, xray0 below, and reads packets from it. It does not forward them: it terminates each connection, opens its own to the same destination from the same host, and copies bytes between the two. { "protocol": "tun", "tag": "ibd-tun", "settings": { "name": "xray0", "address": ["192.168.10.1/24"] }, "sniffing": { "enabled": true, "routeOnly": true, "destOverride": ["http", "tls", "quic"] } } The device carries nothing by itself. Traffic reaches it through an ip rule and a routing table. XrayUI installs its own, and b4 installs its own for a set in Network interface mode. The rule priority decides which one applies, not the order in which the services were set up.

b4's capture filter. For forwarded traffic, Capture Interfaces under Settings > Core > Packet Engine compares the interface a packet leaves by. Once anything routes into the tunnel, that is xray0, so a list naming the uplink excludes everything the tunnel carries. See Which interface is which. b4's marking. A set with routing on marks the packets to its addresses. This is the part the web interface shows. The ip rule list. The kernel walks the rules from the lowest priority number up and stops at the first one that gives a route. b4's rule has priority 10000 + table number. XrayUI in TUN mode adds one at priority 51 for the whole local subnet: 51: from 192.168.1.0/24 lookup 250 10169: from all fwmark 0x4d05/0x27fff lookup 169 Table 250 has a default route, so every packet from the local network ends there, and b4's rule is never reached, whatever mark the packet carries. b4's interface reports nothing, because b4's own rules are correct. warning Two services that both do policy routing do not merge. The one with the lower priority number takes every packet its selector matches. ip rule on the router shows the real order; neither web interface does. Every mark and ip rule of b4, and the values of Xray, XKeen and XrayUI, are in Packet marks.
Both arrangements below work. A mixture of the two gives a set that marks traffic and changes nothing.

XrayUI's rule for the subnet stays. Every client's traffic goes through the tunnel, and b4 handles the DPI bypass of whatever still goes out directly. Capture Interfaces under Settings > Core > Packet Engine: none selected. The uplink there switches b4 off for the whole local network, because none of that traffic leaves by the uplink any more. Enable Routing on b4's sets: off. Its rule would never be reached.
documents.s: Xray routes everything, b4 only bypasses DPI

documents.t: b4's sets pick the destinations, and the tunnel carries only those. The rule for the subnet on the Xray side goes: in XrayUI by turning off its transparent routing for the subnet, by hand by not adding a from <subnet> lookup <table> rule. Left in place, it takes every client's traffic before b4. Capture Interfaces under Settings > Core > Packet Engine: none selected. On the set, DNS & Routing > Traffic Routing: Output Interface xray0, Source Interfaces none selected unless the set covers one segment, and Router's own traffic at Automatic. Xray still needs a route to its own server that does not lead back into the tunnel: the /32 exception XrayUI writes into its table, which both arrangements keep. Automatic keeps the router's own connections out of the tunnel, because Xray opens its own connection to each destination from the router, and routing it back into xray0 loops. Route it too is safe only when Xray sends none of the set's destinations to a freedom or direct outbound. See Router's own traffic.
documents.s: b4 decides what goes into the tunnel

documents.t: A set routed into a TUN, TAP or WireGuard interface does not run its bypass strategy: the segment b4 would change is the inner one, which never reaches the network as b4 wrote it. Its connections end with [routed->xray0] on the Logs page, and flags:routed finds them on the Traffic page. The strategy tabs keep their settings, which do not apply while the set routes into the tunnel. In NFQUEUE mode, a connection that another service sends into such an interface gets no strategy either; see Packets that leave by another route.
documents.s: Packet manipulation with a tunnel egress

documents.t: Each time xray starts, XrayUI adds this rule to the top of mangle PREROUTING: iptables -t mangle -I PREROUTING 1 -p tcp -m socket --transparent -j DIVERT DIVERT marks the packet 0x10000 and accepts it. The rule matches every packet addressed to a local transparent socket, which includes the connections b4 diverts to its own listeners: sets in the Upstream SOCKS5 proxy and Telegram over WebSocket (built-in) modes, and the Telegram over WebSocket switch. A packet the rule accepts never reaches b4's rule, and where no ip rule sends mark 0x10000 to the router itself, it leaves by the default route. The client's connection then never completes its handshake with b4's listener. On iptables b4 keeps its routing jumps above every rule in mangle PREROUTING that matches local sockets. When such a rule appears above them, the next firewall check moves b4's jumps back and logs a warning naming the rule. The check runs at the Firewall Monitor Interval (seconds) under Settings > Core > Firewall, 10 seconds by default. Until then the Telegram over WebSocket card reads Not working and names the rule, and Check again on the card moves the jumps back at once. With the monitor off, at interval 0 or with Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup on, only Check again or saving the settings restores the order. iptables -t mangle -L PREROUTING -n --line-numbers The order is right when every b4r_*_pre line comes before DIVERT.
documents.s: XrayUI's TPROXY rule and connections b4 diverts

documents.t: Each command runs on the router and answers for one layer: # 3. which table decides, for a client address ip rule ip route get 1.1.1.1 from 192.168.1.100 iif br0 # 2. whether b4 marks anything: packet counters on the set's chain iptables -t mangle -L -n -v | grep b4r_ nft list table inet b4_route # 1. whether b4 sees the clients at all: the Traffic page ip route get follows the real rules. A destination that comes back with a table b4 did not create does not reach b4's rule. A destination outside every set that still goes to the tunnel device is routed by another service, and a test of b4 against it measures that service.

b4 installs on Linux routers, computers and servers. Linux, OpenWrt, ASUS Merlin and Keenetic use the same installer script, run over SSH. It detects the platform and the processor architecture. On MikroTik and in Docker, b4 runs as a container. Platform Page Notes Any Linux distribution Linux Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Alpine, Arch and others, with systemd, OpenRC or SysV init OpenWrt 18.06 or newer OpenWrt A USB drive or extroot is recommended, since internal storage is small ASUS routers with Asuswrt-Merlin ASUS Merlin Needs Entware on a USB drive Keenetic routers with OPKG Keenetic Needs Entware and the Netfilter components MikroTik with RouterOS 7.21.1 or newer MikroTik A container on ARM64 or AMD64, with external storage formatted as Ext4. The official image or the community image Any system with Docker Docker Host network mode The memory, kernel and architecture requirements are listed under Requirements. After installation, the web interface listens on port 7000: http://<device address>:7000, for example http://192.168.1.1:7000 on a router. First steps continues from there.
Updating, backups, removal and the installer's diagnostics are described under Updating, backing up and removing.
The image is lavrushin/b4 on Docker Hub.

A docker-compose.yml file: services: b4: image: lavrushin/b4:latest container_name: b4 network_mode: host cap_add: - NET_ADMIN - NET_RAW - SYS_MODULE volumes: - ./config:/etc/b4 restart: unless-stopped Start: mkdir -p config docker compose up -d
mkdir -p config docker run -d \ --name b4 \ --network host \ --cap-add NET_ADMIN \ --cap-add NET_RAW \ --cap-add SYS_MODULE \ -v ./config:/etc/b4 \ --restart unless-stopped \ lavrushin/b4:latest

Parameter Purpose network_mode: host b4 works with the host's network stack directly NET_ADMIN Managing netfilter and the firewall rules NET_RAW Raw sockets SYS_MODULE Loading kernel modules -v ./config:/etc/b4 Keeps the configuration on the host

docker compose logs -f b4 # logs docker compose restart b4 # restart docker compose down # stop docker compose pull && docker compose up -d # update The update dialog of the web interface does not update a container. A container started with docker run is updated by pulling the new image and creating the container again.

After the start, the web interface is at http://localhost:7000 on the host, or at the host's address from another machine. The port is set under Settings > System > Web Server in Port, or in config/b4.json, see Configuration file.
A Keenetic router with OPKG support. Entware. The Netfilter components, see below.
Open the router's web interface. Open System settings. Turn on the OPKG package manager component.
Attach a USB drive to the router. Install Entware through the package manager. The Keenetic help has the details.
documents.s: Older models, with a USB drive

documents.t: KeeneticOS does not ship every netfilter module b4 needs, so two components are turned on before b4 is installed. The components are available only under the admin account. In the router's web interface, open System settings > Component options. Search the components for netfilter, and turn on Kernel modules for Netfilter if it is not on yet. Turn on Xtables-addons for Netfilter, which appears once the Netfilter modules are on. Apply the changes, then reboot the router or reload the components. Over SSH, install the iptables userspace: opkg install iptables

Over SSH on the router: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh The installer detects the architecture: mipsle_softfloat on older models (MT7621), arm64 on newer ones (aarch64). Without Entware Without Entware, b4 goes to /tmp, which is cleared on every reboot. Entware keeps b4 installed across reboots.
/opt/etc/init.d/S99b4 start /opt/etc/init.d/S99b4 stop /opt/etc/init.d/S99b4 restart
What Where Binary /opt/sbin/b4 Configuration /opt/etc/b4/b4.json Service /opt/etc/init.d/S99b4

KeeneticOS rebuilds its firewall from time to time and removes b4's rules with it. The installer adds a hook that makes b4 restore them as soon as the rebuild ends. The log lines this leaves are explained under Router platforms.
On KeeneticOS with a kernel before 4.18 (4.14 before 4.14.173), b4 copies DNS queries instead of holding them. What that changes is described under Router platforms.

After the service starts, the error log shows whether anything failed: cat /var/log/b4/errors.log The errors and their fixes are listed under Router platforms. With no errors, the web interface is at the router's LAN address, on port 7000.
The installer works on any distribution: Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Alpine, Arch and others.

As root: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh Or with wget: wget -qO- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh The installer puts the binary in /usr/local/bin and the configuration in /etc/b4. Without prompts, with the default settings: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --quiet Without a terminal, such as under cron or over ssh without -t, the installer runs as if --quiet were given.
systemctl start b4 systemctl stop b4 systemctl restart b4 systemctl status b4 systemctl enable b4 # start on boot Logs: journalctl -u b4 -f

documents.t: rc-service b4 start rc-service b4 stop rc-service b4 restart rc-update add b4 default # start on boot
/etc/init.d/b4 start /etc/init.d/b4 stop /etc/init.d/b4 restart /etc/init.d/b4 status

The NFQUEUE engine needs kernel modules that usually load when the service starts. When they do not, they can be loaded by hand: modprobe nfnetlink_queue modprobe xt_NFQUEUE modprobe nf_conntrack To check: lsmod | grep nfqueue On a kernel without these modules, the TUN engine is the alternative, see Packet engine.
In an LXC container, the kernel modules are loaded on the host. The container's configuration needs: lxc.cgroup2.devices.allow: c 10:200 rwm features: nesting=1,keyctl=1
An ASUS router with Asuswrt-Merlin firmware. Entware on a USB drive.
Attach a USB drive to the router. Connect to the router over SSH: ssh admin@192.168.1.1. Run amtm. Choose ep to install Entware. The amtm page has the details.
With Entware in place: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh
/opt/etc/init.d/S99b4 start /opt/etc/init.d/S99b4 stop /opt/etc/init.d/S99b4 restart Entware starts the service when the router boots.
What Where Binary /opt/sbin/b4 Configuration /opt/etc/b4/b4.json Service /opt/etc/init.d/S99b4
Without Entware, b4 goes to /jffs/b4 and does not start on boot: the binary has to be started by hand. /jffs is usually limited to about 60 MB, so a USB drive with Entware is the usual choice.
On MikroTik RouterOS 7, b4 runs as a container. RouterOS sends the traffic of chosen clients through it.
RouterOS 7.21.1 or newer, on ARM64 or AMD64. External storage (flash, SSD or HDD) formatted as Ext4. The router's internal memory is not enough for containers.

Besides the official lavrushin/b4 image, the community image wiktorbgu/b4-mikrotik is built for RouterOS and follows b4 releases with the same version tags. Compared with the official image: b4 runs as an OpenRC service, so it restarts without stopping the container; the firewall backend, nftables or iptables-legacy with ipset, is picked from the kernel modules RouterOS exposes; the priorities of the main and default routing rules are fixed, which RouterOS 7.22 passes into containers in a form that breaks policy routing; a companion container, wiktorbgu/dnsproxy-mikrotik, forwards DNS over DoH. Its setup is described on its page. wiktorbgu maintains it, not the b4 project, and its build sources are not published, so its contents cannot be checked against this repository. The steps below use the official image.

The steps use these values. They are replaced with the ones of the local network: Parameter Value Bridge network 192.168.210.0/24 Bridge gateway 192.168.210.1 Bridge name bridge-docker Container IP 192.168.210.10 Interface name B4 LAN network 192.168.100.0/24 DNS server 192.168.100.1 Routing table to_b4 Disk /usb1 Client list b4users
A bridge for the container network: /interface/bridge add name=bridge-docker port-cost-mode=short /ip/address add address=192.168.210.1/24 interface=bridge-docker network=192.168.210.0
A virtual Ethernet interface on the bridge: /interface/veth add address=192.168.210.10/24 gateway=192.168.210.1 name=B4 /interface/bridge/port add bridge=bridge-docker interface=B4
A routing table with a route through the container: /routing table add disabled=no fib name=to_b4 /ip route add check-gateway=ping gateway=192.168.210.10 routing-table=to_b4

The traffic of the clients in the b4users list goes through the container: /ip firewall mangle add chain=prerouting action=mark-connection \ new-connection-mark=b4_connections passthrough=yes connection-state=new \ dst-address-type=!local src-address-list=b4users in-interface-list=LAN \ place-before=0 /ip firewall mangle add chain=prerouting action=mark-routing \ new-routing-mark=to_b4 passthrough=no connection-mark=b4_connections \ in-interface-list=LAN log=no place-before=1 FastTrack skips mangle rules, so it is limited to unmarked connections: /ip firewall filter set [find action=fasttrack-connection] connection-mark=no-mark
/container/mounts add name=b4_etc src=/usb1/docker/b4-mounts/etc dst=/opt/etc/b4 The directory /usb1/docker/b4-mounts/etc has to exist on the disk.

The registry: /container/config set registry-url=https://registry-1.docker.io tmpdir=/usb1/docker/pull The container: /container add remote-image=lavrushin/b4:latest interface=B4 \ root-dir=/usb1/docker/b4-mikrotik mounts=b4_etc \ cmd="--config /opt/etc/b4/b4.json" start-on-boot=yes \ logging=yes dns=192.168.100.1 Once the image is pulled: /container start [find tag~"b4"] Where the provider intercepts DNS on port 53, public resolvers inside the container do not help. DoH on RouterOS works around it, with the container pointed at the bridge gateway, dns=192.168.210.1: /ip dns set use-doh-server=https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query verify-doh-cert=yes
The devices that go through b4 are added to the b4users list: /ip firewall address-list add list=b4users address=192.168.100.50 /ip firewall address-list add list=b4users address=192.168.100.51

Open the web interface at http://192.168.210.10:7000. Turn on NAT Masquerade under Settings > Core > Firewall. The masquerade interface stays at its default, all interfaces. Without masquerade, RouterOS sends the server's replies straight to the client, past the container. b4 then never gets the TLS ClientHello of a connection, and its strategies do not run. With masquerade, the connections leave the container from its address, 192.168.210.10, so rules after the container on RouterOS cannot tell the clients apart.

After the container starts, the web interface is at http://192.168.210.10:7000. Less disk wear USB flash drives and SD cards wear out with writes. Log Directory on the Logging card under Settings > System > Service set to /tmp/log/b4 keeps the logs in RAM. They are then lost on reboot.

RouterOS filters and translates everything that arrives from the WAN before it reaches the bridge. A b4 port, such as 3128 of the MTProto proxy, is reachable from outside only through a dst-nat rule towards the container: /ip firewall nat add chain=dstnat action=dst-nat in-interface-list=WAN \ protocol=tcp dst-port=3128 to-addresses=192.168.210.10 to-ports=3128 Expose to internet in b4 changes only the firewall inside the container and does not replace this rule, see Access from the internet.

/container stop [find tag~"b4"] /container remove [find tag~"b4"] /container add remote-image=lavrushin/b4:latest interface=B4 \ root-dir=/usb1/docker/b4-mikrotik mounts=b4_etc \ cmd="--config /opt/etc/b4/b4.json" start-on-boot=yes \ logging=yes dns=192.168.100.1 The configuration is on the mount point and stays when the container is created again.

A set can hand its traffic to a SOCKS5 proxy in another container on the same bridge, such as Xray, sing-box or mihomo with a SOCKS5 inbound. The set's Routing mode is Upstream SOCKS5 proxy, with the other container's address, for example 192.168.210.20, and its SOCKS5 port. RouterOS needs no extra rules: b4 reaches the proxy inside bridge-docker, and only the proxy's own connections go out through RouterOS. See Sending sites through a SOCKS5 proxy.
documents.s: Sending a set to another container

documents.t: Step 4 picks the traffic by client. To pick it by destination, such as a site's subnets, the destinations go into an address list, and the marking rules match it in place of b4users: /ip firewall address-list add list=via_b4 address=203.0.113.0/24 /ip firewall mangle add chain=prerouting action=mark-connection \ new-connection-mark=b4_connections passthrough=yes connection-state=new \ dst-address-type=!local dst-address-list=via_b4 in-interface-list=LAN \ place-before=0 /ip firewall mangle add chain=prerouting action=mark-routing \ new-routing-mark=to_b4 passthrough=no connection-mark=b4_connections \ in-interface-list=LAN log=no place-before=1 The route through the container stays in table to_b4 from Step 3. A route to the container in the main table does not work: the container sends its traffic back to RouterOS, and the main-table route returns it to the container instead of the WAN. The marking rules apply only to packets from the LAN interface list, so the packets the container sends back leave through the main table. bridge-docker is not in that list after Step 1. If it has been added, this rule keeps the container's packets out of the marking rules. It is added after them, so that place-before=0 puts it on top: /ip firewall mangle add chain=prerouting action=accept \ in-interface=bridge-docker place-before=0 b4 on a separate Linux machine needs the same layout: a subnet of its own, on its own RouterOS port, VLAN or bridge, with RouterOS as its default gateway; the route in to_b4 pointing at the machine; NAT Masquerade on in b4, as in Step 8; its interface out of the LAN interface list, or exempted by the same accept rule with its name in place of bridge-docker. On the clients' own subnet, the machine hands the server's replies straight to the clients, and RouterOS stalls or breaks their TCP connections.
documents.s: Routing chosen destinations through the container

documents.t: Everything b4 sends back to RouterOS leaves through the main route, whatever its set. A set's own DSCP value marks its packets, and by it RouterOS sends that set's traffic through another route, such as a VPN. Routing into the container, above, needs nothing of the kind. The value is turned on with Enable per-set DSCP on the set's DNS & Routing tab, here 31. wg-vpn stands for the VPN interface and via_vpn for its routing table: /routing table add disabled=no fib name=via_vpn /ip route add gateway=wg-vpn routing-table=via_vpn /ip firewall mangle add chain=prerouting action=mark-connection \ new-connection-mark=b4_dscp31 passthrough=yes connection-state=new \ connection-mark=no-mark in-interface=bridge-docker \ src-address=192.168.210.10 dscp=31 /ip firewall mangle add chain=prerouting action=mark-routing \ new-routing-mark=via_vpn passthrough=no connection-mark=b4_dscp31 \ in-interface=bridge-docker /ip firewall mangle add chain=prerouting action=mark-connection \ new-connection-mark=b4_other passthrough=yes connection-state=new \ connection-mark=no-mark in-interface=bridge-docker src-address=192.168.210.10 /ip firewall mangle add chain=postrouting action=change-dscp new-dscp=0 \ out-interface-list=WAN /ip firewall mangle add chain=postrouting action=change-dscp new-dscp=0 \ out-interface=wg-vpn /ip firewall nat add chain=srcnat action=masquerade out-interface=wg-vpn Rule What it does The first mark-connection Marks a connection from b4 whose first packet carries the value. connection-mark=no-mark keeps a connection already marked b4_other from moving to the VPN halfway, which would make it start over mark-routing Sends the marked connections into via_vpn. in-interface=bridge-docker keeps the server's replies, which share the connection mark, out of the VPN The second mark-connection Marks b4's other connections as b4_other, which keeps them out of FastTrack. FastTrack skips the change-dscp rules. In exchange, none of b4's traffic is fast-tracked change-dscp on WAN Clears the value before the internet change-dscp on wg-vpn Clears the value before the tunnel. Without it, the value reaches the VPN server inside the tunnel masquerade on wg-vpn Gives the connections the address of the VPN interface The FastTrack limit from Step 4 is required. Without it the marked connections are fast-tracked and leave through the main uplink with the VPN's source address. When the accept rule for bridge-docker from Routing chosen destinations is at the top of mangle prerouting, the three prerouting rules never see b4's packets. They go above it, with this added to each (the quotes are required): place-before=[find where action=accept in-interface="bridge-docker"] Variations: A second uplink instead of a VPN: the route in via_vpn points at the uplink's gateway, and the last two rules name its interface in place of wg-vpn. More values: each value needs its own mark-connection rule. A value that goes another way also needs its own connection mark, mark-routing rule, table, and the last two rules for its interface. b4 on a separate machine: its interface and address replace bridge-docker and 192.168.210.10. Reverse path filter: /ip settings rp-filter=strict drops the replies that come back through the VPN. loose and the default no let them in. In this layout the devices resolve names through RouterOS, so b4 learns the addresses of a set's domains only from TLS and QUIC names and from its own lookups. A connection to an address b4 has not learned yet stays on the main route. IP, GeoIP and ASN targets give a connection the value from its first packet. The rules were tested on RouterOS 7.24.5, for IPv4.
documents.s: Routing a set's traffic by its DSCP value

documents.t: A container that does not start, an unreachable web interface, traffic that does not reach the container and an engine that does not start are covered under Router platforms.
OpenWrt 18.06 or newer. Free space for the binary. Internal storage (the overlay) is often small, and the installer warns when less than 2 MB is free. A USB drive or extroot is recommended.

Over SSH on the router: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh When curl is missing: opkg update && opkg install curl ca-certificates Or with wget: wget -qO- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh The BusyBox wget that OpenWrt ships does not support HTTPS. The full version installs with: opkg update && opkg install wget-ssl ca-certificates
The installer tries to load the modules b4 needs. When it warns The kernel cannot queue packets to b4, it also prints the packages to install. The usual ones are below.
apk add kmod-nft-queue kmod-nft-nat kmod-nft-compat kmod-nft-conntrack

opkg update opkg install kmod-nft-queue kmod-nft-conntrack nftables-json coreutils-nohup For versions without nftables: opkg install kmod-nfnetlink-queue kmod-ipt-nfqueue iptables-mod-nfqueue iptables-mod-conntrack-extra
Installed modules may still need to be loaded by hand. A command that prints nothing has loaded its module: modprobe nft_queue modprobe nft_ct modprobe xt_connbytes
/etc/init.d/b4 enable # start on boot /etc/init.d/b4 start /etc/init.d/b4 stop /etc/init.d/b4 restart The service keeps running after the SSH session closes, so screen or nohup is not needed.
What With /opt (extroot or USB) Without external storage Binary /opt/bin/b4 /usr/bin/b4 Configuration /opt/etc/b4/b4.json /etc/b4/b4.json
After the start, the web interface is at http://<router address>:7000, for example http://192.168.1.1:7000.
A third-party package, luci-app-b4, adds b4 to the LuCI interface. It is in alpha and covers part of the features. The b4 web interface on port 7000 stays available.
A service that does not start, Could not process rule, slow speed and flow offloading are covered under Router platforms.
b4 updates from the web interface or with the installer script. An update keeps the settings, and a backup made before it is the usual precaution.

The bottom of the side menu shows the running version. When a newer stable release is out, it reads Update available, with both version numbers. Download a backup under Settings > System > Backup, see Backing up the settings. Click the version at the bottom of the side menu. The Version Management dialog opens. Pick a release in Select Version. Include pre-releases adds test builds to the list. Click Upgrade, or Downgrade for an older release. b4 runs the installer, which downloads the release, replaces the binary and restarts the service. The page reloads when b4 is back. The file update.log in the log directory, /var/log/b4 by default, records the last update started here. Don't Show Again hides the notice about that release in the current browser. The dialog cannot update b4 in Docker, where it shows the docker pull command instead, see Docker. It also refuses to update a b4 that was started by hand rather than as a service. When the router cannot reach GitHub, Downloading b4 when GitHub is blocked describes mirrors and Install from a file instead.

Over SSH, as root: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --update To a specific release, older ones included: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --update v1.46.5 The installer sets the current binary aside, stops the service, puts the new version in place and starts it again. A new binary that does not run is replaced by the previous one. The settings stay as they are. On MikroTik and in Docker, an update replaces the container, see MikroTik and Docker.

The Backup sub-tab under Settings > System holds the backup tools, described under System: Button What it does Download Backup Saves the configuration directory as a .tar.gz archive Upload & Restore Writes such an archive back. A restart applies it Download safe copy Saves b4.json alone, with passwords and tokens masked, for sharing The backup archive holds the passwords, tokens and secrets unmasked, so it is kept private. An update started from the web interface also saves a copy of b4.json next to it, named b4.json.bak.v<version> after the version it replaced.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --remove The installer stops b4, clears the firewall and routing rules b4 installed, and removes the service and the binary. When b4 cannot be stopped, nothing is removed. At the end the installer asks whether to delete the configuration directory, /etc/b4 or /opt/etc/b4, and keeps it unless the answer is yes. warning --remove --quiet deletes the configuration directory without asking. Without a terminal, such as under cron or over ssh without -t, --remove stops with an error unless --quiet is given.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --sysinfo The installer prints the system, the installed version and the state of the kernel modules. In the web interface, System Info under Settings > System > Service shows b4's own report, see System Info.

When neither curl nor wget can verify GitHub's certificate, and installing CA certificates does not help, the installer asks before it downloads over unverified TLS. With --quiet it stops instead. B4_ALLOW_INSECURE_TLS=1 in the environment allows the download for that run. A checksum fetched over the same connection only shows that the download is not corrupted.

The packet engine is the part of b4 that sees traffic. It reads the first packets of each connection, matches them against the sets and applies the strategies. Packets reach it in one of two ingestion modes, NFQUEUE or TUN, selected under Settings > Core > Packet Engine. Both depend on firewall rules that b4 installs and keeps in place.

In NFQUEUE mode, iptables or nftables rules hand packets to netfilter queues, and b4 reads them. b4 reads one queue per worker thread, numbered upward from Queue Start Number: 537 to 540 with the defaults. Only the start of each connection is queued. TCP Connection Packets Limit and UDP Connection Packets Limit under Settings > Core set how many packets, 19 and 8 by default. With iptables the count uses the connbytes match. The fakes and split segments b4 sends into a connection count toward the limit as well. A limit below these defaults is raised to them when the configuration is saved. The limits apply to every set.
