b4 fetches the prefixes itself from RIPEstat, the RIPE NCC data service: the prefixes the ASN originates as seen by the RIS route collectors, without announcements that only a few collectors see. Private, reserved and documentation ranges and default routes are dropped, a prefix inside a wider one is dropped, and two adjacent halves of a larger prefix are merged into it. The browser never contacts RIPEstat. The result is kept in asn_cache.json in the directory of the configuration file. Every set that names the ASN and every browser share the file, and the ASN labels on the Traffic page come from it. A file that is not valid JSON at start is moved aside to asn_cache.json.corrupt, and the ASNs the sets reference are fetched again.

Event What happens b4 starts asn_cache.json loads without a network request, and the sets use its prefixes however old they are. After a reboot without internet access, the sets keep matching the last known prefixes Right after start, then every hour A background check fetches each ASN that any set references, enabled or not, whose entry is missing or older than 20 hours. ASNs are fetched one at a time A set gains an ASN without prefixes The check runs at once A fetch fails The last good copy stays in use. The next attempt follows after 30 seconds, and the wait doubles with each further failure, up to one hour The prefixes change Every set that references the ASN is expanded again, and the firewall rules are refreshed An answer without prefixes is refused. An answer that covers less than half the address space known before, counted in IPv4 addresses or in IPv6 /64 networks, is held back. It is taken only after three fetches in a row, an hour apart, return the same shrink. Until then the previous list stays in use, so a gap in the RIPEstat data does not empty a set. Refresh from RIPEstat in the set editor follows the same rule: it keeps the previous list and reports the shrink, and only the background check can accept it.

An ASN without cached prefixes contributes no addresses, and the set does not match that network's traffic until the first fetch succeeds. The set editor and the set card show it as unresolved. A set whose domains, addresses, categories and ASNs all resolve to nothing matches nothing: it does not act on every connection to its ports, its MSS clamp is not installed, and its routing rules appear once a target resolves.

The prefixes join the set's address list after the GeoIP categories and before the addresses entered by hand. The set's IP Version Filter applies to them strictly: with IPv4 only the IPv4 prefixes are loaded, with IPv6 only the IPv6 ones. From there an ASN behaves like the same prefixes entered as IP addresses: the DPI bypass, routing, blocking, packet duplication and the MSS clamp all use them, and an ASN counts as an IP target for the scope of the MSS clamp. A set with ASN targets and no domains cannot be kept working by the watchdog, which confirms the set that handles a site by its host name.
documents.s: How the prefixes join a set

documents.t: No size limit is enforced. A large network expands into thousands of prefixes. Each prefix is an element of the firewall sets that routing, packet duplication and the MSS clamp build, and an entry in b4's address matcher. On a small router this costs memory and load time. The Networks (ASN) panel on Bypass IPs warns above 2,000 prefixes or 16,777,216 IPv4 addresses.

A set with Enable Routing on steers its traffic with firewall rules, packet marks and policy routing. The fields are described on DNS & Routing. Every mark bit, ip rule priority and table of b4 is listed in Packet marks.

Every rule b4 installs for a set matches the destination address. Source interfaces and source devices only narrow whose traffic reaches the rule, so a set with no domain or IP target gets no rule, and the log says so. Source How the address enters the set IP, CIDR, GeoIP and ASN targets Written on every configuration sync, removed when they leave the targets DNS answers for the set's domains Forwarded or pinned answers that b4 sees, and the answers of the set's DNS redirect. Kept for Resolved IP TTL (seconds) b4's own lookups The set's domains, resolved when routing is turned on, through the set's resolver when it has one. See Lookups b4 makes itself TLS and QUIC names The destination of a connection whose ClientHello or QUIC Initial names a domain of the set, other than a private address that no set's Bypass IPs list; over QUIC, no private address is learned at all. That connection has already left by the normal route; later ones follow the set. A subdomain matched this way is resolved in full. Not in Block (blackhole) mode, which blocks such a connection by its name instead A set with IP priority keeps its addresses from the sets below it in the list when neither is limited to source devices. Those sets do not learn them from DNS answers, b4's own lookups, TLS and QUIC names or escalation. The sets on that set's escalation chain are the exception and learn them. IP, CIDR, GeoIP and ASN targets are never affected. With the NFQUEUE engine, a forwarded or pinned answer that brings new addresses is held until they are written to the set, at most 250 ms each time b4 sees it, so the connection that follows usually takes the set's route. An answer from the set's DNS redirect goes out after the addresses are written, without the limit. With the TUN engine the answer is not held, and the first connection to a new address can leave before the address is in the set.

Marking. The set's chain in PREROUTING, b4r_<set>_pre, marks forwarded traffic to the set's addresses, only from the source interfaces when the set has them. Its chain in OUTPUT, b4r_<set>_out, gives the mark to the packets b4 injects for the set's destinations, which would otherwise leave by the normal uplink, and to the router's own traffic unless Router's own traffic keeps it out. Policy routing. An ip rule sends the mark to the set's routing table, whose default route points at the output interface, or at the set's gateway on it. Masquerade. POSTROUTING masquerades the set's traffic leaving through the output interface, so the replies return through it. An egress IP replaces it with SNAT.

Each set gets a mark from a hash in 0x100-0x7EFF, counted up from 0x66 when every hashed value is taken, and a table in 100-249. Both come from the interface name, the egress IP, the gateway and the kill switch, and stay the same across restarts. Sets that agree on all four share them. b4 skips a table that holds routes it did not add, as the VPN clients of Asuswrt-Merlin do in this range, a table named in an rt_tables file (/etc/iproute2/rt_tables, rt_tables.d/*.conf, and the same under /opt/etc/iproute2, /usr/share/iproute2 and /usr/lib/iproute2), and one that another service's ip rule looks up. It logs the move to the next candidate. routing.fwmark and routing.table in the configuration file pin both values when both are set, the mark lies within 0x27FFF, is not 0x24BAB (Telegram over WebSocket), does not contain every bit of the queue mark and does not equal its bits under 0x27FFF.

When the output interface is a tunnel that is up, a TUN or TAP device or WireGuard, b4 leaves the set's packets alone, as in proxy mode: no faking, fragmentation or desync, no SYN health check, dead-IP escalation, IP block detection or TCP duplication. The segment it would change is the inner one, which the router wraps or terminates. The connection is logged with routed-><iface>. A set routed to a plain interface, a set whose output interface exists but is down, and a domain-only set with no IP targets keep the strategy. A set limited to source interfaces or source devices hands off like any other: the packet engine matches on the destination alone.

A proxy with a TUN inbound, such as Xray, sing-box or a tun2socks client, terminates each connection and opens its own to the destination from the router. With the router's traffic routed, b4 marks that connection and sends it back into the TUN the proxy reads. Every turn has a fresh source port, so the kernel sees no repeat, and each turn costs the proxy another socket until memory runs out. Automatic leaves the router's own traffic on the normal route when the output interface is a TUN or TAP device. b4 recognises one by /sys/class/net/<iface>/tun_flags, which the kernel creates for every device opened through /dev/net/tun. WireGuard, PPP, VLANs and physical interfaces cannot re-dial a connection, and Automatic routes the router's traffic into them. A proxy that reaches some of the set's destinations directly (a freedom or direct outbound, a bypass rule, its own DNS) loops the same way. Route it too on a TUN device logs a warning and puts a rate limit ahead of the marking: 200 new router connections per second per destination list, counting only connections to the set's addresses. The limit goes on TUN and TAP devices and on interfaces that do not exist yet when the rules are built, never on a plain interface or WireGuard. On iptables it needs xt_hashlimit, which b4 loads, and warns about when missing. A set with a source interface or included source devices never routes the router's own traffic. An exclude list does not scope the set that way.

When the output interface disappears, the kernel removes the default route of the set's table. The mark rule finds an empty table, the lookup falls through to the main table, and the set's traffic leaves through the normal uplink. The rules still look correct. The kill switch adds blackhole default metric 4096 behind the real route. When the interface goes away, the blackhole drops the set's traffic; when it returns, b4 puts the real route back. A set with the kill switch on gets a table of its own, so it does not blackhole its neighbours. Two sets pinned to the same routing.table still share it, and the switch is then on for both if it is on for either.

An egress IP replaces the set's masquerade with SNAT --to-source, pinned to the output interface so a multi-WAN failover cannot send the packets out another uplink with this source. The device upstream routes by that source; b4's host needs no tunnel and no extra table. b4 adds the address to the output interface, puts it back when the interface loses it, for example on a DHCP renewal, and removes it when no set uses it. It sends an ARP probe first. When another host answers, or the address cannot be added, b4 logs a warning and keeps masquerading. An address configured by hand is used as it is and never removed. The upstream device routes that source, for example with ip rule add from 192.168.1.51 lookup 100 on Linux, or a mangle rule with src-address and action=mark-routing on RouterOS. A router upstream with strict rp_filter and no route back for that address drops the packets before any policy rule. This is the usual reason a correct-looking setup moves no traffic. An IPv4 egress IP rewrites IPv4 only. With Enable IPv6 Support on, the set's IPv6 traffic still leaves through the output interface, masqueraded; an IPv6 address in its place moves the rewrite to IPv6. With IPv6 support off, the set has no IPv6 rules, and its IPv6 traffic takes the normal route. With the TUN engine on the whole default route the setting has no effect.

Gateway (optional) gives the set's table default via <gateway> dev <interface> in the gateway's address family. Without a gateway, the default route goes via the gateway b4 finds on the interface, or is default dev <interface> when there is none. The other family keeps that route: with an IPv4 gateway, the set's IPv6 route is the one it has without a gateway, and the other way round. A gateway in a family whose support is off is ignored, and b4 logs a warning. A save checks only the form of the address. It refuses: anything but one IPv4 or IPv6 address, such as an address in brackets or with a prefix length; a %zone on an IPv4 address, and a %zone that names an interface other than the set's output interface; an unspecified, loopback or multicast address, and 255.255.255.255; the set's own egress IP. When b4 installs the set's rules, it checks the gateway against the router's addresses and its main routing table: A gateway is refused when it is Reason in the log One of the router's own addresses. A link-local gateway is compared only with the output interface's own addresses is one of this router's own addresses Not on a network the output interface reaches directly is not on a network <interface> reaches directly The network or broadcast address of an IPv4 network up to /30, or the network address of an IPv6 network shorter than /127 is the network address of <prefix>, is the broadcast address of <prefix> The interface reaches a gateway directly when the gateway lies in the prefix of an address on the interface, or under a route of the main table through the interface that has no gateway of its own, host routes included. The prefix of an address added with noprefixroute counts only through such a route. An IPv6 link-local gateway is also reachable from an interface with a link-local address of its own. A refused gateway counts as no gateway in its family, for the route and for the guard below. While the interface is up and has a link, b4 logs one warning that names the set, the gateway, the interface and the reason. When the gateway becomes usable, b4 logs that the set now uses it. b4 runs the check at start, on every save, when the output interface comes up and when the firewall monitor sees the interface's address change. A set without a gateway leaves every packet that arrives on its output interface unmarked: devices on that interface's network never follow it. A usable IPv4 gateway changes that for IPv4 when the output interface is of the Ethernet type, as Ethernet ports, bridges, VLANs, Wi-Fi and TAP devices are (/sys/class/net/<interface>/type is 1). Such a set leaves alone packets addressed to the router itself and IPv4 packets from the gateway, and marks the IPv4 traffic of the other devices on that network. With several such sets on one interface, each also leaves alone the IPv4 traffic of the other sets' gateways. IPv6 that arrives on the output interface never follows the set, with an IPv6 gateway as well. On interfaces of other types, such as TUN devices, WireGuard and PPP, the gateway only sets the route. Sets routed through an interface lists the rules. A set with a usable IPv4 gateway on an Ethernet-type interface also drops the IPv4 ICMP redirects the router sends out of that interface. A redirect would point the devices there at the gateway directly, past b4. Sets that differ only in the gateway get separate marks and tables. Two sets pinned to one routing.table with different gateways overwrite each other's default route, and b4 logs a warning. A gateway that passes the check but does not forward the traffic, such as a mistyped address of another device on the network, breaks the set: packets leave, no reply comes back, and the rules look correct.

Listener. b4 opens a transparent listener on a port derived from the set's mark. Diversion. TPROXY rules in PREROUTING send TCP to the set's addresses, and UDP with Route UDP through upstream on, to the listener; an ip rule and a local route deliver it locally. The router's own addresses, broadcast and multicast are never diverted, so a set matching every address leaves the router's DNS, DHCP and web interface reachable. Where the kernel rejects the address-type match, b4 lists the router's addresses instead and logs it. While the firewall monitor runs, b4 rebuilds the rules with a new list when those addresses change. Relay. For each connection b4 opens a SOCKS5 CONNECT to the upstream and copies bytes both ways. The router's own connections reach the listener by a loop through lo, unless the set is limited to source devices or source interfaces. Proxy sets and Telegram over WebSocket lists the marks, rules and ports. With Route UDP through upstream off, b4 answers the set's UDP to port 443 with ICMP port unreachable, and browsers fall back to TCP. Otherwise a site that advertises HTTP/3 in alt-svc would be reached over QUIC directly, and the browser would keep that for the header's lifetime. With the option on, a set with Block QUIC (force TCP) on its UDP tab gets the same refusal: the diversion leaves UDP to port 443 out, and the rest of the set's UDP still goes to the listener. In both cases no later set that matches the same address diverts that UDP to port 443 either. The refusal is per address family, the IPv6 half only with Enable IPv6 Support on. It also applies to the router's own connections, unless the set is limited to source devices or source interfaces. With the option on and an upstream without UDP ASSOCIATE, the set's UDP is dropped, and b4 logs a warning.

With Send domain name to upstream on, the CONNECT carries a host name whenever b4 can tie one to the connection: The SNI or Host the connection carries is sent only when backed by a DNS answer b4 saw for the address in the last 30 minutes, or by the set's domain list. VLESS Reality, ShadowTLS and Telegram's fake-TLS proxies present an unrelated site's name, and sending it would lead there. A connection without a readable name, where the server speaks first (SMTP, IMAP, FTP), takes the device's own DNS answer for the address, then a name learned from a matching ClientHello, then a name b4 resolved for the set. It waits 250 ms for a ClientHello first, unless the device resolved exactly one name for the address or nothing could back a name. A name pinned in the set goes by its address. A name the upstream refuses, as a Tor exit does, is repeated with the address. UDP always carries the address. While some proxy set sends names, b4 records the question name of every A and AAAA answer on UDP port 53 it sees, and of the answers of a set's DNS redirect. The [proxy] line in the log carries a name either way; tls= appears only when b4 read the ClientHello. Tor with SafeSocks 1 refuses connections by address and logs Your application (using socks5 to port 443) is giving Tor only an IP address. Connections b4 cannot name, for example from a device with encrypted DNS that opens an address the set matches by IP, still arrive by address. Tor's SOCKS port has no UDP ASSOCIATE.

A client of b4's SOCKS5 proxy that asks for a host name a proxy set matches is handed to that set's upstream without the firewall rules. The name follows the rules above; with Send domain name to upstream off, b4 resolves it through the set's resolver, or the router's, and sends the address. A .onion name is never resolved locally and never goes direct. Fall back to direct on upstream failure applies when the upstream cannot be reached, not when it refuses a destination. This works without a DNS answer, so also in TUN mode and for names that exist only behind the upstream. The first set that matches the name decides. It has to be in proxy mode with its listener running, carry the router's own traffic (no source interfaces, no included source devices) and not use domain-only matching. A request by address, or for a name the deciding set does not cover, is opened by the router like any of its connections.

An upstream running on the router connects to its server from the router, so a set whose targets include that server, such as 0.0.0.0/0 or a broad GeoIP category, would loop. b4 recognises such a connection by the process that listens on the upstream's port, and sends it directly. An upstream host given as a name is resolved for this check, and 0.0.0.0 counts as the router. For an upstream on another device, a connection from that device goes direct when the set targets 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, or when b4 is relaying a connection to the same destination through that upstream at the moment. A server address inside a broad GeoIP set is not recognised; excluding the device under source devices leaves its traffic alone. The log names the set and the process, or the device, the first time. A mark on the upstream's outbound sockets with any bit under 0x27FFF, such as Xray's sockopt.mark set to 255, keeps its traffic out of the diversion altogether. See Next to other services.
documents.s: A set that covers its own upstream

documents.t: Each diverted connection is accepted, held for the dial timeout and closed. b4 logs it at most once a minute, and once more when the upstream answers again (reached its upstream ... again after N failed attempts): tproxy: set "TMDB" cannot reach its upstream 10.8.0.1:1080 (1 consecutive failures), traffic matched by this set is not getting through: dial upstream: dial tcp 10.8.0.1:1080: i/o timeout Copy JSON in System Info copies the same state under upstreams, with reachable, consecutive_failures and last_error.

With net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables at 1, the kernel runs the IPv4 PREROUTING rules for traffic entering through a network bridge, such as br-lan or docker0, inside the bridge code, and not again at the IP layer. The TPROXY rule assigns the connection to b4's listener in that pass, and the IP layer drops the assignment. The packet is still delivered locally, but no socket takes it: connections from the devices behind the bridge hang, with no connection line in the log. The router's own connections are diverted as usual. net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables does the same for IPv6. The per-bridge attributes nf_call_iptables and nf_call_ip6tables under /sys/class/net/<bridge>/bridge/ turn the pass on as well: it runs when either the global setting or the attribute is 1. This breaks the proxy mode, the Telegram over WebSocket mode and the Telegram over WebSocket switch. While one of them is active and bridge netfilter is on for a bridge with ports, b4 logs a warning naming the bridge, System Info shows it in the Bridge netfilter row, and the Telegram over WebSocket card warns. On OpenWrt the dockerd package turns both settings on at boot through /etc/sysctl.d/12-br-netfilter-ip.conf. They are turned off at runtime, and the same lines in /etc/sysctl.conf, applied after /etc/sysctl.d, keep them off after a reboot: sysctl -w net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=0 sysctl -w net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables=0 printf 'net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=0\nnet.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables=0\n' >> /etc/sysctl.conf Two Docker configurations rely on bridge netfilter: a network created with icc=false, whose containers are no longer isolated without it, and a disabled userland proxy, where without it a container cannot reach the ports other containers on its network publish. OpenWrt's default Docker configuration uses neither. In either one, dockerd sets the settings back to 1 each time it sets up an affected network, at every start too, so they do not stay off.

Backend Needs What b4 creates nftables nft The b4_route table with prerouting, output and postrouting chains, and address sets with interval and timeout iptables + ipset iptables, ipset Rules in the mangle and nat tables and an ipset of type hash:net per set; iptables-legacy is checked too Routing uses the backend of Firewall Engine, on Auto-detect the one b4 found for its other rules. Without ipset or iptables, routing falls back to nftables whenever nft is present. With neither backend, or without the ip command, b4 logs a warning at each start and save and installs nothing. b4 looks these commands up once per run, so a tool installed later takes effect after a restart. The b4 Docker image carries nft, iptables and ipset. Nothing is created for routing, not even the b4_route table, while no enabled set has routing on and the Telegram over WebSocket switch is off.

b4 installs the routing rules at start, on every save, and when the firewall monitor finds them missing. When the backend rejects the base of the rules, such as the b4_route table, no set is installed: [ERROR] Routing: failed to ensure base during sync (nftables): ensure table: ..., it will be retried When only some sets fail, each gets a line, Routing: failed to ensure rule for set '<name>' during sync: ..., and the others are installed. b4 retries after 10, 20, 40, 80, 160 and 320 seconds, then every 10 minutes. The retries log at the trace level. At the info level a cycle leaves three lines: Line Level When Routing: failed to ensure base during sync ... or Routing: failed to ensure rule for set ... ERROR The first failure of a configuration Routing: the routing sync keeps failing; b4 retries it every 10m0s ... WARN The sixth retry fails, 10 minutes 30 seconds after the first failure Routing: the routing sync that failed has been retried successfully INFO A retry succeeds A save or a restart starts the cycle over. While a retry after a failure at the base is pending, the firewall monitor leaves the routing rules alone. A kernel without what the backend needs, such as nftables without the inet family or iptables without the ip_set module, fails every retry until the kernel or the backend changes. The Routing Sets row under Firewall in System Info shows how many routing sets are installed, and the backend. While installing fails, the rows below give the error of the base or of each set, when the failure began and the next attempt, and the missing tool, usually ipset, when its absence makes routing use nftables.
documents.s: When the rules cannot be installed

documents.t: When routing is turned off or a set is removed, b4 removes the set's ip rule, its routes, the jumps from the base chains, and the chains and address sets it created. When b4 stops, it cleans both backends of leftover rules.
How a set's own DSCP value is written, which packets carry it and the rules behind it are described in DSCP rules.

b4 (Bye Bye Big Bro) is a service for Linux routers and computers. It helps open sites that an internet provider blocks with DPI (Deep Packet Inspection), and it can send chosen sites through a VPN or a proxy. It is managed from a web interface in the browser. Installed on a router, b4 covers every device on the network, with no setup on the devices themselves.

Helps open blocked sites. A set changes how the packets of chosen sites look to the provider's DPI. The site receives the same data. See Unblocking a site. Routes chosen sites through a VPN or another interface. See Routing sites through a VPN or another interface. Sends chosen sites to a SOCKS5 proxy, such as Xray or sing-box. See Sending sites through a SOCKS5 proxy. Blocks ads and unwanted sites for the whole network. See Blocking ads and sites. Sends the DNS queries of chosen domains to another resolver. See DNS. Carries Telegram through its own proxy or bridge. See Telegram. Limits any of this to chosen devices. See Applying b4 to selected devices.

It changes nothing until a set targets sites. It does not provide a VPN or an upstream proxy. Route sets use a VPN interface that already exists, and the Upstream SOCKS5 proxy mode a proxy that already runs. No packet change helps when the provider blocks a site's addresses. Discovery then reports address blocked, and only a route or proxy set opens the site. It does not see DNS that a device encrypts itself, such as secure DNS in a browser or Android Private DNS. The DNS settings of the sets do not apply to such lookups. IPv6 connections skip the sets until Enable IPv6 Support is turned on under Settings > Core > Packet Engine.

b4 checks the first packets of each connection against the sets. A connection that no set matches passes unchanged. A matched connection is handled by the kind of its set: Key concepts explains sets, strategies and the set kinds.

The pages of the web interface, in the order of its menu: Page What it is for Dashboard Whether b4 runs, which sets match traffic, and what needs attention Sets The list of sets and the set editor Discovery Finds a strategy for sites that do not open and turns it into a set Community Sets that other b4 users published, applied in one step Watchdog Checks the sites of chosen sets on a schedule and finds a new strategy when they stop opening DPI Detector Reports what the provider blocks and how Traffic The connections b4 sees, live, with the set each one matched Logs The b4 log in real time Settings The packet engine, devices, firewall, web interface and backups

Requirement Value System Linux on a router, a computer or a server, or Docker. The supported platforms are listed under Installation Kernel 3.13 or newer, with NFQUEUE support (nfnetlink_queue). Without it, the TUN engine is the alternative and needs /dev/net/tun and iptables Memory 64 MB free Disk About 30 MB for the binary, plus the configuration and the GeoSite and GeoIP databases Privileges root Architectures amd64, 386, arm64, armv5, armv6, armv7, mips, mipsle, mips_softfloat, mipsle_softfloat, mips64, mips64le, loong64, ppc64, ppc64le, riscv64, s390x
The Logs page shows the b4 log as it is written.

Control What it does Filter logs... Shows only the lines that contain the text, ignoring case. ERROR, WARN, INFO, TRACE, DEBUG Show or hide the lines of each level. Each chip counts its lines. Streaming / Paused Pauses the stream and resumes it. Clear Logs Removes the lines shown in the browser. The log on the router is not affected. P or Pause pauses and resumes the stream, Ctrl+X or Delete clears it.

A trace saves the log of one session to a file, for a bug report. Click Start trace. Reproduce the problem. Click Stop & save. The browser downloads the trace file. Download last trace downloads the last trace again. The file starts with the b4 version, a system diagnostics snapshot and the enabled sets, followed by the log lines written during the session. A trace stops by itself after 15 minutes. Only the last trace is kept. Reporting a problem lists what else a bug report needs.
Log Level in the Logging card under Settings > System > Service decides how much detail the log carries, see Logging.

b4 carries Telegram traffic in three ways. They are independent and can run at the same time. MTProto proxy: a proxy server on b4 that Telegram connects to with a secret. Every Telegram client supports it, from anywhere its port is reachable, such as a phone on mobile data. Telegram over WebSocket: one switch that relays Telegram from every device behind b4 and from the router, with nothing to set up on the devices. Telegram Desktop WEB proxy: the MTProto proxy served as an ordinary HTTPS site, for Telegram Desktop 7.1.1 and later.

MTProto proxy Telegram over WebSocket WEB proxy Set up in Settings > Telegram MTProto Proxy card Telegram over WebSocket card, or a set's routing mode Telegram Desktop WEB proxy card On the device A proxy entry with a secret Nothing A proxy entry from a link Devices covered Any Telegram client, inside the network or outside it Every device behind b4, and the router itself Telegram Desktop 7.1.1 and later Needs the MTProto proxy on Yes No Yes Needs a public hostname Only for devices outside the local network No Yes, with a publicly trusted certificate Needs TPROXY in the kernel No Yes No On the home network, Telegram over WebSocket needs nothing on the devices. A phone away from home needs the MTProto proxy. The WEB proxy suits b4 on a VPS with a hostname and a certificate of its own.

All three reach Telegram through the shared Telegram upstream settings. A Cloudflare Worker is the route to add when media does not load, and a DC Relay helps where the WebSocket routes are blocked as well. Telegram problems lists symptoms and their fixes, and Settings > Telegram describes every field.
This tutorial goes from opening the web interface to a set that opens a blocked site. It starts once b4 is installed and running.

Open http://<address>:7000 in a browser. <address> is the address of the router or computer b4 runs on, for example http://192.168.1.1:7000. On that computer itself, http://localhost:7000 works too. When a username and password were set during installation, sign in with them. When HTTPS was turned on during installation or under Settings > System > Web Server, the address starts with https://. A browser warns about a self-signed certificate, and the warning can be accepted. The dashboard opens. With no sets yet, the Sets panel reads No sets yet: b4 changes nothing until a set targets sites. The Dashboard page describes every panel.

Sets that other b4 users published can be tested before b4's own strategies. Discovery does this while the Community Hub is on. Open Settings > Integrations and turn on Enable Community Hub in the Community Hub card. Click Save Changes. Community then appears in the side menu, and Discovery shows Try community sets first, on by default: it tests up to three published sets for each site before the built-in strategies. With the hub on, b4 syncs the catalogue from hub.b4core.app. What leaves the router lists what the hub receives.

Click Find a strategy with Discovery on the Sets panel, or open Discovery in the side menu. Type the address of a site that does not open into Site or URL and press Enter. Several sites can go in at once, separated by commas. Click Start. b4 tries its strategies on the sites. A run takes from one to ten minutes, depending on the provider. When it ends, every site gets a verdict: Verdict Meaning and next step confirmed 3 of 3, not confirmed A strategy made the site load. The next section applies it no bypass needed The site loads without b4. There is nothing to apply address blocked The provider blocks the site's addresses, and no strategy can help. The site needs a set that sends it through a VPN or a proxy intercepted by the gateway A device in front of b4 answers for the site. b4 has to run on that device. When b4 runs on the router itself, only a proxy set helps does not resolve The name has no address, as with a typo nothing found No strategy loaded the site. Discovery describes what to try next

Click Apply as a set on the card of a site with a strategy found. Check the rows under The set will. They describe what the set does. Keep the suggested Set name or type another one. Click Create set.

Open the site in a browser on a device in the network. Open Traffic in the side menu. The Set column shows the name of the new set next to the site's domain. The Sets panel of the dashboard counts the connections the set matched as well. When the site still does not open, Unblocking a site lists the next steps. A browser that had the site open before keeps reusing its old connections, see The browser opens new connections.

Adding sites to a set: more domains, or whole GeoSite categories. Keeping sets working: the watchdog and escalation. Securing the web interface: it has no password until one is set. Key concepts: sets, targets, strategies and the set kinds.

A set ties a list of targets, such as domains, addresses or networks, to what b4 does with their traffic: a DPI bypass strategy, a route through another interface or a proxy, or a block. The Sets page lists the sets and opens the set editor. Guides that start here: Unblocking a site, Adding sites to a set, Blocking ads and sites, Importing from zapret or byedpi and Sharing a set.

Control What it does Enable All / Disable All Turns every set on or off at once. Search sets... Shows only the sets whose name, domains, GeoSite categories or ASNs contain the text. Select Selects several sets. Delete removes the selected sets after a confirmation, and Cancel leaves the selection. Import Builds sets from a byedpi or zapret command line, see Importing from zapret or byedpi. Create Set Opens the editor for a new set.

The handle at the top left of a card drags the set to another position. When several sets could match the same traffic, b4 picks the most specific match, not the first set in the list, and prefers a set limited to source devices. The order decides only between matches that are equally specific. Routing is the exception: the length of the range plays no part there. Sets limited to selected devices or source interfaces come first, and among sets of the same kind the one higher in the list wins. The order also matters for a set with IP priority on. Connections to its addresses stay with it even when a set lower in the list matches the domain. How sets match traffic describes the full order of checks.

A click on a card opens the set in the editor. Part Shows Switch and number The switch turns the set on or off. The number is the set's position in the list. Name and targets The set's name and a summary of its targets. Route line What the set does with the traffic it matches: Default route for a set that only applies a bypass strategy, the interface or socks5 proxy it routes through, Telegram bridge, or block with the block action. Facet rail The marks along the top of the card: Target, Split, Fake, Route, DNS and Escalate. A mark opens a summary of that part of the set, with a link to its tab in the editor. Compare across sets above the list opens the same part on every card at once. Badges escalates to names the backup set, and fallback for names the sets that use this one as their backup. N ASN unresolved means an ASN has no prefixes yet. Watchdog appears while Keep this set working with the watchdog is on for the set, and opens the watchdog page. Imported shared set and Community set mark a set that came from someone else. The menu at the top right of a card holds: Item What it does Edit Opens the set in the editor. Duplicate Creates a copy of the set right after it. The copy starts with IP priority off. Compare Opens Compare Sets with this set and another side by side. Differences only hides the fields that match. Find a strategy Opens Discovery for the set. Not shown for a set that routes its traffic. Delete Deletes the set after a confirmation.

The top bar holds the set's name. Save Changes, or Create Set for a new set, saves it, and so does the round button at the bottom right. Back and Cancel return to the list without saving. Tab What it holds Targets Which traffic the set applies to: domains, GeoSite categories, addresses, GeoIP categories, ASNs and source devices. TCP The DPI bypass strategy for TCP, on the General, Splitting and Faking sub-tabs. UDP Which QUIC and other UDP traffic the set matches, and what b4 does with it. DNS & Routing The DNS redirect, routing through an interface or a proxy, blocking, and the set's DSCP value. Escalation A backup set for the sites this set keeps failing on. Discovery The addresses Discovery tests for the set, the last search for it, and the watchdog switch. Import/Export The set as JSON, and a shared set for other people.

The tab shows the set as JSON under Set Configuration JSON. Copy JSON copies it. A JSON pasted into the field and loaded with Import replaces the content of the editor, and it takes effect after Save Changes. The JSON is for moving a set between one's own routers. It leaves out what only makes sense on this router: the source devices, and with them the set's own DSCP value; the Escalation settings, which point to other sets; the IP priority switch: a set the JSON is imported into keeps its own; the watchdog switch. The Discovery addresses are carried, and the watchdog switch of the set the JSON is imported into stays as it was. These are set again on the other router. A set can use a payload file that this router does not have. A warning after the import then names the file, and the fake packets use a built-in payload until it is uploaded under Settings > Payloads. A set for someone else is a shared set, which leaves out everything tied to this router. With the Community Hub switched on under Settings > Integrations, the same tab prepares one. The Import field accepts both forms.

A block set stops the traffic it matches instead of sending it anywhere. It blocks ad and tracker domains, unwanted sites or addresses for every device on the network and for the router itself, and it needs no interface or proxy.

The devices resolve names through the router. A device with encrypted DNS of its own is still blocked by the server name in its connections, see When it does not work. For GeoSite categories such as category-ads-all, the GeoSite database loaded under Settings > Geodat Settings. For IPv6, Enable IPv6 Support turned on under Settings > Core. Without it, blocking covers IPv4 only, see IPv6.

Open Sets and click Create Set. On the Targets tab, add what to block: domains or regexp: patterns, IP addresses and CIDR ranges, GeoSite categories such as category-ads-all, or GeoIP categories. Adding sites to a set lists the ways. On the DNS & Routing tab, open Traffic Routing and turn on Enable Routing. Set Routing mode to Block (blackhole). Pick the Block action, see Block options. Reject (fail fast) is the usual choice for ads. Click Create Set. Changes apply without a restart.

Source Interfaces in the same Traffic Routing section limit the set to traffic that arrives on the selected interfaces, such as the bridge of a guest network. Devices on other interfaces and the router's own connections are then not blocked, and the other sets handle their traffic. Which interface is which explains the interface names.

A set with a broad list of ad and tracker domains and the category-ads-all category, already in block mode. To use it, create a set, open its Import/Export tab, paste the JSON below, click Import and save the set. The category needs the GeoSite database. {"b4_version":"1.65.0","name":"adblock","fragmentation":{"strategy":"none"},"faking":{"sni":false},"targets":{"sni_domains":["ad.mail.ru","advertronic.io","vu.okcdn.ru","adkernel.com","adfox.ru","nr-data.net","rubiconproject.com","adition.com","mc.yandex.com","log.strm.yandex.ru","analytics.yahoo.com","criteo.com","taboola.com","ad4m.at","1rx.io","hbx.media.net","media.net","adform.net","analyticsengine.s3.amazonaws.com","analytics.s3.amazonaws.com","ad.doubleclick.net","analytics.google.com","api.bugsnag.com","app.bugsnag.com","browser.sentry-cdn.com","app.getsentry.com","ads-api.twitter.com","log.byteoversea.com","log.fc.yahoo.com","adtech.yahooinc.com","appmetrica.yandex.ru","metrika.yandex.ru","fingerprintjs.com","px.srvcs.tumblr.com","device-metrics-us.amazon.com","cdn.cookielaw.org","consent.cookiebot.com","sdk.privacy-center.org","cdn.privacy-mgmt.com","api.impact.com","cdn.dynamicyield.com","widget.intercom.io","bnc.lt","bingads.microsoft.com","ads.microsoft.com","snap.licdn.com","ct.pinterest.com","geolocation.onetrust.com","consent.trustarc.com","app.usercentrics.eu","advertising-api-eu.amazon.com","fls-na.amazon.com","advertising.yandex.ru","ironsource.mobi","is.com","pangleglobal.com","posthog.com","o0.ingest.sentry.io","lr-ingest.com","mineralt.io","pixel.quora.com","qevents.quora.com","ads.vk.com","advertising.apple.com","ads.huawei.com","ngfts.lge.com","xp.apple.com","cmp.osano.com","consentcdn.cookiebot.com","zenaps.com","clientstream.launchdarkly.com","match.adsrvr.org","smartyads.com","adcolony.com","mouseflow.com","edge.fullstory.com","stats.wp.com","adsrvr.org","c.bing.com","app-measurement.com","cdn.segment.com","quantcast.com","rudderstack.com","snowplowanalytics.com","adjust.com","singular.net","wzrkt.com","ads.pinterest.com","ads.x.com","ads-sg.tiktok.com","tracking.rus.miui.com","cookiebot.com"],"ip":["5.255.255.77/32"],"geosite_categories":["category-ads-all"]},"enabled":true,"routing":{"enabled":true,"mode":"block"}}

The Block action decides what a device sees. Reject (fail fast) is the default. Option What the device sees Reject (fail fast) The connection fails at once: a TCP reset, or ICMP unreachable for UDP and QUIC. A page gives up on an ad slot right away. Drop (silent blackhole) Nothing comes back: the connection times out, and a lookup of a blocked name gets no answer. b4 blocks a site in three ways: DNS. A lookup of a blocked domain gets the answer that the name does not exist (NXDOMAIN), or no answer with Drop (silent blackhole). This covers every device whose DNS goes through the router. Server name. A device that already has an address, from encrypted DNS or a cache, is still stopped: b4 reads the server name in the TLS or QUIC handshake and fails the connection. Address. IP addresses, CIDR ranges and GeoIP categories are blocked in the firewall. The first two work by name, so other sites on the same servers as a blocked host keep working. Blocking by address on a shared CDN blocks every site behind that address.

On a device, the blocked site or ad does not load, and the rest of the page does. The dashboard shows the Blocked panel while a block set is enabled: Domains lists what was blocked, Devices the devices that tried to reach it. Connections that the firewall drops once a blocked site's addresses are known are not counted there. The set's row in the Sets panel shows how many DNS lookups it blocked. On the Traffic page, blocked packets carry the block label, and answers the set replaced carry the sinkhole DNS label. Ad-blocking test pages show the result in a browser. With the browser's own ad blocker turned off, they show what the block set catches: superadblocktest.com adblock.turtlecute.org getblockify.com obfusgated.com paileactivist.github.io adblocktester.pages.dev A block set stops lookups and connections and does not change pages, so test items that check hidden page elements pass only with a browser extension.

A device still opens a blocked site. The device may use encrypted DNS of its own (secure DNS in the browser, Android Private DNS) or a cached address. b4 still stops it by the server name, but not over IPv6 while IPv6 support is off, see IPv6. Turning encrypted DNS off on the device, or IPv6 support on in b4, closes the gap. Over QUIC, the block holds for the whole connection only while the row QUIC drop holds for the whole connection under Kernel Capabilities in System Info reads available. Where it reads unavailable, the row names what the router lacks. A device with a VPN of its own is not blocked. Traffic inside a tunnel the router cannot see is out of b4's reach. A GeoSite category blocks nothing. The GeoSite database is not loaded, or does not contain the category. Too much is blocked. A regexp: pattern can catch far more than intended, and so can an address on a shared CDN. A domain target keeps the block narrow.

Block rules are written only for the address families b4 handles. Enable IPv6 Support is off by default, and a block set then writes no IPv6 rules: DNS still hides the name from devices that resolve through the router, for A and AAAA lookups alike. A lookup that reaches the router over IPv6 itself passes unchanged. The server name of IPv6 connections is not checked. Address targets are blocked for IPv4 only. A device that already holds an IPv6 address of a blocked host therefore reaches it over IPv6. With Enable IPv6 Support on under Settings > Core and the service restarted, blocking covers both families. This is not the same as turning IPv6 off for the network, which is a router setting outside b4.

The Discovery tab of the set editor holds the pages Discovery tests for the set, the last search for it, and the switch that puts the set under the watchdog. Keeping sets working walks through it. A set that routes its traffic to a proxy or an interface applies no bypass strategy, so the tab is read-only for it.

Address adds a page that Discovery fetches when it searches a strategy for the set. The watchdog checks the same pages. Rule Effect Up to 5 addresses, one per host The field is disabled once the list is full. A domain Becomes https://<domain>/. A full URL Kept with its path. Only http and https addresses of public hosts Local and private addresses are refused. A strategy found on these pages applies to every domain the set targets, although only these pages were tested. For a set built on a GeoSite category, that is every entry of the category. Useful addresses are pages that represent the set, such as the main page of each service it covers, and pages that do not open without b4. A page that loads without b4 cannot show whether the set works. A set created by Discovery keeps the addresses it was found on. Use these addresses as the set's discovery URLs, in the Discovery apply dialog, stores the tested addresses in an existing set. Watch through <set> on the watchdog's older per-domain list adds the address of a domain. Discovery addresses describe the local network and stay on the router. A set shared or published to the Community Hub carries none, and an update from the hub keeps the local ones. The Import/Export JSON carries the addresses, but not the watchdog switch.

Suggest loads up to ten candidate addresses, one per host. Each one names its source: Saved for this set; From an earlier search for this set; From the DPI Detector site list, for sites of the DPI Detector list that the set matches; A domain listed in the set; A known page of a service in the set's geosite categories. Add puts a suggestion in the list. A suggestion for a host that another set handles names that set: a strategy written into this set does not affect it. A set whose targets are only large lists, such as ru-blocked, usually gets no suggestion, and a page has to be added by hand. Suggest and Find a strategy need a saved set.

Find a strategy opens Discovery with this set picked and its addresses in the field. Unsaved changes to the set are lost when Discovery opens. The Find a strategy item of the set card's menu on the Sets page does the same.

Keep this set working with the watchdog puts the set under the watchdog. The set's Discovery addresses are then checked on a schedule. When they keep failing, the watchdog searches for a new strategy, writes it into the set, checks the addresses again, and undoes the change if they still fail. Enable Watchdog under Settings > Discovery has to be on as well. While it is off, the set's switch can stay on, but nothing is checked. Condition When it does not hold The set is enabled The switch stays on, and the set is not checked until it is enabled. The set has Discovery addresses The switch stays on, and nothing is checked until an address is added. The set routes no traffic The switch turns off when the set is saved. The set is not limited to specific devices by an include list The switch turns off when the set is saved. The router's own check carries no device MAC and never matches such a set. The set targets domains or GeoSite categories The switch stays on, but the set is not checked. A set of only IP addresses, GeoIP categories or ASNs cannot be checked by name. A caption under the switch names the condition that fails. Once the set is saved with the switch on and Enable Watchdog is on, the tab shows its watchdog status and the time of the last check. It also shows the last heal with the strategy it wrote, and Open the watchdog. On the Sets page, the card of a watched set carries a Watchdog badge coloured by the status. A heal can change the set while the editor is open on an older copy. Saving that copy is refused with an offer to reload, which discards the unsaved changes.

Last search for this set shows the most recent Discovery run for the set: its verdict, when it ended, the strategy it found, and which addresses it covered. Open in Discovery opens Discovery with the set picked.

When a set keeps failing to open a site, escalation switches that site to a backup set. Name lookups and connections for the site then go through the backup. After a while, b4 tries the original set again. Keeping sets working shows how escalation fits with Discovery and the watchdog. A typical pair is a light set for most sites and a heavier one for the sites that need it. The backup does not have to be another bypass strategy: it can route through a proxy or an interface, or carry a pinned address or another DNS server for the site.

Field What it does Default Escalate to set The backup set. None turns escalation off. A disabled set is marked disabled: the link stays and sits idle until the set is enabled again. A set that handles only calls is not offered. None Sets can form a chain, A to B to C: b4 moves a site along it as each set fails, up to eight steps. A backup set limited to source devices is used only for those devices, and other devices stay on the original set. The tab suggests turning on RST Injection Protection in this set. It keeps the current page working while b4 detects the block.

Each trigger counts on its own, and whichever reaches its limit first switches the site over. Field What it counts Default Unanswered TLS handshakes How many times the same connection resends its ClientHello without an answer. 3 Handshake wait A resent ClientHello older than this also counts as unanswered. 3000 ms Forged resets Resets for the same site that b4 judges injected rather than sent by the server. 3 Reset counting window Resets count only within this time. 30 s Unusable DNS answers NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL or answers without an address for the same domain, after which the backup set resolves it. 2 A fourth trigger has no field: connection attempts to an address go unanswered, and the address does not answer the router either when b4 tests it. No bypass strategy helps such an address, while a backup set that routes the site elsewhere or pins another address does. For DNS, IPv4 and IPv6 lookups count separately, and an empty answer to an IPv6 (AAAA) lookup does not count, since a site without IPv6 answers that way. Lookups other than A and AAAA are not counted.
Field What it does Default Remember switch for How long a site stays on the backup set before b4 tries this set again, 5 to 1440 minutes. 60 min

The switch is per site. It applies to the host name that failed. Other sites on the same server stay on the original set. The backup takes over the whole site. Lookups use its pinned addresses, DoH server or forwarding, connections use its bypass strategy, and its routing applies. b4 writes the addresses it knows for the site into that routing. A set with IP priority keeps its connections. A connection that a set with IP priority keeps follows an escalation only to a backup on that set's own chain or ranked above that set. Between sets without source devices, a backup below such a set and off its chain never learns that set's addresses for its routing or DSCP value. Backups of the sets ranked above such a set are best placed above it or on its chain, when they route traffic or have a DSCP value. A backup placed there also takes the connections such a set keeps when their site escalates to it. IP priority has the details. The failed request is lost, the next one works. For the DNS trigger, the lookup that trips the switch is already answered by the backup set. The site comes back after Remember switch for. Clear on the dashboard's Active Escalations panel sends every site back at once and forgets the counted resets and DNS failures. Reset counters on the dashboard leaves the switches as they are. Escalation reacts to failures only, so the first failure of a site is still a failure. It does not replace Discovery, which finds a working strategy in advance. The log records each switch with its reason, for example: escalation: ntc.party is not getting through with ntc.party (no usable DNS answer), switching it to ntc.party backup
documents.s: How a site moves and comes back

documents.t: b4 reads a byedpi or zapret command line, or a whole configuration file, and turns it into sets. b4 is an independent implementation that shares no code, configuration format or option names with either tool, so the import is a translation: some options land exactly, some approximately, and some have no counterpart. The report lists what became of each option. This is not the Import/Export tab of the set editor, which moves a b4 set between b4 installations, see Sets.

The command line or configuration file of byedpi (ciadpi 0.13 or 0.15 to 0.17) or zapret (nfqws). Any other tool is refused with a message that names it. zapret2 is refused too: it keeps its strategies in Lua scripts, not in options. The domains the source tool works on. A host list is a file on the other machine, and the import cannot read it.

Open Sets and click Import. Paste the source into Command line. It accepts: an option list, such as -Ku -a1 -An -s1+s, with or without the program name; the ExecStart= and Environment= lines of a systemd unit; a variable such as NFQWS_OPT="..."; a whole configuration file, unedited, such as /opt/zapret/config, /opt/etc/nfqws/nfqws.conf or the Windows .bat that starts winws. Leave Source tool and Version on Detect automatically. When the report says Version guessed and the result looks wrong, pick the version by hand: byedpi changed the meaning of several options between 0.13 and 0.15. Click Analyze. Nothing is saved yet. Read the report, see The report. Enter the domains, see Domains. Shared domains go to the first set that takes targets and has no host list of its own, and each set has its own Domains (optional) field. The report warns when no set takes the shared domains. Click Create N sets. Importing moves domains away from existing sets A domain works in one set only. When an imported set claims a domain that an enabled set already targets, the domain is removed from that set. The message after the import names the sets that lost domains. The imported sets are placed ahead of the existing ones.

byedpi and zapret split a configuration into profiles, and each profile becomes a separate set, in the same order. byedpi starts a profile with -A/--auto: "try this when the previous attempt failed". The sets are linked with Escalation, and only the first one needs domains. byedpi's triggers on an HTTP redirect or a TLS error are reported as approximated. zapret starts a profile with --new, an alternative chosen by its own filters. These sets are independent. A byedpi profile limited to UDP, without filters of its own, joins the set that handles the rest of the traffic, since one b4 set covers both protocols. A configuration file is read the way its launch script reads it, so the sets follow the profiles the source machine runs. Commented-out alternatives, variables of another daemon such as tpws, and host list placeholders such as <HOSTLIST> are reported, not converted. An alternative is imported by uncommenting it and analyzing again.

A b4 set acts only on its targets. A byedpi command line usually has no host list, and a zapret one points at a file on its machine, so the import asks for domains per set. A set left without targets is created disabled, unless it handles only calls. A fallback set gets no domain field. It is reached through escalation from the set before it, and the same domains would make it compete with that set. A set for calls gets no domain field either. Such a set comes from a zapret profile with --filter-l7 naming discord or stun. The profile covers UDP only and has no host list or ipset of its own. The set gets (auto: STUN request) as its fake payload. With a --filter-udp port list, it handles only calls and is created enabled when the profile sends fakes. Without a UDP port list, it is created disabled, with Calls on Pass call setup. Its report row says to add the ports, choose Handle only calls in Calls and enable the set. The Discord line --filter-udp=19294-19344,50000-50100 --filter-l7=discord,stun --dpi-desync=fake becomes the voice set of Discord voice calls. Only one set acts on a domain. Profiles that share a host list and differ only by port become sets that are created disabled and named in the report. Each needs its own domains, or it can be deleted. A host list file (--hostlist=..., -H ...) is named next to the domain field of its set. Its contents are copied from the other machine and pasted there. A fake payload file (--dpi-desync-fake-tls=/opt/.../tls_clienthello.bin) is replaced by a built-in payload. The original can be uploaded under Settings > Payloads. An all-zero hex pattern becomes b4's all-zero payload.

Every option gets one row that says what became of it. The percentage above the report weighs mapped options fully and approximated ones partially, and leaves out the options that do not apply. Result Meaning Mapped b4 has the same thing. The b4 fields it set are listed under the explanation. Approximated The closest b4 behaviour was used. The row says how it differs. No equivalent b4 cannot express this. Not applicable The option configures the other tool's own process, such as its listening port or daemon mode, and means nothing for b4. No effect The option was read but changes nothing, in the source tool as well, or a later copy of it overrides it. Not recognized Not a known option for this tool and version. Invalid The value could not be read. These do not carry over: Automatic TTL (--dpi-desync-autottl, byedpi's hop count probing). b4 sends fakes with a fixed TTL, taken from --dpi-desync-ttl when the source has one. Changes to plain HTTP (--hostcase, --domcase, byedpi's --mod-http). Exclusion lists (--hostlist-exclude, --ipset-exclude). b4 has no exclusion list, so those entries are kept out of the set targets by hand. Packet ranges (--dpi-desync-start, --dpi-desync-cutoff, byedpi's --round). b4 has the same packet limits for every set, TCP Connection Packets Limit and UDP Connection Packets Limit under Settings > Core. Negated port filters (--filter-tcp=~80). A b4 port filter lists the ports to act on. Proxy settings of byedpi, which is a SOCKS5 proxy: its listening address, buffers and connection limits.

The new sets appear on the Sets page ahead of the existing ones. The result is a starting point, not a verified configuration: the provider, the route and the blocking differ between the source machine and this one. A Discovery run on the imported domains confirms whether the strategy works here, and finds a better one when it does not.

No set carries a strategy. The report says that none of the options that do the bypass were recognized. This happens with a variant of the tool with a different option syntax. Such a configuration is worth sending to the b4 issue tracker. A set passes traffic unchanged. The report warns when sets got no bypass options at all. Such a set changes nothing until a strategy is set on its TCP tab or found by Discovery. The sites do not open. The imported strategy does not work on this network. Unblocking a site shows the next steps.

The DNS & Routing tab of the set editor decides which resolver answers the set's domains and where the set's traffic goes. Guides that use it: Routing sites through a VPN or another interface Sending sites through a SOCKS5 proxy Passing sets to another router DNS, for resolvers, pinned addresses and ECH Blocking ads and sites

The sub-tab sends the DNS queries for the set's domains to a resolver of the set's own. Other domains keep the resolver the device uses. Field What it does Default Enable DNS Redirect Sends the queries for the set's domains to the resolver below. Off Resolver type Plain DNS (UDP) for a resolver's IP address, DNS-over-HTTPS for a DoH URL. Plain DNS (UDP) Fail closed when the resolver is unreachable On, the set's names stop resolving while the resolver is down. Off, b4 answers from the last good reply or from the device's own resolver. Off DNS Server IP, DNS-over-HTTPS URL The resolver, typed or picked from the recommended list. Empty Fragment DNS Queries Splits each query into IP fragments, for DPI that reads names in DNS queries. Off Remove ECH keys from DNS answers Browsers then send an ordinary ClientHello. See Removing ECH keys. Off Domain and addresses Pinned addresses in hosts file order: 157.240.0.174 www.instagram.com. A pin applies only to names the set targets, also with the redirect off. Empty

The sub-tab sends the set's traffic through a network interface or a SOCKS5 proxy, relays it to Telegram, or blocks it. Field What it does Default Enable Routing Turns routing on for the set. Off Routing mode Network interface, Upstream SOCKS5 proxy, Telegram over WebSocket (built-in) or Block (blackhole), described below. Network interface Source Interfaces Limits the set to traffic that arrives on the selected interfaces, such as the LAN bridge. See Which interface is which. None, every interface Resolved IP TTL (seconds) How long an address learned for the set's domains stays in the set. IP targets stay as long as the set lists them. 3600 Routing matches destination addresses: the set's IP, CIDR, GeoIP and ASN targets, and the addresses b4 learns for its domains. A set higher in the list with IP priority on can keep its addresses out of what this set learns. A set with no domain, IP or ASN target routes nothing, and the tab warns about it. The exception is block routing on a set that handles only calls: it blocks the calls the set takes. Source Devices only limit whose traffic the set takes: routing everything a device sends also needs Match any IP address under Targets > Bypass IPs.

The set's traffic leaves through the selected interface, such as a WireGuard or OpenVPN tunnel or a second uplink. Field What it does Default Output Interface The interface the set's traffic leaves by. One that is down or missing is marked unavailable, and the set's routing stops until it is back. None Egress IP (optional) Rewrites the source address of the set's traffic. b4 adds the address to the output interface itself. The device upstream then routes by that source. Empty Gateway (optional) The device on the output interface's network that receives the set's traffic, such as a VPN gateway or another router. Empty uses the gateway b4 finds on the interface, or a plain route through it. Empty Router's own traffic Whether the router's own connections to the set's addresses use the output interface too. See below. Automatic Kill switch Drops the set's traffic while the output interface is gone. See below. Off Traffic that arrives on the output interface itself does not follow the set. With an IPv4 address in Gateway (optional) on an Ethernet port, bridge, VLAN, Wi-Fi or TAP interface, IPv4 devices on that network follow the set too, apart from the gateway itself. b4 ignores a gateway that is outside the interface's network or is one of the router's own addresses, and logs the reason. See Gateway and Sites through a VPN on another device. When the output interface is a tunnel that is up, such as WireGuard or a TUN or TAP device, b4 leaves the set's packets alone: the strategy tabs have no effect, and the set's connections end with [routed->wg0] on the Logs page. A set routed to a plain interface, such as a second uplink, keeps its bypass strategy. Router's own traffic​ The setting covers connections the router opens itself, such as package updates or a proxy running on it. Traffic from the devices on the network follows the set either way. Value What happens Automatic The router's own traffic follows the set, except into a TUN or TAP device read by a program on the router, such as Xray or sing-box Route it too Always follows the set Leave it alone Always takes the normal route The exception prevents a loop: a proxy behind a TUN device opens its own connection to each destination, which would go back into the same TUN until the router runs out of memory. See Using b4 with Xray or XrayUI. The field is greyed out on a set limited to a source interface or to included source devices, which never takes the router's own traffic. Kill switch​ Without the kill switch, the set's traffic leaves through the normal uplink with the router's real address while the output interface is gone, for example while a VPN client reconnects. With it on, that traffic is dropped. Other traffic is not affected, and routing resumes by itself when the interface returns.

b4 takes over the set's TCP connections and opens each one again through a SOCKS5 proxy, such as Xray or sing-box on the router or on another host. The set's bypass strategy does not apply in this mode. The router's own TCP connections to the set's addresses go through the proxy as well. This includes the lookups of a DNS over TLS resolver on the router when its server is in the set. A set limited to a source interface or to included source devices leaves them alone. Field What it does Default Upstream SOCKS5 host The proxy's host name or address, 127.0.0.1 for a proxy on the router itself. Empty Upstream SOCKS5 port The proxy's port, commonly 1080. 0 Username (optional), Password (optional) For a proxy that requires authentication. Empty Send domain name to upstream Sends the proxy the host name instead of the address when b4 can tie a name to the connection. Names pinned in the set always go as addresses. TCP only. On Route UDP through upstream Sends the set's UDP through the proxy too. Off, or with Block QUIC (force TCP) on the UDP tab, b4 refuses the set's QUIC, and browsers fall back to TCP. Off Fall back to direct on upstream failure Connects directly while the proxy cannot be reached. Off Requirements​ This mode, the Telegram over WebSocket (built-in) mode and the Telegram over WebSocket switch need TPROXY support in the kernel. On OpenWrt with nftables it comes from kmod-nft-tproxy and kmod-nft-socket, with iptables from kmod-ipt-tproxy, kmod-ipt-socket and iptables-mod-tproxy. Keenetic firmware has the modules. kmod-nft-fib, or kmod-ipt-extra with iptables-mod-extra, lets the rule skip the router's own addresses by type; without them b4 lists the addresses. System Info on Settings > System > Service shows under Kernel Capabilities whether Transparent proxy (TPROXY) is available, and names the missing packages. Verifying that it works​ A connection the set sends through the proxy ends with [proxy] on the Logs page. Without that line the connection was not diverted, usually because its address is not in the set. See Checking the result. When the upstream itself is down​ While the proxy does not answer, every connection to the set's addresses hangs and fails, on every TCP port, including other sites on a shared CDN address. The dashboard shows Set X: proxy ... unreachable and upstream down. See When the upstream is down. Connections through the built-in SOCKS5 proxy​ A client of b4's own SOCKS5 proxy that asks for a host name a proxy set matches goes straight to that set's upstream. See The built-in SOCKS5 proxy. Bridge netfilter​ With bridge netfilter on, as OpenWrt's dockerd package sets it, connections from devices behind a network bridge such as br-lan hang in this mode and in the Telegram modes. See Bridge netfilter for the fix.

The set's Telegram traffic is relayed over Telegram's WebSocket edge, with no proxy in the Telegram app. The switch on Settings > Telegram does the same for every device without a set. See Telegram over WebSocket.

The set's traffic never leaves the router. Block action decides how: Reject (fail fast), the default, ends the connection at once, and Drop (silent blackhole) lets it time out. See Blocking ads and sites.

The DSCP block at the bottom of Traffic Routing writes the set's own DSCP value into the packets sent to the set's addresses, with routing on or off. The router in front of b4 reads the value and routes the set's traffic, for example through a VPN. See Passing sets to another router.

Field What it does Default Enable per-set DSCP Writes the set's value. Turned on with the value at 0, it fills in the first of 7, 31, 6 and 25 that no other set and no Set DSCP uses. Off DSCP value 0-63. 0 clears the field. 0 The value replaces the value of Set DSCP under Settings > Core > Firewall in those packets, whether Set DSCP is on or off, and the interface list there limits it too. The value stays on this router: a shared set never carries it.

7, 31, 6 and 25 keep normal priority in Linux Wi-Fi, cake and pfifo_fast; the hint under the field lists where other values land. pfSense cannot match these four, and there AF11-AF13 (10, 12, 14) disturb traffic least. Sets meant for different routes need different values.

The value goes by destination address alone, whatever the protocol and port: the set's IP, CIDR, GeoIP and ASN targets, and the addresses b4 learned for its domains. A set higher in the list with IP priority on can keep its addresses out of what this set learns. A CDN address shared by several sites carries the value for all of them. See Which packets get the value for overlapping sets.

A packet to an address b4 has not written for the set yet leaves without the value. A domain's address is written when b4 sees its DNS answer. Where the devices' DNS does not pass through b4, as with b4 in a container on MikroTik, IP, CIDR, GeoIP and ASN targets give the value from the first packet.

The block names the reason, and the switch cannot be turned on while it holds. No value is written: in the Upstream SOCKS5 proxy, Telegram over WebSocket (built-in) and Block (blackhole) modes; for a set with source devices, included or excluded, or with routing limited to Source Interfaces; for any set while Device Filtering is on with a device selected; for a set with no domain, IP, GeoIP or ASN target, or with Domain-only matching and no IP, GeoIP or ASN target; while Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup is on. Through a tunnel such as WireGuard, the router in front of b4 sees only the tunnel's packets, which usually do not carry the value.
documents.s: When the value is not written

documents.t: See Reading the value on the next router. Linux with nftables​ See Linux with nftables. RouterOS​ See Routing a set's traffic by its DSCP value.
documents.s: Reading the value on the next router

documents.t: With iptables, the sets' values need the ipset command and the xt_set kernel module. The rules and their cost per packet are in Firewall rules and cost.
See How routing sets work, DSCP rules and Packet marks.
The Routing Sets row under Firewall in System Info shows how many routing sets are installed, and the error while installing fails. See When the rules cannot be installed.
documents.s: When the rules cannot be installed

documents.t: A shared set is a set in a form that can be handed to another b4 user. It is one JSON document with the strategy, the targets and the payload files the set uses, and nothing tied to the router it came from. The same form is what Publish to hub sends to the Community Hub. The plain JSON of the Import/Export tab, described under Sets, copies a set as it is, routing included. It suits moving a set between one's own routers. Both forms are pasted into the same field, and b4 tells them apart.
On the router the set comes from, the Community Hub is on: the Share with other b4 users section is shown only then, see Switching it on. The router that imports the set needs no hub.

On the router the set comes from: Open the set and go to the Import/Export tab. In Share with other b4 users, click Prepare shared set. Read Check before sharing and Left out of the shared set, and correct the set where needed. Click Copy or Download, and pass the JSON on. On the router that receives it: Open Sets and click Create Set. Go to the Import/Export tab, paste the JSON into Set Configuration JSON and click Import. Read Notes from the import, and check the other tabs. Click Create Set.

A shared set is built from a list of allowed settings. The preview names every setting that was dropped, and why. Carried: the TCP, UDP, fragmentation and fake packet settings, with port filters; the targets: domains, addresses, geosite and geoip category names, ASNs, the TLS and IP version filters; the DNS redirect, with its DoH URL and pins for the set's own domains; the MSS clamp; block mode, since a block set carries nothing private. Left out: routing to an interface, a proxy or the Telegram bridge, with the proxy's address and credentials; device filters and escalation; the DNS server address the set redirects to, and IP block detection; the Discovery addresses, the watchdog switch, the IP priority switch and the set's own DSCP value; the set's id and its enabled state. ASNs travel as numbers. The router that imports the set fetches their address ranges itself. Domains that look private to the sharing network are reported, not removed: a single label such as nas, an IP address in the domain list, or a name ending in .lan, .local or .home. They mean nothing on another network and are worth deleting before the set is passed on.

A set whose fake packets use a captured ClientHello carries that file inside the shared set, so the importing router sends the same fake packets. A file is carried only when it parses as a TLS ClientHello with a server name, or as a QUIC Initial with a readable ClientHello, and only up to 16 KB. When the file is missing on the sharing router, the set is shared without it, and both sides use the built-in payload. On import, the file appears under Settings > Payloads, named after the protocol and the server name, such as tls_www_google_com.bin. An existing file with the same name and other contents is never overwritten: the new file gets a short hash suffix.

The import runs on the router and lists every change under Notes from the import: A shared set in a newer format is refused. Settings this b4 does not know are dropped, and values it does not accept are replaced by defaults. The b4 version the set needs is compared with the running one. Each payload file must match its hash. Geosite and geoip categories missing from this router's databases are named. A category name means what the local database says, which can differ between the sources under Settings > Geodat Settings. ASNs whose address ranges this router has not fetched yet are named. They match nothing until b4 fetches them, which starts once the set is saved. A pin for a domain the set does not target, or for a private address, is dropped. The remaining pins are listed, to be checked on the DNS & Routing tab before saving. A DNS redirect to a DoH resolver outside the known public list is dropped. Settings a shared set leaves out are removed even when the JSON was edited by hand to include them. A shared set imported into an existing set keeps that set's own DSCP value, and turns its IP priority switch off.

The card of the imported set on the Sets page shows Imported shared set. Once the strategy is changed in the editor, the chip reads Imported shared set, edited. Targets, port filters and pins can be changed without that.

The shared set could not be imported: ... names the reason, such as a format from a newer b4. Invalid JSON format means the pasted text is not valid JSON. Command lines from byedpi and zapret are a different import, described under Importing from zapret or byedpi.

The Targets tab decides which traffic the set applies to. It has three sub-tabs: Bypass Domains, Bypass IPs and Source Devices. Adding sites to a set shows the ways to fill this tab, including from the Traffic page and the dashboard. How sets match traffic describes how b4 chooses between sets that target the same site.

The Bypass Domains sub-tab holds domain names and GeoSite categories, and the filters that apply to the whole set. Field What it does Default Match any domain Adds regexp:.*, which matches every domain. A domain that another set lists is still handled by that set, so this set takes only what no other set claims. For routing, it covers only the addresses this set has resolved, not every address. Off Domain-only matching Matches the domains only by the server name in the handshake, never by their IP address. Useful on shared CDN addresses, where a neighbouring domain on the same IP would otherwise get this set's strategy. A routing set with this on routes only the addresses listed explicitly. Off TLS Version Filter Any, TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3, compared with the highest version the client offers. For a match by domain it is a preference: among the sets that list the domain, one whose filter fits comes first. For a match by address, a set whose filter does not fit does not take the connection.
