Any IP Version Filter Any, IPv4 or IPv6, a preference for matches by domain and by address alike: among the matching sets, one whose filter fits comes first. Shown while both IPv4 and IPv6 support are on under Settings > Core. An ASN target then loads only the prefixes of the chosen family. Any Manual Bypass Domains Domain names, added with Enter. A domain covers its subdomains, so a leading *. is removed. Several domains can be pasted at once, separated by commas or new lines. A regexp: entry takes a regular expression. Empty Bypass GeoSite Categories Ready-made lists of a service's domains from the GeoSite database, such as youtube or discord. Needs the database loaded under Settings > Geodat Settings. A click on a category shows its domains. Empty Edit List opens all manual entries as text, one per line. When a domain is already in another set, a warning names that set.

The Bypass IPs sub-tab holds addresses, GeoIP categories and ASNs. Field What it does Default Match any IP address Adds 0.0.0.0/0, and ::/0 while IPv6 support is on, which match every address. For DPI bypass, a narrower range in another set is handled by that set, so this set takes only what no other set claims. For routing, a narrower range in another routing set gets no such priority, so the two are best not combined. Off IP priority A connection to an address the set lists, by IP, GeoIP category or ASN, stays with this set even when a set lower in the list matches its domain. Shown while TLS Version Filter on Bypass Domains is Any. Off Manual Bypass IPs Addresses and CIDR ranges, such as 192.168.1.100 or 10.0.0.0/8, entered the same way as domains. Other text, such as an AS number, is refused. Empty Bypass GeoIP Categories Address ranges from the GeoIP database, by country or by network. Needs the database loaded under Settings > Geodat Settings. Empty IP priority suits servers that carry only this set's sites, such as the Google Global Cache nodes in a provider's own network. Shared CDN ranges and large networks carry many sites, and the switch is best left off there. With the Google network AS15169 as a target, for example, the set would also keep youtube.com and every other Google service from the sets below it. Sets that rank above this one still take connections by name. A set limited to source devices ranks above every set without them. Among sets of the same kind, the one higher in the list ranks first. IP priority does not apply to a connection that matches the set only through Match any IP address. IP priority describes the exact rules.

The Networks (ASN) panel on Bypass IPs holds the set's ASN targets. An ASN (autonomous system number) identifies the network of one operator: AS15169 is Google, AS13335 is Cloudflare. An ASN target makes the set match every address range, or prefix, the network announces. b4 fetches the prefixes from RIPEstat, refreshes them daily and keeps the last good copy when a fetch fails. Field What it does Add ASN, or find one by IP Takes a number (15169), the number with its prefix (AS15169) or an IP address. For an address, b4 lists the networks that announce it, and a button such as Add AS15169 adds one. The address itself is not added. ASN rows Each ASN in the set with its holder, the number of IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes, the approximate number of IPv4 addresses and the time of the last update. Refresh from RIPEstat fetches the prefixes again, Show prefixes lists them, and Remove from the set removes the ASN. When a lookup fails, the error is shown, and Add anyway, resolve later still adds the ASN. b4 retries in the background. Until a fetch succeeds, the ASN adds no addresses to the set, and the set's card shows N ASN unresolved. Private and reserved numbers are refused, since no public network announces them. For routing, where two sets of the same kind cover the same addresses, the set higher in the list wins, and sets limited to selected devices or source interfaces come before the others. A set with ASN targets and no domains cannot be kept working by the watchdog, which identifies a set's sites by their names. How sets match traffic describes where the prefixes come from and how they are refreshed. Large and shared networks A large network expands into thousands of prefixes, which costs memory on a small router. The panel warns above 2,000 prefixes or 16,777,216 IPv4 addresses. A cloud, hosting or CDN network such as AWS, Google Cloud, Cloudflare, Akamai or Hetzner carries many unrelated services. Its ASN also catches every other site hosted there, public DNS resolvers such as 8.8.8.8 and 1.1.1.1 included. A domain target, or a narrower set placed above, keeps the set to the service meant.

The Source Devices sub-tab limits the set to traffic from selected devices. Applying b4 to selected devices shows the setup. Field What it does Default Device table The devices with their MAC address, IP address and name. offline marks a device not on the network now. The set applies to the traffic of the selected ones. None selected All devices except selected Applies the set to every device except the selected ones. Off With no device selected, the set applies to all traffic. A set limited to devices takes priority over a set without devices that targets the same site. A device that has left the network for good is removed from this set by clearing its checkbox, or from every set by forgetting it under Settings > Core > Devices. Devices found in the router's ARP table are matched by their MAC address. A device added by hand has no MAC address on the network, so it is matched by the IP address entered for it. Such a device needs a fixed or reserved address, and it cannot be matched when a router between it and b4 replaces its source address. Without a working ARP table, the tab says so, and filtering by source device does not work. Source devices do not select traffic on their own Source devices decide whose traffic the set applies to, not which traffic. A routing set whose only target is a source device routes nothing. To route everything from a device, Match any IP address is turned on in the Bypass IPs sub-tab. Traffic the router itself sends never comes from a source device, so such a set leaves it alone.

The TCP tab holds the set's DPI bypass strategy for TCP connections, such as HTTPS. It has three sub-tabs: Sub-tab What it holds General The segment delay and port filter, packet duplication, IP block detection, RST injection protection and MSS clamping. Splitting How b4 splits the first data packet of a connection, the TLS ClientHello. Faking Fake packets that DPI reads and the server discards, and changes to the real ClientHello. Discovery tests strategies against a blocked site and writes the values that work into a set. The strategy it suggests is the first one to try, and manual changes on these sub-tabs are for tuning it. A set can send its traffic through a proxy, or through a tunnel interface that is up, on the DNS & Routing tab. b4 then leaves its packets alone: splitting, faking, packet duplication and IP block detection do not apply.

The Faking sub-tab sends fake packets that DPI reads and the server discards, and it can change the real ClientHello. Each technique is a separate panel. Discovery picks the fake settings, the TTL included, for the strategies it finds, and manual changes are for tuning. Fake payloads are generated and uploaded under Settings > Payloads.

Fake ClientHello packets sent before the real one. DPI reads the fake, and the real ClientHello passes unnoticed. Field What it does Default Enable Fake SNI Sends fake packets before the real ClientHello. On Fake Packet Count How many fakes to send, 1 to 20. 1

Field What it does Default Fake Payload Type What the fake carries, see the table below. Preset: Google (classic) Match Fake Size Builds the fake from the real ClientHello with the payload's domain fitted to the length of the real name, so both have the same size. A payload that is not a ClientHello is repeated or cut to that size. Off Randomize TLS Random Replaces the 32-byte Random field of the fake, so that it differs from the real one. Off Duplicate Session ID Copies the Session ID of the real ClientHello into the fake. Off The last two are under Fake Packet TLS Modification, shown for every payload type except Random. Payload type The fake carries Random Random bytes. Preset: Google (classic), Preset: DuckDuckGo A ClientHello for that site. Preset: STUN A STUN request. My own Payload File A ClientHello generated or uploaded under Settings > Payloads, chosen in Generated Payload. All Zeros Zero bytes. Inverted Original The real ClientHello with every bit inverted. Generated from Domain A ClientHello generated for the domain entered in Domain.

The How the server rejects it section decides why the server discards the fake while DPI reads it. Field What it does Default Fake Strategy How the fake becomes unusable to the server, see the table below. Past Sequence Sequence Offset How far the sequence number is moved, for Random Sequence and Past Sequence. 10000 Timestamp Decrease How much the TCP timestamp is decreased, for TCP Timestamp. 600000 Fake TTL The TTL of the fakes, 1 to 64. It has to reach the DPI and expire before the server. SYN MD5 Signature, OOB, UDP fakes, the Combo decoy, Overlap Length and Post-ClientHello RST use it too, also with Fake SNI Packets off. 7 Apply Fake TTL Uses Fake TTL whatever the strategy. Without it, the TTL applies only with the TTL strategy. Off MD5 Signature on Fake Puts the TCP MD5 option on the fake. DPI still reads it. A server that checks the option discards the fake, and one that does not takes it as data unless the fake strategy stops it. Off Strategy Why the server discards the fake TTL The fake expires on the way and never reaches the server. Random Sequence Its TCP sequence number is random. Past Sequence Its sequence number is one the server has already processed. TCP Check Its TCP checksum is wrong, and it acknowledges data the server never sent. MD5 Sum It carries a TCP MD5 option. A server that does not check the option takes the fake as data. TCP Timestamp Its TCP timestamp is too old. On a connection without TCP timestamps, as from Windows by default or to a server that refuses them, the fake goes out as with TCP Check instead, and the log shows a warning that names the set and the device. The right TTL depends on how many hops away the DPI is. Discovery finds it, and for manual tuning 3 is a starting point.

Fake SYN packets sent during the TCP handshake, before the real connection starts. An aggressive technique: fake SYNs can upset some network equipment. Field What it does Default SYN Fake Packets Sends fake SYN packets during the handshake. Off SYN MD5 Signature Sends a fake SYN with a TCP MD5 option before the real handshake, at Fake TTL from Fake SNI Packets. Off SYN Fake Payload Length 0 sends the header only, a larger value adds a fake TLS payload, up to 1200 bytes. 0 SYN Fake TTL The TTL of the fake SYNs of SYN Fake Packets, 1 to 100. 7

Fake TCP control packets with broken checksums and a low TTL. They confuse DPI that tracks connections, and the server drops them. Field What it does Default Desync Mode Which packets to send, see the table below. Disabled Desync TTL 1 to 50, low enough for the packets to expire before the server. 7 Desync Packet Count Fake packets per desync with RST Packets, FIN Packets or ACK Packets, 1 to 20. The two combined modes send a fixed set. 3 Post-ClientHello RST Sends a fake RST after the ClientHello, to remove the connection from the DPI's tracking table. Off Mode What it sends RST Packets Fake RSTs, so DPI takes the connection as torn down. FIN Packets Fake FINs with old sequence numbers, so DPI takes the connection as finished. ACK Packets Fake ACKs with random future sequence and acknowledgment numbers. Combo (RST + FIN) RST, FIN and ACK packets in sequence. Full (RST + FIN + ACK) A fake SYN, then RST, PSH and URG packets.

Fake ACK packets with changed TCP window sizes, sent with a low TTL before the real packet. Field What it does Default Window Mode Disabled. Zero Window sends a window of 0, then 65535. Random Window sends 3 to 5 fakes with sizes from the list. Oscillate goes through the list in order. Escalate grows from 0 to 65535 in steps. Disabled Custom Window Values The list for Random Window and Oscillate, values 0 to 65535. An empty list uses the defaults. 0, 1460, 8192, 65535

For DPI that slows a connection down once about 15-20 KB have come from the server. b4 sends fake packets towards the server that DPI sees and that expire before they reach it. Field What it does Default Incoming Mode Disabled. Fake Packets sends a broken ACK for every incoming data packet. Reset Injection, FIN Injection and Desync Combo send fake RST, FIN, or RST, FIN and ACK once the incoming data reaches the threshold. Disabled Corruption Strategy How the fakes of Fake Packets are made unusable: Bad Checksum, Bad Sequence, Bad ACK, Random for each packet, or All Corruptions. The other modes rely on Fake TTL alone. Bad Checksum Fake TTL 1 to 20. 7 Fake Count Fake packets per injection, 1 to 10. 3 Threshold Min, Threshold Max The incoming data, in KB, that triggers an injection. Each connection picks a value between the two. Not used by Fake Packets. 14, 14 In NFQUEUE mode, while any enabled set has an incoming mode other than Disabled, the server's first packets reach b4 on every connection b4 sends fakes or split segments into, whichever set takes the connection. While no set has one, only the SYN-ACKs and resets of those connections reach b4. See Packet marks.

Changes the real ClientHello, not a fake, so that it does not match known DPI signatures. warning Mutation changes the ClientHello that reaches the server. When a site stops opening after mutation is turned on, turning it off is the first check. Field What it does Default Mutation Mode Disabled, Random (random extension order and noise), GREASE Extensions, Padding, Fake Extensions (unknown TLS extensions), Fake SNIs (extra server names) or Advanced (All), which combines them with all their settings. Disabled GREASE Extension Count 1 to 10. 3 Padding Size The size of the ClientHello with padding, 256 to 16384 bytes. 2048 Fake Extension Count 1 to 15. 5 Add Fake SNI Extra server names put into the ClientHello next to the real one. ya.ru, vk.com, max.ru
The General sub-tab of the TCP tab holds the settings that apply whatever splitting or faking method the set uses.

Field What it does Default Segment 2 Delay Delay between the pieces b4 sends, in milliseconds. A range makes each connection pick a random value from it. 0 Port Filter The TCP ports the set acts on, such as 443 or 80,5222,8000-9000, and a list without 443 leaves HTTPS out. Empty means every port b4 captures: 443 and the ports any set lists. Empty Drop SACK Options Removes the Selective Acknowledgment option from TCP headers. Some DPI uses it to put fragments back in order. Off Empty line before HTTP method For plain HTTP on port 80: puts an empty line before the request and shortens the User-Agent by two characters to keep the length. Inspection that expects the method at the start of the request no longer finds the Host header. Needs a User-Agent header, and suits nginx servers. Off

For providers that slow traffic down by dropping some outgoing packets to certain address ranges, such as Telegram's. b4 drops the original packet and sends several copies instead. Field What it does Default Enable Packet Duplication Sends each packet of the set's TCP connections as several copies. The duplicated packets get none of the set's other bypass techniques. Off Copy Count How many copies to send, 1 to 10. 3 The Traffic page labels duplicated packets dup.

Some server addresses are blocked at the IP level: nothing reaches the server, so no bypass strategy helps. A CDN often answers DNS with several addresses of which only some are blocked, and the site then works or hangs depending on the address a device picked. The detection finds such addresses, and the Traffic page labels their connections ip. The other fields appear once it is on. Field What it does Default Enable IP Block Detection Detects destinations that never answer and acts on them. Off Heal DNS answers Also removes unreachable addresses from DNS answers. When every address is unreachable, the last one that worked for the domain is answered instead. Off Detect unanswered SYNs Catches blocks at the address level, where the connection never opens. On SYN Threshold How many unanswered connection attempts before the router tests the address itself. Nothing happens until that test fails too. 3 Retransmit Threshold How many unanswered copies of the ClientHello, the first one included, mark the destination blocked. This covers a block that lets the connection open and then swallows the handshake. A low value can mistake a slow server for a block. 3 Detection Timeout How long, in milliseconds, before a repeated and still unanswered SYN or ClientHello counts as reaching its threshold. With Cache Blocked IPs on, a server that sends nothing back for this long after the ClientHello gets its address checked for a ban. 3000 Healed Answer TTL The TTL written into healed DNS answers, in seconds. A short value lets devices pick up a recovered address quickly. 60 Cache Blocked IPs Remembers blocked addresses, so new connections to them are reset at once instead of waiting. An address blocked for every site name is banned. On How long an address stays marked is set by Retest interval (seconds) under Settings > Core.

Some providers block an address for every site name: the connection opens, but no site on that address answers. In a set with Cache Blocked IPs on, b4 tests whether an address answers for other site names when: IP block detection marks the address blocked (see Retransmit Threshold and Detection Timeout); the server sends nothing back for the Detection Timeout after a device's ClientHello. An address that answers none of those names is banned. A connection still waiting on it is then reset. An address that answers them, even with a refusal, is not banned. An address that IP block detection marked blocked stays in the cache of blocked addresses all the same. Until the Retest interval (seconds) runs out, new connections to it are reset, whatever the site. On some routers b4 cannot see whether a server has answered while the connection is open. There it tests a silent server only after the device gives up on the connection, see Kernel requirements. While an address is banned: New connections to the address and port are reset at once in every set with IP block detection and Cache Blocked IPs on. QUIC to that address and port is refused. A device can then move on to the site's next address, if the site has one. A set that routes through a proxy, or through a TUN, TAP or WireGuard interface that is up, leaves its connections to the address alone. A connection that another service sends into a tunnel is left alone too, see Packets that leave by another route. A set routed to another interface, such as a second uplink, still resets or refuses its connections. DNS answers for the domains of every set leave it out. When every address of an answer is banned, b4 answers with an address that worked for the domain before. When it knows none, the answer passes unchanged. The Traffic page labels the connections b4 resets or refuses ban. A ban lasts 24 hours by default. An address banned again within 30 days after its previous ban ended is banned for 7 days. b4 tests a banned address again at every Retest interval (seconds) and lifts the ban early after three successful tests in a row. Bans stay across restarts and set changes. The Banned addresses panel on the dashboard lists the bans, and Unban lifts one at once. The switch and the ban lengths are on the IP Block Detection card under Settings > Core. When the set's Escalation trigger fires first, the host moves to the backup set, and this set does not check or ban its address. A backup set with IP block detection and Cache Blocked IPs on can still ban it.

Field What it does Default Enable RST Protection Drops connection resets that look injected by DPI rather than sent by the server. Off TTL Tolerance The largest allowed difference between the TTL of a reset and the TTL of the server's replies. 3 RST Injection Protection describes the checks.

Limits the TCP maximum segment size (MSS) for the set's connections. A smaller MSS makes the client send its ClientHello in several segments, which some DPI cannot put back together. Field What it does Default Enable per-set MSS Turns the clamp on for the set. Available once the set has an IP, GeoIP, ASN or source device target. Off MSS size (bytes) The MSS, 10 to 1460. 88 is filled in when the switch is turned on. 88 The MSS is set on the first packet of a connection, before the server name is known. Only IP, GeoIP, ASN and source device targets therefore decide where it applies. Domains, GeoSite categories and the TLS version filter play no part. The set targets The clamp applies to IP addresses, GeoIP categories or ASNs Connections to those addresses Source devices only Every port 443 connection from those devices, wherever it goes Both Connections from those devices to those addresses A set whose IP, GeoIP and ASN targets resolve to no addresses yet installs no clamp until they do. A device added by hand needs a fixed address to scope a clamp. 88 is the value suggested for smart TVs on YouTube. Every segment then carries at most 88 bytes, so large downloads are slow, and when a connection works but crawls, a larger value is the next step. To slow down one device's HTTPS without a set, the per-device MSS does the same. A per-set MSS overrides the per-device and global MSS for the connections it covers.

Some DPI breaks connections by sending a forged TCP reset (RST) in the server's name. The device takes it for a real one and closes the connection. RST injection protection drops resets that do not look like the server's own. It is turned on per set, in the RST Injection Protection section of the General sub-tab. Field What it does Default Enable RST Protection Turns the protection on for the set. Off TTL Tolerance The largest allowed difference between the TTL of a reset and the TTL of the server's first reply, 1 to 20. 3 b4 drops a reset when, for example: it arrives before the server has answered at all; it is not the first reset on the same connection; its TTL differs from the TTL of the server's replies by more than TTL Tolerance, a sign that it came from another point in the network. A tolerance of 3 fits most networks. When b4 drops resets that the server really sent, a larger value is the fix. Each dropped reset appears in the logs with its reason. The protection pairs with Escalation: it keeps the current page working while b4 detects a block, and the Escalation tab suggests turning it on.

The Splitting sub-tab decides how b4 splits the first data packet of a connection, the TLS ClientHello, so that DPI cannot read the server name in it. Discovery tests the methods against a blocked site, and the method it suggests is the first one to try. Manual changes are for tuning.

Field What it does Default Method The splitting method, see the table below. The settings of the chosen method appear under it. Combo Reverse Fragment Order Sends the second fragment first. On Strategy Randomization Pool Methods that b4 picks from at random for each new connection, so that connections differ. An empty pool uses Method. Empty Method What it does Combo Splits at several points, shuffles the segments and adds timing jitter. It can add a decoy and fake packets between the segments. Hybrid Picks Combo, Disorder, Extension Split or First-Byte Desync for each ClientHello, by the split points it finds in it. It has no settings of its own. Disorder Sends the real segments out of order with timing jitter, without fake packets unless Fake Per Segment is on. Extension Split Splits the ClientHello just before the SNI extension. It has no settings of its own and uses Reverse Fragment Order and Segment 2 Delay. First-Byte Desync Sends one byte, waits, then sends the rest, so that DPI gives up before the server name arrives. The wait is Segment 2 Delay on the General sub-tab, at least 100 ms. TCP Segmentation Splits the packet into TCP segments. IP Fragmentation Splits the IP packet into IP fragments. TLS Record Splitting Splits the ClientHello into several TLS records inside one TCP packet. OOB (Out-of-Band) Sends a one-byte fake with the TCP URG flag. DPI that follows the connection reads it as data. The fake goes out at Fake TTL and has to expire before the server, which would drop the real byte at that position. Disabled No splitting. Only fake packets are used, if they are on.

Field What it does Default Smart SNI Split Splits in the middle of the server name. The recommended choice. On Fixed Split Position Splits at this many bytes from the start of the TLS payload, 0 to 50, where 0 turns it off. A range makes each connection pick a random position. With Smart SNI Split also on, the packet becomes three segments. 1

Field What it does Default First Byte Splits after the first byte. On Extension Split Splits before the SNI extension. On SNI Split Splits in the middle of the server name. On Enable Decoy Sends a fake ClientHello with an allowed server name before the real one. The fake has a low TTL, so DPI sees it and the server does not. Off Shuffle Mode Middle Only keeps the first and last segments in place, Full Shuffle reorders all of them, Reverse Order sends the last one first. Full Shuffle First Segment Delay Pause after the first segment, 10 to 500 ms. 30 Jitter Max The largest random delay between the other segments, 100 to 10,000 µs. 1000 Fake Per Segment Sends fake overlapping packets before every segment, not only the first. Fakes Per Segment sets how many, 1 to 11. Off With every split point off, Combo sends the packet in one piece, and the tab shows a warning.

Field What it does Default SNI-Based Splitting Splits around the server name. On Shuffle Mode Full Shuffle or Reverse Order. Full Shuffle Min Jitter, Max Jitter The random delay between segments, in µs. Used while Segment 2 Delay is 0. Max Jitter has to be greater than Min Jitter. 1000, 3000 Fake Per Segment As in Combo. Off

Shown for Combo and Disorder. b4 puts fake bytes in front of a real segment and moves its sequence number back by the same amount. DPI reads the fake bytes as the start of the data, and the server discards them. Combo adds them only to the first data packet of a connection, when that packet starts a ClientHello or an HTTP request. Later requests on the same connection go without them. Field What it does Default Overlap Pattern The fake bytes: None, TLS 1.2 Header, TLS 1.1 Header, TLS 1.0 Header, HTTP GET, Zeros, or Custom hex bytes. None Overlap Length How many pattern bytes to add. 0 turns the overlap off. 0

Field What it does Default Insert Position How many bytes come before the inserted byte, 1 to 50. A range makes each connection pick a random position. While Smart SNI Split is on, as it is by default, the byte goes in the middle of the server name instead. - OOB Byte The byte sent out of band. x
Field What it does Default Record Split Position The size of the first TLS record in bytes, 1 to 100. A range makes each connection pick a random size. -

The UDP tab decides which UDP traffic the set matches, QUIC above all, and what b4 does with it. Its most common use is not a bypass over UDP but refusing QUIC, so that the browser falls back to TCP, where the set's TCP strategies apply.

Field What it does Default Block QUIC (force TCP) Matches every QUIC packet to the set's targets and answers it with ICMP port unreachable. It sets QUIC Matching to By SNI or matched destination and Action Mode to Reject. Off QUIC carries HTTP/3 for YouTube, Google, Discord and other sites. Its packets are encrypted end to end, so b4 cannot desync the handshake the way it does with TLS over TCP: only decoys and a fragmented Initial packet are left, and both are weak. When a provider silently drops UDP to port 443, a video stalls without an error, and nothing tells the browser to stop trying QUIC. Browsers also remember that a host offered HTTP/3 and keep trying QUIC with it. A refusal from the router makes the browser switch to TCP at once. On a set sent through an Upstream SOCKS5 proxy with Route UDP through upstream on, the switch refuses only the set's QUIC, and the rest of its UDP goes through the proxy. The other settings on this tab do not apply to UDP that goes through the proxy.

Field What it does Default QUIC Matching By SNI matches QUIC whose ClientHello carries a server name the set targets, which is also how b4 learns the addresses of those domains. By SNI or matched destination also matches any QUIC packet to a destination the set already matches by IP or port, with no server name needed. By SNI Port Filter UDP ports to match, such as 5000-6000,8000, for VoIP, games and other UDP applications. It also limits the rest of the set: a set with 8443 here does not act on UDP port 443. Empty matches any port, except the ports that only a set for calls lists. Empty Calls How the set treats calls, see the table below. Pass call setup Which calls Shown with Handle only calls: the calls the set takes, see Sets for calls. Discord app and browsers Calls What happens Pass call setup STUN requests, which start calls in browsers and apps, and the Discord app's voice packets pass unchanged. The set's Action Mode still applies to the rest of a call, such as browser audio and video. Handle only calls The set takes no targets and acts only on calls, see Sets for calls. A set with targets cannot choose it. Handle like other UDP STUN requests and the Discord app's voice packets get the set's action like the rest of its UDP. With Drop or Reject, the set blocks calls too. With By SNI and no domains or GeoSite categories on the Targets tab, no QUIC ClientHello can match, and the tab shows a warning. UDP to port 53 is DNS and goes to b4's DNS handling instead.

With Calls on Handle only calls, the set applies its Action Mode, such as fakes, only to the packet that opens each call on the ports in its Port Filter, whatever the address. Which calls decides which calls it takes: Which calls The set takes Discord app and browsers Calls in the Discord app, in browsers and in other apps that start calls with STUN. Discord app Calls and voice channels in the Discord app. Browsers Calls in browsers, Discord in a browser included, and in other apps that start calls with STUN. The rest of a call the set takes belongs to the set: its later packets pass untouched, or are blocked when the set blocks. Fakes go only before the packet that opens the call. Every other packet on those ports is left to the other sets, or passes untouched. A set with an empty UDP Port Filter leaves those ports alone. A call the set takes belongs to it even when another set matches its destination address, such as a GeoIP set that covers the same servers. The same holds when that address belongs to a domain another set handles. A set for calls has three requirements. When it breaks one, b4 refuses to save it, and a warning on the tab names the cause. No targets: no domains, IPs, GeoSite or GeoIP categories and no ASNs. Source devices are allowed. A Port Filter on this tab with the ports the calls arrive on. While it is empty, the warning offers Use Discord ports, which enters 19294-19344,50000-50100. An empty Port Filter on the TCP tab. Without targets, a TCP port filter would make the set act on every TCP connection on those ports. The TCP tab shows a warning too. While Handle only calls is chosen, the tab hides Blocking QUIC and QUIC Matching. With Action Mode on Drop or Reject, or with Block (blackhole) routing on the DNS & Routing tab, the set blocks the packet that opens each call, and a warning says so. The IP Version Filter on the Targets tab limits such a set as well. Choosing Handle only calls changes Fake Packet Payload from (zero fill) or (auto: QUIC Initial) to (auto: STUN request), and any other payload stays. On some networks zero-filled fakes cut Discord calls short. Leaving Handle only calls in the same edit restores the previous payload. When a set without targets leaves Handle only calls and keeps its UDP Port Filter, it acts on all UDP on those ports, and a hint on the tab says so. Discord voice calls sets up such a set step by step.

Field What it does Default Action Mode What b4 does with the UDP the set matched, see the table below. Fake & Fragment Mode What happens Off Matched UDP passes unchanged. b4 still reads the QUIC ClientHello, so a set with domains keeps learning their addresses, for example for routing. Fake & Fragment Decoy packets go before the real one, and the Initial packet is fragmented. Weak against QUIC. Drop The packet is dropped without an answer, and for QUIC so is the rest of its connection. The client falls back to TCP once it stops waiting, usually after several seconds. Reject The packet is dropped, and for QUIC so is the rest of its connection. An ICMP port unreachable goes back to the client, which switches to TCP at once. The recommended way to refuse QUIC. Coalesce QUIC Initial Sends the handshake packet that carries the server name behind a padding packet in the same datagram. Inspection that reads only the first packet of a datagram no longer sees the name. The rest of the connection goes out untouched, and the handshake itself is unchanged. When the set blocks its traffic on the DNS & Routing tab, the block action applies instead of the action mode. In a set with IP block detection and Cache Blocked IPs on, QUIC to a banned address is refused whatever the action mode. Whether the rest of a dropped QUIC connection is dropped too depends on the router. System Info shows it under Kernel Capabilities in the row QUIC drop holds for the whole connection. Where the row reads unavailable, only the first packets of the connection are dropped, and the row shows what the router lacks. Dropped QUIC connections describes the cases. Everything on this tab applies to IPv6 only while Enable IPv6 Support is on under Settings > Core. With it off, b4 sees no IPv6 packets, and a destination that answers over IPv6 keeps working over QUIC there.

Shown in Fake & Fragment mode. Field What it does Default Fake Packet Count How many fakes go before the real packet, 1 to 20. 6 Fake Packet Size The payload size of each fake, 32 to 1500 bytes. 64 Fake Packet Payload What the fakes carry: (zero fill), (auto: QUIC Initial) for a fresh random QUIC Initial in each fake, (auto: STUN request) for a fresh STUN request in each fake, QUIC preset 1, QUIC preset 2, or a payload uploaded under Settings > Payloads. Presets and uploaded payloads are cut or padded with zeros to Fake Packet Size, (auto: STUN request) is padded with random bytes, and 1200 bytes suits (auto: QUIC Initial). (zero fill) Evasion Technique How the fakes are made unusable to the server. UDP fakes always use the set's Fake TTL from TCP > Faking: None sends them without extra corruption, TTL is the same as None, Checksum also breaks the UDP checksum. None Segment 2 Delay Delay between the fakes and the real packet, 0 to 1000 ms. A range makes each connection pick a random value. 0

The Settings page holds the configuration of b4 itself. Sets have their own page and editor. Tab What it holds Core How traffic reaches b4 and what b4 does with it, on the sub-tabs Packet Engine, Devices, Firewall, DNS and SOCKS5 System The service itself, on the sub-tabs Service (restart, System Info, language, logging), Web Server and Backup Geodat Settings The GeoSite and GeoIP databases: sources, downloads and updates Discovery Discovery and the watchdog Telegram Telegram over WebSocket, the MTProto proxy and the WEB proxy Integrations The IPinfo token, the AI assistant, the MCP server and the Community Hub Payloads Payloads for faking The login, HTTPS and the Expose to internet switches are covered in Securing the web interface.

The buttons in the page header act on every tab at once: Save Changes saves the changes of every tab. Discard Changes drops the unsaved changes after a confirmation. Reload loads the configuration from b4 again, which drops unsaved changes as well. While a change is unsaved, Modified shows next to the Configuration title, and the tab with the change shows a dot. Most changes apply on save. Some fields on Core and System, such as Ingestion mode or the web server Port, apply only after b4 restarts. A sub-tab with such a change shows a restart icon with the tooltip Applies after a restart, and the header shows Some changes require a B4 restart to take effect. The message that confirms the save then offers Restart Service.
The Core tab decides how traffic reaches b4 and what b4 does with it. Some fields apply only after a restart, see Saving and restarting. Packet capture explains how the engine works.
The sub-tab decides how packets reach b4, which address families it handles and how much of each connection it reads.

Ingestion mode selects how packets reach b4. A change applies after a restart. Mode How packets reach b4 NFQUEUE (default) Firewall rules hand packets to b4. The usual choice. TUN interface Traffic is routed through a virtual interface that b4 reads. For kernels without the modules NFQUEUE needs. TUN settings​ Shown while TUN interface is selected. Field What it does Default Uplink interface Where b4 sends processed packets. Auto (follow default route) moves with the default route when the WAN or VPN changes. A selected interface pins the uplink. Auto (follow default route) Uplink gateway The gateway of a pinned uplink. Empty takes it from the default route. Empty TUN address Address and prefix of the TUN device. Must not overlap a LAN or VPN subnet. 10.255.0.1/30 TUN device name Name of the interface b4 creates. Must not be the uplink or another existing interface. b4tun0 Capture Interfaces​ Capture Interfaces, shown in NFQUEUE mode, limits b4 to traffic that leaves the router through the selected interfaces. An empty selection, the default, covers every interface and is the usual choice. A VPN client or a tunnel can move traffic to another interface, and traffic outside the selection gets no set. When nothing works after an interface is selected, clearing the selection is the first check, see Capture Interfaces match nothing. See also Which interface is which. When the engine does not start​ When the packet engine fails to start, the web interface keeps working, but traffic passes through the router untouched. The dashboard and the Packet Engine card show the reason. When the kernel lacks the modules NFQUEUE needs, installing them or switching to TUN interface fixes it. b4 retries the start three times within about two minutes, which covers a WAN or VPN that comes up late. Engine start and retries has the details.

IP block detection is turned on per set, on the TCP > General tab. This card holds its global settings. Field What it does Default Retest interval (seconds) How long an address marked unreachable stays marked before it is tested again. Recovery after a block is lifted can take this long. The interval also paces the checks of pinned DNS addresses and of banned addresses. 300 Remember blocked addresses Bans an address that leaves a ClientHello unanswered and answers no other site name either. Applies to sets with IP block detection and Cache Blocked IPs on, see Banned addresses. On First ban (hours) How long an address stays banned the first time. 24 Repeat ban (days) How long the ban lasts when the address is banned again within 30 days after its previous ban ended. 7

Field What it does Default Enable IPv4 Support b4 handles IPv4 traffic. On Enable IPv6 Support b4 handles IPv6 packets, DNS answers and firewall rules. While it is off, sets with Remove ECH keys from DNS answers on still remove ECH keys from IPv6 DNS answers in NFQUEUE mode. Off Force IPv4 for matched domains While IPv6 support is off, b4 removes IPv6 addresses from DNS answers for domains a set matched, so clients reach them over IPv4. On IPv6 support off With IPv6 support off, a targeted site that also answers over IPv6 can be reached over IPv6 past every set. Force IPv4 for matched domains narrows the gap for devices that resolve names through the router, see The IPv4 fallback.

Field What it does Default Queue Start Number The first NFQUEUE number b4 reads. Another value is needed only when another program uses the same numbers. 537 Packet Mark The mark on the packets b4 sends itself, such as fakes, so that they pass its processing unchanged. See Packet marks. 32768 Worker Threads How many workers process packets in parallel, from 1 to 16. 4 TCP Connection Packets Limit How many packets at the start of each TCP connection reach b4, up to 100. The limit applies to every set. 19 UDP Connection Packets Limit The same for UDP, up to 30, for every set. 8

The Device Filtering card limits DPI bypass to selected devices, or excludes selected devices from it. Applying b4 to selected devices explains what the filter covers and how to set it up. Field What it does Default Enable Device Filtering Turns the selection on. While it is off, every device gets DPI bypass. Off Exclude Selected Devices (Blacklist) Off, only the selected devices get DPI bypass. On, the selected devices are excluded from it. Off Vendor Lookup Downloads the IEEE vendor list, about 6 MB, to name each device's manufacturer. A randomized MAC address shows as Private. Off

While filtering is on, the card lists the devices from the router's ARP table and those added by hand. A device that has left the network stays in the list as long as b4 keeps a name, a selection or an MSS value for it, or a set uses it as a source device. Column What it shows Checkbox Selects the device. MAC Address The MAC address, or matched by IP for a device added by hand. IP The current address. manual marks a device added by hand, offline a device not on the network now. Name The name set with the edit icon, otherwise the vendor. Saving an empty field removes the name. MSS An MSS clamp for the device's TCP connections to port 443, from 10 to 1460. Applies whether or not filtering is on. An offline device has a Forget device icon next to its name, and Forget offline above the list forgets several of them at once. Forgetting deletes the name, selection and MSS value b4 keeps for the device and removes it from the source devices of every set. The change applies when the settings are saved. A forgotten device that connects again appears as a new device.

Adds a device that the ARP table does not show, such as one behind another router, by IP Address and an optional Name. Such a device is matched by its IP address. It counts for routing sets, set source devices and its MSS value, but not for DPI bypass, which matches MAC addresses only.
The sub-tab sets how b4 manages its firewall rules, and the rules it adds besides capture.

Field What it does Default Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup For setups that add the rules by hand. In NFQUEUE mode b4 then installs no capture rules, and masquerade, MSS clamping, DSCP, DNS over TCP interception and Expose to internet are off. Off Firewall Engine The backend for the rules of b4. Auto-detect, the usual choice, uses nftables when it works and iptables otherwise. Auto-detect Firewall Monitor Interval (seconds) How often b4 puts back rules that the router's firewall removed. 0 turns this off in NFQUEUE mode. In TUN mode the minimum is 10. 10

The clamp sets the TCP maximum segment size of every connection to port 443, the router's own included. The client's ClientHello then leaves in several small segments. Field What it does Default Enable Global MSS Clamping Turns the clamp on. Off MSS Size The segment size in bytes, from 10 to 1460. 88 A device's value in Available Devices wins over this one, and a set's value, on its TCP > General tab, wins over both.

Masquerading rewrites the source address of forwarded packets to the address of the outgoing interface. Container and gateway setups need it. Field What it does Default Enable NAT Masquerade Turns masquerading on. Off Interface tags Limits it to the selected outgoing interfaces, typically the uplinks. None selected means every interface. None

b4 can write a DSCP value into the packets it sends, so that a router in front of it can tell its traffic apart. Passing sets to another router shows the setup. Field What it does Default Set DSCP Writes DSCP value into the packets this host sends out. Off DSCP value From 0 to 63. Turning the switch on fills in a free value, usually 7, which keeps normal priority on Wi-Fi and on Linux routers. 0 Interface tags The outgoing interfaces that get the values. None selected means every interface except loopback. None A set can write its own value into the packets to its addresses, see DSCP, and the card lists such sets. The value reaches the internet The router that reads the value is expected to reset it on its internet uplink. Otherwise the provider sees it on every connection b4 carries.

The sub-tab holds the DNS settings that apply to every set. The resolver itself is chosen per set, see DNS. Field What it does Default Intercept DNS over TCP Sends DNS over TCP to b4 too. Without it, a client that falls back to TCP skips the set's DNS server. On Listener port The local port for DNS over TCP. Another value is needed only when another program holds it. 5453 Query timeout Seconds to wait for a set's DNS server. 5 Idle timeout Seconds an idle DNS-over-TCP connection stays open. 30 Read/write timeout Seconds for one query or answer on an open connection. 10 Forward timeout Seconds to wait for the client's own resolver when no set matched a TCP query. 5

The sub-tab configures the built-in SOCKS5 proxy. Connections through it leave from the router, and the sets apply to them, see Connections through the built-in SOCKS5 proxy. Field What it does Default Enable SOCKS5 Proxy Starts the proxy. Off Bind Address 0.0.0.0 listens on every address. 127.0.0.1 is the router only. 0.0.0.0 Port The proxy port. 1080 Expose to internet Adds a firewall rule that opens the port to any address, see Access from the internet. Off Username, Password The login of the proxy, set together. Both empty means no login. Empty Allowed Sources The client addresses allowed to connect. Empty means any. Empty A change to Enable SOCKS5 Proxy, Bind Address or Port restarts the proxy and closes its connections.

Add IP or CIDR adds an address or a range, IPv4 or IPv6, and From device adds the address of a known device. Other addresses are refused. A client on the router itself needs 127.0.0.1/32. Chrome and Chromium cannot log in to a SOCKS5 proxy, so a source list is the way to limit them. With a login and a list, a client needs both. The list is not authentication: addresses can be spoofed. It adds no firewall rule either, and binding the proxy to the LAN address is what keeps it off the WAN.

The Discovery tab of Settings has two cards. Testing Configuration holds the timings and the trusted DNS server of Discovery runs. Watchdog turns the watchdog on and holds its timings. Save Changes in the page header saves the tab, see Saving and restarting. No change here needs a restart. A change applies from the next Discovery run, not to one in progress.

Field What it does Default Discovery Timeout Time limit for one fetch of a site. A higher value helps on a slow or unstable connection. 5 sec Config Propagation Delay Pause after Discovery switches to the next strategy, before it fetches through it. A higher value helps on a slow router. The watchdog waits the same time after a heal, before it checks the set again. 1500 ms How many fetches in a row a strategy has to pass is chosen for each run with Confirm each strategy in the Discovery options.

Trusted DNS server, under DNS Configuration, is the resolver whose answers Check DNS for tampering takes as correct. Discovery compares each site's address from the router's resolver with this server's answer. Empty uses the public resolvers built into b4. Form Transport 9.9.9.9, 2620:fe::fe, 127.0.0.1:53053, udp://9.9.9.9 Plain DNS over UDP, repeated over TCP when the answer is truncated tcp://9.9.9.9 Plain DNS over TCP tcp+udp://127.0.0.1:53053 UDP first, TCP when UDP fails https://dns.google/dns-query DNS over HTTPS. /dns-query is added when the URL has no path The port defaults to 53. Plain DNS needs an IP address, and a host name works only in an https:// URL. DNS over TLS is not supported directly: a local DNS proxy that speaks it can be named here instead. When the router's resolver gives a site a wrong address, the proposed set gets a DNS fix. The trusted server itself goes into the set when a set can use it: a public IP address on port 53 that answers over UDP and is not one of this host's own, or an https:// URL. Otherwise the set gets a built-in resolver that returns the correct address, or the correct addresses are pinned in it. The run log says which. With Check DNS for tampering on, a run stops with an error when this server does not answer before it starts. The same field in the Discovery options replaces this one for a single run. How the check decides is described in How Discovery searches.

Enable Watchdog turns the watchdog on or off for every watched set and for the older per-domain list. It is off by default. A set is put under the watchdog on its own Discovery tab, and the switch here has to be on for any set to be checked. The fields below show while the switch is on. Field What it does Default Check Interval How often each watched set or domain is checked while it works. 300 sec Failure Re-check Interval How often a set or domain is checked again after a failed check. 60 sec Healing Cooldown Pause after a search for a new strategy, before the next check of that set or domain. 900 sec Check Timeout Time limit for one check fetch. 15 sec Max Retries Failed checks in a row that start a search for a new strategy. 3 Turning the switch off cancels a search in progress, and that search writes nothing.

Older per-domain list holds domains that the watchdog checks one by one, see Older per-domain list. Add Domain adds a domain or a full URL, and the cross on a chip removes it. The Watchdog page edits the same list.

The Geodat Settings tab downloads and updates the GeoSite and GeoIP databases. With them, a set can target a whole category of domains or addresses instead of single entries, see Adding sites to a set.

Both are databases in the V2Ray format that group entries into named categories. GeoSite (geosite.dat) groups domains. The youtube category, for example, holds youtube.com, googlevideo.com, ytimg.com and the other domains of YouTube. GeoIP (geoip.dat) groups IP ranges, by country or, in b4geoip, by service.

The Source list on each card offers the presets that publish that database, and Custom URL... for any other address of a .dat file. Source Contents Loyalsoldier Domains and IP ranges, China and worldwide RUNET Freedom Domains and IP ranges for the blocking in Russia b4geoip IP ranges by service, GeoIP only For networks in Russia, RUNET Freedom for GeoSite and b4geoip for GeoIP are the recommended sources. The installer offers both by default.

The GeoIP database of the b4 project. It is built automatically from the prefixes each network announces, as RIPE NCC records them. It groups addresses by service, so a set can target one platform: cloud providers: AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, OVH, Scaleway, Oracle Cloud, Contabo, AEZA; CDNs: Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, CDN77; game companies: Roblox, Valve/Steam, Sony/PlayStation, Nintendo, EA, Riot Games, Ubisoft, Epic Games, Wargaming, Bungie, Take-Two, CCP; platforms: Telegram, GitHub, Apple, Adobe, Amazon, Blizzard.

Field What it does Default Destination Directory The directory Update and Upload write the files to, always as geosite.dat and geoip.dat. b4 creates it when it does not exist. The directory of the current files, /etc/b4 when there are none The field is not saved with Save Changes. A new directory takes effect on the next Update or Upload of each card: the file goes to the new directory, and the copy b4 wrote at the old path is deleted. Until then, a hint under the field names both directories.

The Geosite Database and GeoIP Database cards each manage one file. The chip in the card header shows its state: Chip Meaning Active The file exists. Its size and modification time are shown under the path Not Found A path is set, but there is no file at it Disabled No path is set, and the database is off Under the header are the file path, or Not configured, and the source URL. An uploaded file shows Local upload instead of a URL. Control What it does Source Picks a preset, or Custom URL... with the address in the Custom URL field. The choice is stored when Update succeeds Update Downloads the selected source into the destination directory. Sets get the new categories without a restart Upload Writes a .dat or .db file of up to 500 MB from the browser into the destination directory. An uploaded file has no source URL, so automatic updates leave it alone Remove Deletes the file and switches the database off, see below One download runs at a time. A download started while another one runs, from the other card or in the background, fails with another geodata download is already running.

Remove opens the Remove geo database dialog with the path of the file. Confirming deletes the file and clears the path and the source URL. The database stays off until the next Update or Upload, and automatic updates do not bring it back. b4 deletes only a file named geosite.dat or geoip.dat. A file under another name stays on disk, and the database is switched off all the same. The dialog lists the sets that use categories from the database. While such a set exists, the database cannot be switched off. The file is deleted, but the save fails with Failed to save configuration: Configuration is invalid, and the next check for missing files downloads the file again. Removing the categories from those sets first lets the database go. On a router with little storage, removing a database that no set uses frees its full size.

Update replaces a database on demand. Background downloads fetch the stored source URLs, on the Auto-update schedule or to restore a missing file. A download is checked before it replaces the current file. An error or block page, an empty or cut-short file, and a GeoIP file uploaded as GeoSite are rejected, and the current file stays in place. The new copy is written next to the current one, so an update needs free space for both. The files range from about 10 MB to more than 70 MB. When a direct download of a preset fails, b4 repeats it through the update mirrors. A file that is damaged anyway, for example by a full disk, costs only the categories b4 cannot read. Sets keep matching by their other targets, and the log names the categories and sets affected. A missing or damaged file is downloaded again from its source URL, whatever the Auto-update fields say.

Field What it does Default Refresh on startup Shortly after b4 starts, downloads every database that has a source URL Off Schedule Daily, Weekly or Monthly: downloads every database that has a source URL once 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days have passed since the last run Off Last run When a background download last refreshed every database that has a source URL. Update does not change it - Both fields are saved with Save Changes and apply without a restart. Background downloads run only while the web server is on: with its port set to 0, nothing is downloaded, missing files included.

Once a database has a path, the set editor shows its categories on the Targets tab: Bypass GeoSite Categories on the Bypass Domains sub-tab and Bypass GeoIP Categories on the Bypass IPs sub-tab. Each selected category shows how many domains or address ranges it holds, and clicking a GeoSite category opens a preview of its first 100 domains. Targets describes how sets match by category.

Project What it does GeodatExplorer A web application that shows the categories, domains and IP ranges in a .dat file, for checking a category before it goes into a set v2dat A command-line utility that unpacks .dat files into text lists, for scripts

The Integrations tab connects b4 to outside services. AI Assistant lets b4 ask an AI provider about its settings, while MCP server lets an AI application ask b4. Changes are saved with Save Changes in the page header.

Field What it does Default Access token The token for ipinfo.io. With it, the Add to a set dialog of the Traffic page and the dashboard offers Enrich with IPInfo, which shows the organization, host name and location of an address. b4 requests these details from the router. Get a token opens ipinfo.io, where the free tier is enough. Empty

The assistant explains settings inside the web interface. b4 sends the question to the chosen AI provider. While the assistant is on, an AI icon shows next to many fields, most of them in the set editor, and Ask AI to explain this setting opens the answer. Field What it does Default Enable AI assistance The switch in the card header. Off OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, OpenAI-compatible The provider. With OpenAI or Anthropic, the questions and the parts of the configuration they touch leave the router for that provider. With Ollama they stay local while Endpoint points to the router or a computer in the local network. None Model The model, picked from the provider's list or typed in. Empty API key Required for OpenAI and Anthropic, optional for OpenAI-compatible. Set key stores it on the router in a file of its own, not in the configuration. Empty The Advanced section holds the connection details. Field What it does Default Endpoint The address of the provider's API, filled in for each provider. Another value points to another server, such as a self-hosted one. Per provider Max tokens The longest answer, in tokens. 1024 Temperature From 0 to 2. Lower values give more predictable answers. 0.2 Timeout (s) How long one request may take. 120 While the provider cannot be used, for example without a key, the card shows the reason.

The MCP server lets an AI application, such as Claude Desktop, Cursor or LM Studio, read the state of b4 and, when allowed, change its settings. The model runs in that application, so b4 needs no API key for it. Connecting an AI assistant shows the setup. Field What it does Default Enable MCP server The switch in the card header. The server uses the port of the web interface. Off Access token The token the AI application presents. Generate creates one, Regenerate replaces it. Without a token, the application needs a web login while one is set, and that login ends when b4 restarts. Without either, anyone who reaches the port can use the server, including changes and probes when they are allowed. Empty Allow configuration changes Lets the AI change the sets and the MTProto, SOCKS5 and logging settings, not only read them. Credentials and all other settings stay read-only. Off Allow active probes Lets the AI make b4 fetch a domain and run Discovery, which sends real traffic from the router. Off Client configuration The entry to paste into the AI application, with the address and the token. -

The connection to the Community Hub, where b4 users publish sets and report whether they work. Community Hub describes the card in full. Field What it does Default Enable Community Hub Adds the Community page, the hourly sync and the Share with other b4 users section of the set editor. Off Hub mirrors Addresses of the same hub, one per line, tried in order. Empty means https://hub.b4core.app. Empty Hub public key Only for a self-hosted hub with its own key. The key of hub.b4core.app is built in. Empty Hub status shows the catalogue, the last sync with its error and the hub addresses, and Sync now syncs at once. Author identity shows the key that signs the sets and reports sent from this router. Show recovery code gives the code that moves this key to another router, where Restore from code takes it in.

An AI application such as Claude Desktop, LM Studio, Cursor or Jan can read b4's state over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It then answers questions about it: which set matches a domain, whether traffic reached b4, what the log says. The model runs inside that application. b4 contacts no AI provider and needs no API key.

An AI application that connects to MCP servers over HTTP. Access from that application to the b4 web interface. The MCP endpoint uses the web server's address, port and TLS certificate, and it is unreachable while the web server is off. An application that connects from a local computer. claude.ai, ChatGPT on the web and connectors added in Claude Desktop's settings connect from their vendor's cloud and cannot reach a router on a home network.

Open Settings > Integrations and turn on Enable MCP server on the MCP server card. Click Generate next to Access token. Click Save Changes. The token is stored only on save. Click Copy under Client configuration. The entry holds the endpoint, which is the address the web interface is open at followed by /api/mcp, and an Authorization header with the token. Paste the entry into the MCP configuration of the AI application. VS Code reads .vscode/mcp.json in the workspace, or the user-level mcp.json. Its inputs block makes the editor ask for the token instead of keeping it in the file: { "inputs": [ { "id": "b4-token", "type": "promptString", "description": "b4 MCP token", "password": true } ], "servers": { "b4-asuswrt": { "type": "http", "url": "https://192.168.1.1:7000/api/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:b4-token}" } } } } LM Studio uses the same kind of file with mcpServers as the top-level key and no type. Several entries can sit side by side, for example a router and a local instance: { "mcpServers": { "b4-asuswrt": { "url": "https://192.168.1.1:7000/api/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <token>" } }, "b4-local": { "url": "http://localhost:7000/api/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <token>" } } } } An application without an equivalent of inputs keeps the token in the file as plain text, so such a file does not belong in a repository.

While a token is set, it is the only credential the MCP endpoint accepts, and no other part of b4 accepts it. It keeps working when b4 restarts. Regenerate replaces it, and the application then needs the new one. Without a token, the endpoint accepts the login token of the web interface instead. That token expires after a day without use and is discarded on every restart, so an application set up with it soon loses access. The token on an untrusted network The token travels in a header of every request. Over plain HTTP anyone on the network path can read it and reuse it, so without HTTPS the port belongs on a trusted network only. With no MCP token and no username and password under Settings > System > Web Server, anyone who reaches the port can use the server: read b4's status, configuration and diagnostics, and make changes and run probes when those are allowed.

By default the assistant only reads. It can report b4's status and counters, show the configuration and the sets, and check which set covers a domain. It can also look up GeoSite and GeoIP categories, read the recent connections, the error log and the update log, and run diagnostics. API and MCP tools lists every tool and the permission it needs. The assistant can look up b4's REST API too, for tasks its tools do not cover. While the web interface has a username and a password, calls to that API need them. b4 tells the assistant to ask the user for them first. With them, the assistant can do everything the web interface can, whatever the switches below allow. Skills for AI assistants give the assistant step-by-step instructions for common tasks with these tools, such as finding why a site does not open or writing a bug report.

Two switches on the card widen what the assistant may do. Both are off by default, and each works without the other. Switch What the assistant may do Allow configuration changes Change the settings inside sets, the MTProto and SOCKS5 settings and the logging settings. Create, move, enable and delete sets, edit their targets, and undo its own changes Allow active probes Make the router fetch a domain to see whether it loads, and run Discovery to find a working strategy. Private and local addresses are refused A change goes through the same checks as a save in the web interface and applies at once. It appears under Recent changes on the dashboard as AI agent changed a setting. Some settings stay out of the assistant's reach whatever the switches say, because a wrong value could cut off access to the router or open it to the internet: credentials, the web server settings and the MCP settings; the capture engine and the firewall backend; the Expose to internet switches, and any change that would open a port while one of them is on; packet marks, routing tables and DSCP values; a set's id, its Discovery addresses and its watchdog switch, which only the watchdog actions change, under their own permissions; the log directory and the locations of the geodata files. API and MCP tools gives the details.

Asking the assistant to undo a change, such as "that made it worse, put it back", restores the configuration from before its last change and applies it at once. Asking again goes one more change back. The history covers only changes made over MCP since b4 started, and edits in the web interface are not part of it. An undo is refused when the configuration changed after the change being undone: in the web interface, by the watchdog or by another tool. Changes on the MCP server card do not count, and an undo leaves that card's settings as they are. It is also refused when it would turn a watchdog on, or bring back addresses a watchdog checks, while Allow active probes is off. Once that switch is on and saved, the same undo goes through.

Tool output may be passed on to a third-party model, so b4 removes passwords, tokens and secrets from it. Host names and URLs are passed as configured, and the diagnostics include the router's hostname, its interface addresses and its firewall rules. API and MCP tools lists what is removed.

A question such as "Is b4 running, and which capture engine is active?" gets an answer with the version and the capture engine. Each tool call adds a line to the log on the Logs page, with the tool and the address of the caller.

The application cannot connect. The MCP server is off, the token in the application differs from the saved one, or the web server's port cannot be reached from that computer. The Logs page shows each refused request with the reason. The token itself never appears in the log. A test request gets 405. The endpoint answers POST only, so a GET from a browser or a script gets 405. This is normal. A web page cannot reach the endpoint. A request from a browser page is accepted only when the page's origin is b4's own address written as an IP address or localhost. AI applications send no origin and are not affected. A host name is allowed by adding it to the allowed origins in the configuration file. The assistant says it cannot change a setting. Allow configuration changes is off, or the setting is one that MCP never changes. The assistant lacks a tool after a switch was turned on. A switch takes effect when the settings are saved, without a restart, but an application that was already connected keeps the list of tools it received when it connected. Reconnecting the application to the MCP server fetches the current list.

The Telegram tab of Settings sets up the three ways b4 carries Telegram traffic and how b4 reaches Telegram's data centres. The guides under Telegram walk through each setup. The Secrets and Telegram Desktop WEB proxy cards appear while the MTProto proxy is on.

The card turns on Telegram over WebSocket for the whole network, with no set involved. Field What it does Default Enable Telegram over WebSocket Relays Telegram from every device behind b4, and from the router itself, through the bridge. Device filtering applies. The MTProto proxy is not needed. Off The header shows Save to apply until the settings are saved. After that it reads Working, or Not working with the missing part named when the pointer rests on it. The Bridge status box shows: Item Shows Listener port The bridge's port, 13443, and the address families it listens on, or not running Active connections Bridged connections open right now Telegram ranges How many address ranges are in use, their source (telegram.org, b4 mirror, saved copy, GeoIP file or built-in list) and when they were updated Relayed sessions How many sessions the bridge relayed, and when the last one was Counters line Passed on undecoded, data center dial failures and closed without a handshake, shown once one is above zero. See The counters under the bridge status Button What it does Check again Repeats the kernel's TPROXY check, then installs the bridge's firewall rule or moves it back above another program's rule Refresh addresses Downloads Telegram's address list at once, and reports the number of ranges or the error Each warning above the box is explained under The Telegram over WebSocket card shows a warning.

The MTProto proxy that Telegram connects to with a secret. The card's fields are hidden until its switch is on. Field What it does Default Enable MTProto Proxy Starts the proxy server. Off Bind Address The address the proxy listens on. 0.0.0.0 accepts connections on every address, 127.0.0.1 from this host only. 0.0.0.0 Port The port Telegram connects to. 3128 Expose to internet Adds a firewall rule that accepts connections to the port from any address, over IPv4 and IPv6. Off adds no rule and blocks nothing. See Access from the internet. Off Fake SNI Domain The domain the proxy's TLS handshake presents, and the site that a connection failing the secret check is passed to. New secrets are generated for it. storage.googleapis.com

Field What it does Default Max Connections The most client connections open at once, probes included. Each Telegram client uses several. The WEB proxy is not limited by it. 2048 TCP User Timeout (sec) Closes a client connection after this long with unacknowledged data, so a phone that left the network is noticed in about two minutes. -1 turns it off. 120 Idle Timeout (sec) Closes a relayed session after this long with no traffic in either direction. -1 turns it off. 300 In both timeouts, 0 uses the default.

One entry for each person lets access be given and withdrawn one person at a time. The log names the secret each connection used. Field What it does Default Switch Turns the entry on or off. A client with a switched-off secret is rejected. On Name / comment A name for the entry, shown in the log and on the Traffic page. Empty Max networks Refuses new connections to the secret once it is in use from this many networks at once. Devices behind one internet connection count as one network. 0 means no limit. 0 Secret The secret itself. Generate Secret replaces it with a new one for the current Fake SNI Domain. Only fake-TLS secrets, hexadecimal and starting with ee, are accepted. Generated Add secret adds an entry with a generated secret. The share button (Share connection link) opens the link and QR code, see Adding the proxy in Telegram. The bin button (Remove secret) deletes the entry.

The WEB proxy serves the MTProto proxy as an HTTPS site for Telegram Desktop 7.1.1 and later. Field What it does Default Enable the WEB carrier Serves the proxy on the relay hostname. Off Relay hostname A public DNS name used only for the relay, with a publicly trusted certificate on port 443. No scheme, port or path; punycode for international names. Empty Relay port Empty: the relay is served on the web interface's port, on the relay hostname only. A port: the relay gets a listener of its own, where any other name or IP address gets the placeholder page. Filled with 443 when the carrier is first turned on. Empty Expose to internet Shown while a relay port is set. Opens the relay port to connections from any address. Without a relay port, the relay is reachable from outside only when the web interface is exposed. Off Certificate for the relay hostname Shown while a relay port is set. Certificate file and Private key file in PEM format, used on the relay port only. Empty: the web server's certificate. Empty Placeholder page The page every visitor other than Telegram sees. An uploaded HTML file of up to 1 MiB replaces the built-in page, and Remove restores it. Built-in

How b4 reaches Telegram's data centres, for the MTProto proxy and Telegram over WebSocket alike, even while the proxy is off. The routes are explained under Telegram upstream. Field What it does Default Transport mode How the MTProto proxy reaches Telegram: Direct TCP, Auto (WebSocket → TCP) or WebSocket only. Telegram over WebSocket always uses Auto. Auto (WebSocket → TCP) DC Relay host:port of a VPS that forwards to the data centres, shown for Direct TCP and Auto (WebSocket → TCP). The ? button shows the socat commands. Not used by Telegram over WebSocket. See DC Relay. Empty Cloudflare Worker domain One or more *.workers.dev names, separated by commas. See Cloudflare Worker relay. Empty Let sets process Worker connections Shown once a Worker domain is set. Lets a set whose targets cover the Worker apply its DPI strategy to b4's connections to it. See DPI processing. Off Custom WebSocket domain A domain that relays WebSocket traffic to Telegram. b4 adds kws1., kws2. and so on for each data centre. Empty Telegram WS edge IP (advanced) Replaces the address of Telegram's own WebSocket edge. 149.154.167.220 Fronting name for Telegram's WS edge (advanced) A TLS name, such as sprinthost.ru, tried on Telegram's edge when the handshake under its own names goes unanswered. See Fronting name for the WS edge. Empty (off) Test connection tries each configured route to data centre 2 and lists the result of each. Test direct TCP tries data centre 2 over direct TCP, without the DC Relay.

Field What it does Default CF proxy fallback Uses a rotating pool of Cloudflare-proxied domains for the data centres that Telegram's own edge does not serve. On CF proxy domain list URL Where the pool is refreshed from, hourly. tg-ws-proxy's list DC list fallback mirror Fetches Telegram's data-centre list from the mirror below when Telegram's own endpoint is unreachable. On DC list mirror URL The mirror. The default one is hosted by the b4 author and receives the requesting IP address, nothing else. The b4 author's mirror Bridge Handshake Wait (sec) How long Telegram over WebSocket waits for a client's first byte before closing the connection. -1 waits indefinitely. 180 b4 downloads these lists only while the MTProto proxy, Telegram over WebSocket or an enabled set in its routing mode is on.

The tab applies on Save Changes, without restarting the service. A change to Enable MTProto Proxy, Bind Address, Port, Fake SNI Domain, Transport mode, Custom WebSocket domain, the WS edge IP, the fronting name or a CF proxy setting restarts the MTProto proxy. Secrets apply without a restart. A secret switched off or removed loses its open connections. The WEB proxy's switch and hostname apply from the next request. A new relay port or certificate restarts only the relay's listener.

The Payloads tab keeps the files that fake packets can carry instead of a built-in payload. A payload is generated from a domain name or uploaded as a file. Generating, uploading and deleting act on the router at once, without Save Changes.

Some strategies send a fake packet ahead of the real one. The DPI inspects the fake, and the set's Fake Strategy keeps the server from accepting it, see Faking. The data the fake carries is the payload. TLS payloads serve the fakes a set sends over TCP, QUIC payloads the fakes it sends over UDP.

The Fake Payload Type field of a set, under TCP > Faking > Fake SNI Packets, picks what the fake carries: Type Contents Random 1200 random bytes, new for every connection Preset: Google (classic) A recorded TLS ClientHello for www.google.com. A new set starts with this type Preset: DuckDuckGo A recorded TLS ClientHello for staticcdn.duckduckgo.com Preset: STUN A STUN Binding Request, with no TLS in it My own Payload File A payload from this tab, picked in the Generated Payload field All Zeros 1200 zero bytes Inverted Original The data of the real packet with every bit inverted Generated from Domain A ClientHello built like the ones on this tab, for the name in the set's Domain field While My own Payload File has no payload picked or its file cannot be read, and while Generated from Domain has no name, the fake carries Preset: Google (classic). The payload type of a Discovery result is the one to start from.

The card builds a TLS ClientHello for the name in Domain. Typing a name, such as youtube.com, and clicking Generate or pressing Enter adds the payload to the list. The ClientHello is built on the router. No connection is made, and the name is not resolved or checked. An http:// or https:// prefix and a path are dropped, and the name is lowercased. Each name holds one payload per protocol: when the name already has a TLS payload, generated or uploaded, the tab keeps it and reports that it exists. Every generated ClientHello has SNI as its first extension. The generator is built for a TSPU shortcut: when SNI is the first extension, the name is checked against an allow-list, and an allowed name takes a fast path. Whether the shortcut applies depends on the provider's equipment.

The card adds a payload from a .bin file. Field What it does Name/Domain The name the payload is listed under in sets and in Discovery. Nothing ties it to the contents of the file. When the field is empty, choosing a file fills it from the file name: tls_youtube_com.bin gives youtube.com Protocol TLS (for TCP fakes) or QUIC (for UDP fakes). Choosing a file sets it from the first bytes of the file Choose File... Opens the file picker Upload Sends the file. Available once a file is chosen and a name is set The file has to be smaller than 64 KB and not empty. b4 stores it as it is, without checking the contents. An upload under a name and protocol that already exist replaces that payload without asking. A shared set carries its payload file only when the file parses. For TCP fakes that is a TLS ClientHello with a server name, for UDP fakes a QUIC Initial with a readable ClientHello, at most 16 KB either way. Payloads installed from a shared set appear on this tab.

TCP fakes. On the set's TCP tab, Faking sub-tab, with Enable Fake SNI on, the Fake Payload Type My own Payload File shows the Generated Payload field. It lists every payload on this tab by name and size. UDP fakes. On the set's UDP tab, with Action Mode set to Fake & Fragment, Fake Packet Payload sets the body of the fake packets: Option Body (zero fill) Zeros. A new set uses this option (auto: QUIC Initial) A new QUIC Initial with random contents for every fake QUIC preset 1, QUIC preset 2 Built-in QUIC Initials of 1200 and 1357 bytes A payload from this tab Listed as [quic] example.org (1250 bytes), QUIC payloads first The body is always Fake Packet Size long: a longer payload is cut, and a shorter one is padded with zeros.
