A new set sends 64 bytes, so a full QUIC Initial goes out whole only once the size is raised to its length. UDP describes the other fake settings.
documents.s: Using a payload in a set

documents.t: The Captured ClientHello as the fake payload field in the Options of the Discovery page offers the TLS payloads from this tab. Discovery tries the picked payloads before its built-in ones, and a strategy found with one of them uses My own Payload File with that payload. A run that finds nothing with the built-in payloads can be repeated with payloads generated for several names.

The list shows every payload on the router, whether generated, uploaded or installed from a shared set, with its name, size, protocol and the time it was added. The buttons are icons, and the names below are their tooltips. Button What it does View/Copy hex Opens Payload Hex Data with the payload in hex. Copy & Close copies it to the clipboard Download .bin Saves the payload as a file Delete Deletes the payload at once, without confirmation Refresh list Reloads the list from the router Clear all captures Deletes every payload after a confirmation Deleting a payload that a set uses Deleting a payload does not change the sets that refer to it. At the next start or configuration save, b4 logs an error for the missing file, and those fakes fall back to Preset: Google (classic) over TCP and to zeros over UDP.

Payloads are files in the captures/ directory next to the configuration file, and payloads.json in that directory lists them. The tab shows what payloads.json lists, so a .bin file copied into the directory by hand does not appear. Uploading the file adds it.

By default the web interface opens without a password for anyone who reaches its port. A login and HTTPS protect it, and the Expose to internet switches decide whether it, or a proxy of b4, can be reached from the internet.
Access to the web interface. For HTTPS, a certificate and its private key as PEM files on the router.

Open Settings > System > Web Server. Under Authentication, fill in Username and Password. Click Save Changes. The web interface asks for the login from then on. The login applies only while both fields are filled. A session lasts until b4 restarts or until it goes unused for 24 hours. A new password does not end the sessions already open, a restart does. After 5 failed logins within 15 minutes, logins from that address are refused for 5 minutes. The fields are described under Web Server.

Without HTTPS the login, the password and every session cross the network unencrypted. Copy the certificate and the key to the router, for example into the directory of the configuration file. Open Settings > System > Web Server. Enter their paths in TLS Certificate and TLS Key. Click Save Changes, then Restart Service. Open the web interface at the same address with https://. A self-signed certificate is enough on a local network: openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout server.key -out server.crt -days 365 -nodes -subj "/CN=b4" The key must be an unencrypted PEM file. A save is refused when a file is missing, the key has a passphrase or the certificate does not match the key. openssl pkey -in key.pem -out key-plain.pem removes the passphrase. b4 reads the files when it starts, so a renewed certificate takes effect after a restart.

Each listener in the table below has an Expose to internet switch next to its port, off by default. With it on, b4 adds a firewall rule on the host it runs on that accepts TCP connections to that port from any address, IPv4 and IPv6. b4 puts the rule back after the router reloads its firewall, and removes it when the switch is turned off or b4 stops. The switches apply on save. Listener Switch Opens the port only when Web interface Settings > System > Web Server A username and a password are set MTProto proxy Settings > Telegram > MTProto Proxy The proxy is on WEB proxy relay port Settings > Telegram > Telegram Desktop WEB proxy The MTProto proxy and its WEB proxy are on, and Relay port holds a port SOCKS5 proxy Settings > Core > SOCKS5 The proxy is on with a login or Allowed Sources, and the web interface, if it runs, has a login To open the web interface: Set a login and turn on HTTPS, as above. Turn on Expose to internet under Settings > System > Web Server. Click Save Changes. The web interface port also serves the API, the MCP server and, without a relay port of its own, the WEB proxy relay, so the switch exposes them together. A changed port moves the rule at the next restart. A SOCKS5 client can connect to any address, the router's own ports and the web interface included. That is why exposing the proxy needs a login on the web interface as well. SOCKS5 sends its own login unencrypted. The rule covers TCP only, so on a host that drops incoming connections, UDP through the proxy does not work from outside. With a switch off, b4 adds no rule, and it does not block the port either. On a host that accepts incoming connections, such as a VPS without a firewall, every listener on 0.0.0.0 is reachable from the internet whatever the switch says. A listener stays private through its Bind Address, a LAN address or 127.0.0.1, or through the host's own firewall. Without a login Anyone who reaches the web interface without a login gets full control of b4. b4 refuses to expose the web interface without a username and a password, but on a host without a firewall the default 0.0.0.0 is reachable from the internet anyway.

The rule opens the port on the host b4 runs on and nowhere else. Situation What it takes Carrier-grade NAT: a WAN address in 100.64.0.0/10 No connection from the internet reaches it over IPv4. A public IPv6 address on the WAN is not affected. A router or modem in front: a private WAN address such as 192.168.x.x A port forward on that device as well, where the provider allows one. A cloud firewall: AWS security groups, Azure network security groups, Google Cloud firewall rules, Oracle Cloud security lists A rule in the provider's firewall as well. b4 in a MikroTik container A dst-nat rule on RouterOS, see MikroTik. firewalld that owns its nftables table, as on Fedora 42, RHEL 10 and Debian 13 Opening the port in firewalld: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=<port>/tcp, then firewall-cmd --reload. The log names these commands. Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup on Nothing: b4 adds no rule, and the switches are greyed out. How the rules are placed is described under Packet capture.

The web interface asks for the login in a private browser window. With HTTPS, the address opens with https://. The log records every change on a line starting with Expose:. It names the ports opened, a switch that is on but opened nothing, and rules put back after a firewall reload. For the MTProto proxy, the Share MTProto connection dialog warns when the port is not open.

The login is refused after a few attempts. The address is locked out for 5 minutes. The password is forgotten. b4 keeps only its hash. With b4 stopped, removing the web server's username and password from the configuration file and starting b4 again turns the login off. The interface still opens over HTTP. The dashboard shows Web server TLS is not usable, serving plain HTTP instead with the reason, such as a moved or replaced file. The port does not open from outside. The Expose: lines in the log give the reason, and What the switch cannot open lists the causes outside the router.
The System tab holds the settings of the service itself, on the sub-tabs Service, Web Server and Backup. Some fields apply only after a restart, see Saving and restarting.
The sub-tab has two cards, Service and Logging.

Restart Service restarts b4 after a confirmation. The web interface is unavailable for a few seconds and reloads once b4 answers again. b4 restarts through its service manager, such as systemd or an init script, when it has one. Otherwise, in Docker for example, it restarts itself in place, and the container does not restart. The Service Manager row of System Info shows which way applies.

System Info opens the System Diagnostics dialog, a report on the router and on b4. Section Contents System Host name, distribution, kernel, architecture, CPU and memory, and a Container row when b4 runs in one B4 Version, build, Service Manager, process ID, memory use and uptime Process Memory, threads and open files of the b4 process Paths The b4 binary, the configuration file, the data directory, the error log and the geodata files Geodata The GeoSite and GeoIP databases and the ASN cache Engine NFQUEUE or TUN, the start error when the engine failed, and with TUN its device and capture Firewall The firewall backend, the routing sets installed, Flow Offloading, how often b4 restored its rules, and the rules of b4 Network The interfaces with their state and addresses Kernel Modules, Kernel Capabilities Whether the modules b4 uses are present, and the packages that provide a missing one Firewall Tools (at least one needed), Required Tools, Optional Tools Which commands b4 found, with their versions Storage Free space and read-write state of the usual mount points When Flow Offloading shows that offloading bypasses b4, the router moves connections to a fast path before b4 has seen the packets it needs, and b4 does not see that traffic. Copy JSON copies the whole report, for a bug report for example. It is not masked: it holds the host name, the addresses and MAC addresses of the interfaces, the firewall rules and the proxy address of each proxy set. What can be private lists what each part of a bug report holds.

Field What it does Default Language The language of the web interface, English or Русский. English Time Zone The time zone of the timestamps in the log. Auto (system default) uses the zone of the system. Auto (system default) Memory Limit A soft cap on the memory b4 uses: auto or empty for half of the system memory, a size such as 128MiB, 256m or 1g, or off. Near the cap b4 frees memory more often, and going over it does not stop b4. auto Update mirrors Comma-separated https addresses tried before the built-in mirrors when a download from GitHub fails, see Downloading b4 when GitHub is blocked. Empty A Memory Limit below 32 MiB is raised to 32 MiB. The same floor applies to auto on a router with less than 64 MiB of memory.

The Logging card sets how much b4 logs and where the log goes. Field What it does Default Log Level How much b4 logs. Error logs errors and warnings, Info adds the main events, Trace adds the details of packet and DNS processing, and Debug adds debug output. Info Log Directory The directory for errors.log, which keeps errors and start-up warnings, and update.log, which keeps the last update started from the web interface. Empty turns file logging off. /var/log/b4 Instant Flush Writes every log line at once instead of in batches. On Syslog Sends the log to the system log as well, tagged b4. Off Info is the usual level, and Trace or Debug the level for diagnosing a problem. At Error, the Logs page shows only errors and warnings. The Traffic page does not depend on the level, except for DNS queries, which it shows from Info on. The command-line flags --log-dir, --instaflush and --syslog override these fields, see Command-line flags.

The sub-tab configures the server of the web interface, which also carries the API and the MCP server. Securing the web interface shows how to set up the login, HTTPS and access from the internet. Field What it does Default Bind Address The address to listen on. 0.0.0.0 is every address, IPv4 and IPv6. 127.0.0.1 is the router only. 0.0.0.0 Port The port of the web interface. A port that another program or another b4 listener uses is refused on save. 7000 Expose to internet Adds a firewall rule that opens the port to any address. Needs a username and a password, see Access from the internet. Off TLS Certificate The path to the certificate file, .crt or .pem. With both TLS fields empty, the interface is served over plain HTTP. Empty TLS Key The path to the private key file, .key or .pem, without a passphrase. Set together with the certificate. Empty

Field What it does Default Username The login name. Empty turns the login off and deletes the stored password. Empty Password The password, stored only as a hash. A blank field keeps the stored password. Empty The login applies only while both fields are set. Without a TLS certificate, the login and the session cross the network unencrypted. The card warns in both cases.
The sub-tab saves, restores and resets the configuration.

Download Backup saves a .tar.gz archive of the configuration directory. Besides the configuration, it holds the history of Discovery and of the DPI Detector, the payloads and the banned addresses. The GeoSite and GeoIP databases, the vendor list of device filtering and the Community Hub author key stay out. The author key moves to another router with its recovery code, see Integrations. The archive holds secrets The archive holds the configuration as it is, with the password hash, the tokens and the secrets, and the stored AI API keys. The safe copy is the file for sharing.

Upload & Restore takes a .tar.gz backup of up to 50 MiB and writes its files into the configuration directory. A file in the archive replaces the current one, and other files stay. b4 keeps no copy of the configuration it replaces, so a fresh backup first preserves it. The Restart B4 Service dialog opens after the restore. The restored configuration takes effect with the restart. A save before the restart writes the old configuration over it.

Download Configuration saves the configuration b4 runs with as one JSON file, in the format of the configuration file. Button Content Download safe copy The configuration with credentials, secrets and the host names of the router and of the owner's relays masked, for sharing when asking for help. Sets, with their domains and proxy addresses, stay as they are Download as is The full configuration, with the password hash and every token and secret Safe copy​ The safe copy removes the web interface password and puts [redacted] in place of: usernames, passwords, tokens and secrets; the host names of the router and of the owner's relays; credentials and paths in URLs, and private DNS-over-HTTPS addresses; the update mirrors. Sets with their targets, strategies and proxy addresses, devices, interfaces and ports stay as they are. b4 refuses to save a configuration that still holds [redacted] in a masked field. A configuration file with it does not load. b4 then starts with default settings and keeps only the port and bind address of the web server, so the web interface opens without a login. The next save replaces the file.

Reset returns the configuration to its defaults after a confirmation. It keeps: the sets; the web server settings, with the login, the language and the MCP server; the geodata settings. Everything else returns to its default: the Core tab, the rest of System, the Discovery and Telegram tabs, IPinfo, the AI assistant, the Community Hub and the dashboard layout. Files beside the configuration, such as the histories, the payloads and the stored AI keys, stay. Fields that need a restart take effect after the next one.

A Cloudflare Worker is a small relay that runs on a free Cloudflare account under a *.workers.dev name. b4 reaches every Telegram data centre through it. It is the route to add when media, stickers or reactions do not load: data centres 1, 3 and 5 have no WebSocket edge of their own, and where the CF proxy pool is unreachable too, a Worker is their only WebSocket route. Cloudflare can end a Worker's connection in the middle of a session. b4 therefore tries a Worker last among the WebSocket routes and sets aside one that goes quiet. A Worker is a fallback, not the main route. This Worker is not the one under Update mirrors, which stands in for GitHub for b4's own downloads and runs a different script.

A free Cloudflare account. cloudflare.com, cloudflare.dev and workers.dev reachable from the network. For the MTProto proxy, Transport mode set to Auto (WebSocket → TCP) or WebSocket only. Telegram over WebSocket always uses Auto.

Create a free Cloudflare account. Under Compute > Workers & Pages, create a Worker from the default template and deploy it. Replace the Worker's code with the script below and deploy it again. Make sure the Worker's compatibility date is 2026-04-07 or later. In b4, open Settings > Telegram and enter the Worker's domain, such as name-1234.username.workers.dev, in Cloudflare Worker domain on the Telegram upstream (shared) card. Several Workers are separated by commas. Click Save Changes. tg-ws-proxy keeps a step-by-step guide with screenshots: CfWorker.md.

import { connect } from "cloudflare:sockets"; function toBytes(data) { if (data instanceof ArrayBuffer) { return new Uint8Array(data); } if (typeof data === "string") { return new TextEncoder().encode(data); } if (data && typeof data.arrayBuffer === "function") { return data.arrayBuffer().then((ab) => new Uint8Array(ab)); } return new Uint8Array(); } const ignore = () => {}; export default { async fetch(request, env, ctx) { if ((request.headers.get("Upgrade") || "").toLowerCase() !== "websocket") { return new Response("Expected websocket", { status: 426 }); } const url = new URL(request.url); if (url.pathname !== "/apiws") { return new Response("Not found", { status: 404 }); } const dst = url.searchParams.get("dst"); const pair = new WebSocketPair(); const client = pair[0]; const server = pair[1]; server.accept(); const socket = connect({ hostname: dst, port: 443 }); const tcpReader = socket.readable.getReader(); const tcpWriter = socket.writable.getWriter(); socket.closed.catch(ignore); tcpReader.closed.catch(ignore); tcpWriter.closed.catch(ignore); server.addEventListener("message", async (event) => { try { await tcpWriter.write(await toBytes(event.data)); } catch { try { server.close(1011, "tcp write failed"); } catch {} } }); server.addEventListener("close", async () => { try { await tcpWriter.close(); } catch {} try { socket.close(); } catch {} }); const pump = (async () => { try { while (true) { const { value, done } = await tcpReader.read(); if (done) { break; } if (value) { server.send(value); } } } catch { } finally { try { server.close(); } catch {} try { tcpReader.releaseLock(); } catch {} try { socket.close(); } catch {} } })(); ctx.waitUntil(pump); return new Response(null, { status: 101, webSocket: client }); }, };
Test connection on the Telegram upstream (shared) card lists a result for each route. The Worker's line starts with wsworker:// and shows its latency, or the stage where it failed.

Cloudflare reports The Workers runtime canceled this request because it detected that your Worker's code had hung. The compatibility date is earlier than 2026-04-07. From that date on, the runtime answers a closing frame by itself. The stream stops after the first few kilobytes. Some networks slow down workers.dev: the handshake completes, then the data stalls. b4 sets a Worker aside for ten minutes after two stalls within five minutes. When a set already has a strategy that works for Cloudflare, Let sets process Worker connections applies it to the Worker connections too, see DPI processing. The log line of a stall is described under The upstream goes silent mid-session.

The script accepts a WebSocket on the /apiws path and opens a TCP connection to port 443 of the address b4 asks for, the port every Telegram data centre listens on. The loop that carries data back from Telegram is handed to ctx.waitUntil(), so the runtime does not cancel it as soon as the handler returns. The closed promises get an empty catch, so a socket that Cloudflare reclaims does not log unhandled rejections. A stateless Worker still does not suit long sessions: waitUntil extends execution by about 30 seconds, and a large download can be cut. For a connection that has to outlive a request, Cloudflare offers a Durable Object with WebSocket hibernation.
The WebSocket transport and the Cloudflare Worker relay are inspired by tg-ws-proxy.

A DC Relay sends the MTProto proxy's direct connections to Telegram through a VPS. It is for b4 inside a censored network where Telegram's addresses and the WebSocket routes are both blocked. The VPS runs only socat, a TCP forwarder: no keys and no Telegram software.

A VPS outside the censored network that b4 can reach. Five free ports on the VPS, one for each main data centre, open in its firewall. Transport mode set to Direct TCP or Auto (WebSocket → TCP) on the Telegram upstream (shared) card. WebSocket only makes no direct connections, so the relay has no effect there. The relay serves the MTProto proxy only. Telegram over WebSocket does not use it.

Install socat on the VPS: apt install -y socat In b4, open Settings > Telegram and enter DC Relay on the Telegram upstream (shared) card: the VPS address with a base port, such as my-vps.com:7007. Click the ? button beside the field. The DC Relay socat setup dialog shows a ready socat command for each data centre. Click Copy all and run the commands on the VPS. Open the ports that the dialog lists on its last line in the VPS firewall. To keep the commands running after a reboot, start them from /etc/rc.local or a systemd unit. Click Save Changes in b4. Each command forwards one VPS port, the base port plus the data centre's number minus one, to that data centre's port 443. Media data centre 203 shares the port of data centre 2 and needs no command of its own. With Auto (WebSocket → TCP), b4 tries the relay first and the WebSocket routes after it. A WebSocket connection that b4 keeps open in advance is still used before the relay.

The dialog's Address family switch chooses whether the commands connect to Telegram over IPv4 or IPv6. IPv6 is for a VPS that reaches Telegram over IPv6 but not over IPv4. The switch changes only the Telegram side of each command: # IPv4 socat TCP-LISTEN:7007,fork,reuseaddr TCP:149.154.175.50:443 & # IPv6 socat TCP-LISTEN:7007,fork,reuseaddr TCP6:[2001:b28:f23d:f001::a]:443 & The listening side follows the DC Relay address. An IPv6 address there is written in brackets, [2001:db8::1]:7007, and the commands then listen over IPv6 as well. Media data centre 203 has no IPv6 address and goes through the command of data centre 2. When media stops loading after a switch to IPv6, that one command goes back to IPv4.

Test connection on the Telegram upstream (shared) card tries data centre 2 over each configured route, the relay included. Test direct TCP tries it without the relay, which separates a relay problem from a Telegram one.
When connections through the relay fail, socat is not running on the VPS, a port is closed in its firewall, or the relay address is wrong. The log line and the checks are under Dialling fails.

The MTProto proxy is a Telegram proxy server on b4. Telegram connects to it with a secret, from the local network or from outside, such as a phone on mobile data. Every Telegram client supports it. To the network, a connection looks like HTTPS to the domain set as Fake SNI Domain.

For devices outside the local network, the proxy port is reachable from the internet. Expose to internet opens it on the b4 host. A router or modem in front of the host also needs a port forward, and a WAN address behind carrier-grade NAT cannot be reached over IPv4 at all. See Access from the internet. The clocks of the b4 host and of the devices agree within two minutes. NTP on both keeps them so.

Open Settings > Telegram. On the MTProto Proxy card, turn on Enable MTProto Proxy. Set Port. The default is 3128. 443 is a common choice, since the traffic already looks like TLS. For devices outside the local network, turn on Expose to internet. Keep the default Fake SNI Domain, or enter a domain that is reachable from the network and carries ordinary traffic. On the Secrets card, click Add secret. The new entry comes with a generated secret. Enter a name for the person or device in Name / comment. Click Save Changes. A secret for each person lets access be withdrawn one person at a time: each entry has its own switch and its own link, and the log names the secret a connection used. Only fake-TLS secrets, hexadecimal and starting with ee, are accepted. A secret in another format, such as one copied from another proxy, is skipped, and the log shows skipping invalid secret. Some changes, such as a new port, restart the proxy on save. On a VPS outside the censored network, Direct TCP in Telegram upstream is enough. On a router inside it, the default Auto (WebSocket → TCP) reaches Telegram without a VPS, and a DC Relay is the next step when WebSocket is blocked as well.

On the Secrets card, click the share button of a secret (Share connection link). At the top of the dialog, choose Local network for devices on the same network, or Internet for devices outside. Internet fills in the public address b4 finds, and a DDNS name can be typed instead. Open the tg://proxy link on the device, or scan the QR code. To add the proxy by hand, open Settings > Data and Storage > Proxy > Add proxy > MTProto in Telegram and enter the b4 address as Server, the port and the secret.

In Internet mode, the share dialog warns when the link is not expected to work from outside, and names the cause. A test from the same Wi-Fi says nothing about access from outside, because many routers do not loop a connection to their own public address back to the local network. A phone on mobile data connects from outside. The Telegram panel of the dashboard shows the networks, connections and traffic of each secret. The Traffic page shows the proxy's connections with the secret's name.
Telegram problems covers each symptom: Telegram sits at "Connecting", the client is rejected, Telegram turns the proxy off, or dialling fails.

A connection that fails the secret check, such as a probe by the network, is passed through to the Fake SNI domain on port 443, so the real site answers it rather than b4. Data that is not a TLS handshake at all is dropped.

Telegram's lines in the log carry the [tg-bridge] tag, and the lines of one connection share a counter, such as [tg-bridge c=1f]. The proxy's handshake lines, proxy fake-TLS handshake OK and proxy fake-TLS failed, appear only at the debug level.

A working session of the MTProto proxy logs one line per client: [tg-bridge c=3] proxy relay [phone] 192.168.1.50:51234 <-> DC2 via ws:kws2.web.telegram.org No such line. The connection does not reach b4. From outside, nothing arrives until Expose to internet is on for the proxy port, and a router or modem in front of the host also needs a port forward. In Internet mode the share dialog names the causes it detects, and What the switch cannot open lists the ones no rule on the b4 host fixes. The line appears, and Telegram still waits. The problem is between b4 and Telegram. Test connection on the Telegram upstream (shared) card shows which routes work.

[tg-bridge c=7] upstream answered -444 (invalid DC) for a DC 2 session: the route does not end at the data center the client asked for, cutting it and ranking the route down Cause: the session reached another data centre than the one the client asked for. b4 keeps the code from the client, ranks the route down and lets the client reconnect over another route. Fix: a run of these lines for one data centre means every route to it ends in the wrong place. Another route helps: a Cloudflare Worker domain or a custom WebSocket domain. Through Telegram over WebSocket, b4 corrects the data centre by itself, see Which data centre a session goes to.
documents.s: Telegram says the proxy is misconfigured and turns it off

documents.t: Cause: Telegram's own WebSocket edge serves data centres 2 and 4 only. Media for foreign channels comes from data centre 1, and 203 carries media too. Fix: a Cloudflare Worker domain, with CF proxy fallback left on.
documents.s: Media, stickers or reactions do not load

documents.t: At the debug level, the log shows the reason: [tg-bridge c=4] proxy fake-TLS failed from 192.168.1.50:51234: HMAC verification failed for all secrets The secret in Telegram matches no enabled secret in b4. The fix is the link from the share dialog, or turning the secret's switch on. [tg-bridge c=4] proxy fake-TLS failed from 192.168.1.50:51234: timestamp out of range: diff=214s The clocks of the device and the b4 host differ by more than two minutes. NTP on both fixes it. With every secret switched off, the proxy logs secrets: 0 at start-up and closes every connection at once.

[tg-bridge c=9] upstream silent for 8s with 512 B awaiting an answer, cutting the relay Cause: the route accepted the client's requests and stopped answering, as a Cloudflare Worker does when Cloudflare ends its connection. Fix: b4 cuts the session, and sets a Worker aside for ten minutes after two such sessions within five minutes. For a Worker that stalls often, see Cloudflare Worker relay.

[tg-bridge c=2] proxy dial DC 2 failed: dial tcp 149.154.167.51:443: i/o timeout Direct TCP without a relay: Telegram's addresses are blocked. Auto (WebSocket → TCP), WebSocket only or a DC Relay gets around it. With a DC Relay: socat is not running on the VPS, its port is closed, or the relay address is wrong. Test direct TCP tries without the relay and tells the cases apart.

The card reads Working when the bridge's firewall rule is installed, its listener runs and no other program's rule sits above it. Otherwise it reads Not working, and resting the pointer on it names the missing part. A warning above the Bridge status box names the cause. The first four below stop the bridge; the others leave it running.
documents.s: The Telegram over WebSocket card shows a warning

documents.t: This kernel has no TPROXY support. The bridge needs the tproxy and socket kernel modules. The warning names the packages that add them: on OpenWrt, kmod-nft-tproxy and kmod-nft-socket; for other systems, see Routing requirements. After they are installed, Check again repeats the check and installs the rule. The Transparent proxy (TPROXY) row in System Info on Settings > System > Service shows the same result.

Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup is on in Settings > Core > Firewall, so b4 installs no firewall rules at start-up, the bridge's included. Saving the settings installs them only until the next restart. Turning the setting off fixes it.

The bridge listener on port 13443 failed, followed by the error. The fixed port could not be bound, for example because another process holds it. b4 keeps retrying, and Telegram takes the normal path meanwhile. netstat -ltnp on the router names the process, where the build supports -p. When only IPv6 fails, a note says that IPv4 goes through the bridge and IPv6 takes the normal path. b4 tries IPv6 again only when the listener restarts, for example after b4 restarts.

Not working names a rule such as DIVERT, which takes the bridge's connections. XrayUI adds one each time xray starts. b4 moves its rule back above it at the next firewall check, and Check again does it at once. With Firewall Monitor Interval (seconds) at 0, only Check again or saving the settings restores the order. Background: Using b4 with Xray or XrayUI.
documents.s: Another program's rule sits above the bridge

documents.t: Bridge netfilter is on for, followed by network bridges such as br-lan. Telegram on the devices behind them stays at "Connecting", while the router's own Telegram works and the status reads Working. Sets in the Upstream SOCKS5 proxy mode are affected too. On OpenWrt, the dockerd package turns the setting on. System Info on Settings > System > Service shows how to turn it off, and Bridge netfilter describes the effect on Docker.
documents.s: Bridge netfilter is on for a network bridge

documents.t: Neither core.telegram.org nor the b4 mirrors answered. The warning shows the error and the source of the list still in use, which stays, with the built-in list always part of it. b4 tries again by itself, and Refresh addresses tries at once.
documents.s: The address list could not be downloaded

documents.t: The bridge has not been verified with the TUN engine. Relayed sessions on the card and the Telegram bridge entries on the Traffic page show whether Telegram reaches it.

The warning lists the sets in the Telegram over WebSocket (built-in) mode, disabled ones marked off. While the switch is on they add nothing, since the switch already sends Telegram from every device into the same bridge. Such a set, unless it is limited by an included source-device list, still keeps the bridge's connections to its targets out of DPI processing, see DPI processing.
documents.s: Sets use the Telegram over WebSocket routing mode

documents.t: The line under the Bridge status box appears once a counter is above zero. Counter Counts What to do Passed on undecoded Connections that were not MTProto, such as HTTPS to Telegram's web hosts, and sessions b4 could not map to a data centre. They go on to the Cloudflare Worker or directly. Nothing: a growing count is not a fault in itself. data center dial failures Sessions for which no route to Telegram connected. The log shows bridge dial DC <n> failed. The causes under Dialling fails, apart from the DC Relay, which the bridge does not use. closed without a handshake Connections that closed, or stayed silent for the whole Bridge Handshake Wait (sec), before sending anything. Nothing: Telegram opens connections before it needs them. A shorter wait produces more.
documents.s: The counters under the bridge status

documents.t: Voice calls go over UDP, which the bridge does not take. QUIC is not rejected, so a client that uses QUIC to a Telegram address passes the bridge by. IPv6 goes through the bridge only while Enable IPv6 Support is on in Settings > Core > Packet Engine. Devices excluded by device filtering keep the normal path. A set limited to devices or source interfaces that covers Telegram addresses handles its devices first. An address outside the list in use does not go through the bridge.
documents.s: Some Telegram traffic does not go through the bridge

documents.t: Cause: a block set covers Telegram addresses and is not limited to source interfaces or to an included list of source devices. It then also blocks the router's own connections to those addresses, the bridge's connections to Telegram among them. Fix: limiting the block set to source interfaces or to an included list of source devices, or removing Telegram's addresses from its targets.
documents.s: A block set stops the bridge

documents.t: The set mode needs TPROXY like the switch, see TPROXY support is missing. The set needs the telegram GeoIP category and a configured GeoIP database. A set that names a category without a database is rejected on save. A set limited to source interfaces or devices leaves out the router's own connections, Telegram Desktop on the router included.
documents.s: A set in the Telegram over WebSocket mode steers nothing

documents.t: Cause: the relay answers everything it does not recognise with the placeholder page and logs nothing: a hostname that does not match, a missing or wrong token, an ordinary page request, or a reached carrier limit. A working relay logs: [tg-bridge] web carrier up from 203.0.113.9 (secret=desktop) [tg-bridge] web proxy new stream 1 from 203.0.113.9 Fix: when neither line appears, one of the requirements is not met: the MTProto proxy is on and its listener started; the web server runs, or a relay port is set; the hostname reaches b4 over trusted TLS on port 443, with its Host header intact; the link comes from the share dialog.
documents.s: The WEB proxy hostname shows a placeholder page

documents.t: The Telegram upstream (shared) card decides how b4 itself reaches Telegram's data centres. The MTProto proxy and Telegram over WebSocket both use it, so it applies even while the proxy server is off. The defaults are Auto (WebSocket → TCP) with CF proxy fallback on.
A Cloudflare account, only for a Cloudflare Worker. A VPS outside the censored network, only for a DC Relay.

Open Settings > Telegram and find the Telegram upstream (shared) card. Choose the Transport mode for the MTProto proxy. Direct TCP suits a host that reaches Telegram's addresses directly, such as a VPS outside the censored network. Auto (WebSocket → TCP) is the choice for a censored network. When media, stickers or reactions do not load, enter a Cloudflare Worker domain, see Cloudflare Worker relay. Keep CF proxy fallback on, under Fallback sources. Click Save Changes. A new transport mode, custom WebSocket domain, WS edge IP, fronting name or CF proxy setting restarts the MTProto proxy. Transport mode What it does Direct TCP Connects to the data centres directly, or through the DC Relay when one is set. Auto (WebSocket → TCP) Tries the WebSocket routes first, then direct TCP. WebSocket only Uses the WebSocket routes only, with no direct TCP and no DC Relay. Telegram over WebSocket always uses Auto (WebSocket → TCP) and never the DC Relay, whatever the card says.

Test connection tries each configured route to data centre 2 and lists the result of each, with its latency or the stage where it failed. Test direct TCP tries data centre 2 over direct TCP without the DC Relay. Comparing the two separates a problem of a route from a problem of Telegram.

Symptom Fix Media, stickers or reactions do not load A Cloudflare Worker domain, with CF proxy fallback on The handshake with Telegram's own edge is dropped for its names, while its address is reachable A fronting name Telegram's own edge does not answer at its default address Another address in Telegram WS edge IP Direct TCP and the WebSocket routes are all blocked A DC Relay The log lines that identify each case are under Telegram problems.

A domain that relays WebSocket traffic to Telegram, for a self-hosted relay next to the shared CF proxy pool. b4 adds kws1., kws2. and so on for each data centre, so the names have to resolve for every data centre in use.

Telegram's own WebSocket edge is reached at one address, 149.154.167.220, for every data centre it serves. Telegram WS edge IP (advanced) replaces that address for a network where the default one does not answer. It takes a host or an IP address without a port. The custom WebSocket domain is not affected.

Where DPI drops the handshake for the names of Telegram's edge while the edge's address stays reachable, b4 can present another name in the TLS handshake. Fronting name for Telegram's WS edge (advanced) sets that name, such as sprinthost.ru, the one tg-ws-proxy uses. The field is empty, and fronting off, by default. b4 tries the name only after a handshake under Telegram's own names went unanswered, and keeps a connection only when it ends on a telegram.org certificate. Fronting does not help when the network blocks the edge's address outright, or when its DPI forwards the connection by the name it sees.
documents.s: Fronting name for the WS edge

documents.t: CF proxy fallback uses a rotating pool of Cloudflare-proxied domains for the data centres Telegram's own edge does not serve. CF proxy domain list URL is where the pool is refreshed from, hourly. The default is tg-ws-proxy's list on GitHub. DC list fallback mirror fetches Telegram's data-centre list from a mirror when Telegram's own endpoint is unreachable. The default mirror is hosted by the b4 author and receives the requesting IP address, nothing else. DC list mirror URL sets another mirror, and turning the switch off removes the fallback.

For each data centre, b4 builds a list of routes and tries them in this order: Direct TCP, first, when the mode is Direct TCP, or Auto (WebSocket → TCP) with a DC Relay set. Telegram's own WebSocket edge, which serves data centres 2 and 4 only. The custom WebSocket domain. The CF proxy pool, while CF proxy fallback is on. The Cloudflare Worker domains. Direct TCP, last, in Auto (WebSocket → TCP) when it was not placed first. The routes overlap, and the first one to connect carries the session. A route that keeps failing is skipped by later sessions for a while. For data centres 1, 3, 5 and 203, WebSocket means the custom domain, the CF proxy pool or a Worker. Media in foreign channels is therefore the first thing to fail when none of them is reachable. Direct TCP needs a host that reaches Telegram's addresses. Most are in 149.154.0.0/16, data centre 203 is at 91.105.192.100, and data centres 4 and 5 are reached in 91.108.4.0/24 and 91.108.56.0/24. These addresses are built into b4. Refreshing the data-centre list changes how b4 matches an address to a data centre, not where it connects.

The WEB proxy serves the MTProto proxy as an ordinary HTTPS site on a hostname of its own. Telegram Desktop 7.1.1 and later loads that site in a hidden window and carries all of its connections through it, so the client opens no MTProto connection and the traffic looks like a browser visiting a website. The proxy's secrets and its upstream apply as usual. The hostname needs a publicly trusted certificate on port 443, so the WEB proxy suits b4 on a VPS more than a router behind carrier-grade NAT.

The MTProto proxy is on, its port is free, and it has at least one secret. A public DNS name points at the b4 host and is used for nothing else. b4 answers every path on that name, so the web interface is not reachable there. A publicly trusted TLS certificate for that name is served on port 443, either by b4 itself or by a reverse proxy in front of it. The reverse proxy keeps the Host header, or sets X-Forwarded-Host, and allows the WebSocket upgrade on /api/v1/ws. A self-signed certificate is not enough.

Open Settings > Telegram. The Telegram Desktop WEB proxy card is shown while the MTProto proxy is on. Turn on Enable the WEB carrier. Enter the Relay hostname: a bare name, with no scheme, port or path. An international name goes in its punycode (xn--) form. Check Relay port. Turning the carrier on fills it with 443, the port Telegram connects to. See Relay port. Under Certificate for the relay hostname, enter the Certificate file and Private key file for the hostname. Left empty, the relay uses the web server's certificate. On a router, turn on Expose to internet under Relay port. When the relay port is not 443, forward WAN port 443 to it. Click Save Changes. On the Secrets card, click the share button of a secret, copy the link in the WEB · Telegram Desktop 7.1.1+ row, and add it in Telegram Desktop. The link has the form https://t.me/webproxy?server=<hostname>&secret=dd<32 hex characters>. It carries another form of the secret than the list shows, so a link assembled by hand does not work, and the share dialog is the only source. The relay has no login of its own: anyone who holds the link can use the proxy. Renaming the hostname breaks every link The link is bound to the relay hostname. After Relay hostname changes, every link handed out stops working and has to be shared again.

Telegram always opens https://<hostname>/ on port 443, and the link carries no port. Public port 443 therefore has to lead to the relay: the relay port set to 443, a forward from 443, or a reverse proxy on 443. Relay port Effect A port, usually 443 The relay gets a listener of its own. Any other name or an IP address on that port gets the placeholder page, so the web interface is not reachable through it. Empty The relay is served on the web interface's port, on the relay hostname only. Whatever brings public port 443 to that port also brings the web interface, and its login page answers on the public IP address. On a router, the usual layout is a relay port with Expose to internet on, and a forward from WAN port 443 when the relay port is not 443. The web interface port is neither exposed nor forwarded, so the interface stays reachable only from the local network. The relay port uses the web server's certificate unless Certificate for the relay hostname holds one. A public certificate on the web server makes the web interface HTTPS-only, with a browser warning on every visit by IP address. A certificate under Certificate for the relay hostname goes to the relay port only, and the web interface keeps its own.

Every visitor that is not Telegram sees a plain "Service status" page, the same on every b4 installation. Placeholder page on the card replaces it with one HTML file of up to 1 MiB, and Remove restores the built-in page. The relay answers every path with that same file, so styles and images have to be inside it. The file is kept as webproxy_page.html next to the configuration file. A file copied there by hand is served the same way, and deleting it restores the built-in page.

Opening the hostname in a browser shows the placeholder page even when the relay does not work, so it proves nothing. The log confirms a working relay: [tg-bridge] web carrier up from 203.0.113.9 (secret=desktop) [tg-bridge] web proxy new stream 1 from 203.0.113.9 Connections carried this way appear on the Traffic page as MTProto, with the secret's name.

Only the placeholder page shows, and the log has no web carrier up line. See The WEB proxy hostname shows a placeholder page. Nothing answers over TLS on port 443. The certificate or key does not load, and the log says so. On the web interface's port, b4 then falls back to plain HTTP, and a relay port of its own does not start at all. A phone has no WEB proxy entry. Telegram's mobile apps do not support it and use the MTProto link from the same dialog.

Telegram over WebSocket relays Telegram from every device behind b4, and from the router itself, over Telegram's WebSocket edge, with Cloudflare routes behind it. Nothing is set up in Telegram on the devices, no VPS is involved, and the MTProto proxy does not need to be on.

TPROXY support in the kernel: the tproxy and socket modules. On OpenWrt they come with kmod-nft-tproxy and kmod-nft-socket, and Routing requirements lists the packages for other systems. b4 manages the firewall: Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup is off in Settings > Core > Firewall. For Telegram over IPv6, Enable IPv6 Support is on in Settings > Core > Packet Engine. Without it, Telegram over IPv6 takes the normal path. No set and no GeoIP or GeoSite file is needed. The bridge has not been verified with the TUN engine.

Open Settings > Telegram. On the Telegram over WebSocket card, turn on Enable Telegram over WebSocket. The card shows Save to apply. Click Save Changes. The switch takes effect without a restart. The bridge then covers every device behind b4 and the router itself. Device filtering applies: with an allow list, the selected devices and the router are bridged; with a deny list, the selected devices keep the normal path. A set bridges only some devices or interfaces instead, see below.

The card's header reads Working. Not working names the missing part when the pointer rests on it. Relayed sessions in the Bridge status box grows while Telegram is in use. On the Traffic page, bridged connections appear under the set name Telegram bridge, with the Telegram bridge label. No set of that name exists in the set list. The Telegram panel of the dashboard shows the relayed sessions and failures. The contents of the card are described under Settings > Telegram.

A warning on the card names the cause. Each one is explained, with its fix, under Telegram problems. Media, stickers or reactions do not load. Telegram's own edge serves only some data centres, and a Cloudflare Worker covers the others. Voice calls go over UDP and are not bridged, and neither is QUIC. Some Telegram traffic does not go through the bridge lists every case. A block set covers Telegram addresses. Unless it is limited to source interfaces or an included list of source devices, it also blocks the bridge's own connections, see A block set stops the bridge.

The routing mode Telegram over WebSocket (built-in) feeds the same bridge from one set, limited to the set's devices or interfaces. While the switch is on, such a set is redundant, and the card says so. Open Sets and create a set. On the Targets tab, add the telegram GeoIP category. The GeoIP database has to be configured, otherwise the set is rejected on save. On the DNS & Routing tab, turn on Enable Routing and set Routing mode to Telegram over WebSocket (built-in). Select Source Interfaces on the same tab, or source devices on the Targets tab. With both empty, the set covers every device. Click Create Set. Source scoping leaves the router out A set limited to source interfaces or devices does not bridge the router's own connections, Telegram Desktop on the router included. Device filtering has no such effect. Connections such a set carries appear on the Traffic page under the set's own name, with the same Telegram bridge label. Only the GeoIP category steers Telegram into the bridge: a GeoSite category adds nothing for it.
documents.s: Limiting the bridge to some devices or interfaces

documents.t: The bridge takes TCP connections to Telegram's address ranges into its listener on port 13443, reads the MTProto session and relays it through the Telegram upstream. For bridged sessions the transport mode is always Auto (WebSocket → TCP), and the DC Relay is not used.

The ranges always include a list built into b4. On top of it, b4 uses the first source that works: the list Telegram publishes at core.telegram.org, the same file from the b4 mirrors, the last downloaded copy, or the telegram category of the GeoIP file. The list is refreshed once a day, and Refresh addresses downloads it at once. Telegram ranges on the card shows the source in use.

Telegram Desktop names its data centre at the start of a connection. The Android app does not, so b4 takes the data centre from the address the connection was sent to. When Telegram answers that such a session belongs to another data centre, b4 sends later sessions for that address to the other data centre at the same site.
documents.s: Which data centre a session goes to

documents.t: Connections from devices reach the bridge untouched: no faking, fragmentation or desync applies to them. The bridge's own connections to Telegram, and those of the MTProto proxy, depend on the route: Route DPI processing Telegram's WebSocket edge, direct TCP to a data centre An ordinary set whose targets match applies its DPI settings Cloudflare-proxied domains, a custom WebSocket domain None. No set applies its DPI settings A Cloudflare Worker None, unless Let sets process Worker connections is on A set that covers Cloudflare for other sites therefore leaves these routes alone, apart from the Worker while that switch is on. A set in the Telegram over WebSocket (built-in) mode, unless it is limited by an included source-device list, leaves the bridge's connections to its targets unmodified.

Every TCP connection to a Telegram range enters the bridge, plain HTTPS to web.telegram.org or t.me included. A connection that is not MTProto, or that b4 cannot map to a data centre, goes on unchanged to its original address, through a Cloudflare Worker when one is set and the port is 443, or directly. The card counts these as Passed on undecoded.

The switch comes before every routing set that is not limited to devices or interfaces, so a catch-all set that sends everything through a VPN does not take Telegram away from the bridge. A set limited to devices or source interfaces still handles its own devices first, which keeps one device's Telegram on another route.

The table names the page where each problem is solved. A site that does not open is covered on this page. Symptom Where it is solved A site does not open, or stopped opening A site does not open Status on the dashboard reads Engine failed Engine failed No packets reached b4 in the last N min, or the Traffic page shows nothing while devices are in use b4 does not see traffic Another message under Needs attention on the dashboard Needs attention Telegram does not connect, or media do not load Telegram problems The service or its container does not start, or a problem specific to OpenWrt, Keenetic or MikroTik Router platforms None of the above, or b4 itself seems at fault Reporting a problem
The checks go from the quickest to the slowest. The first one that fails points to the cause.

Status on the dashboard reads Running in normal operation. Engine failed means that the packet engine did not start: the web interface works, but traffic passes through the router untouched, and no set applies. The card under the status strip shows the error, and Engine failed lists the fixes.

Open the site on a device behind the router. Open Traffic and find the site's domain. The Set column shows the set it matched. The Traffic page shows Cause and fix The site's domains without a set The set is off, or the site loads from domains that are not in it. The + next to a domain adds it to a set, see Adding sites to a set. Another set That set handles the site, and the strategy of the intended set does not apply to it. Unblocking a site shows how to write the strategy into the set that handles the site. Nothing from the device b4 does not see the device's traffic, see b4 does not see traffic. Domains not in any set on the dashboard's Activity panel opens the Traffic page with only the connections no set matched.
documents.s: 2. The site's connections reach a set

documents.t: b4 handles only the first packets of a connection. A connection the browser opened before the set existed, or while the strategy did not work yet, gets no bypass, and the browser keeps reusing it. It keeps DNS answers for a while as well. In Chrome, Edge and other Chromium browsers: Open chrome://net-internals/#sockets and click Flush socket pools. Open chrome://net-internals/#dns and click Clear host cache. Reload the site. A full restart of the browser has the same effect, in Firefox as well. On Windows, ipconfig /flushdns also clears the system's DNS cache. An address typed without https:// has one more trap. Chrome tries HTTPS first and falls back to plain HTTP when HTTPS fails, for example while the site is blocked. After that it keeps choosing HTTP for the site for some time, and the address bar can suggest the http:// address. The strategies Discovery finds are tested over HTTPS, so over plain HTTP a blocked site usually stays blocked. Typing the address with https:// opens the site over HTTPS. Shift+Delete (Shift+Fn+Delete on a Mac) removes the http:// suggestion from the address bar.

b4 sees the DNS queries that devices send to port 53. A device with encrypted DNS, such as secure DNS in the browser or Android Private DNS, bypasses b4. The DNS options of the sets then do not apply to it: another resolver, pinned addresses, the IPv4 fallback. Turning encrypted DNS off on the device fixes it, see What b4 sees. flags:dns in the filter of the Traffic page shows the lookups of the sets' domains and what b4 did with each, see Checking the result. A device whose lookups never show there uses encrypted DNS. When the provider's DNS answers the site with wrong addresses, a set can send its domains to another resolver, see Sending a set's domains to another resolver. The DPI Detector shows whether DNS answers are forged. A device keeps an answer it already has until the answer expires.

While Enable IPv6 Support is off, b4 handles IPv4 only, and a connection over IPv6 skips every set. When the router has IPv6, the dashboard shows IPv6 traffic skips all sets under Needs attention. Force IPv4 for matched domains removes the IPv6 addresses of the sets' domains from DNS answers. A device with encrypted DNS, or with an address it already has, still connects over IPv6. Enable IPv6 Support under Settings > Core > Packet Engine brings IPv6 into the sets. In TUN mode, IPv6 always skips b4.

YouTube, Google, Discord and other sites load over QUIC (HTTP/3), which runs over UDP. On the Traffic page, such connections show UDP next to the site's domain. b4 has only weak means against QUIC. Block QUIC (force TCP) on the set's UDP tab refuses QUIC, and the browser switches to TCP at once, where the set's strategy applies.

A site that opened with its set and stopped later, while the Traffic page still shows that set, points to a strategy that no longer works. Find a strategy in the set card's menu, or on the set's Discovery tab, opens Discovery with the set picked. Unblocking a site walks through a run. Keeping sets working lets the watchdog search for a new strategy and write it into the set on its own.

Some blocks no strategy passes. Discovery marks them on the site's card: address blocked: connections to every address of the site fail. intercepted by the gateway: the first hop in front of b4's host answers the connection itself. When that hop is another router, b4 has to run on it, or b4's host has to be excluded from its redirect. Such a site needs another way out: Routing sites through a VPN or Sending sites through a SOCKS5 proxy. When the gateway intercepts and b4 already runs on the main router, only a proxy helps. The DPI Detector shows how the ISP blocks a site.

When a page opens without its styles or images, the other hosts it loads them from can be blocked too. The Discovery result card lists the page hosts that the strategy opens, and Apply in the Discovery history offers them again.

A set with the fake strategy TCP Timestamp relies on TCP timestamps, and Windows sends none by default. On a connection without them the fake goes out as with TCP Check, and the Logs page shows a warning that names the set and the device. When the site stays blocked on that device, netsh interface tcp set global timestamps=enabled in an administrator console turns timestamps on. Another fake strategy for the set is the other way. The strategies are described in Faking. When every check passes and the site still does not open, Reporting a problem lists what to collect for a bug report.
documents.s: 10. The site fails only on some devices

documents.t: Problems that belong to one router platform, by the symptom. The installation itself is described on the platform pages.
Check that the kernel modules are installed and loaded, see Kernel modules. Read the log: logread | grep b4

b4 fails while it adds its rules. The cause may be a broken table left from an earlier run that failed. To delete it and start b4 again: nft delete table inet b4_mangle 2>/dev/null /etc/init.d/b4 restart
On some devices Software flow offloading, under Network > Firewall in LuCI, affects how fast b4 works. Both positions of the switch are worth a try.

Flow offloading moves an established connection to a fast path that skips the firewall hooks b4 works from. Turning it off fixes this, but on weaker hardware it costs a lot of throughput. b4 needs only the first packets of a connection: 19 for TCP and 8 for UDP by default, set by TCP Connection Packets Limit and UDP Connection Packets Limit under Settings > Core > Packet Engine. Offloading can start after them: In /usr/share/firewall4/templates/ruleset.uc, find the line: meta l4proto { tcp, udp } flow offload @ft; Replace it with: meta l4proto { tcp, udp } ct original packets ge 40 flow offload @ft; Reload the firewall: fw4 restart The limits of this approach: The threshold, 40 here, has to stay above b4's packet limits. A higher limit in b4 puts connections on the fast path before b4 is done with them. The rule reads conntrack accounting. When sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_acct returns 0, the counter stays at zero and nothing is offloaded at all. A set with Enable Packet Duplication on its TCP tab inspects the whole connection, so no threshold fits it. The file belongs to the firewall4 package. A package upgrade or a sysupgrade overwrites it. System Info under Settings > System > Service, and the installer's diagnostics, show the threshold they find and compare it with b4's limits.
documents.s: b4 runs but sees no traffic, with flow offloading on

documents.t: The error log is /var/log/b4/errors.log.
The Netfilter components are not fully on. Both Kernel modules for Netfilter and Xtables-addons for Netfilter have to be on, see Netfilter components.
documents.s: xt_connbytes kernel module is not available

documents.t: b4 holds DNS queries in its queue after conntrack. A device that asks for a name's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses at once then often loses the second answer. The brackets give the reason, such as a module that did not load, xt_NFLOG or nfnetlink_log. System Info shows DNS queries copied, not held (NFLOG) as unavailable under Kernel Capabilities, with the missing modules and the component to turn on. The fix is in Netfilter components.
documents.s: b4 cannot copy DNS queries with NFLOG (...)

documents.t: KeeneticOS rebuilds its firewall on its own: on a UPnP renewal, a WAN reconnect, or a change to a policy or a component. Each rebuild removes b4's rules. The installer places 50-b4.sh in /opt/etc/ndm/netfilter.d/, and this hook makes b4 restore its rules as soon as the rebuild ends. Without the hook, b4 finds them missing at its next check, every Firewall Monitor Interval (seconds), 10 by default. Log line Meaning Tables rules missing after a firewall rewrite, restoring..., then Tables rules restored successfully The hook reported a rebuild, and b4 put its rules back. Normal Tables rules missing, restoring... at the WARN level The check found the rules gone with no signal from the hook. Either 50-b4.sh is missing, or something other than KeeneticOS removed the rules Expose: the rules opening ... were missing from ..., usually after the firewall was reloaded; restored them The rules of Expose to internet were put back. It follows every rebuild, also with a working hook TUN: capture chain B4_TUN lost N of M rules (removed outside b4) ... In TUN mode, the capture chain was rebuilt. It follows every rebuild as well The same check can be started by hand: kill -USR1 $(cat /var/run/b4.pid)
documents.s: The log reports b4's rules missing

documents.t: On KeeneticOS with a kernel before 4.18 (4.14 before 4.14.173), b4 does not hold DNS queries. It takes a copy of each one and acts on the resolver's reply. At start the log says: IPTABLES[iptables]: KeeneticOS runs its raw table after conntrack (kernel 4.9-ndm-5), so b4 copies DNS queries with NFLOG (group 537) instead of holding them in its queue This is normal, and System Info shows DNS queries copied, not held (NFLOG) as available. What it changes: The router's resolver still gets every query and caches the real answer, also for a name that a set blocks, pins or sends to its own resolver. Devices that ask the router get b4's answer instead. A device that asks a resolver outside the router gets b4's answer only when that resolver replies. A nat rule that moves DNS to another port is not supported. After a firewall rebuild, queries pass without a copy until b4 restores its rules, see above. With a later kernel, b4 holds DNS queries in its queue and logs no such line. How b4 handles DNS explains the difference.
documents.s: The log says b4 copies DNS queries with NFLOG

documents.t: The commands refer to the names of the MikroTik setup.
Check its status: /container print. Read its log: /log print where topics~"container". Check that the disk is formatted as Ext4.
Check that the container runs: /container print. Check that RouterOS reaches it: /ping 192.168.210.10.
documents.s: The web interface does not open

documents.t: Check the client list: /ip firewall address-list print where list=b4users. Check the marking rules: /ip firewall mangle print. Check the route: /ip route print where routing-table=to_b4. Check that FastTrack is limited to unmarked connections, see Step 4.
documents.s: Traffic does not go through the container

documents.t: Check that the route to the container is in table to_b4, not in the main table, see Routing chosen destinations. Check that bridge-docker, or the interface of a separate b4 machine, is out of the LAN interface list, or that its packets are exempted from the marking rules as shown there.
documents.s: Destinations routed through the container do not open

documents.t: NAT Masquerade is off in b4, so the server's replies bypass the container. Step 8 turns it on.
documents.s: Traffic reaches the container, but nothing changes

documents.t: The error on the dashboard card names the cause. Extension NFQUEUE revision 0 not supported, missing kernel module? means that the kernel RouterOS runs the container on has no NFQUEUE support. Switch to TUN on the same card selects the TUN engine, which needs no queue modules, and restarts b4. See Packet engine.
documents.s: The dashboard reports that the NFQUEUE engine did not start

documents.t: Problems with b4 are reported as issues on GitHub. The bug report form there asks for the b4 version, the platform, the System Info report and a log trace. A trace recorded while the problem happens shows what b4 did with the traffic.

Item Where The b4 version At the bottom of the side menu System Info System Info under Settings > System > Service, then Copy JSON in the System Diagnostics dialog, see System Info A log trace The Logs page, see Recording a trace The set involved Copy JSON on the set's Import/Export tab, see Import/Export The configuration, when asked for Download safe copy under Settings > System > Backup, see Safe copy The text of the report says what was expected and what happened instead, which set, device or app is involved, and how often the problem occurs: every time, only on some sites, or only after b4 has run for a while.

A trace holds only the lines of the current log level, so the level goes up first. Under Settings > System > Service, set Log Level to Debug and click Save Changes. On the Logs page, click Start trace. Reproduce the problem, for example open the site that fails. Click Stop & save. The browser downloads the trace file, and Download last trace downloads it again. Set Log Level back to Info. A trace stops by itself after 15 minutes. The file is described under Recording a trace on the Logs page.

Over SSH, the installer prints the system, the installed version and the state of the kernel modules, see Diagnostics: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanielLavrushin/b4/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --sysinfo With file logging on, errors.log in the log directory, /var/log/b4 by default, keeps b4's errors and start-up warnings. Router platforms gives the log commands of OpenWrt and MikroTik.
documents.s: When the web interface does not open

documents.t: Issues on GitHub are public. The items above hold details of the router and the network: Item What it holds System Info The host name, the addresses and MAC addresses of the interfaces, the firewall rules, and the proxy address of each proxy set. It is not masked. Log trace The System Info report, the enabled sets with up to eight of their domains each, and the log lines. The lines name the sites the devices open, with the devices' IP and MAC addresses. A proxy set's proxy address is listed, its login is not. Set JSON The set's domains and addresses. For a proxy set, also the proxy's address, username and password. Safe copy The sets with their domains and the proxy address of each proxy set, the devices with their names and MAC addresses, the interfaces and the ports. Passwords, tokens, secrets and the host names of the router and of the owner's relays are masked. Installer output The host name. Each item is plain text, and a text editor shows what it holds before it is shared. A name or an address that has to stay private can be replaced with a placeholder, the same one wherever it appears.

When the devices' traffic does not reach b4, no set applies, and sites behave as if b4 were not installed. The signs: Status on the dashboard reads Engine failed. Needs attention on the dashboard shows No packets reached b4 in the last N min. While devices are in use, the Traffic page shows nothing, or only the router itself.

The packet engine did not start. The web interface works, but traffic passes through the router untouched. The card under the status strip shows the error, see If the packet engine did not start. b4 retries the start three times by itself. Cause Fix The kernel lacks the modules NFQUEUE needs. Kernel Modules and Kernel Capabilities in System Info name the missing modules and the packages that provide them. Installing the modules, see OpenWrt and Keenetic, or Switch to TUN on the card. TUN needs no queue modules. TUN mode started while the WAN or the VPN was down, and found no default route. One of the automatic retries starts the engine when the link comes up within about two minutes. TUN device name under Settings > Core > Packet Engine is the name of the uplink or of another existing interface. A name that no interface uses, such as the default b4tun0. Once the cause is fixed, Restart b4 on the card starts the engine. On MikroTik, the error and its fix are described under Router platforms.

No packets reached b4 in the last N min means that the engine runs, but no packet reaches it. Cause Fix Skip IPTables/NFTables Setup is on, and the Firewall cell on the dashboard reads Set up externally. In NFQUEUE mode b4 then installs no capture rules. The rules are added by hand, or the switch is turned off under Settings > Core > Firewall. The router's firmware removed b4's rules, and Firewall Monitor Interval (seconds) is 0. In NFQUEUE mode b4 then does not put them back. A non-zero interval, 10 by default. b4 restores missing rules at every check. On MikroTik, RouterOS does not send the traffic to the container. Traffic does not go through the container lists the checks.
The Traffic page shows the router's own connections as Router, or under the router's own address. When nothing else shows while devices are in use, b4 does not see their traffic.
documents.s: The Traffic page shows nothing, or only the router

documents.t: Capture Interfaces under Settings > Core > Packet Engine limits b4 to traffic that leaves the router through the selected interfaces. While the selection matches nothing, b4 inspects nothing, and no set applies. The Packet Engine card then names the interface the traffic leaves by, in a warning that starts with Nothing B4 has seen has left by. Clearing the selection fixes it: an empty selection covers every interface and is the usual choice. See Capture Interfaces.

A VPN client, XrayUI or another service that moves the default route changes the interface traffic leaves by, without touching b4's settings. A Capture Interfaces selection made before that stops matching. When Xray routes the whole network through its tunnel, for example, a selected uplink switches b4 off for every device. The selection stays empty in such setups, see Using b4 with Xray or XrayUI. Which interface is which helps find the setting at fault.
documents.s: A VPN client or XrayUI moved the traffic

documents.t: For the traffic the router forwards, TUN mode needs the iptable_raw and xt_CT kernel modules. On a kernel without them, such as the Synology DSM kernel, b4 captures only the connections the router makes itself. The devices' traffic then gets no bypass strategies, and b4 does not see their DNS queries. Routing and blocking sets still apply to it. System Info shows This device only in the Captured Traffic row under Engine. Where the kernel has the modules NFQUEUE needs, NFQUEUE mode captures the devices' traffic. Packet capture explains the reason.

Flow offloading moves an established connection to a fast path that skips the firewall hooks b4 works from. When the Flow Offloading row of System Info ends with (bypasses b4), the router moves connections to that path before b4 has seen the packets it needs. Turning offloading off fixes it. On OpenWrt, offloading can also start after the packets b4 needs, see Router platforms.

Device filtering. While Enable Device Filtering is on under Settings > Core > Devices, only the selected devices get DPI bypass. With Exclude Selected Devices (Blacklist) on, every device except them gets it. A device left out gets no DPI bypass, and the dashboard does not count its connections. DPI bypass matches devices by MAC address, so a phone with a randomized MAC address counts as a new device. Applying b4 to selected devices lists the other cases. A VPN on the device. Traffic that a device sends through its own VPN client leaves in a tunnel the router does not see into. It is outside b4's reach. When none of these explains the problem, Reporting a problem lists what to collect.

The Watchdog page shows the sets and domains the watchdog checks, their status and its last heals. The watchdog fetches a set's pages on a schedule. When they keep failing, it heals the set: it runs Discovery for it, writes the strategy found into it, and undoes the change if the pages still fail. Keeping sets working shows how to set it up. The watchdog is off by default. Enable Watchdog under Settings > Discovery turns it on for all sets and domains.

A set is watched while Keep this set working with the watchdog is on in its Discovery tab. The set also has to be enabled, have Discovery addresses, route no traffic, not be limited to specific devices by an include list, and target domains or GeoSite categories. The tab names the condition that fails.

A check fetches the set's Discovery addresses through b4, the way a device behind the router reaches them. A set is checked as soon as it is watched, then every Check Interval, and every Failure Re-check Interval after a failed check. An address that another set handles, or that an escalation currently sends to another set, is not counted: a strategy written into this set would not affect it. An address fails when it does not load, answers with an HTTP error such as 451 or 5xx, returns a block page or is cut off. A certificate error, a required client certificate or a private destination makes it Unusable: no strategy changes that, so it is never healed.

After Max Retries failed checks in a row, the watchdog runs Discovery for the set. Heals run one at a time, and a Discovery run started by hand makes them wait. A heal shows on the Discovery page but cannot be stopped there. A heal writes only a strategy that works on every address, and only the bypass strategy, as Writing into an existing set describes. Then the addresses are checked again, and when one still fails, the set's previous strategy comes back. A heal never touches another set. A heal of a set with its own DSCP value tests strategies with that value, as Discovery for the set does. Nothing is written when the set's traffic has moved to another DSCP path by then, as after a change to Set DSCP under Settings > Core > Firewall or to its interface list. After every heal, the set waits for the Healing Cooldown. After three failed heals in a row, the watchdog gives up on the set. Checks go on, but no heal starts until one of these happens: a check finds every address loading; Check now is clicked; the set's watchdog is turned off and on again. A page opened before a heal, such as the set editor, cannot undo it. Its save is refused with an offer to reload, which discards the unsaved changes.

A watched set shows its status here, on its Discovery tab, on its card on the Sets page and on the dashboard. Status Meaning Queued Not checked yet, or waiting for a fresh check after a change. Healthy Every address that could be checked loaded. Degraded At least one address failed. The row shows the failed checks in a row. Search queued Max Retries was reached, and the heal waits for its turn. Searching The heal's Discovery run is in progress. Cooldown A heal failed or wrote nothing, and the next check waits for the cooldown. Cannot verify No address can be checked: each is handled by another set, escalated or unusable. Gave up Three heals failed in a row. Checks continue, heals do not. Each address shows OK, Failed, Other set (with the set that handles it), Escalated, Unusable or Queued. The reason under a set's status says why it is in that state or how the last heal ended: Reason Meaning Handled by another set Another set, or none, handles the addresses, so a strategy written into this set does not affect them. Current strategy works Tested alone, the set's strategy loads the addresses, yet the live check fails. Something outside the strategy is in the way: another set, DNS or IPv6. Nothing was changed. No bypass needed Tested alone, the addresses load without a bypass, yet the live check fails. Same causes as above. Partial A strategy was found for only some of the addresses. Nothing was written. Nothing found The search found no working strategy. Over 20 minutes The search took too long and was stopped. It is tried again after the cooldown. Verification failed The strategy did not pass the live check and was undone. Edited The set changed while the search ran, so nothing was written. Busy Another Discovery run was in progress. The watchdog tries again later. Rules changed b4 was applying or rewriting the firewall rules the search depends on, such as its DSCP rules, so nothing was written. The watchdog tries again later.

Each row of Watched sets opens the set's Discovery tab. It shows the status and the reason, the last check, Last heal with the strategy it wrote, Failed heals and the end of the Cooldown. Show addresses lists every address with its status, the HTTP response and the last error. Check now checks every address at once and clears the cooldown, the failed heals and a give-up. It is unavailable while a heal is queued or running. Stop watching this set turns the set's watchdog off.
The Watchdog card of Settings > Discovery sets the timings for sets and domains alike: Check Interval, Failure Re-check Interval, Healing Cooldown, Check Timeout and Max Retries.

Older domain list holds domains checked one by one. It predates per-set watching and keeps working beside it. A domain is added in the field above the list or under Settings > Discovery. An entry is a domain, checked as https://<domain>/, or a full URL. After Max Retries failed checks, Discovery runs for the domain. A confirmed strategy goes into the first enabled set without routing that lists the domain, or a parent of it, in its domain list. Without such a set, a new set named watchdog-<domain> is created. A domain is never written into a set that routes or blocks traffic. Status Meaning Healthy The domain loaded on the last check. Degraded Failures were recorded, but Max Retries is not reached yet. Healing Discovery is running for the domain. Queued The domain waits for its next check. An entry whose host a watched set already checks reads Checked through set <name>. Watch through <set> moves an entry to the set that handles its host. It adds the address to that set's Discovery addresses, turns the set's watchdog on and removes the entry. Watching the set is the usual choice, since its heal always writes into that set and checks all of its pages together.
